title: The Bond effect? How MI6 fascinates spy watchers around the world | Espionage | The Guardian
description: Britain’s spooks take quiet satisfaction from survey ranking Secret Intelligence Service Europe’s top espionage agency
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Britain’s spooks take quiet satisfaction from survey ranking Secret Intelligence Service Europe’s top espionage agency
Content: Roger Moore as MI6’s James Bond in the 1983 film Octopussy.Photograph: Danjaq/Eon/Ua/Kobal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRoger Moore as MI6’s James Bond in the 1983 film Octopussy.Photograph: Danjaq/Eon/Ua/Kobal/ShutterstockEspionageThe Bond effect? How MI6 fascinates spy watchers around the worldBritain’s spooks take quiet satisfaction from survey ranking Secret Intelligence Service Europe’s top espionage agencyDan SabbaghDefence and security editorSat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 08.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMI6 has the swagger of James Bond; its French equivalent, DGSE, the complexities of the television drama Le Bureau. The film and TV shows may be fictional, but a survey run by a French magazine that placed the British spy agency above the French as No 1 across all of Europe this week is not.L’Express, a news weekly, conducted a Eurovision-style poll of 60 current and former spies from across the continent, plus the CIA and Israel’s Mossad. Each was asked to rank their top five foreign intelligence agencies, in secret, naturally enough. MI6 was first with 251 points ahead of DGSE on 169, with other agencies trailing behind.The result did not surprise Alexandra Saviana, a deputy editor at the publication, specialising in defence and intelligence, but the margin of victory did. “It is a huge point gap,” she said, reflecting the opinions of insiders and allies, 17 of whom are or were agency chiefs in a interconnected, covert ecosystem.At MI6’s headquarters in Vauxhall, London, there has been no sign of a public reaction from its chief,Blaise Metreweli. But there is a quiet satisfaction at the unexpected verdict, not least because the agency values how it is perceived by both allies and adversaries. “Reputation matters a lot in the espionage game,” said a former Whitehall insider.View image in fullscreenMI6’s headquarters in London.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images“British spies fascinateEurope, and beyond,” L’Express explained in its cover story. Saviana added that MI6’s success in the poll was principally down to its record in recruiting and running high-level human sources over generations: a focus on human intelligence in an era dominated by technology, intercepts and satellite monitoring.“The British have the ability to play the long game, to bet on sources over 10 years, a bit like the Russians,” a former French DGSE spy told the magazine, adding “and they have a penchant for underhand tactics” without revealing what they meant.One ex-spy voiced scepticism about the survey and added that a human intelligence service such as MI6 was only as good as the high-value agents on its books. UnderRichard Moore, MI6’s previous chief, there were worries that it no longer had enough. Others, including Saviana, accept that greater credit might have been given to MI6’s sister agency, the signals intelligence experts at GCHQ, but it was not in the poll.MI6’s reputation among its peers, the French publication said, was built on “long standing tradition”, including recruiting cold war assets, most notably the KGB’sOleg Gordievsky, a double agent through late 1970s and early 80s, who helped convince Margaret Thatcher to take Mikhail Gorbachev seriously before he had to be dramatically smuggled into Finland in 1985, his cover finally blown.View image in fullscreenRonald Reagan meeting Oleg Gordievsky, an MI6 cold war asset, in the White House, 1987.Photograph: Eraza Collection/AlamyNot every mole evaded capture. Alireza Akbari, a former Iranian deputy defence minister who had become a British citizen, was arrested on a return to Iran in 2019 and executed in 2023. Prior to his death, he confessed to being an MI6 agent. Though the confessions appeared coerced, spies from a number of countries indicated he was the person who had passed on the existence of theFordow nuclear enrichmentsite in 2008.In the run-up to the 2003 Iraq war, MI6 was accused of simplistically supporting the case for war, promoting what turned out to be false sources, claiming that Iraq’s leader, Saddam Hussein, could attack UK targets within “45 minutes”, and relied on one source who described supposed chemical weapons devices that were remarkably similar to one inthe Hollywood movie The Rock. It was a low point.L’Express argued that MI6 had rehabilitated itself in the run-up to the Ukraine war in February 2022,correctly warningin conjunction with the CIA that Russia was about to invade, while French and German counterparts were sceptical up until the last minute, having misjudged the situation. The chief of the German BND agency even flew into Kyiv the day before the invasion, seemingly unprepared.It reflects MI6’s close and longstanding relationship with the CIA, part of the wider Five Eyes arrangements for intelligence sharing, between the US, UK, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, that are the envy of continental Europe, even allowing for the complexities posed by Donald Trump’s chaotic presidency. “Every other country wants to say they are the sixth eye,” Saviana said.Fiction also has its advantages. Gordon Corera, a co-presenter of The Rest is Classified podcast, recalled that a former MI6 chief once told him a story of a young officer going somewhere far flung, not knowing whether the person he was trying to cultivate spoke English. “As he walked into the room the contact extended his hand and said: ‘Hello, Mr Bond.’ The former chief remarked: ‘I doubt if he would have received such a warm welcome if he’d been from the Belgian secret service.’”Explore more on these topicsEspionageMI6EuropeUK security and counter-terrorismJames BondnewsShareReuse this content

title: Where in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse? | Solar eclipses | The Guardian
description: When, where and how to get the optimal view of the first solar eclipse to be visible across the country this century
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: When, where and how to get the optimal view of the first solar eclipse to be visible across the country this century
Content: Planetarium astronomer Carys Herbert demonstrates wearing Celestron solar eclipse glasses at the Royal Observatory Greenwich, south-east London, before the solar eclipse on 12 August.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenPlanetarium astronomer Carys Herbert demonstrates wearing Celestron solar eclipse glasses at the Royal Observatory Greenwich, south-east London, before the solar eclipse on 12 August.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PASolar eclipsesWhere in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse?When, where and how to get the optimal view of the first solar eclipse to be visible across the country this centuryRachel HallSat 8 Aug 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the first time this century, people across the UK will be able to see an almost total solar eclipse in the evening sky on Wednesday.A solar eclipse occurs when the moon moves between the sun and the Earth, blocking the sun’s light either partly or fully. This year, people in the UK and Ireland will see 90-96% of the sun covered by the moon for the first time since 1999 – and it’s their last chance until 2081.Across north-western Europe, people will see about 88-95% coverage, while spectators in parts of Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain will see a total eclipse for up to two minutes and 18 seconds in duration.In the UK, viewers in the west will see the most of the sun obscured: 95% in Plymouth, 93.2% in Cardiff and 93.1% in Belfast. Spectators in Manchester will see 91.9% and Londoners will catch 91.4%. Farther north and east people will see smaller proportions, with Edinburgh at 90.7%, Newcastle at 90.2%. Shetland will have the lowest coverage at 88%.Map of the best locations in UK to view the solar eclipseRoyal Observatory Greenwich astronomer Jess Lee said that these are small differences, and all “will still be impressive sights”. She recommended finding hills with clear views to the west, for example Parliament Hill, Alexandra Palace or Primrose Hill in London, or rooftop venues.Because the eclipse takes place in August, there’s a stronger chance of clear skies. Tom Morgan, a Met Office meteorologist, said it was too early to be confident, but “given the summer we’ve had a lot of the UK will have reasonable viewing conditions”.At present, there is a higher risk of thick cloud and rain in Scotland and Northern Ireland, while the clearest skies are likely to be towards the south and the east of the UK. “For many it’ll be quite a spectacular and rare event,” he said.For Scotland’s astronomer royal, Catherine Heymans, keeping an eye on the clouds is the secret to scoring the best view, since these could partly or entirely obscure the eclipse.“I plan to check the Met Office’s fantastic online cloud cover forecast as we get closer to the day. I’m ready to hop on a train north, south, east or west to find some cloud-free skies,” she said.Spanish mountain village braces for astrotourists lured by total solar eclipseRead moreGetting to a high point with a clear view of the horizon also helps. “I’d recommend a dress rehearsal in the days before. If you can’t see the sun from your planned viewing spot at 7.30pm because your view is blocked by a hill or a house, then you’ll want to find yourself a different location for the real event,” Heymans added.The most important thing, she stressed, is to wear eclipse glasses and avoid looking directly at the sun.During an eclipse, the sun appears dimmer, making it easier to look at directly. However, solar radiation can still reach and damage the retina, often without causing any pain, so viewers may not realise harm is occurring until it’s too late.Following the 1999 total solar eclipse, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists reportedabout 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems after watching the eclipse.The UK Health Security Agency advises that there are two safe approaches: specialist eclipse viewers or indirect viewing methods.Eclipse glasses or handheld solar viewers must be genuine and sold by a reputable retailer, and should have specially designed filters that meet the international safety standard ISO 12312-2:2015(E), and no scratches, tearing or damage to the lens. Old pairs may not be reusable and sunglasses should never be used.Indirect view methods include viewing the sun’s image projected through a colander or the gaps between tree leaves on to white paper, or using a pinhole pierced in one sheet of card and projected on to another.Sarah Crowther, an astronomer at the University of Manchester, said it was important to remember that the solar eclipse would take place at different times across the UK.It starts at about 6.08pm in Edinburgh and Glasgow, 6.10pm in Belfast, 6.13pm in Manchester and Liverpool, 6.15pm in Birmingham, 6.17pm in London and 6.18pm in Cornwall. Maximum eclipse follows roughly an hour later, ending about 8pm.People might observe the surrounding area going quiet during the solar eclipse, “when animals think it is night because it is darker, which gives a sense of calm. And then there’s an awakening as it gets light again, birds think it is dawn so there could be a dawn chorus,” said Crowther.She added: “I think many people feel a sense of awe when they see an eclipse. It can put the vast scales of the solar system into some kind of perspective.”Explore more on these topicsSolar eclipsesAstronomySpacenewsShareReuse this content

title: The moment I knew: As I packed, our future looked uncertain – then he gave me his fluffy pyjamas | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: Stephanie Casey was an exchange student in Ireland when she met Jack. They quickly became close but as the year drew to a close, her departure loomed
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Stephanie Casey was an exchange student in Ireland when she met Jack. They quickly became close but as the year drew to a close, her departure loomed
Content: Jack and Stephanie Casey at Blarney Castle in Ireland, 2017.View image in fullscreenJack and Stephanie Casey at Blarney Castle in Ireland, 2017.The moment I knewAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knew: As I packed, our future looked uncertain – then he gave me his fluffy pyjamasStephanie Caseywas an exchange student in Ireland when she met Jack. They quickly became close but as the year drew to a close, her departure loomedFind more stories fromthe moment I knew seriesStephanie CaseySat 8 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 20.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2016 I was an Australian student on exchange in Dublin, plotting to fall in love at Trinity College before Normal People made it cool. My housemates had swiped on Jack’s Tinder profile on my behalf, and we met in October for the first time under the Spire on O’Connell Street.Jack couldn’t quite believe I had actually shown up; I was just glad he wasn’t the other lad standing there with the Peaky Blinders haircut and matching tracksuit. We went to a bookshop cafe, where Jack spilled his tea due to nerves and I waxed lyrical about the importance of compulsory voting due to mine. It was sweet, genuine, interesting conversation. When we parted ways, we both did the classic over-the-shoulder, cow-eyed glance back. Jack kept his cool; I panicked and walked straight into a line of kindergarteners on an excursion in the city.The moment I knew: after my mum lost everything in Japan’s tsunami, Trent showered her with tiny kindnessesRead moreSoon we were seeing each other every week, which quickly turned into every day. My room had a view out onto Pearse Street, and Jack would wave to me out of the train window as it pulled into Pearse St station. I’d sign him into the “overnight visitors” book at my dorm (sorry Mum) where we’d watch Australian horror films (Wolf Creek) and Irish comedies (Father Ted). We walked all over Dublin in the cold afternoons that were bluey-gold in the light and smelled like peat fires, Jack taking me to his favourite parks and pubs. We ate spice bags and Vegemite, drank tea and Guinness.My uni friends put my phone on time-out so I could stop texting Jack about the “season finale of America” – Trump 1.0 had just begun – and start studying for exams; my Australian friends wondered if I’d finally cracked and made the whole boy up, given the romantic disaster I’d been at home.View image in fullscreenTogether at the Cliffs of Moher, Ireland in 2019. ‘Our relationship status remained undefined, at least by us. To everyone else … it was clear we were serious about being together’But as the year drew to a close, reality loomed. My visa meant I had to come home in January and Jack still had two more years of study to complete in Dublin. We hadn’t talked about what we were going to do, or what our future looked like.Our relationship status remained undefined, at least by us. To everyone else – from my mum who gently advised me to “give it a chance”, to Jack’s family who I joined for Christmas Day – it was clear we were serious about being together.On the night I was leaving my university accommodation, Jack helped me pack my life – which had quickly become our life – into a straining suitcase. He picked up a pair of his pyjama pants that I coveted and had claimed as my own. They were thick, fluffy, in a blue and green plaid; no Irish clan connection, no fancy label, just a budget pair from Penneys, my other great Irish love. He packed them into my bag, but I protested: “You can’t do that, you love these pants”. He looked at me steadily and said: “Yes, but I love you more.” His words were a simple gift, one that I had never received before, which gave me the answer I didn’t know I was looking for: that we would give it a chance, together.I flew back to Australia a few days later and cried the whole way home. We didn’t have a plan, but we knew we wanted to be together. We talked in the mornings, sent memes to each other during the day and called to say goodnight. We did this for three years. Life might have shrunk to the size of a phone screen, but it had also never felt so large.I visited Jack in Dublin in 2017; he spent six months in Australia doing his own exchange in 2018; we reunited halfway in Vietnam in 2019. In early 2020, Jack moved to Australia – he really took “locking it down” seriously, even before Covid.View image in fullscreen‘We married last year, in Dublin, and around the corner from our first date’: Stephanie Casey and Jack on their wedding day in 2025Since then, Jack has become a citizen, and we’ve bought a house and a puppy together. We married last year, in Dublin, around the corner from our first date.Our love is something I’m so proud of, and it brings me joy every day. There have been sacrifices, hard conversations and long lonely days, but I would do it again. I’m pretty sure Jack feels the same. But perhaps he has just been trying to get his pyjamas back this whole time.Tell us the moment you knewShare your experienceShare your love storyDo you have a romantic realisation you'd like to share? From quiet domestic scenes to dramatic revelations, Guardian Australia wants to hear about the moment you knew you were in lovePlease share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: President Xi never wastes a good crisis. As Iran, Ukraine and Palestine distract the world, he tightens his grip  | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: Ever the strategist, the Chinese leader is taking the offensive, both abroad and at home. That’s bad news for global order, and minorities in his country, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: Ever the strategist, the Chinese leader is taking the offensive, both abroad and at home. That’s bad news for global order, and minorities in his country, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: China's Xi Jinping with Donald Trump during a visit to Zhongnanhai Garden in Beijing on 15 May 2026.Photograph: Evan Vucci/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChina's Xi Jinping with Donald Trump during a visit to Zhongnanhai Garden in Beijing on 15 May 2026.Photograph: Evan Vucci/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionXi JinpingPresident Xi never wastes a good crisis. As Iran, Ukraine and Palestine distract the world, he tightens his gripSimon TisdallEver the strategist, the Chinese leader is taking the offensive, both abroad and at home. That’s bad news for global order, and minorities in his countrySat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.05 EDTShareImagine what would happen if a British prime minister in London told the Scots they could not have their own parliament, national football team or fly the saltire. Or if the Welsh were told their language and poetry were banned and must no longer be taught in schools. The ensuing uproar would probably destroy the United Kingdom. Yet that’s exactly what Xi Jinping, China’s communist emperor, is telling the roughly 125 million members of the 55ethnic and religious minoritieswho together comprise about 9% of the country’s (majority Han Chinese) population.Xi claims his sinicisation policy, embodied in a new “ethnic unity” law, will boost national identity and integration and, by expanding compulsory use of the Mandarin language, improve life and work prospects. Minorities should “hug tightly like pomegranate seeds” to build a strong, united China, he says. But Tibetans, Mongolians,Uyghursand others who value their separate language and customs fiercely object to what they see asforced assimilationinto a conformist, intolerant monoculture dominated by the Communist party’s tunnel vision. For them, it’s ethnic cleansing by another name.The new law has been condemned, though not too loudly, by western governments and more vociferously by rights organisations such asAmnesty International. The death of Lobga Rangzen, a Free Tibet activist whoset himself on firein protest outside the UN in New York last month, briefly drew international attention. But such tragedies are not new. Wholesale repression in Tibet and brutal “re-education” camps in Xinjiang are but two longstanding aspects of Xi’s intensifying nationwide war on dissent, difference and diversity. The law and its harsh penalties, which extend toChinese citizens based abroad, adds legal weight to existing efforts to enforce his and the party’s will (much the same thing these days) by creating a politically compliant, cowed population that dare not answer back.A debilitating fatalism has taken hold in the west about China’s behaviour, whether it involves persecution of minorities, evisceration of democracy in Hong Kong, vindictive prosecutions of pro-democracy activists such as the former Apple Daily publisherJimmy Lai, or vicious suppression of independentChristian churchesand “unapproved” religious groups. It’s as though Xi’s China is now seen as simply too big, too economically powerful and too militarily threatening to influence, let alone contain or control. When China’s internal affairs are the issue, it’s easier to steer clear. Awkwardly balancingtrade against security, and culpably silent on human rights, Britain is far from alone among western democracies in failing to articulate a coherent China policy.But Xi’s increasingly aggressive, uncompromising policies are not confined to domestic matters. In power for nearly 15 years, Xi, 73, is growing ever more confident and abrasive in pursuit of his international legacy bucket list: establishing China asthe dominant global power, relegating the US to second place and making his country the essential hub of a new multipolar security, economic and diplomatic order. His legacy list includes a takeover of Taiwan before he stands down, and unchallenged supremacy across the Asia-Pacific region. It all points one way: to Xi’s coronation as the greatest Chinese leader since Mao Zedong.With the 21st party congress approaching, 2027 could be a big year for Xi – and he is already getting his ducks in a row. His dictatorship looks unassailable. Top regime cadres,meeting this week in secretive conclaveat the Beidaihe seaside resort in Hebei province, are expected to endorse his redoubled drive to enforce loyalty and discipline in the ranks – the official phrase is “sustained advancement of full and rigorous party self-governance”. The Beidaihe gathering, andanother meeting due in October, come amid almost Stalinistpurgesofsenior politicaland military figures.Signs of a more assertive international posture are everywhere. In recent months, China has stoked nationalisttensions with Japanand deliberatelyprovoked the Philippinesin disputed areas of the South China Sea. Its intimidation of Taiwan is unceasing. This week, Japan’s latest defence white paper singled out China as presenting “an unprecedented strategic challenge” and warned the threat was moving closer to home. Admiral Samuel Paparo, head of US Pacific Command,fired a broadsideat China’s “coercive actions” in pursuit, he said, of regional dominance.Xi is now actively challenging the US and the west on several other fronts. China is reportedly planning toprovide Iranwith up to 400 shoulder-fired missiles and new air defence systems. It is already materially assisting Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. And an emboldened Beijing is deploying the sort oftrade weaponsbeloved of Donald Trump. Last year it restricted exports of vital rare earth minerals, to Washington’s great alarm. Only this week, China hit back at Trump’s new tariffs byblocking sales of drone technology.Xi’s ever more bullish stance owes much to Trump’s trashing of the post-1945 global order, disdain for international law and national sovereignty (as seen in Venezuela and Greenland), andstrained relationswith traditional allies such as Japan, South Korea and European Nato countries. Many now view the US as an unreliable partner. For China, Trump’s shifting focus away from Asia and towards the western hemisphere is a golden opportunity to be exploited while it lasts. That may be one reason why Xi has taken the unusual step of agreeing to visit Trump in Washington next month, so soon after their May meeting in Beijing.The main focus of the summit is expected to be artificial intelligence, amid US worries that it is in danger oflosing the AI race. According to Chinese commentators, at least, Trump asked for the meeting after China agreed AI partnerships with 28 countries, mostly from the global south. AI is “probably the biggest thing anybody’s ever seen”, Trump said last month. “Whoever wins that race is probably going to win, period.” By which he presumably means, win the 21st century’s superpower crown.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe summit is likely to confirm the impression left bythe last one: that Xi, outmanoeuvring Trump on Asia-Pacific security and Taiwan, accumulating geopolitical clout, and winning trade and tech wars, is well on the way to fulfilling his ambition of gaining the upper hand over the US. Yet in the end, Xi is still an unelected autocrat, a thug in a suit who relies on force to stay in power. He’s failing to deliver economically and, as in India and elsewhere, young urban Chinese may not tolerate his old-school brand of suffocating authoritarianism indefinitely. Who knows? Perhaps his ethnic unity law may ultimately prove a step too far – as it certainly would in Britain.All should be on their guard. Xi, no friend of the west, may be morphing into an outright enemy while all eyes are onIran, Gaza and Ukraine. Symbolically if not yet physically, a dangerously unconstrained Xi is shutting the door on peaceful coexistence at home and abroad.Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsXi JinpingOpinionChinaHuman rightsTariffsAI (artificial intelligence)Asia PacificDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Planting seeds of peace: teenagers from conflict-torn world build bridges at summer camp | Young people | The Guardian
description: UK hosts decades-old event for first time where many participants are from opposite sides of global disputes from Israel and Palestine, to India and Pakistan
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: UK hosts decades-old event for first time where many participants are from opposite sides of global disputes from Israel and Palestine, to India and Pakistan
Content: The campers stayed at a boarding school in Tavistock for three weeks in an experience many said was challenging but life-changing.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe campers stayed at a boarding school in Tavistock for three weeks in an experience many said was challenging but life-changing.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianYoung peoplePlanting seeds of peace: teenagers from conflict-torn world build bridges at summer campUK hosts decades-old event for first time where many participants are from opposite sides of global disputes from Israel and Palestine, to India and PakistanJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentSat 8 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the surface it looks like a normal summer school in theDevoncountryside, with teenagers playing volleyball in the sun, doing arts and crafts in the hall, and preparing for the night’s talent show.But behind the scenes, intensive discussions are taking place. Many of these teenagers come from opposite sides of historical national conflicts – from Israel and Palestine, India and Pakistan.Every day at Seeds of Peace they spend two hours in dialogue sessions with each other, sharing their personal experiences, their pain and trauma, and trying to find the common ground that unites them. Over the course of three weeks, that is 32 hours in a room discussing heavy topics and trying to build bridges.“You won’t find them sitting with maps and facts and books,” said Eva Armour, Seeds of Peace’s executive director. “They’re talking about their own lived experiences – that’s how the learning is happening. You can’t debate someone else’s lived experience the way that you might debate what happened in the war.View image in fullscreenEva Armour, Seeds of Peace executive director, with global youth programme lead, Qasim Aslam.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian“It’s almost embarrassingly simple how well this model works, but we need to invest in this work even a fraction of what we’re investing in the aftermath of war.”The Seeds of Peace summer camp, for teenagers aged 14 to 17 from eight different countries including the UK, has been running for 30 years but this is the first time it has been held in Britain.Founded in 1993 by the American journalist John Wallach, it usually takes place in the US but political uncertainty meant organisers felt the UK was a safer bet this year.View image in fullscreenThe 14- to 17-year-olds at the camp, who come from all over the world, are known as ‘seeds’.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian“Picking a country to host this is one of the enormous challenges,” said Qasim Aslam, the global youth programme lead. “If you pull up a map, there are very few countries where all parents from all eight countries would be comfortable sending their kids, and where we can get visas for all participants.”Coming to the end of their three-week stay at a Devonshire boarding school in Tavistock, many of the campers – known as “seeds” – said the experience had been challenging but life-changing.View image in fullscreenMika, 17 from Israel: ‘Facing someone who is supposed to be my enemy, but she’s just a girl like me – it’s difficult.’Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianMika, a 17-year-old from Israel, said she was glad she attended even though she had not come closer to answering her questions about peace. “Now I’m thinking, did I really expect three weeks to fix it all?“Facing someone who is supposed to be my enemy, but she’s just a girl like me – it’s difficult,” she said. “I could just not know about it and go and have fun in another summer camp and it would be way easier. But I prefer knowing it and starting to work through it for what I believe.“If one day maybe I have the power to change something, I don’t want to be ignorant. I want to know the pains of everyone.”View image in fullscreenHala, 16, is Palestinian and from Jerusalem: ‘It was hard at first, I thought I was betraying something deep down inside of me.’Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianHala, a 16-year-old Palestinian from Jerusalem, said it was the first time she had met Israelis “outside of checkpoints, raids and IDF uniforms”.“It was hard at first, I thought I was betraying something deep down inside of me,” she said. “But when I got to know these people, I realised they have very different views about their government. And we like the same movie. We have so many things in common.”View image in fullscreenEsther, 17, from Belfast: ‘It’s really powerful to hear from people themselves.’Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianEven for those coming from outside the main conflict zones, the experience has been enlightening. “I have never had the chance to speak to people from different countries like Israel and Palestine before – you never know how the media censors stuff so it’s really powerful to hear from people themselves,” said Esther, a 17-year-old from Belfast. “I feel like I’ll be much less quick to judge people now.”For some participants, the act of attending is fraught with difficulty. Ahmad, a 26-year-old Palestinian camp counsellor who previously attended as a teenager, said he would not be speaking about his summer trip back home.View image in fullscreenThe act of attending can be fraught with difficulty for some.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian“For some people, it feels like you’re betraying your country, because you’re trying to make peace with the people who are killing you at the same time,” he said. “You can’t just go home and expect people to understand Seeds of Peace in a second. You need to be here to understand that.”While camp organisers aim to get a diverse range of teenagers, they admitted there were limits to how accessible they could be – English language skills are required so the dialogue sessions can be most effective.The cost to attend the summer camp is $9,000 (£6,700), although many of those attending receive scholarships to cover the vast majority of this fee. And in some countries there is a competitive application process. “We’re trying to identify young people that could be influencers in their respective communities in the future,” said Aslam.Many past attenders have gone on to become politicians, ambassadors and business leaders, taking the skills they learned at Seeds of Peace with them into their work.View image in fullscreenPast attenders have gone on to become politicians, ambassadors and business leaders.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianOver the past three decades, the organisers have worked in areas such as the Balkans, Cyprus, Greece, Turkey and Afghanistan, tailoring their camps to respond to geopolitical events. They also do year-round work and regional camps in place where need is greatest.“It feels like it’s getting harder for people to be able to talk to each other across differences,” said Armour. “After 7 October [attacks on Israel by Hamas], we actually got a lot of calls from schools and institutions saying we don’t really know how to talk to each other about this, can you help?”View image in fullscreenJoud, 17, from Jordan: ‘I learned how to listen and understand, not just respond.’Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianJoud, a 17-year-old from Jordan attending for the second year, said the camp had enabled her to have healthy debate with her family for the first time, and she had become good friends with a Jewish girl from the US, which she “never expected”.“Our social identities are complete opposites. But we connected in many different ways, and I learned how to listen and understand, not just respond,” she said.“In what situations are 14- to 17-year-olds with very opposing ideologies and opinions sat down together in a room for two hours talking about things that maybe the leaders of their own countries don’t have the courage to sit down and talk about?”Explore more on these topicsYoung peopleDevonPeace and reconciliationInternational relationsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The market is dead’: why aren’t flats in England selling? | Property | The Guardian
description: Figures show most leasehold flats in England do not find a buyer within six months, despite slashed prices
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Figures show most leasehold flats in England do not find a buyer within six months, despite slashed prices
Content: Most flats listed for sale in England are leasehold.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMost flats listed for sale in England are leasehold.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesProperty‘The market is dead’: why aren’t flats in England selling?Figures show most leasehold flats in England do not find a buyer within six months, despite slashed pricesRupert JonesSat 8 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘The market is dead for flats,” says Susan Young*, who has been trying for some time without success to sell her two-bed flat in a popular Devon seaside resort.The first-floor property is in “immaculate condition”, Young says, thanks to the £15,000-£20,000 spent on renovations. It has “superb views” across the beach. And, perhaps most crucially, it is a freehold flat, so is untainted by the controversies associated with the discreditedleaseholdsystem.“Despite not needing to buy (that is, no chain) and dropping the price to well under what I paid for it, I have only had four viewings in nine months,” says Young, a former teacher, who moved in 2023 but now needs to relocate for family reasons.She paid £300,000 for the property and currently has it on the market for £280,000.She does not want to reduce the price any further and, if there are no viewings by the end of the summer, she intends to take the flat off the market and put it back on next year when, hopefully, there will be more interest from buyers.View image in fullscreenIs the market for flats in England dead?Photograph: Realimage/AlamyShe says the flats market is moribund even though hers is in a block of six where each flat owns a sixth of the freehold and they set their own management fee. “It is very dispiriting.”Meanwhile, Louisa, who lives in London, has been trying to sell her leasehold flat for two and a half years. The sale recently fell through for a third time after several months of negotiations when the buyers demanded she knock £10,000 off the price.She initially feared having to “sell at a massive loss, losing all my deposit and preventing me from buying in the near future. My property is above a barber shop, and I have been told that banks will not lend mortgages above these, leaving me in a position looking for reasonable cash offers.”However, there is now some hope as she has found a cash buyer. “So I’m currently going through the process again, but I’ve stated that I will only give the sale a few months before giving up and trying to rent it out. This will be attempt number four.”Louisa bought the flat for £200,000, and the sale that fell through recently was for £145,000.View image in fullscreenSome owners of flats in England have cut the price several times to no avail.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian“It’s a one-bed flat, and I now have a two-year-old daughter. This situation has meant we are unable to leave my family home, where we have been staying. I just want to move on and give my child a bedroom.“I’m not buying again in the near future. I’m quite traumatised from the experience.”Young and Louisa are just two of the Guardian readers who responded to a recent call-out asking about their experiences of trying to buy or sell a flat in recent months.Many of the respondents said the same thing: they have been trying – and trying – to sell a flat. Some have cut the price several times but to no avail; others have been left in the lurch when buyers pulled out.Some are owner-occupiers; others are small landlords who are trying to leave the rental sector.So what’s happening?In June, the property website Zoopla issued data showing that the average price of a house was up 43% since 2016 across the UK, but flats had increased by 10% over the same period.Zoopla said “uncertainty around leasehold inEnglandis affecting the pricing of flats versus houses” and that flats were taking longer to sell as a result.Most flats listed for sale in England are leasehold. And the longlist of scandalsand controversies associated with this form of ownership – from high service charges and ground rents and hefty one-off bills to cladding issues, costly lease extensions and difficulty buying freeholds – has prompted government action.However, aban on new leaseholdproperties in England and Wales is unlikely to come into force until after the next election, and concerns about cost and complexity are clearly having an impact now.We asked Zoopla to crunch the numbers on flats not selling and why. It found that across most of England, the majority of leasehold flats listed for sale in 2025 had not sold within six months.View image in fullscreenThe property website Zoopla says ‘uncertainty around leasehold in England is affecting the pricing of flats versus houses’.Photograph: larigan/Patricia Hamilton/Getty Images“London was worst – about 87% unsold – followed by the south-east (85%) and the east of England (84%),” Richard Donnell, the Zoopla executive director, says. The average was 80.5%.As to why many flats are struggling to find buyers, Donnell says it is not only the leasehold issue, which reinforces the preference for buying a house where possible. It is also to do with who is buying and who is selling.“Flats take longer to find buyers because the natural buyer (the first-time buyer) and the natural seller (often an investor with no urgency to move) may want two different prices,” he adds.For example, in London, most first-time buyers are looking for flats, not houses, as flats are their main route into ownership, Donnell says. “But investor-owned flats are being priced above the typical first-time buyer budget (£450,000 v a £425,000 budget). So even though flats are what buyers there want, the ones investors are selling are out of reach.”In addition, thousands of aspiring homeowners are finding themselves shut out of the flats market owing to banks’ increasingly restrictive mortgage lending rules, says William Coe at the mortgage broker Cleerly. At the same time, he adds, surveyors are increasingly “down valuing” flats – creating yet another barrier for buyers.“I’ve been told I need to drop the price by another £30,000 as small flats just aren’t selling”Barbara Doolan*, who lives in Sussex, has owned a flat in a small block in Croydon for 20 years, and has always rented it out.She tried to sell the flat in 2024 but had no joy, despite cutting the price twice. She says she had no choice but to rent it out again, and had a “terrible experience” with the tenant, who defaulted on the rent and illegally sublet it.“I’ve considered selling again … and the market is even worse now. Three agents have said I’d need to drop the price by another £30k to get some interest as small flats like this just aren’t selling.”“A combination of factors has left ordinary small landlords like us trapped”Angie West and her wife own two flats in London, one of which they bought 20 years ago as a buy-to-let investment. At the time they both worked in the voluntary sector and neither had a private or workplace pension, so they hoped the flat would provide them with some financial security in retirement.West, who is now semi-retired, says that in late 2024 they put it on the market for £325,000. There followed a difficult period during which they reduced the asking price several times and had two separate buyers pull out.double quotation markBuyers can pull out at any stage for almost any reason, with no financial consequence to themAngie WestWith costs mounting, they later decided they would have to rent the property out again. More costs were racked up, and the current tenants recently gave notice and are due to leave this month.“We intend to try selling the flat again but are very worried about what will happen if it does not sell … What concerns me most is that the combination of falling flat values, repeated failed sales, leasehold costs, licensing requirements and increasing complexity in the rental sector has left ordinary small landlords like us trapped,” says West, who lives in south London.“The whole process feels incredibly insecure. Buyers can pull out at any stage for almost any reason, with no financial consequence to them, while sellers are left paying legal fees, management pack costs and other expenses.”Top tips on how to sell a flatView image in fullscreenMost first-time buyers in London are looking for flats, not houses.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianKnow your market“Chat to your agent about what local first-time buyers can actually afford and who is buying flats and what they are prepared to pay,” Zoopla’s Donnell says.Price realistically from day oneBuyers have a lot of choice, so getting the asking price right is crucial. “The key to selling a flat successfully in the current market is pricing competitively from day one,” says Colleen Babcock, Rightmove’s property expert. “Our research shows that nearly three-quarters of homes that have sold so far this year have done so without a price reduction.” So if you list a property at an optimistic price, thinking you can always reduce it later, “you’re putting yourself at an immediate disadvantage”.Major on all the benefitsThe buying agent Henry Pryor says that aside from the obvious – “make it clean, make it tidy, make it desirable, make it smell of freshly baked bread and coffee …” – sellers should also emphasise the property’s “lock up and leave” benefits. Lock up and leave means requiring very little in terms of daily maintenance – for example, a flat that doesn’t have a garden or lots of rooms or areas to clean.Be on top of your service charge historySome potential buyers will ask for (at least) three years of service charge accounts (where relevant). So sort these out before you list the property and be ready to explain the trend, Donnell says. A recent Zoopla analysis showed that the typical leaseholder pays £1,900 a year in service charges, plus £200 a year in ground rent. If your service charges or ground rent are relatively low, then point this out, Rightmove says.Lease length mattersAbout a fifth of leasehold listings have less than 100 years left on the lease, according to Zoopla. Leaseholders have the statutory right to extend their lease at a cost that rises quickly once a lease drops below 80 years, it adds. “For flats with less than 85 years remaining, consider applying to extend the lease before listing,” Donnell says. TheLeaseholdand Freehold Reform Act 2024 will make it cheaper and easier to extend a lease, but it’s not yet clear when these measures will come into force. The government last month said the changes would go live “as soon as possible”.Six may be the magic number“You should always be able to attract an investor by pricing your property so that a buyer would generate a 6% or better yield,” Pryor says. You need to work out what your flat would rent for (local estate agents should be able to provide that information), he says. Then work out what capital value would generate a 6% or better yield. To do this, take the annual potential rent – the per calendar month figure x 12 – then multiply this by 100, then divide by 6. “That’s where you need to pitch your asking price,” Pryor says, although he adds “hopefully you will do better” than that and actually find a buyer who really likes your flat.* Name has been changedExplore more on these topicsPropertyHousing marketHouse pricesLeaseholdFirst-time buyersReal estateEnglandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: One of UK’s best fossil collections sold overseas in ‘loss to the nation’ | Fossils | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Lack of funds left British museums unable pay eight-figure sum for collection, which went to Abu Dhabi institution
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Exclusive: Lack of funds left British museums unable pay eight-figure sum for collection, which went to Abu Dhabi institution
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesFossilsOne of UK’s best fossil collections sold overseas in ‘loss to the nation’Exclusive: Lack of funds left British museums unable pay eight-figure sum for collection, which went to Abu Dhabi institutionNicola DavisScience correspondentSat 8 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.02 EDTShareOne of the most important collections of UK Jurassic fossils ever compiled has been sold to a museum in Abu Dhabi, the Guardian can reveal, in what British experts have described as a loss for the nation.The collection, which was amassed by a private fossil collector, consisted of 318 specimens, including ichthyosaurs, fish and crustaceans among other creatures, some of which could be new species.The fossils were initially offered for purchase to the Natural History Museum (NHM) in London and to Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales) for what was described by one source as an “eight-figure sum”.Neither institution bought the collection, with both citing a lack of funding. An email seen by the Guardian suggested the NHM had “no money at all” for acquisitions.One curator said that while there had long been a hope that the collection could be kept in the UK, it also posed issues around storage space, curatorial time and packaging materials.“I don’t blame the collectors at all. That’s all they can do. They can’t sit on these things forever,” the curator said, adding that the issue was expected to occur again and again as collectors get older and look for a suitable home for their life’s work.“Whose responsibility is it to fund our heritage and the preservation of our heritage? Because otherwise it could get lost,” they added.The extensive collection is understood to come from a sequence of rocks known as the Lower Lias, from Lyme Regis, Charmouth, and the south-west of the UK.It was compiled by Chris Moore, a private Dorset-based collector with experience ofhunting fossils in the area. In emails seen by the Guardian the collection is described as “stunning”.View image in fullscreenIchthyosaur fossil.Photograph: Martin Shields/AlamySome countries, including Mongolia and Brazil, consider all fossils found in those countries in recent decades to be property of the state – a situation thathas led to international disputesover repatriation of fossils housed abroad. However, this is not the case in the UK.Richard Butler, a professor of palaebiology at the University of Birmingham who was not involved in the sale, said the collection was of national significance. “This is one of the most important collections of fossils ever made on the world-famous Jurassic Coast of Dorset. It would have been wonderful to see these fossils on display and engaging the public in a UK museum.”He added: “This sale raises important questions about whether more should be done to preserve important and irreplaceable natural heritage such as this for the benefit of the UK public.”Britain’s Jurassic gold rush: the fossil hunters chasing fortunes on Dorset’s beachesRead moreIn theUnited Arab Emirates, the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi confirmed it had bought a collection from Moore, which went on display in November 2025. A spokesperson for the museum said the Lower Jurassic rocks of the UK preserved some of the best examples of marine life from when what is now the Dorset coast was roughly at the same latitude as north Africa.“All natural history museums around the world tell this story, often using fossils from multiple countries to help narrate their journey through time. If we are to tell a 4.2bn-year story of the evolution of life on Earth, all museums must travel both spatially and temporally with their collections,” the spokesperson said.“A large majority of the Chris Moore collection is already on public display in the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi in the Mesozoic Gallery (Age of Dinosaurs Gallery).”Lyme Regis is part of theJurassic Coast, a Unesco world heritage site, that is rich with fossilsthat date back to between 200m and 145m years ago. The area has a long history of private fossil collecting, with notable figures including Mary Anning – a pioneering palaeontologist and fossil dealer whose triumphs included the discovery of the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaurusin 1823.While approaches vary across the UK nations, modern fossil collectors along England’s Jurassic Coast are encouraged to follow the west Dorset fossil collecting code and the Undercliffs national nature reservefossil collecting code.Fossils initially belong to the owner of the land on which they are found, legal ownership is typical transferred to collectors who adhere to such codes and recording schemes – a situation that reflects the valuable role collectors are deemed to have in finding fossils that might otherwise never be recovered.View image in fullscreenSunset at Durdle Door in Dorset’s Jurassic coast.Photograph: Loop Images/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesBut whilehighly valuable archeological findsturned up by activities such as metal detecting can be classified as treasure – and therefore must be reported to the relevant authorities within 14 days of discovery – the same is not true for fossils, even those deemed to be key scientifically important fossils, known as category 1.According to the west Dorset fossil collecting code of conduct, collectors “who intend to sell or otherwise dispose of their category 1 specimens must first offer them to UK registered museums for a period of six months. If no purchase has been agreed by this time, the collector will be free to offer the specimen elsewhere.”However, such codes are not legally binding and even if followed, as Moore did, fossils found in the UK can be sold by collectors to private individuals, museums or other buyers – including those overseas. Moore was approached for comment.According to the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DDCMS), only objects that are over 50 years old and are manufactured or produced require an individual cultural property export licence, and there are no export requirements specific to the sale of fossils.A quick search of online marketplaces reveals a plethora of fossils, with small ammonites selling for as little as a few pounds.But some fossils can also fetch colossal sums: in 2020, Stan the T rex, now also housed atthe Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, was sold for a then record-breaking $31.8m (£23.6m), while in July this year another T rex skeleton nicknamed Guswas sold at Sotheby’s for $50.1m.These figures are far beyond the budget of most museums, with such specimens instead snapped up by private buyers – including business people and celebrities. Among those known to have bought dinosaur fossils are the actors Leonardo DiCaprio, Nicolas Cage andRussell Crowe– although Cage later returned the rare dinosaur skull he had bought to Mongolia, after it emerged it hadbeen illegally removed from the country.View image in fullscreenA Tyrannosaurus Rex dinosaur skeleton that was auctioned by Christie’s in New York in 2020.Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesFossils have also become popular on social media, with hunters using platforms such as TikTok to share videos of themselves cracking open rocks in a “fossil or no fossil?” reveal. Some accounts have several million followers.Finding a fossil is only the first step on the road to a sale: as the NHM in London notes,painstaking mechanical and chemical preparation is neededto turn it one into a museum-grade exhibit. Only dedicated fossil hunters have the tools and skills to prepare fossils –and Moore is among them.Many experts support the status quo for fossil collecting and sales, arguing that a ban on collecting would mean many important specimens would remain undiscovered and could result in a black-market for fossils – rather than allowing collectors to work with academics.View image in fullscreenAn ammonite at the fossil graveyard at Lyme Regis in Dorset.Photograph: Loop Images/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesThere is no suggestion the sale of the Moore collection to the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi has broken any rules.Yet Dr Erin Maxwell, an expert in Early Jurassic marine vertebrates based at the State Museum of Natural History in Stuttgart said the sale was a blow. “Such a sale in my opinion represents a loss to the UK, as fossils represent part of the natural [or] cultural heritage of the region and country from which they originate.“The loss is somewhat offset by the fact that these fossils are going to a museum rather than into the collection of a wealthy individual.”Maxwell added that there were other options for countries such as the UK where fossils are not automatically considered property of the state.“I think it is important for the state to have the right of first refusal on acquiring the collection on an at-cost basis prior to export – rather than the currently grossly inflated market price,” she said. “However, if the state declines, then sale to a foreign museum is a best-case scenario.”Phil Davidson, a palaeontologist at Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre in Dorset, said the priority was that fossil specimens of key scientific interest were in public collections, such as museums, so they could be described by teams of international experts, noting most scientific journals did not allow specimens to be described if they were within a private collection.“All the researchers I have talked to have said the same thing: the location of where the museum collection is housed is secondary,” Davidson said.“Countless specimens of scientific importance are housed outside their country of origin. Often this was because the specific researchers are based in other countries, or that they do not have the capacity or need to focus on other pressing priorities”.Davidson also stressed the importance of keeping the Moore collection together, adding the specimens come from a world heritage site “and this heritage is for everyone and not limited to lines on a map”.

title: Iran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz as deal still out of reach | Strait of Hormuz | The Guardian
description: Tehran urges US to ‘correct its behaviour’ as UAE says one of its ships targeted by Iranian missile
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tehran urges US to ‘correct its behaviour’ as UAE says one of its ships targeted by Iranian missile
Content: Tehran, Iran. An Iranian statement said the US must never threaten the country again.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTehran, Iran. An Iranian statement said the US must never threaten the country again.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesStrait of HormuzIran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz as deal still out of reachTehran urges US to ‘correct its behaviour’ as UAE says one of its ships targeted by Iranian missileGuardian staff and agenciesSat 8 Aug 2026 17.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 20.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, while theUnited Arab Emiratessaid one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile, as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach on Saturday.Iran’s politburo-like body known as the supreme national security council said the strait of Hormuz will not open until the United States “corrects its behaviour”, and its state broadcaster published a statement from the council’s secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who is also a commander in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).The US must never threaten Iran again, the statement said, and must permanently end the war with Iran and its armed allies in the region. The US must lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area. It also must “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets.Iran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in warRead moreThere was no immediate comment from the US, which has wanted an acceptable deal on the strait before ending the blockade. According to the interim deal signed in June, a schedule to end sanctions and a plan for compensation would be part of the final deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets.The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said on Saturday that they were close to reaching anagreement on navigation, “specifically the determination of a transit route”. But the waterway’s reopening is contingent on other conditions, he said, in remarks shared on social media, and blamed the situation on what he called the US violation of the interim deal.Oman, which is mediating and has made relatively few comments on the talks, said in a statement on Saturday that the discussions were continuing “in a positive and constructive atmosphere”, and condemned attacks on ships on the strait.Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait and wants to charge users for passage, repeatedly attacking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route.The US opposes any Iranian tolls in the strait, though the June deal allows Tehran to hammer out arrangements for the “future administration” of Hormuz in conjunction with fellow coastal state Oman.The 60-day period to negotiate a final deal will end in just over a week but could be extended.Iran has said it was close to reaching a separate deal with Oman to manage the strait, which runs between the two countries.Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian, a relative moderate, said he believed now was the best time for an agreement.“There is cohesion, strength, and unity in the country, and as far as I know, Iran is considered victorious and powerful in this war,” Iranian news agencies quoted him as saying.Continued attacks in the strait, which was free to sail through before the war, led to the collapse of an April ceasefire, and mediators have since urged both sides to return to the terms of the June memorandum.The strait, which is crucial to global supplies of oil and natural gas, had been considered an international waterway before the war. Ship transits remain low.Meanwhile, a vessel owned by Abu Dhabi’s state-owned Adnoc oil and gas company was attacked while sailing through the strait of Hormuz, Emirati authorities said earlier on Saturday. The foreign ministry said Iran fired the missile as part of attacks on commercial shipping.Adnoc said in a statement that there were no casualties following the attack early on Saturday. The company said more than a dozen of its vessels have been attacked by missiles and drones while using the strait since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. One crew member has been killed and 20 others wounded, it said.Adnoc did not elaborate on the location of the attack or any damage.Later, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre said a vessel east of the town of Khasab, Oman had been struck by a projectile that caused a fire that was put out, and the vessel and crew were safe. It was not clear whether this was the Adnoc incident.Explore more on these topicsStrait of HormuzIranOmanUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricaUnited Arab EmiratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Explosive’ wildfire forces 20,000 people to flee as British Columbia declares state of emergency | Canada | The Guardian
description: Fast-moving fire displaces people in western Canada, burning homes as it races through towns on Okanagan Lake
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fast-moving fire displaces people in western Canada, burning homes as it races through towns on Okanagan Lake
Content: Smoke rises from the Bald Range wildfire over a residential street in Summerland, British Columbia, Canada, on 7 August.Photograph: Terry Fries/ReutersView image in fullscreenSmoke rises from the Bald Range wildfire over a residential street in Summerland, British Columbia, Canada, on 7 August.Photograph: Terry Fries/ReutersCanada‘Explosive’ wildfire forces 20,000 people to flee as British Columbia declares state of emergencyFast-moving fire displaces people in western Canada, burning homes as it races through towns on Okanagan LakeAssociated PressSat 8 Aug 2026 18.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish Columbia declared a state of emergency on Saturday as a fast-moving wildfire destroyed homes, trapped residents and forced more than 20,000 people to flee communities along Okanagan Lake in westernCanada.The premier, David Eby,announced the emergencyas more than 100 wildfires burned across the province, nearly half of them out of control in hot, windy weather and prolonged drought.The entire community of Summerland, home to about 12,000 people, was ordered evacuated overnight, along with about 8,000 people in and around nearby Peachland. Officials had not determined how many homes were destroyed.Eby said some residents became trapped and had to be rescued, while search-and-rescue crews continued looking behind the fire lines for anyone else who may have been caught.“I know many families are facing an unimaginable day today,” Eby said. “People have lost their homes. And many people have been displaced. Others are waiting for news about loved ones.”Cliff Chapman, director of wildfire operations for the BC Wildfire Service, said firefighting helicopters were diverted to rescue people who could no longer escape by road. He said the outcome would have been significantly worse without cooperation among agencies responding to the fire.The Bald Range wildfire was first reported on Friday evening but grew to about 50 sq km (19 sq miles) within hours, overwhelming the smaller community of Faulder and covering the roughly 15km (9 miles) to Summerland at extraordinary speed.Chapman described fire conditions across British Columbia as “explosive” and warned that other communities could face fires similar to the one that forced the evacuation of Summerland.Kelly Greene, British Columbia’s emergency management minister, said the state of emergency gives the province additional powers, including the ability to restrict travel and secure accommodations for evacuees that might otherwise be unavailable.Erick Thompson, an emergency official with the regional district of Okanagan-Similkameen, called it one of the “quickest-moving, fastest-growing” wildfires the region had experienced.Thompson eventually had to abandon the emergency operations center and evacuate his own family. “I had to leave the EOC to come and get my family to leave this area. We’re heading south,” he said in a video posted early Saturday from his vehicle as traffic backed up around him.Videos posted on social media appeared to show multiple homes burning as residents fled along roads with flames on both sides.One homeowner, Kerry Gold, and her husband, Mike Elsinga, fled at about 12.30am after watching flames spread beyond nearby mountains.“It’s scary. It’s moving fast,” Gold said.The couple, who recently moved from the city of Vancouver, had packed bags, prepared a carrier for their cat and planned to help a disabled friend evacuate.“You want to stay here and protect your home, but you also don’t want to get caught in it,” Elsinga said.Canada has endured increasingly destructive wildfire seasons in recent years, forcing mass evacuations and repeatedly sending smoke across large parts of Canada and the United States.Explore more on these topicsCanadaWildfiresAmericasShareReuse this content

title: Fifa launches new attack on media over alleged ‘concerted effort’ to undermine Gianni Infantino  | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: Fifa has issued a new statement alleging there is a ‘concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president’ as pressure increases on Gianni Infantino
Author: David Hills
Headline: Fifa has issued a new statement alleging there is a ‘concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president’ as pressure increases on Gianni Infantino
Content: Fifa has issued a new statement defending its under-fire president, Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Jaime Saldarriaga/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFifa has issued a new statement defending its under-fire president, Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Jaime Saldarriaga/AFP/Getty ImagesGianni InfantinoFifa launches new attack on media over alleged ‘concerted effort’ to undermine Gianni InfantinoFifa issues statement defending under-fire president‘Insinuation should not be presented as fact’David HillsSat 8 Aug 2026 18.17 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 18.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa has issued a new statement alleging there is a “concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president” as pressure increases onGianni Infantino.Fifa president Gianni Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged ‘lover’Read moreThe governing body issued the statement in response toUefa confirming on Saturdaythat a “departure payment” was made to a female employee who is alleged to have been in a relationship with Infantino while he was the organisation’s general secretary – allegations Fifa dismissed as “categorically untrue”.The Daily Telegraph reported on Friday night that the woman received a six-figure sum following the alleged relationship with Infantino. In a statement, Uefa confirmed a payment was made along with covering the fees for an MBA course, which it said was “in line” with regulations at the time.Fifa told the Telegraph that “any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory”, and late on Saturday issued a new, broader statement attacking Infantino’s critics.A Fifa spokesperson said: “The Fifa president was democratically elected by Fifa’s member associations and continues to serve with their mandate. It is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president.“Those who do not have the support of Fifa’s member associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through Fifa’s established democratic processes. Recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning Fifa and its president. Speculation and insinuation should not be presented as fact, and repetition does not make an allegation true.”Two weeks that rocked Fifa: how Gianni Infantino unravelled, day by dayRead moreDefending Infantino as a leader who has “dedicated more than 30 years of his professional life to European and world football”, the statement added: “Fifa welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to distort facts, amplify unsubstantiated allegations or manufacture distractions designed to undermine progress.“Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading, Fifa will challenge it directly and vigorously. Fifa’s responsibility is to its 211 member associations and to football around the world. We will not be distracted or diverted from strengthening the organisation, delivering for our member associations and continuing the work of making football truly global.”Pressure has continued to mount on Infantino after theexposure and collapse of his planto seek private investment in a company which would run Fifa’s competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cups. Fifa has said it will not accept any challenge to Infantino’s position before the election next March.Uefa’s threat that its 55 member countries could boycott Fifa competitions remains in place, with the European confederation saying on Thursday that the withdrawal of the scheme “changes nothing”.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Navy says it is spending 25% more time monitoring Russian vessels around UK waters | Royal Navy | The Guardian
description: Warning of increased activity as patrols spent 21 days in July shadowing Moscow’s ships in Dover Strait and North Sea
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Warning of increased activity as patrols spent 21 days in July shadowing Moscow’s ships in Dover Strait and North Sea
Content: HMS Mersey tracking the Russian Admiral Grigorovich frigate.Photograph: UK MOD Crown copyright/Royal Navy/ReutersView image in fullscreenHMS Mersey tracking the Russian Admiral Grigorovich frigate.Photograph: UK MOD Crown copyright/Royal Navy/ReutersRoyal NavyNavy says it is spending 25% more time monitoring Russian vessels around UK watersWarning of increased activity as patrols spent 21 days in July shadowing Moscow’s ships in Dover Strait and North SeaNadeem Badshahand PA MediaSat 8 Aug 2026 16.03 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 16.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheRoyal Navyhas warned of increasing Russian activity around the UK’s waters after it spent 21 days in July monitoring Moscow’s ships.Naval operations to monitor Russian vessels increased by 25% last month compared with the previous year, with warships making repeated voyages through the strait of Dover and the North Sea.Offshore patrol vessels HMS Tyne, HMS Mersey and HMS Severn, alongside Wildcat helicopters from 815 Naval Air Squadron and Merlin submarine-hunting aircraft, were deployed throughout the month to shadow Russian frigates Neustrashimy and Admiral Grigorovich, which are tasked with escorting so-called “shadow fleet” tankers.Last month, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in its annual report that Royal Navy vessels had been “activated” 116 times in the year to March 2026, shadowing 61 Russian warships and 28 merchant vessels around the UK’s waters.This reflected a 30% increase in Russian naval activity over the previous two years and included operations to deter the spy ship Yantar, which was spotted near undersea cables off Scotland last November.Vladimir Putin has been accused of using the Kremlin’s shadow fleet of ageing vessels to evade international sanctions on its oil and fund the war in Ukraine.The increase in Russian naval activity follows theseizure of the tanker Smyrtosby Royal Marines in June, the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel.The MoD said the diversion of ships from Russia to escort shadow fleet vessels meant the country was “using up valuable operational capacity to constantly guard cargo”.The UK has already imposed sanctions on more than 500 vessels, and Russia’s oil and gas revenues fell by 24% year on year in 2025.HMS Tyne was also tasked with monitoring the Neustrashimy as it carried out a live-firing exercise outside British and French waters on 20 July.Another ship, the frigate HMS Somerset, has been involved in monitoring Russian activity in the North Atlantic as part of a four-month Nato deployment searching for submarines, alongside helicopters from the Navy’s Fleet Air Arm.Somerset’s commanding officer, Cmdr Matt Millyard, said on Saturday: “This deployment demonstrates exactly what the Royal Navy exists to do: protect the UK and our allies from wherever our interests are threatened.“I am immensely proud of every single member of the ship’s company for what we have achieved over the past four months.”Explore more on these topicsRoyal NavyMilitaryRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Scratch of the day: local football season postponed due to ‘rock hard’ pitches | Drought | The Guardian
description: Drought and record heat have forced the Norfolk and Suffolk league to move kick-off to the end of August as the ground is deemed too dangerous to play on
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Drought and record heat have forced the Norfolk and Suffolk league to move kick-off to the end of August as the ground is deemed too dangerous to play on
Content: Dried-out football pitches can be found across all England after high temperatures and no rain.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAView image in fullscreenDried-out football pitches can be found across all England after high temperatures and no rain.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PADroughtScratch of the day: local football season postponed due to ‘rock hard’ pitchesDrought and record heat have forced the Norfolk and Suffolk league to move kick-off to the end of August as the ground is deemed too dangerous to play onMatthew WeaverSat 8 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis summer’s record drought has forced a football league to delay the start of its season because “rock hard” pitches are a danger to its players.The 2026/27 season in the Anglian Combination League of 85 amateur teams in Norfolk andSuffolkwas due to start next weekend.But on Friday after an urgent meeting, theleague’s board announcedit had unanimously decided to postpone the start of the season until the end of August, because most of the clubs’ pitches are dried out and too dangerous to play on.It said a number of pre-season friendlies have had to be cancelled because of the drought and matches that have gone ahead have led to “many injuries”.In a statement addressed to all leagues clubs, players and officials, it confirmed the start of the season will be delayed until 29 August.“The rationale behind this decision is to protect the welfare of players, officials and all associated with the match day, in what has been the driest and hottest July since records began in 1836,” the league chair, Dale Brown, said in the statement. “Most of our league clubs pitches are grass and the ground conditions are extremely dry and pitches rock hard.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEurope’s dry riverbeds and scorched earth – in picturesRead moreBrown added: “This was a very difficult decision to reach and one that will not please all clubs.”The league’s decision comes after a series of record-breaking heat waves and exceptionally low rainfall have left much of England and Wales visibly parched and the ground as hard as concrete.Record temperatures were experienced in May and June, andJuly was the driest month since records began. A drought was declared inhalf of England last monthwith many water companies imposing hosepipe bans. Such a ban by Anglian Water which covers Norfolk and Suffolk, has been in force since 11 July.Aerial images have shown dried out parks and sports fields devoid of any signs of green, with the exception of golf clubs, some sports clubs, and private schools who enjoycontroversial exemptions from hosepipe bans.The Met Office forecasts another heatwave next week, with temperatures set to reach 36C in parts of East Anglia and south-east England by next Thursday. There is no sign of much-needed rain, although humidity is expected to increase next week.The FA does not hold figures on the number of leagues that have been forced to postpone the start of next season because of the drought. It said it was a matter of individual leagues and county football associations.Explore more on these topicsDroughtUK weatherNorfolkSuffolkClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hunter Biden talks about how his father’s cancer has spread and is causing him pain | Joe Biden | The Guardian
description: Joe Biden’s prostate cancer is reportedly ‘debilitating’, even as ex-president continues to speak out on public issues
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Joe Biden’s prostate cancer is reportedly ‘debilitating’, even as ex-president continues to speak out on public issues
