Content: Then president Joe Biden and his son Hunter embrace in the Oval Office of the White House on 24 July 2024.Photograph: Evan Vucci/EPAView image in fullscreenThen president Joe Biden and his son Hunter embrace in the Oval Office of the White House on 24 July 2024.Photograph: Evan Vucci/EPAJoe BidenHunter Biden talks about how his father’s cancer has spread and is causing him painJoe Biden’s prostate cancer is reportedly ‘debilitating’, even as ex-president continues to speak out on public issuesStaff and agenciesSat 8 Aug 2026 15.17 EDTFirst published on Sat 8 Aug 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormer US presidentJoe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread to other parts of his body and is causing him pain, even as he continues to speak out on public issues, his sonHuntersaid in an interview.In a wide-ranging interview with the BBC broadcast late on Friday,Hunter Bidengrew emotional as he discussed his father’s condition, describing it as very sad to watch.“The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further,” he said. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects.”Joe Biden appears to discuss sensitive information on tape with ghostwriterRead moreJoe Biden, 83, was the oldest man to serve as US president and his age was a source of concern for much of his four years in office. He and his White House advisers have faced intense criticism for allegedly concealing the extent of his health issues, especially after he was forced to abandon his bid for re-election after a disastrous debate with his eventual successor, Donald Trump.The former president revealed his cancer diagnosis in May of last year, less than four months after he left the White House.Hunter Biden said the diagnosis had been tough on the family.“It’s really sad to watch,” Biden said. “The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good.”But Biden said his father remains “out there”, speaking publicly about the issues that are important to him.“He’s still doing his thing,” he said. “He so believes in this country.”Biden also expressed gratitude for the pardon his father granted him because if he had not, Trump would have sought retribution against him, he said. But he also acknowledged that it was not good for the former president’s legacy or the American people.“It is something that is easily criticized and for good reason,” Biden said. “All I know is that I’m grateful he did it for me, and all I can say to anybody out there is, what would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me?”Joe Biden will publish a memoir, Promise Me, America, after the midterm elections.The Associated Press contributedreportingExplore more on these topicsJoe BidenHunter BidenCancerUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI to pause some work on AI model Astra due to security concerns | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Agent found to be able to find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, and to carry out cyber-attacks
Author: Eric Berger
Headline: Agent found to be able to find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, and to carry out cyber-attacks
Content: ‘The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them.’Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them.’Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAI to pause some work on AI model Astra due to security concernsAgent found to be able to find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, and to carry out cyber-attacksEric BergerSat 8 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTFirst published on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI will pausesomework on an artificial intelligence model because of security concerns, the company stated on Friday, following a series of incidents in which AI agents have escaped containment.The company had evaluated the agent, Astra, and found “significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity”, which had moved to a “critical” threshold where it can find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, or devise and execute cyber-attacks when given only a “high level desired goal”.OpenAI stated that the model was not involved in an incident in which one of its AI agentswent rogueduring a test, accessed the open web and hacked a startup, Hugging Face. The company discovered other instances in which autonomous agents had escaped containment,Reuters reportedin July.Google DeepMind enters a new era as co-founder Demis Hassabis shifts AI roleRead moreThe reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them. Still, critics of the AI industryhave warnedthat such disclosures from OpenAI and its competitors Anthropic and Meta could be designed to generate hype about the technology’s power and thus spur additional interest from investors.To prevent potential rogue behavior from AI agents,OpenAIis “implementing stricter security controls for higher-capability models and associated activities, including isolated testing environments, restricted network and tool access”, the company’s blogpost stated. It will also install “enhanced model weight protections and encryption, additional monitoring and detection capabilities”.The company will pause internal activities involving Astra that do not meet these new requirements.“We’re committed to working alongside governments, safety institutes, and civil society to ensure that the frontier capabilities of models like Astra, and those that follow, are deployed responsibly and broadly for the benefit of all humanity,” the company stated.Metaalso disclosedthis week that one of its models hacked another company during cybersecurity testing. And the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) announced on 4 August that agents powered by OpenAI and Anthropic had senttargeted emailsto software developers in an attempt to pass a cyber challenge.“These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world,” theinstitute statedin a blogpost.The organisation cautioned that the models’ sending of harmful software was not a case of a “model escaping its secure test environment” but rather that the group had intentionally permitted internet access to “best assess the maximum capability of models”.Still, the “behaviour was possible, sustained and new; that alone warrants attention”, the AISI said.The reports emerged while the Trump administrationwas finalizinga framework on how to test AI models for safety and cybersecurity risks. OpenAI and Anthropic, which have increased competition from China and other tech firms, have argued that open-source models, meaning those that allow anyone to see and modify the underlying program code, pose asecurity riskand pushed for additional federal regulations on them.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAInewsShareReuse this content

title: Train operators to crack down on ‘donutters’ and other digital ticket cheats | Rail fares | The Guardian
description: South Western and GTR announce fightback after move away from paper tickets increases fare dodging
Author: Esther Addley
Headline: South Western and GTR announce fightback after move away from paper tickets increases fare dodging
Content: ‘Short-faring’ is a trick by which passengers buy a last-minute digital ticket only for the final part of their journey so they can exit barriers.Photograph: Ashley Cooper pics/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Short-faring’ is a trick by which passengers buy a last-minute digital ticket only for the final part of their journey so they can exit barriers.Photograph: Ashley Cooper pics/AlamyRail faresTrain operators to crack down on ‘donutters’ and other digital ticket cheatsSouth Western and GTR announce fightback after move away from paper tickets increases fare dodgingEsther AddleySat 8 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 06.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is more than one way to commit fraud and, for some rail travellers, it has been as simple as a couple of taps on their phone as their train approaches its destination.That telltale last-minute purchase of a digital ticket – for the shortest journey that will allow them to bleep through the gates, regardless of how far they have travelled – is one of a number of illegal wheezes that train operators are trying to eliminate, with the enthusiastic backing of the government department that will directly oversee most of England’s rail services when they are renationalised next year.View image in fullscreenDeanna Smith (left) said fare dodging was ‘just like tax dodging – we all fall victim to their behaviour’. Pictured with Daniel Pizarro.Photograph: Andrew Hasson/The GuardianTwo rail companies, South Western Railway (SWR) and GTR, which operates Thameslink, Southern and other services, this week introduced measures to clamp down on “short-faring” – a trick by which passengers buy a last-minute digital ticket only for the final part of their journey, even if they boarded in a station without barriers much further away.Don’t bother trying to download a digital ticket from Vauxhall to Waterloo, the terminus for many trains to London from the west – or on a number of other routes, apparently including from Norwood Junction to London Bridge, where many services from the south coast hit the capital. For those and some other routes, you will now need to collect a physical ticket from a physical ticket machine, after operators found that up to 95% of tickets on some short routes were being used fraudulently.Fare evasion on Britain’s railways did not begin with digitisation – you don’t need a QR code to vault a barrier or hide in the toilet from a ticket inspector. But the increasing reliance on digital ticketing has widened some of the loopholes for those minded to cheat – and added to an ever-growing problem for train companies.View image in fullscreenKatie Bell and Nicola Garrett. Garrett said she was annoyed by fare dodging.Photograph: Andrew Hasson/The GuardianUp to £400m is lost to fraud each year on the rail network, according to the Department for Transport, through high-tech and decidedly low-tech methods. As well as short-faring, operators point to “quick scanning” (buying a ticket on your phone seconds before being approached by an inspector), “tailgating” (squeezing behind a paying customer as they pass through a ticket gate) and “donutting”, a scam by which a passenger buys a cheap ticket covering the first part of their journey and another covering the last, but avoids paying the higher cost of the full trip. A former senior executive at HSBC, Joseph Molloy,received a suspended sentenceearlier this year for using this technique 740 times to commute between Orpington in Kent and London Bridge, saving him £5,911 over 11 months.“It’s quite a big problem, because we’re coming to terms with a completely different form of ticketing,” said therailway commentator and authorChristian Wolmar. “No longer do you go to the ticket office and buy little red and yellow cards. You now buy online, and that affords these new opportunities. The system is clearly open to abuse.”Though a push to reduce staff numbers has been a factor, he says, “how you tackle this is very difficult because you can’t have guards at every stop. It’s through digital analysis that they are going to find a solution to this.”The government appears to agree, widening the introduction earlier this month ofan app that calculates ticket faresby tracking the user’s phone. While currently being trialled on a number of routes in the East Midlands and Yorkshire, the technology could eventually be brought in acrossGreat British Railways, the public body that will take over the running of the soon-to-be renationalised network, expected to be up and running next year.“Fare evasion is illegal and selfish – it actively makes journeys worse for all rail passengers by diverting money that could otherwise be used to improve services,” said the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander. “We are committed to tackling ticket cheats, and that’s one of the expected benefits of expanding our digital ticketing app to more people across the trial areas.”Her department has also recently given £33m for new or enhanced ticket gates at “fare dodger hotspots” across England, and hasclosed a loopholethat allowed some passengers to dishonestly claim a refund even though they had used a service.SWR said its introduction of new anti-fraud measures came after one intervention at Brighton station found that half of those travelling on the wrong ticket were using the short-faring scam.To passengers disembarking at the station on Friday morning, a clampdown on cheats was very welcome. “Obviously fares go up anyway because of inflation, but they are probably pushing up our fares as well, so we all suffer,” said Deanna Smith, who had travelled on Thameslink with her partner to visit a coffee festival. “It’s just like tax dodging – we all fall victim to their behaviour.”Nicola Garrett, who was on a day trip to Brighton with a friend from her home town of Leigh-on-Sea, said: “I’m someone who has always paid for everything, so I get a bit pissed off [by fare dodging]. Nobody seems to think that they have to pay for anything these days. It’s just like, if you can get away with doing it, why wouldn’t you?”Explore more on these topicsRail faresRail industryRail transportTransportConsumer affairsTransport policyEnglandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Britain’s Jurassic gold rush: the fossil hunters chasing fortunes on Dorset’s beaches | Fossils | The Guardian
description: Social media and soaring prices are fuelling a fossil-hunting boom, with rare discoveries worth thousands of pounds
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Social media and soaring prices are fuelling a fossil-hunting boom, with rare discoveries worth thousands of pounds
Content: Searching for fossils on Dorset beachFossilsBritain’s Jurassic gold rush: the fossil hunters chasing fortunes on Dorset’s beachesSocial media and soaring prices are fuelling a fossil-hunting boom, with rare discoveries worth thousands of poundsNicola DavisScience correspondentSat 8 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBent double at the waist, Martin Curtis combs a stretch of aDorsetbeach with the concentration of a man searching for a lost cufflink or wedding ring.The search is meticulous – and with good reason. What he hopes to find could be far more valuable than an errant piece of jewellery. Curtis is searching instead for the telltale spiral of an ammonite, the star-shaped rod of a crinoid or rocks of a particular shape and colour that suggests there is something very special inside. He is hunting fossils.Along Charmouth beach and elsewhere on the Jurassic Coast, families with children, seasoned collectors and lone day-trippers peer intently at the ground in search of traces of creatures that lived 190m years ago. While some are here for fun, a growing number are here for business.View image in fullscreenA selection ofCurtis’s discoveries.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianThat growing professional interest reflects the rising popularity and value of Jurassic fossils, creating a thriving marketplace that has made some collectors social media celebrities and others very wealthy.A Guardian investigation this week revealed that one of Britain’s most significant collections of Jurassic fossils was recentlysold to a museum in Abu Dhabifor what is believed to be an eight-figure sum.One of UK’s best fossil collections sold overseas in ‘loss to the nation’Read moreThe collection, amassed by the private fossil collector Chris Moore, included 318 specimens, some of which may represent species previously unknown to science. The sale was described by some experts as a loss for the nation.Yet while British museums lacked the funds to acquire Moore’s collection, wealthy institutions in the Gulf did not. For the fossil hunters combing Charmouth beach, it is another reason to scrutinise every promising item of unusual shape, colour and texture.Fossil hunting – and the industry that has grown around it – is not a modern pursuit. Perhaps England’s best-known fossil hunter and dealer, Mary Anning, was born at nearby Lyme Regis in 1799 and madebreathtaking discoveries along this coastline, including the first complete plesiosaur skeleton – a huge long-necked marine reptile that lived during the Jurassic period before becomingextinct alongside most dinosaurs 66m years ago.View image in fullscreenMartin Curtis searching the coastline for fossils. He later spots a 190m-year-old belemnite.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianAnning has not been forgotten. Her name and image are everywhere, from information boards along the seafront to the colourful Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre overlooking the beach. Here, fossil collecting is largely encouraged.“On the rapidly eroding West Dorset coast, fossil collecting is essential if specimens, some of which may be of great scientific value, are to be saved from damage or destruction by the sea,” notes the West Dorset fossil collecting code of conduct.View image in fullscreenFossil hunting is a popular pastime on the Jurassic Coast, with some discoveries showing up on social media.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianAnd just as Anning sold many of her discoveries, fossils are still bought and sold today. Downstairs is a shop where small ammonites can be picked up for a few pounds, while larger specimens, painstakingly prepared within their surrounding rock, sell for several hundred. Provided hunters follow the code of conduct, ownership of fossils passes to the finder.“Professional collectors have the most time, are able to react quickly to events that uncover the fossils – ie: storms and landslides – and have a great deal of local knowledge. But they need to sell their finds in order to earn a living,” the code notes.It is easy to understand how fossil hunting becomes addictive. As we comb the beach, Curtis points to a smooth, brown, bullet-shaped object: the fossilised remains of a squid-like creature known as a belemnite.“That belemnite’s 190m years old. And we are the only three people to ever see that creature,” he says.View image in fullscreenMartin Curtis: ‘I spent a lot of my childhood on the beach with my father.’Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianA little later, I spot a sparkling curve nestled among the pebbles and prise out a tiny ammonite, glittering with iron pyrite. It is the size of a penny and, though it is probably worth very little, I feel as if I have won the lottery.As a professional guide and fossil hunter, Curtis knows these beaches intimately. “I spent a lot of my childhood on the beach with my father, finding fossils a bit further down the coast that way in Kimmeridge,” he says.As an adult, he returned to the coastline while caring for his eldest daughter. “I could take her out on the beach, walk along for two hours looking for fossils [while she was] fast asleep in the backpack,” he says.View image in fullscreenCharmouth beach’s unique geological and natural factors make it an ideal place to find fossils.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianHe later turned his hobby into a business, using his mountain leader qualifications to run guided fossil walks and selling specimens he has painstakingly revealed from the surrounding rock using air chisels and iron-powder air abrasion.“I’m a big ammonite fan. They are my favourite fossils, and I’ve got loads of rocks at home with some really nice big special ammonites in, waiting to be prepared,” he says.Progressing along the beach, we pass the remnants of huge mudslides, where it is clear there are many for whom fossil collecting is a more than a casual pastime. Hammers are swung, chunks of sticky mud broken apart and carefully examined. This is fossil hunting in earnest.Curtis says TikTok and Instagram have transformed the activity in recent years. Social media is awash with videos of fossil hunters cracking open rocks on Britain’s beaches.View image in fullscreenCurtis says Covid staycations fuelled a rise in fossil hunting.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian“It’s really changed the scope of fossil hunting down here. It’s now making it a lot harder because it’s introducing a lot more people to fossil hunting. I’ve been running walks here for 10 years now and the change [during that time] is quite significant,” he says, adding that the influx of fossil hunters during Covid staycations accelerated the trend.Curtis believes parts of the coastline are being over-collected. “The erosion rate is struggling to keep up with the amount of people on the beach, because of the conditions,” he says, noting that fresh material is not being exposed quickly enough. And when new material does appear, word spreads quickly on social media. “So even on a[good day], there’s going to be twice as many people here.”View image in fullscreenSome fossil hunters have amassed impressive collections, with specimens displayed in UK museums and beyond.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianCompetition among professional fossil hunters is intense, with experts keeping an eye on one another as they inspect new falls and vie for the finest discoveries. It is perhaps not surprising that rare finds or beautifully prepared specimens can command substantial sums.“As fossil hunters, [when] we come to the beach, we are collecting to try to earn money. Maybe selling a few bits … online. But generally, we are collecting for ourselves. And if we find anything good, we keep it,” Curtis says.Some fossil hunters have amassed remarkable collections. Figures such as Moore have become big names in the fossil-hunting world, with his specimens displayed in museums locally and beyond, and counting David Attenborough among his friends.View image in fullscreenFossils for sale in the local shop.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianThe recent sale has cemented Moore’s status as one of the Jurassic Coast’s leading collectors. But his collection is unlikely to be the last to leave Britain. As the country’s professional fossil hunters grow older,more private collections are likely to be in need of new homes.Perhaps unsurprisingly for a man used to handling relics from millennia gone-by, Curtis is philosophical about his friend’s collection being sold overseas. “It’s always sad when things like that go abroad” said Curtis, adding that Moore had worked hard on his collection. “The key thing is it’s being enjoyed by someone,” he said. “It’s all well and good having a good collection, but it’s no good stuck in a box somewhere.”There is a striking irony here. The remains of creatures that have been hidden in these shores for 190m years are now being sold to countries whose modern wealth is derived from plumbing their own oily depths.Yet down on the beach in Dorset, the international marketplace feels a long way away. For Curtis, size isn’t everything – it’s all about the next swirl in the sand. “[A discovery] doesn’t have to be big. It just generally needs to be special. And the more you get into fossil hunting, the fussier you become,” he says.Explore more on these topicsFossilsBiologyEvolutionDorsetEnglandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The night Belfast burned: how the Northern Ireland race riots unfolded  | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: A stabbing in June sparked another summer’s night of racial violence, stoked by loyalist groups. How did the unrest erupt – and why do many fear it will happen again?
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: A stabbing in June sparked another summer’s night of racial violence, stoked by loyalist groups. How did the unrest erupt – and why do many fear it will happen again?
Content: Cars and homes set on fire during protests in BelfastNorthern IrelandThe night Belfast burned: how the Northern Ireland race riots unfoldedA horrific knife attack on a street in June sparked another summer’s night of racial violence, stoked by loyalist groups. How did the unrest erupt – and why do many fear it will happen again?Hannah Al-OthmanandRory Carrollin BelfastSat 8 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 04.28 EDTShareShortly after 10.30pm on Monday 8 June, as a summer twilight lingered overBelfast, a horrific scene unfolded on Kinnaird Avenue: a man straddled and repeatedly stabbed a figure lying on the ground in a bloody assault that ended only after onlookers intervened.Others captured the drama on cameraphones and uploaded the footage to social media. Once seen, the grainy images were hard to forget, and by dawn on Tuesday 9 June they were ricocheting around X, WhatsApp, Facebook, Telegram and other platforms.Many commentators highlighted one aspect: the assailant was black, the victim white.Police had a suspect in custody – he was initially identified as a refugee from Somalia, later corrected to Sudan – but this did not stem a cascade of outrage. What, commentators demanded to know, about other foreign men of “military age” inNorthern Ireland? Had they been “vetted”? What “alien culture” had they imported?0:41Bus set on fire as disorder flares up in Belfast – videoBy 9.30am a message – an exhortation – was being widely shared. “All business to close at 5.30pm tonight. No excuses.” It listed 25 locations around Northern Ireland for people to gather at 7pm. “Please forward [to] all men of the age of 18 and over. Wear dark clothing … and be prepared to fight or be arrested.”It was an invitation to a pogrom.Far-right agitators, such as Elon Musk and Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known by his alias Tommy Robinson, amplified calls to protest, and those interventions were prominent in the coverage that followed.Through a combination of interviews with witnesses and people who responded to the unrest, on-the-ground reporting in loyalist strongholds and at far-right rallies in Northern Ireland, and analysis of messages sent by figures connected to the extreme right, the Guardian has established the most complete picture yet of how a single incident of horrific violence precipitated the crisis. And it suggests that organisers in Belfast needed no encouragement or direction. This was their show.Drawing onprevious eruptions of violence– this was to be the third consecutive summer of racial disturbances in Northern Ireland – the organisers issued further instructions: leave mobile phones at home and deactivate dashcams and doorbell cameras.A map locating the Belfast attackBy early afternoon, schools were sending children home, public transport was halting and steel shutters were clanging down over foreign-owned barber shops, supermarkets and other businesses.As families sat down for dinner, crowds gathered at designated roundabouts and intersections in loyalist areas across the city.At about 7.30pm a woman with a megaphone on the Shankill Road recited the Lord’s Prayer to several hundred people, some draped in union flags. They marched through terraced sidestreets and halted outside the home of a Romanian family. A nearby Black family, anticipating trouble, had already fled and asked neighbours to move their car.The Romanian family’s windows had been “put out” twice before, but the family had refused to leave. The previous night’s stabbing had nothing to do with the Romanians but somehow alchemised into what one woman in the crowd called “the last straw”.Dozens of boys and men wearing hoods and masks surged forward. Some launched bricks through windows, others shoved fireworks through the letterbox. A woman inside, visible to the crowd, watched helplessly as her home came under attack. The family’s car went up in flames, then men in balaclavas broke down the door.Women and children in the mob observed proceedings. “There’s wee girls inside,” said one. In contrast to race riots in England and Belfast in 2024, and inBallymena last year, the violence was not recorded or streamed on mobile phones. A teenage boy who ignored the injunction against filming was dragged aside and chastised.Similar scenes played out across Belfast. In the east of the city, families from Ukraine, Romania, Poland and Sudan left. Properties and vehicles, including a Glider bus, were set ablaze and plumes of smoke rose into the night.1:00Cleanup footage shows aftermath of Belfast anti-immigration violence – videoOn arterial roads and by roundabouts, crowds lit bins and set up roadblocks to question and intimidate suspected foreigners. In Sandy Row, central Belfast, Ethiopian and Chinese residents fled and arsonists burned a Syrian supermarket. On Crumlin Road, in the west, Ugandan health workers and Nigerian families sought refuge. In some places the police were absent or stayed back and it was left to community volunteers to navigate the mobs and escort families to safety.At around 10pm the violence abated and crowds began to disperse. Some whooped in jubilation, others surveyed the smouldering debris with satisfaction. A point, they said, had been made. Rain began to fall, helping emergency crews to douse the embers of gutted homes and vehicles.View image in fullscreenA couple stand outside a house as a vehicle burns on McMaster Street, in east Belfast.Photograph: PANew loyalismThe riot should not have come as a surprise. Northern Ireland was primed for it. “We could see it coming,” said Daniel Holder, the director of the Committee on the Administration of Justice (CAJ), a Belfast-based advocacy group. “It wasn’t unprecedented, it was an escalation of an existing pattern.”An escalation, and a learning curve. Drawing on lessons from 2024 and 2025, the agitators refined their methods to hit more targets and reduce the chance of arrest.Far-right allies in England and the US were taking notes. Enrique Tarrio, the former head of the militant US group Proud Boys, recently visited and interviewed activists for a documentary. And last month, the Advance UK-affiliated YouTuber Sarah White was streaming multiple events in Northern Ireland, including an Orange Order march and an anti-migrant protest in Portrush.The Northern Ireland “model” is not necessarily transferable. It has taken a unique mix – the legacy of the Troubles, xenophobia, social media platforms and state acquiescence – to create the toxic climate.Damage to homes, cars and public transport after Belfast riotsUntil the 1998 Good Friday agreement the region was almost entirely white and native-born. As sectarian violence eased, immigrants trickled in. By the 2021 census, 3.4% of the population was from a minority ethnic background – small compared with 19% in England, but the sight of people from Africa, Asia and the Middle East still came as a jolt.Many immigrants settled in working-class loyalist areas where the population was declining, property was cheaper – and paramilitary groups endured. Despite a state-sponsored “transitioning” process, the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) and Ulster Defence Association (UDA) split into sub-groups that continued to deal drugs and coercively control communities.View image in fullscreenA man is escorted from his home in Belfast after rioters set fire to cars and buildings.Photograph: PA“Peace” walls between Catholic and Protestant neighbourhoods still stand, underlining the persistence of traditional sectarian divisions, but the waning IRA threat weakened loyalist paramilitaries’ claims to be community defenders, prompting them toseek a new bogeyman to justify their existence.“Loyalism has always been a reactionary ideology based on keeping out ‘foreign’ influence,” said Stephen Millar, an academic and author of Performing Paramilitarism: Loyalist Songs, Conflict, and Culture War in Northern Ireland. “The pivot from [opposing] Irish nationalism to anti-migrant rhetoric is, to some extent, internally consistent, and serves to keep loyalism ‘relevant’, trading one form of racism for another.”Sporadic attacks and harassment against minority ethnic families – paint bombs, smashed windows, “locals only” graffiti, threatening posters – have proliferated over the past decade, especially in County Antrim, where healthcare workers from Africa were among those targeted.That turned out to be the warm-up for afull-scale riot in BelfastinAugust 2024 – a copycat response to mayhem in England after the killing of three girls in Southport. Then in June 2025,Ballymena, 25 miles outside Belfast, eruptedafter two Roma teenagers were charged with rape (the charges were later dropped).View image in fullscreenProtesters wore masks and hoods to obscure their identities.Photograph: Peter Morrison/APJune’s eruption completed a grim summer hat-trick.Jon Boutcher, the chief constable of thePoliceService Northern Ireland (PSNI), said the overall picture of paramilitary involvement in the most recent trouble was “inconsistent” but that paramilitaries were present.However, many say the police have been slow to recognise, at least in public, the role of paramilitary groups in controlling the violence. Holder said: “To anyone on the ground, that was very obvious from the start.”The UDA and UVF are fractured. Some factions urged restraint – that is partly credited with keeping Ballymena calm this summer – but independent observers say other factions orchestrated much of the violence. Firefighters had no doubt about paramilitary influence and sought permission from their leaders before tackling blazes, sources said.The ferrying of teenagers to and from flashpoints was further evidence of orchestration, said Chris Quinn, Northern Ireland’s children’s commissioner. “There’s been a long history of child criminal coercion and child criminal exploitation.”Such children should not escape legal consequences but they too were victims, said Quinn. Some heeded the call to riot to service debts, including drug debts, he said. Another source, a youth worker, said paramilitary groups paid boys £100 to join the rioting.View image in fullscreenAI-generated anti-Islam murals in Newtownabbey.Photograph: Paul Faith/The GuardianInstead of Catholics, it was now people of colour in the crosshairs of loyalist groups, said Michaela Rafferty, of Anaka, a women’s group that helped escort besieged families to safety. “There has been a sectarian element, obviously, through our years of Troubles and violence. Now that focus has kind of moved to brown and black people.”AI-generated anti-Islam murals have appeared in loyalist strongholds such as Moygashel and Newtownabbey. “Islam is Heathen, Islam is Satanic — A New Evil Has Arisen,” says one, “Not welcome, not wanted, not here,” says another.New methodsAgitators have refined their methods. Most rioters in Ballymena last year wore masks or hoods but footage uploaded by participants and onlookers helped police identify and charge dozens of rioters. The lesson was not lost on the recent rioters in Belfast – they banned filming and made greater efforts to conceal identifying details, such as tattoos.Through trial and error they also discovered that without a galvanising incident, such as a brutal crime allegedly committed by a foreigner, calls for mass mobilisation tended to flop, and this punctured morale.On the ground in the Belfast riots - podcastRead moreInstead, they set up online community groups and joined existing ones to drip-feed anti-foreigner sentiment, said Dessie Donnelly of rabble.coop, a Belfast-based tech cooperative that tracks online xenophobia. “Ballymena was a watershed. You had loads of groups springing up online and a far-right network emerging.”Before the most recent riot, posts about dark-skinned men in parks, and foreigners moving into houses of multiple occupation (HMO) on particular streets, proliferated. The tactic distilledIslamophobiato a hyper-local level, said Donnelly. “It prepares people for when there is an animating event.”Activists in Belfast, Bangor, Coleraine, Derry, Newtownabbey, Portadown and other towns formed online “clusters” that shared and amplified posts and infiltrated online forums for loyalist bonfires and marching bands, said a researcher with Accountability Project Northern Ireland, a group that monitors online hate.Last summer, the watchdog noticed that a Portadown-based Facebook group was circulating ascreenshot of council-owned HMO properties– a ready-made hitlist of addresses that rioters used in June.1:36Belfast protests: police use water cannons against rioters in Northern Ireland - videoBurgeoning attacks – in the year to 31 March, police recorded 2,367 race incidents and 1,507 race crimes, the highest on record – created a sense of foreboding as summer approached, said Naomi Green, the Northern Ireland-based assistant secretary general of the Muslim Council of Britain (MCB). “We thought it was going to get quite scary very quickly, and it did.”A week before the riot, anti-racism organisations convened an emergency meeting in Belfast because they feared trouble, said Holder. The marching season loomed and there was “a huge buildup” of racist activism on- and offline, he said. “For a third successive summer, it was waiting on an excuse.”The attack at Kinnaird Avenue provided the spark. For foreigners who had been previously targeted there was a sense of inevitability, on the afternoon of 9 June, to what came next. “We’ve been sharing the same messages all day: go home early, stay inside, don’t go out,” Mohammed Mahmoud, 39, said as a crowd gathered near his Sandy Row grocery store.The aftermathThe violence that night gave way to an eerie calm the next day. Central Belfast was like a ghost town, with most businesses remaining shut in expectation of fresh strife. A familiar message duly began to circulate on social media. “All business to close … wear dark clothing.”View image in fullscreenTorched homes and vehicles the day after the riotsPhotograph: Charles McQuillan/Getty ImagesIn fact, Belfast remained largely quiet on the night of 10 June but in Glengormley, 7 miles north, a mob tried to march on the Chimney Corner hotel, which had been used to house asylum seekers, and fought against police in riot gear. The crowd hurled bricks and rocks, lit bonfires in the street and torched a vacant house. Police used water cannon and plastic bullets to drive them back.Around 11pm the violence dwindled and stopped, as if someone had turned off a tap. That was the last disturbance in June. But in some ways the aftermath has been just as troubling.In a poll by the thinktank More in Common, 8% of people in Northern Ireland said it was justified to burn migrants out of their homes and 11% agreed with intimidating them out of an area. Forty-one per cent said they sometimes feel like a stranger in their own country and three-quarters worry about asylum seekers entering Northern Ireland.Conleth Burns, the associate director and Ireland lead for More In Common, said polling in England showed similar results. “You’ve got a similar number of people in lots of societies who think that this level of violence against migrants is justified.”View image in fullscreenA United Against Racism rally in Belfast on 13 June.Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/ReutersNorthern Ireland, however, has far fewer foreigners and people of colour than England, which shows that even small numbers can have an outsized impact, said Burns. Most people expressed concern about immigration, racism and violence, he added. “People don’t see [those views] as being contradictory.”TheInstitute for Strategic Dialogue, which tracks extremism and misinformation, said the unrest turbo-charged far-right activism online. Posts that promoted claims of anti-white police bias surged to more than 200,000 in the first two weeks of June compared with 104,000 in the whole of May, it said in a report published this week.The main parties at Stormont strongly condemned the violence but critics say the executive failed to prepare for the crisis.“This was the third time in two years,” said Donnelly. “They should have known something would happen, it was building up.”Even though the Police Service of Northern Ireland had struggled to contain unrest in previous years it was still under-resourced, said Donnelly. “There was no acknowledgment that immigrants had been systematically attacked twice and that it would happen again.”Holder said Stormont’s response had downplayed the gravity of the crisis. “You’d expect a racist pogrom to be the key issue for the institutions to deal with over the summer, and putting in emergency measures to prevent that happening again. But no, there’s no sense of urgency.”Aerials from Belfast during anti-immigration protest following knife attack – watch liveLiz Griffith, the head of migration justice at the Northern Ireland Law Centre, said the devolved government had failed to update anti-racism legislation and downgraded a long-awaited policy document.The strategy now focused on “race relations”, which Griffith said was “a discredited term now; it is woefully out of date and has been out of date since the 1970s”.“It’s as if this was to do with somehow the relationships of people not getting on with each other,” Holder said. “That the people having the brick put through their window need to improve their relationship with those putting the brick through the window.”The Stormont executive had failed to bring forward hate crime and race equality laws in line with the rest of the UK.“The law in itself does not prevent racism but it’s the bedrock on which all your other initiatives rest,” Griffith said. “It’s been updated in England, Scotland and Wales, and ours is just antiquated. There’s constant talk of consultation after consultation to update this legislation, but it has just got stuck, it’s never moved.”In the face of this inaction, many want Andy Burnham, the new prime minister, to step in. “Unless Westminster intervenes at this point and ensures that there are protections, and legal protections, and consequences for some of this behaviour, unless there is some accountability here, it’s going to continue,” Green said.Many migrants and refugees think another eruption is likely but some try to remain optimistic. Suleiman Abdulahi, the founder and director of Horn of Africa People’s Aid Northern Ireland, has endured many attacks and reported 12 of them, most recently on 26 June. None have resulted in a prosecution but he did not wish to condemn his adopted home. “I’m not saying the Northern Ireland people – the majority – are racist. The majority are hospitable.”Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.
