title: ‘She’s the voice of a really particular moment’: how Phoebe Bridgers became her generation’s defining songwriter | Phoebe Bridgers | The Guardian
description: The US songwriter’s third album has drawn rave reviews, she counts Taylor Swift as a fan and pop bears the imprint of her wit and pathos. Her peers explain how she did it
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: The US songwriter’s third album has drawn rave reviews, she counts Taylor Swift as a fan and pop bears the imprint of her wit and pathos. Her peers explain how she did it
Content: ‘Her music is so precise and weird and beautiful’ … Phoebe Bridgers performing on The Tonight Show With Jimmy Fallon, 15 July 2026.Photograph: NBC/Todd Owyoung/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Her music is so precise and weird and beautiful’ … Phoebe Bridgers performing on The Tonight Show With Jimmy Fallon, 15 July 2026.Photograph: NBC/Todd Owyoung/Getty ImagesPhoebe Bridgers‘She’s the voice of a really particular moment’: how Phoebe Bridgers became her generation’s defining songwriterThe US songwriter’s third album has drawn rave reviews, she counts Taylor Swift as a fan and pop bears the imprint of her wit and pathos. Her peers explain how she did itKatie HawthorneSat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis week, indie star Phoebe Bridgers releases her long-awaited third album, six years since her pandemic-era breakthrough. Alongside a slew of glittering reviews for Lost Weekend, includingfive stars from the Guardian, with it comes her first solo charting single in the UK – although the Californian musician’s influence runs far deeper than reviews or record sales could measure. Just how did a RuneScape-referencing, Halloween-costumed Berklee drop-out become the most influential songwriter of the 2020s?Bridgers’ idiosyncratic writing has shaped the sound of the decade. Her second album Punisher, released in June 2020 (and recorded many months before), spookily anticipated that strange, lonely year: in her eerie double-tracked vocals (a nod to Bridgers’ musical hero, Elliott Smith), Bridgers sang of empty shopping malls and conspiracy theories over lush, unsettling music made from watery electric guitar, Mellotron, strings, screams and birdsong. Today, Bridgers’ distinctive mix of dry wit and pathos is traceable in the lyrics of pop’s new chart toppers, such as Olivia Rodrigo andGracie Abrams, while heavyweights across generations and genres, including Paul McCartney, Taylor Swift and SZA, have clamoured for collaborations. “Sheisthe reference now,” Swifttold the Guardian in 2022.“She’s the voice of a really particular moment,” says author Carmen Maria Machado, who first met Bridgers when she attended an event for Machado’s prize-winning memoirIn the Dream House. There is a kinship between Machado’s prose and Bridgers’ lyrics – both are candid, haunted, unafraid to get gruesome – and it resulted in Machado publishing a short story to accompany Punisher. “Phoebe’s never looking directly on, rather looking askance,” says Machado. “Her music is so precise and weird and beautiful; it’s a prayer or an ode to this place that we’re living in, while also watching it fall apart.”Phoebe Bridgers: Lost Boys – videoReviews for Lost Weekend have highlighted the album’s deeply personal subject matter – it discusses the death of Bridgers’ father, and the end of her engagement to actor Paul Mescal – but also Bridgers’ enduringly surreal sense of humour. When performing single Lost Boys on the Tonight Show, she played it first with a band of children, who were fizzing with excitement, and then again in an acoustic arrangement with veteran folk legend Dan Reeder. The effect was trippy, sweet and faintly morbid: distinctly Phoebe.For Naomi McPherson, a member of synth-pop three-piece Muna, it’s this mixture of matter-of-fact and magical that makes Bridgers so distinct. “It’s infuriating and inspiring how good she is,” McPherson says, pointing to a forthcoming Lost Weekend song with a line about turning down the stereo volume to better parallel park: “To be able to put that in a song in a way that isn’t stupid, but is actually brilliant and somehow deeply touching, is an enormous feat.”Muna signed to Bridgers’ record label Saddest Factory in 2021, joining a cohort of imaginative, predominantly queer musicians united under Bridgers’ mentality of “getting cool stuff out to people as fast as possible”. Singer-songwriter Claud (whose song A Good Thing soundtracked the finale to queer romance series Heartstopper) was the label’s first signee. They emphasise the value of Bridgers’ support at a vital time for both artists: “I knew I could trust her opinions and instincts for my project, because I love everything she does with hers.”The label was rolled into parent company Dead Oceans earlier this year after a trademark dispute, but its lasting influence reflects Bridgers’ determination to change the music industry for the better – as didher supergroup, Boygenius, formed with songwriter friends Lucy Dacus and Julien Baker. Together the trio played their biggest stages to date and clinched three Grammy awards, while Bridgers took the award ceremony as an opportunity to condemn former Recording Academy boss Neil Portnow, who had beenaccused of sexual assault, for his disparaging“step up”comment towards women in music: “Rot in piss!”View image in fullscreenFrom left: Bridgers, Lucy Dacus and Julien Baker of Boygenius accepting the award for best rock performance at the 2024 Grammy awards.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APBridgers’ plain-talking has won her a passionate fanbase, many of whom are easily spotted by their matching ghost tattoos – a reference to the cover of her 2017 debut Stranger in the Alps – and her concerts are intense: Claud, who has toured with Bridgers, describes “crowds of tens of thousands where you can actually hear a pin drop”. It tracks, then, that Bridgers decided to promote Lost Weekend not with sit-down interviews but a series of secretive pop-up shows across the US, taking the new songs straight to fans.‘We have to nurture each other’: how Olivia Rodrigo and Gen Z reinvented the power balladRead moreFan Baleigh Epperly, an environmental advocate, DJ and co-founder of queer, female-led local DJ collective Their House, “freaked out” when Bridgers rolled in to play at the Loud, a 500-capacity venue in her home town of Huntington, West Virginia. “We never get shit,” she laughs, saying it meant “everything” that Bridgers was visiting “the overlooked places, the places where she knows her fans are”.The tiny shows were first come, first served, capped at $50 a ticket, and mobile-phone free. Epperly says they all sat cross-legged, watching Bridgers play as if it were a house show. “It was the talk of the town, literally,” she marvels, predicting that the performance will have a lasting impact on young musicians who may have internalised damaging stereotypes about Appalachia: “If Phoebe is good enough for West Virginia, then you’re good enough to play here, to live here, to be from here.”Muna’s Katie Gavin describes Bridgers’ influence in similar terms. “She’s an aspirational songwriter for me. Seeing her make art makes me want to do it, which is what the best music does.”Explore more on these topicsPhoebe BridgersIndienewsShareReuse this content

title: Stretchy, supportive and completely chafe-free: the sportswear real people swear by | Fitness | The Guardian
description: From leggings that don’t roll down to bras that keep everything in, keen amateur cyclists, weightlifters and swimmers reveal the bits of kit they can’t do without
Author: Sarah Phillips
Headline: From leggings that don’t roll down to bras that keep everything in, keen amateur cyclists, weightlifters and swimmers reveal the bits of kit they can’t do without
Content: Lucy Law, Amy Smith and Sally Gulliford at a Zumba class in Bristol.View image in fullscreenLucy Law, Amy Smith and Sally Gulliford at a Zumba class in Bristol.FitnessStretchy, supportive and completely chafe-free: the sportswear real people swear byFrom leggings that don’t roll down to bras that keep everything in, keen amateur cyclists, weightlifters and swimmers reveal the bits of kit they can’t do withoutWords:Sarah Phillips. Portraits: Fabio De PaolaSat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.What is the perfect sports kit? That is the question we set out to answer, talking to sport and fitness enthusiasts all over the country. From Zumba dancers in Bristol to marathon runners in Leeds and gym bunnies in Thurrock, we asked different groups for the activewear they swear by and why it works for them.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Sea swimmers in Felixstowe had conflicting views about wetsuits, but all swore by brightly coloured tow floats and swim caps. Boxers in east London were united on the best kind of glove, but had different takes on clothing choices. Cyclists in the Wirral had differing levels of bike-collecting addiction, but agreed on the benefits of being Mamil (middle-aged men in Lycra).Finding the right kit is a matter of trial and error, and what is comfortable for one person can be sensory torture for another. Cost can also be an issue, but spending more doesn’t always equate to a better experience, as these interviews show.Above all, what is clear is that when you do find perfection, it can enhance how you feel about yourself when participating in any given sport. All that’s left to do iseither bulk buy or devise a very efficient washing system.Here is some inspiration to get you started …The Zumba dancersWhen Sally Gulliford first plucked up the courage to start going to Zumba in Bristol in 2019 with her daughter, she didn’t want to stand out. “I wore baggy clothes and stood at the back,” says Gulliford, 57, who is a civil servant and lives in the village of Backwell near the city.Amy Smith, who takes the class, reassured Gulliford that everyone would be focused on the instructor doing the moves at the front. The 38-year-old from Bristol had herself only recently regained the confidence to teach, and to wear tight-fitting workout clothes, having started leading classes after the birth of her two daughters. She decided her sessions would be held in a nightclub in the dark: “This creates an atmosphere where people not only feel like it’s a party, which it should be, but lose their inhibitions more. It is like a girls’ night out – we compare outfits and ask where things are from.” The clothing choices of attendees reflect this disco atmosphere. “I wear bright colours now,” Gulliford says. Her daughter still goes, too: “And borrows my gear.”“You want to completely submerge in the workout,” says Lucy Law, 35, a psychological therapist from Yeovil, who has been going to classes since 2024. This is why the right attire is key: “You don’t want to be worrying about your back fat or your side boobs, or anything rubbing.”With all the jiggling about, a sturdy bra is crucial; all the women agree thatM&S’s Goodmove ultimate support non-wired sports bra(worn by Smith and Gulliford, above centre and right,£15) is the best. The zip-front design ensures “you’re not going to fall out”, Gulliford says. Law also rates theF&F active zip-front high support sports bra(seen on her above left,£18), “because it’s so soft”.Gulliford saysZumba Wear’s mesh tops(worn by Smith, above centre,from £24.70)are popular to keep cool andHalara’s skortsandskort dresses(worn by Law, above left, from £17.95) work well for bum-shaking. “You don’t want something to feel like a wetsuit,” Law says, “but you want it tight enough that it flows with your body. A massive one for me, especially with trousers or shorts, is rolling down at the top. I pull them up to suck the belly in and I don’t want to be spending the workout pulling them up.”Gymshark’s Light Hold Leggings(£38) andMatalan’s Souluxeleggings(from £12.50) do the job: “They do not move on your tummy.”Dressing up for Zumba has helped the women to feel good about themselves. “It has definitely given me a lot more confidence in how I look at myself and what I wear,” Gulliford says.To find Amy Smith’s online and in-person classes, follow her on Instagram atZDP_AmyThe Guardian fashion desk recommends …View image in fullscreenMarks & Spencer Goodmove sports bra£15 at M&SView image in fullscreenAdidas boxy mesh T-shirt£33 at Adidas£33 at AsosView image in fullscreenMarks & Spencer bubble hem skort£15 at M&SView image in fullscreenSweaty Betty Power 7/8 gym leggings£44 at Sweaty BettyThe city runnersView image in fullscreenNico Junior, Habiba Hassan and André Lance of the Lost Culture running club in Leeds“I’m not going to lie and say that I don’t feel the heat; I absolutely do,” says Habiba Hassan, 26, of pounding the pavements of Leeds with theLost Culture running club. “It can be quite difficult at times, especially when we are doing long distances, and in the summertime.”Hassan, an NHS dietitian who completed this year’s London marathon, says that her running look has evolved as modest activewear has improved. “What was available five years ago is very different to now,” Hassan says. “I’m not in a position where I have to wear a men’s oversized T-shirt any more. There are brands that cater for me.” Hassan sources breathable tops that are intentionally loose-fitting, such as herHaya Active essential training top(above centre, £39). She is always being asked where she got her loose trousers:they arePromoveryoga trousers with pockets(above centre, £27.99).The founder of the club,André Lance, 35, says that while they are an undeniably stylish group, participants are encouraged to prioritise more practical considerations when dressing for training sessions and races. He wearsKiprun’s 2 in 1 long-distance trail running shorts(seen on Nico Junior, above left, £39.99) – which have an inner layer “that feels like it stops chafing, which is a positive” – and an oversized, aerated T-shirt, along with basic running shades or a skullcap in winter.Chafing is a concern for Hassan, too, especially as “where I chafe changes year on year”. She finds “softer, buttery fabrics” are better.Adidas’scushionedsocks(£8 for three pairs) help on long runs.Junior, 28, who works in tech and runs with the group, sings the praises of hisCorosPace 4 GPS sport watch(above left,£229): “You can determine on a run whether you’re doing too much and it helps you to pace yourself.” Hassan has just moved from an Apple Watch to aGarmin Forerunner 55 GPS(£111.99), saying it is more tailored to running. Lance usesJBL’s Endurance Race 2earbuds(£59.99), which “stay in my ear all the way”; Junior prefersBeats By Dre’s Powerbeats Pro 2(£249.99). They go around the ear and, he says, stop his head feeling heavy on long runs.Vests are handy for trail runs and races, to carry gels and other items. Hassan loves theSalomon Active Skin 4runningvest(£95). “It has lots of zips, which are really good for your keys,” Hassan says, “and deeper pockets for your phone. At the back, there is a really deep pocket if you want to carry extra layers or a coat. It distributes the weight, which is why I love it so much, because I found that belts hitting against your tummy can cause abdominal pain. It comes with soft water bottles that are like pouches.”They all save carbon-plated trainers for racing. “I wearPuma Deviate Nitro 4running shoes(as does Junior, above left,£150) for training,” Lance says, “as they are more centred on comfort and stability. For race day,Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4 shoes(above right,£154) have knocked minutes off my time. It feels like I’ve got magic powers.”Lost Culture running club meet in Leeds on a Tuesday, Wednesday and Sunday;instagram.com/lostculture.runThe Guardian fashion desk recommends …View image in fullscreenPuma modest oversized tee£38 at PumaView image in fullscreenOn performance T£75 at OnView image in fullscreenFree People Carpe Diem shorts£38 at Free PeopleSums Club merino socks£21 at Sums ClubThe boxersView image in fullscreenManuela Campbell, Mackenzie Qu and Ailsa Mullins at Hot Girl Boxing in east London“The high you get from sparring is like nothing I’ve experienced before,” says Mackenzie Qu, a 23-year-old from Hackney who works in retail, “and I’ve played a lot of sports.” One of the downsides is that boxing involves a lot of gear, explains Qu, who took up the sport last October, signing up toHot GirlBoxingin east London. “I’ve survived OK so far without a lot of it, but if I take it any more seriously, I’m going to have to invest in gloves at least.” It is definitely worth borrowing gloves to start, says Ailsa Mullins, 34, the coach at Hot Girl, but you need to be “prepared for the stench of putting on gloves that 30 people sweated in before you!”For Qu’s first fight in November, they plan to wear Muay Thai-style shorts (with a high elastic waist and silky flared leg openings) with a bright yellow waistband, found at a branch ofTraid. “I thrift most of the sportswear I own,” Qu says, adding thatOxfam,CrisisandBritish Heart Foundationshops are the best for unearthing treasures.Also preparing for the November fight is Manuela Campbell, 43, who lives in east London and works for a trade organisation. As the name of the club suggests, “I get really hot, so at this time of year I am usually in something sleeveless. If it’s not sweltering, I prefer a baggy shirt: I don’t want my top to ride up. I like to keep it loose, so there’s a bit of airflow,” she says.Mullins wears a sports bra: “I like something with high coverage that’s quite compact – anything that can push you in – because your chest is in the striking zone.” She ratesGymshark’sEveryday seamless racerback sports bra(£28), andLululemonis another go-to brand.Campbell is prepared to indulge in decent gloves – she just got new ones made by Rival – which last for around two years. “All the Hot Girls wear Rivals,” Mullins says. “They are a really good entry-level glove.” She recommends theRV7 Fitness Plus bag gloves(£54.99) she’s wearing above left.Having a good supply of wraps – worn under gloves for extra protection – is non-negotiable. “I stockpile wraps,” says Campbell, who owns leopard-printHot Girl-branded versions andMeister’s Semi-elastichand wraps(£7 a pair). Gum shields are also a must if sparring. Head guards are always worn in fights, but Campbell feels safer wearing them more generally: “My brother has been doing martial arts for years and I don’t want my nose to look like his.”When it comes to footwear,Campbell and Mullins favour boxing boots. “If you’re going to stick at it, get those first,” Mullins says. “You can borrow most other things but your own pair of boots will make such a difference.”Adidas’sBox Hog classic shoes(above left and right,£60) are her favourites.The boxers all find the act of getting dressed to box inspiring: “There is something about the ritual of wrapping your hands before starting a session,” Campbell says, “that makes you feel very powerful, and capable of a lot more than what people have told you. I was told from a very young age that I wasn’t a sporty girl – turns out I’m actually quite athletic.”Hot Girl Boxingholds sessions in Hackney, east London, on Tuesdays and Saturdays.The Guardian fashion desk recommends…View image in fullscreenAndanola oversized T-shirt£38 at AdanolaView image in fullscreenSuzi Wong classic SW amateur boxing shorts£24.99 at Suzi WongView image in fullscreenEverlast Pro Elite boxing boots£69.99 at Sports Direct£99.99 at Get the LabelView image in fullscreenVuori energy top£60 at Vuori ClothingThe sea swimmersView image in fullscreenAmanda Bowden, Seamus Bennett and Jenny Saltmarsh of the Swimscapes swimming club in FelixstoweAmanda Bowden, 59, from Felixstowe, Suffolk, got into sea swimming on “a bit of a whim”, when someone invited her to do it to mark her 50th birthday: “I lasted about seven minutes, then didn’t do it again for a year.” After getting the bug properly, though, Bowden signed up for a 6km swim and it took off from there.There was one slight problem: she struggled to find swimwear “in colours and coverage that reflected how I wanted to present myself”. As asewing school owner, the obvious thing to do was to make her own swimsuit – using specialist material, sourceable from companies such asFunki Fabrics. She wore it when she swam the Channel solo at the age of 56 – “It had a teal background with white polka dots and red crabs all over it” – and has made others since (above left). If buying a costume, she says, it’s essential to try it out first: “Rotate your arms and move about in it. Bend over and see if your boobs come out. If you’re an endurance swimmer, look for something lined, with well-finished edges. The more bands and straps there are, the more risk of chafing.”Bowden is part of theSwimscapes clubin Felixstowe, as is Jenny Saltmarsh, 52, a health and safety consultant. Saltmarsh is a fan ofFunkita swimsuits, which come in fun patterns (like the one above right) and fit her well. In winter, she opts for aZone3 Ti+ thermal high neck swimsuit(£75). Neither swimmer wears a wetsuit: “Too much faff,” Saltmarsh says, though, without one, Bowden laughs, “it can be a bit brutal”.Seamus Bennett, 61, a swimming coach and councillor who set up Swimscapes in 2012, wears anOrca wetsuit(above centre,from £149) from March to June. He recommends a proper, flexible swimming one: “A general surfing or sailing suit may actually hinder you.”In summer, he likesFunky Trunks’ Jammers(£39.95). He feels the cold in his hands, so wearsLomoTri-Xneoprene gloves(£21), but avoids boots, which he says “slow you down”.There are safety concerns to swimming all year round. To help, Bowden uses “a highly visible tow float and a bright cap, so people can see me”, while Saltmarsh wearsSurfEars 4.0 vented earplugs(£54.95) to avoid surfer’s ear, “bony growths, from cold water coming in”. Bennett recommendsGarmin’sepix Pro Gen 2watch(above centre, £299.99), which he says has a better battery life than others, and Bowden favoursCrocsfor navigating the stony shore. As for goggles, Bennett wearsArenaCobra TriMirror triathlon swipe goggles(above centre, £68.99), because “the anti-fog lasts a long time and they’re really clear and comfortable”. In open water, Saltmarsh wears “polarisedZone3 Venator-X swimgoggles(above right, £35) and a “necessary evil” swimming cap – the brighter the better.How do they feel about the divisive issue of changing robes? Saltmarsh says she loves herDryrobe(above right,£175). “Everybody in my house has one – even the dog. My friends got me a badge: ‘All dry robe, no knickers.’” Bowden, of course, made her own.Swimscapes meet on Saturday and Sunday all year round, plus Monday May-Oct;facebook.com/FelixstoweSwimscapesThe Guardian fashion desk recommends …View image in fullscreenSpeedo Vanquisher 3.0 mirror goggles£29 at Speedo£19.99 at AmazonView image in fullscreenSwimcore jammers£37.50 at SwimcoreView image in fullscreenFinisterre Kaia 2mm Yulex swimsuit£140 at FinisterreView image in fullscreenTwo Bare Feet long cuff swim gloves£19.99 at Two Bare Feet£24.99 at AmazonThe weightliftersView image in fullscreenWilf O’Donoghue, Lauren Briggs and George Barrett at the Alternative Movement gym in Thurrock, EssexLauren Briggs, 30, from Thurrock in Essex, hadn’t been to a gym before she lost both her legs after having sepsis in 2021. “I’d never done any sport before,” says Briggs, who also lost her admin job in the aftermath of her illness. Now she goes toAlternative Movement, an adaptive gym five minutes from her home, four times a week for group and individual PT sessions. Briggs is able to deadlift more than her own weight, and has taken part in a triathlon and an adaptive competition.“Being a bilateral amputee, I really overheat,” she says. “Because I’ve lost two of my extremities, the heat doesn’t dissipate; it all comes up through my body and head. I find that tight clothing insulates you more, so I try to wear airy clothes that don’t cling to me too much.” She opts for loose and light materials, and wears “quite a lot ofAdidas” (such as the T-shirt above centre) because she likes their sweat-proof material. Shorts work better than leggings with her prosthetic legs – she’s a fan of theseHalara SoftlyZero Airy super high waisted 2-in-1 yoga shorts(£19.95). “They’ve got tight shorts inside but they are still loose, so it’s good for when you are getting up and down off the floor. Sometimes with baggy shorts, being female, I feel a bit exposed.“I have very sweaty hands,” Briggs adds, which can make lifting tricky, “so gloves do help. But I also use chalk, such asBear Grip’sliquid chalk(£8), because with the gloves, when you’re sweating in them, it can sometimes cause friction and you get blisters. With the chalk, you don’t.”Another Alt Movement gym-goer, Wilf O’Donoghue, 17, who is a student, says he prefers sweat-proof T-shirts and elasticated shorts, and Uniqlo is his go-to: “It’s affordable and easy to work out in.” He likes these shorts (above left) and theDry-Ex T-shirt(£19.90).George Barrett, 24, believes having a uniform for the gym helps him to stick with it, as a person with autism spectrum disorder: “Comfort and routine is baked into our identity.”M&S shortsandUnder Armourvests meet his sensory needs, and he usesSennheiserin-ear headphones(above right, from £34.99) to cancel out any noise: “I mainly listen to music with a lot of power behind it.” As for footwear, Barrett says hisSkechers Slip-ins trainers(above right, £90) are “loose and breathable”.Briggs has found the best gym shoes for her areRAD’s One V2(£130), which she’s wearing above and says are good all-rounders. “For weightlifting, I’ve realised that your footwear is crucial.”There are adaptive clothing ranges, including atPrimark, but not all offer sportswear and most are on the pricey side, according to Briggs. “As soon as you market something as adaptive or for the disabled community, the prices do seem to hike up quite drastically,” she says. “A lot of disabled people, we’re not working, we’re on benefits, and we’re paying premium prices for something just to be able to live our day-to-day life – that’s not really fair.”Alternative Movement offers a range of sessions at different times across the week at its gym in Grays, Thurrock, Essex;altmovement.co.ukThe Guardian fashion desk recommends…View image in fullscreenNakedfeel Origin yoga shorts£18 at Crzy Yoga£15 at AmazonView image in fullscreenPrimark adaptive wireless bralette£10 at PrimarkView image in fullscreenNext inclusively sized slim fit cargo joggers£34 at NextView image in fullscreenAdidas Supernova Rise 3 adaptive running shoes£130 at Adidas£130 at AsosThe Sunday cyclistsView image in fullscreenSimon ‘Bob’ Smith, John Moore and Chris Weatherston of the Brombay Bicycle Club in WirralIn 2016, a group of friends from Bromborough, Wirral, signed up for theLiverpool-Chester-Liverpool bike ride. Most had not ridden much before, or not for a while, and their first training ride, which they were very proud of, was 11 miles. “We had mountain bikes and were wearing Aldi’s best gear from the middle aisle,” laughsJohn Moore, 62, who works at the University of Manchester.After the race, they agreed they had enjoyed it so much, they would go for weekly Sunday rides around Cheshire and north Wales. “We used to look at road cyclists and say we’re never going to be like them, we’re never going to be Mamils [middle-aged men in Lycra],” Moore says. “But six months later, we all started. I suppose it’s more aerodynamic.” Simon “Bob” Smith, 61, who is retired, agrees: “There’s no flapping.” Chris Weatherston, also 61 and retired, thinks it’s more comfortable. “Not to look at, admittedly,” Moore adds.Over a curry atWirral Tandoori, Brombay Bicycle Club was born. One member, Garry Swaby, a graphic designer, came up with a concept for the club jersey, converting the Indian flag. The curry house even sponsored the kit. They got the design printed on aL’Etape Jersey(above centre, £50). Quickly, bikes were upgraded and, inevitably, collections grew, turning it into an expensive hobby. “I’ve got six bikes,” Smith admits. “I’ve got seven,” Weatherston says.Moore has just two and says he loves hisGiant TCR Advanced 2(£1,839):“It’s light, has a carbon fibre frame and handles really well.” If you are starting out, go for a main brand and read reviews, Smith says, and take it for a test drive if the shop will allow you to, Weatherston suggests.Padded cycle shorts are a must, with the group rating theCastelli Endurance 4 Short(£140) – “You can ride for hours in it,” Smith says, adding that, when not in the club kit, “I like myCastelli Climber’s 3.0 SL2 Jersey(above left, £41.99). It looks great, is lightweight and breathable, and has UV protection.” As for helmets, Smith, who has “come off a couple of times”, favoursSpecialized’s Align II(£45).Finding a decent saddle –theSLRBoostTM Superflow(£134.99) – for added comfort has been a gamechanger, Moore says, and hisMavicshoes with cleats(above centre, from £101.98) “make a massive difference”. Smith gets “sore palms after a few hours”, so needsgloves(above left, from £18), adding, “Glasses are important, not just to look cool, but to stop getting bits in your eyes.” Moore has“Oakley sunglasses that are brilliant”, theRSLV 141s(above centre, £188). The club’s local bike shop,K Cycles, is their first port of call for kit and advice.This summer, the club marked 10 years of cycling together by returning to do the Liverpool-Chester-Liverpool again, in memory of Chris Lewis, a member who died in June. They proudly wore the Brombay Bicycle kit. “Our dazzling apparel definitely gets noticed,” Moore says. “At a time when flags can be divisive, it is great to wear something flag-based that gets such positive reactions.”Find a group near you atcyclinguk.org/local-groupsThe Guardian fashion desk recommends…View image in fullscreenSantini windproof vest£54 at Santini CyclingView image in fullscreenCastelli arm warmers£29.95 at CastelliView image in fullscreenLe Col sport jersey£47 at Le ColView image in fullscreenRapha core cargo shorts£72 at RaphaExplore more on these topicsFitnessWomen's sportswearMen's sportswearHealth & wellbeingCyclingSwimmingRunningfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Lip-smackingly sour’: the best (and worst) supermarket cottage cheeses, tasted and rated | Cheese | The Guardian
description: Creamy, high-protein and all over our socials, cottage cheese is having a moment. We test the best …
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Creamy, high-protein and all over our socials, cottage cheese is having a moment. We test the best …
Content: It might be hard to believe, especially for those of a certain age, but cottage cheese has become cool.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.View image in fullscreenIt might be hard to believe, especially for those of a certain age, but cottage cheese has become cool.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.The FilterCheeseReview‘Lip-smackingly sour’: the best (and worst) supermarket cottage cheeses, tasted and ratedCreamy, high-protein and all over our socials, cottage cheese is having a moment. We test the best …The best supermarket vine tomatoesTom HuntSat 8 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.When I was growing up, cottage cheese was tasteless and mostly only eaten by dieters. Its recent revival in the UK, most likely driven by social media, has similar health reasons at its root – the current protein obsession in gym bros and weight watchers alike – butcottage cheese has become cool. The flavourless squeaky varieties of yesteryear are still around, but a whole new category now exists on supermarket shelves that is unabashedly fatty, rich and full of flavour, with artisanal complexity and a lacto-fermented sour twang.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.I scored these based on flavour; the more complex and sour, the better, especially when balanced with a rich, sweet and creamy suspension. None of these products were bitter.Texture is also key. I find tough, squeaky curds a bit unappetising, but I do enjoy them with a bit of size, and the silkier, the better. Some of the products were less like cottage cheese and more like a grainy yoghurt. It’s rare I give five out of five, especially when a product is not organic. However, there was one today that was so good it deserved the award.As usual, marks were also given for transparency, traceability and provenance; plus sustainability certification and, importantly, value – though even the most expensive products were relatively well priced. The quality, taste and range of cottage cheese on the market is now exceptional.The best supermarket cottage cheeseBestoverall:The Estate Dairy cottage cheese made with jersey milkView image in fullscreen£2.60 for 450g at Ocado (58p/100g)★★★★★A wonderfully rich, unctuous and creamy cottage cheese made with live cultures, and the milkandcream of jersey cows on the Cholmondeley estate in Cheshire by this B Corp-certified dairy. A dense mixture with large, firm and plentiful curds. Protein content 10%.Best bargain:Asda cottage cheeseView image in fullscreen£1.58 for 300g at Asda (53p/100g)★★★☆☆Very creamy, extra-large, super-soft curds. Made with British milk and salt. Wonderfully silky and soft with a rich, creamy quality and classic sour edge. Protein content 9.1%.And the rest …Essential Waitrose natural cottage cheeseView image in fullscreen£1.75 for 300g at Waitrose (58p/100g)★★★★☆An excellent and consistently thick and creamy cottage cheese with large, silky curds. Sweet, rich and sour. Made with British milk and salt only. Protein content 10.3%.Co-op high protein cottage cheeseView image in fullscreen£2.10 for 300g at Co-op (70p/100g)★★★★☆An extra-thick cottage cheese with large-to-small curds that make up the sauce. Very creamy and stiff, but with lovely soft curds and a fresh taste. Made with British milk and enriched with cream and creme fraiche. Joint highest protein content: 12%.Longley Farm Yorkshire cottage cheeseView image in fullscreen£2.19 for 250g at Morrisons (88p/100g)£2.20 for 250g at Waitrose (88p/100g)★★★★☆Large, very firm curds with a thick layer of cream on top. Made in Yorkshire by Longley Farm, established in 1948, from milk and salt. It has a high fat content, making it rich and creamy. Protein content 10.3%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAll Things cottage cheese naturalView image in fullscreen£1.60 for 240g at Ocado (67p/100g)£1.85 for 240g at Sainsbury’s (77p/100g)★★★★☆Complex and creamy like a sour mascarpone. A super thick, creamy texture with large, soft curds suspended in the cream. It’s made with British grass-fed milk, cream, pink Himalayan salt, as well as lactic cultures that give it a lip-smackingly sour twang, balanced with the sweetness and richness of the cream. Protein content 10%.Graham’s the Family Dairy cottage cheese naturalView image in fullscreen£1.65 for 300g at Tesco (55p/100g)£1.65 for 300g at Ocado (55p/100g)★★★☆☆Extra sweet and very firm curds of mixed sizes, which make up a thick, creamy sauce. A classic, sharp, sour twang. Made from just Scottish milk and salt. Joint highest protein content of 12%, and winner of a one-star Great Taste award 2025.Milbona cottage cheese naturalView image in fullscreen£1.39 for 300g at Lidl (46p/100g), in store only★★★☆☆A dense, fresh and creamy cottage cheese with small, soft curds and a layer of cream sitting on top. This one has a lovely, clean, lactic sour taste. Made simply with milk and salt. Protein content of 11.5%. Produced in the EU.Piątnica Serek Wiejski cottage cheese naturalView image in fullscreen97p for 200g at Asda (49p/100g)£1.25 for 200g at Sainsbury’s (63p/100g)★★★☆☆Very firm medium- to large-size curds, suspended in a sweet, very mild cream. Less sour than most, with a clean, fresh milk flavour. Made in Poland. Protein content 11%.Emporium cottage cheese naturalView image in fullscreen£1.39 for 300g at Aldi (46p/100g), in store only★★☆☆☆Medium-sized, firm curds suspended in cream and creme fraiche. Although it has a light, fresh taste and yoghurt-like consistency, it has a complex and sour flavour. Protein content 11.9%.Explore more on these topicsCheeseThe FilterFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Water Colour review – an elegant, expertly handled study of depression | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Milly Sweeney’s award-winning two-hander about an art student and a kitchen porter draws power from its clever structure and light touch
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Milly Sweeney’s award-winning two-hander about an art student and a kitchen porter draws power from its clever structure and light touch
Content: Doesn’t overstate its case … Molly Geddes and Ryan J Mackay in Water Colour.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenDoesn’t overstate its case … Molly Geddes and Ryan J Mackay in Water Colour.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewWater Colour review – an elegant, expertly handled study of depressionTraverse theatre, EdinburghMilly Sweeney’s award-winning two-hander about an art student and a kitchen porter draws power from its clever structure and light touchMark FisherSat 8 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is rare to come out of a show raving about the structure, but the unusual plotting distinguishes Milly Sweeney’s two-hander. The young playwright’s theme is the way everyday social pressures – the stress of completing an art degree show, the anxiety of starting a job – can take a toll on mental health. With sensitivity, she traces the step-by-step process that might take someone from depression, compounded by circumstance, to thoughts of suicide.Her characters are Esme (Molly Geddes) – friendless at Prestwick Academy, isolated at Glasgow School of Art – and Harris (Ryan J Mackay), seemingly on the up after landing a job as a kitchen porter in a Michelin-star restaurant.The novelty in Water Colour, namedbest new play in the 2026 Cats awards, is that the two young people are unknown to each other. Their stories play out independently, except for the significant moment when they cross, one inadvertently helping the other at the point of greatest need. It is built with the elegance of a figure of eight.A Trial: After An Enemy of the People review – Wagner Moura upends Ibsen and keeps us guessingRead moreA joint venture by the Byre theatre, Pitlochry Festival theatre and the Traverse, it is punchily performed by Geddes and Mackay, who help narrate each other’s stories to create the illusion of their happening at the same time. She plays his tyrannical head chef, while he plays her opinionated tutor, the two revelling in their malevolent caricatures in Sally Reid’s buoyant production.This lightness of touch leavens the play’s serious intent. When Esme is suffering from debilitating inertia, still in bed at 3pm, Harris is the partying carouser with money to burn. The roles are reversed as the play loops round on itself, illustrating the fragility of our emotional health without overstating the case. It is a clever piece of writing, brisk and confident, portraying isolation even as it celebrates the power of mutual support.AtTraverse theatre, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreMental healthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: From Love Me Tender to Kevin Bridges: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: Vicky Krieps puts her heart on the line in Anna Cazenave Cambet’s romantic drama, and the Glaswegian comedy superstar is back on stage for a massive UK tour
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Vicky Krieps puts her heart on the line in Anna Cazenave Cambet’s romantic drama, and the Glaswegian comedy superstar is back on stage for a massive UK tour
Content: A French connection … Vicky Krieps and Antoine Reinartz in Love Me Tender.Photograph: Peccadillo PicturesView image in fullscreenA French connection … Vicky Krieps and Antoine Reinartz in Love Me Tender.Photograph: Peccadillo PicturesGoing out, staying inCultureFrom Love Me Tender to Kevin Bridges: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadVicky Krieps puts her heart on the line in Anna Cazenave Cambet’s romantic drama, and the Glaswegian comedy superstar is back on stage for a massive UK tourSat 8 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Contents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaLove Me TenderOut nowVicky Krieps heads up Anna Cazenave Cambet’s drama about a woman who splits amicably from her husband to follow her dream of becoming a writer, but then falls for a woman – at which point, the ex-hubby files for sole custody of their child. Also starring Monia Chokri and Antoine Reinartz.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Edinburgh international film festivalVarious venues,13to 19 AugustThe world’s oldest continuously running film festival returns with a programme that includes 10 films competing for a £50K prize; plus the UK premieres of I Want Your Sex by Gregg Araki and Lance Hammer’s Queen at Sea; and special guests doing talks including Kenneth Branagh, Ewan McGregor and Bruce Dern. There’s also a screening and club-night celebration for Trainspotting’s 30th anniversary.Ice Cream ManOut nowEli Roth directs a slasher about an ice-cream man who turns children into homicidal maniacs. You’re probably either in or out by this point but, in case it makes a difference, the film stars Ari Millen of Orphan Black fame as the titular dispenser of summer treats.A Child of My OwnOut nowA true-crime docudrama based on the real-life case of a Mexican woman who abducted a baby from the hospital where she worked as a nurse. Chilean director Maite Alberdi’s factual account is interwoven with a telling of the story from the perpetrator’s point of view.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenUrine for a treat … Joji.Photograph: Evers PundJojiDublin,11 August; London,13 August; touring to 16 AugustThe Japanese-Australian YouTube prankster turned serious musical artist arrives in arenas in support of February’s fourth album of ornate electronic ballads, Piss in the Wind. The night’s singalong moment is likely to be Glimpse of Us, which is now on 1.8bn Spotify streams and counting.Michael CraggJohn Grant with Richard HawleyKelvingrove Bandstand, Glasgow,10 AugustOriginally brought together in 2023 as part of the Manchester international festival, Grant and Hawley reunite for this unique collaboration celebrating the work of late country star Patsy Cline. With Cline’s songs steeped in romance and heartbreak, expect them to come to life anew on a Glasgow bandstand.MCThe Galloping CureFestivaltheatre, Edinburgh,9 to 12 AugustAdvertised as “an opera for the opioid age”, this is the latest collaboration between Missy Mazzoli, one of the most successful composers working in opera today, and librettist Royce Vavrek, dubbed “the indie Hoffmannsthal”. Its world premiere production by Scottish Opera is a musical must-see at this year’s Edinburgh international festival.Flora WillsonDenys Baptiste, Gary Crosby, Cassie KinoshiBristol Beacon: Lantern Hall, 8 AugustJoining the BBC’s wider Proms season, this live-broadcast Radio 3 Bristol concert showcases successive generations of African-Caribbean jazz artists who have transformed the UK scene over the past half-century. Soulful Coltrane-inspired saxophonist Denys Baptiste, Jazz Warriors co-founder Gary Crosby and saxophonist/composer Cassie Kinoshi highlight this diversely creative gig.John FordhamGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenFigures of fun … Kira Freije’s Unspeak the Chorus.Photograph: Rob HarrisKira FreijeModernArtOxford, to 16 AugustIt’s your last chance to catch a clutch of exhibitions this week before they close, including strange, lifesize figures frozen in moments of emotional anguish created by Freije, who is nominated for this year’s Turner prize.New Contemporaries 26Mima, Middlesbrough, to 16 AugustThere’s no better place to spot the art stars of the future than the annual New Contemporaries exhibition, which brings together work by recent graduates and early-career artists.Rachel Maclean: They’ve Got Your EyesFact, Liverpool, to 16 AugustThis Scottish artist combines film and sculpture, fairytale and horror for a terrifying immersive exploration of AI and how it’s tearing apart the idea of art and authorship.Flare-UpGoldsmith’s Centre for Contemporary Art, London, to 16 AugustHealth and illness are the focus of this show about the body and disability, featuring a stellar lineup of artists including Derek Jarman, Félix González-Torres and Racheal Crowther.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenBetween the sheets … Alan Cumming and Shirley Henderson in rehearsals for A History of Paper.Photograph: Chris KeatchA History of PaperPitlochry Festivaltheatre,9 Augustto 19 SeptemberOliver Emanuel and Gareth Williams’s thoughtful and romantic new musical charts a burgeoning relationship between a man and woman through the scraps of paper they leave behind – tickets, letters, menus and shopping lists. title: This burning summer is the proof: the voices of climate denial aren’t just delusional, they’re deadly | Sadiq Khan | The Guardian
description: Look at our blazing forests and parched cities. Green policies aren’t a ‘luxury’, and we can’t burn more oil and gas. People need the truth, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Author: Sadiq Khan
Headline: Look at our blazing forests and parched cities. Green policies aren’t a ‘luxury’, and we can’t burn more oil and gas. People need the truth, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Content: Parched grass near the Houses of Parliament in London, 3 August 2026.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenParched grass near the Houses of Parliament in London, 3 August 2026.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionClimate crisisThis burning summer is the proof: the voices of climate denial aren’t just delusional, they’re deadlySadiq KhanLook at our blazing forests and parched cities. Green policies aren’t a ‘luxury’, and we can’t burn more oil and gas. People need the truthReport: Sadiq Khan calls on Andy Burnham to commit to climate action as pressure grows over North Sea oilSat 8 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 13.47 EDTShareEurope is burning. This summer, an unprecedented series of heatwaves hasswept throughthe continent and across many parts of the globe. The consequences have been nothing short of catastrophic. In recent weeks deadly blazes have torn through France, Greece and Spain, killing firefighters, forcing people from their homes and robbing them of their livelihoods.With Tuesday marking Britain’s 34th day of temperatures exceeding 30C (86F) this year, the UK has also found itself reckoning with ferocious heat. Wildfires have forced evacuationsin Suffolkandthe Cairngorms. In London – where parks have become burnt, brittle and brown – hundreds of grass fires have put our firefighters under pressure like never before. In July, the weather station at Kew Gardens recorded its first ever month without rain since it started operating in 1871. As rivers run dry and reservoirs run low, farmers are warning of food shortages amid the deepening drought. Withthousands of deathsalready estimated to be linked to the extreme heat we saw in May and June alone, it’s likely this figure will climb higher still.The terrifying scenes we’ve seen so far this summer are the latest part of a pernicious long-term pattern. This is the third drought London has experienced in the past five years. Across the world, the past 11 years have been the 11 hottest ever recorded – and with a super strengthEl Niño forming in the Pacificwhich could pour yet more fuel on the fire, that trend is all but certain to continue. The climate emergency is here – and no one can say they didn’t see it coming.When I was first elected mayor back in 2016, I warned that our rapidly warming world would be the defining challenge of our time. I was the first mayor of a global city todeclare a climate emergency. Since then, a coalition of climate deniers and delayers has been relentless in condemning the green policies I’ve introduced. When I announced my intention to expand the Ulez – creating thelargest clean air zonein the world – they unsuccessfully attempted to drag down the debate and whip up a crude culture war. On social media, people were blinded by a dark blizzard of disinformation designed to discredit climate action. Radicalised by what he’d seen online, one man even detonated ahomemade bomb, destroying a Ulez camera in a shocking act of domestic terrorism.Looking back now, it feels like the fierce fight over Ulez marked the beginning of something else: a new age of extreme climate scepticism. In the years since, the horrifying reality of the climate crisis has come into sharp relief – and yet somehow the clamouring voices of denial and delay have grown louder than ever. Having dismissed climate change as a “con job”, Donald Trump has sought to sabotage global climate action, withdrawing the United Statesfrom the Paris agreementfor the second time, cutting support for clean energy, and boosting oil and gas production. In the UK, where cross-party consensus on the climate crisis has collapsed, his ideas have been echoed by opposition politicians and rightwing populists who veer wildly between denialism and fatalism. As some claim the climate crisis is a hoax, others insist it’stoo late to act.Both arguments are bogus. The climate crisis is getting worse, but inLondonwe’ve shown that – with courage and creativity – we can prepare ourselves for its impacts. We’ve planted more than 640,000 trees across the capital, shading our streets from the summer sun. We’ve embraced rewilding while creating and improving more than 2,000 football pitches’ worth of green space, providing natural drainage to prevent flooding. And just last month, we set out a plan to clean up our rivers and create safe swimming sites where Londoners can cool down in the heat. We have more zero-emission buses than any city in Europe and about a third of our country’s electric charging points.At the same time, since I’ve been mayor our city’s carbon emissions have fallen by about a quarter, while our economy has continued to grow. And last year the Ulez helped us to get levels of nitrogen oxide – one of the most toxic pollutants in our air–within legal limitsalmost two centuries before experts predicted we would. Between 2019 and 2024, estimated deaths associated with air pollution in Londonfell by an estimated 40%.Through C40 Cities, a network of almost 100 global cities I co-chair, London is working side by side with cities around the world to take on the climate emergency – from rolling out new green buses to boosting the supply of renewable energy – but we cannot do this alone. National governments across the globe must step up and meet the gravity of this moment with renewed focus, funding and resolve. This includes our own government, which should reassure the public by reaffirming its commitment to net zero and making clear that it will continue to reduce our reliance on oil and gas and to invest in green projects.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExtreme heat breaks temperature records in central and eastern EuropeRead moreThe most common refrain I hear from climate deniers is that green policies are some kind of luxury divorced from the worries of working people who are just trying to get by. But the idea that you can separate the climate crisis from the cost of living is patently absurd. What happens when droughts cause food prices to rise and when oil-price shocks squeeze household budgets? When hospitals are overwhelmed by vulnerable people struggling in the heat? When railways and roads buckle, workplaces close and schools are shuttered? The notion that climate action represents “woke nonsense” relies on the ridiculous premise that the climate crisis isn’t real – or that if it is, we won’t feel its impact on our lives. This year has proven just how wrong that is.We are living in an era of extremes, and my fear is that – without urgent action – the worst is still to come. In this context, climate denial and delay isn’t just delusional – it’s deadly. Because it won’t be President Trump and the fossil fuel companies paying the price for failure – it will be the rest of us. If we are to protect our planet and the people who call it home, we must turn the tide on climate denial by preparing for a hotter future and embracing net zero like never before.Sadiq Khan is mayor of LondonExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionClimate science scepticism and denialExtreme heatSadiq KhanLondonAir pollutionLow emission zonescommentShareReuse this content

title: Private pensions are a publicly subsidised gift to the wealthy | Phillip Inman | The Guardian
description: John Healey should equalise the tax break on pension savings to stop inequalities from widening
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: John Healey should equalise the tax break on pension savings to stop inequalities from widening
Content: ‘Do standard-rate taxpayers know that they get half the subsidy for pension saving that higher-rate taxpayers receive? Probably not.’Photograph: Steve Vidler/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Do standard-rate taxpayers know that they get half the subsidy for pension saving that higher-rate taxpayers receive? Probably not.’Photograph: Steve Vidler/AlamyPensions industryPrivate pensions are a publicly subsidised gift to the wealthyPhillip InmanJohn Healey should equalise the tax break on pension savings to stop inequalities from wideningSat 8 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 14.43 EDTSharePrivate pensions are a privilege for the lucky few and a curse for everyone else. Sold as a saviour for what would otherwise be a ruinous old age, they have become pernicious financial vehicles that allow an older generation to hoodwink younger generations, who also seek security in their latter years.To make matters worse, saving by the better off is enhanced by state subsidies, widening the divide between rich and poor in retirement while driving a wedge between the generations.AsJohn Healeyscours the public finances for ways to boost spending on defence, social care (and the rest) before the autumn budget, he should put considering equalising the tax break on pension savings top of his list.Do standard-rate taxpayers know that they get half the subsidy for pension saving that higher-rate taxpayers receive? Probably not.Official figures published last month show that the cost of income tax relief on pensions soared from £48bn in 2022-23 to £60bn in 2024-25, an increase of a quarter in just two years. About £40bn is swallowed up by higher-rate taxpayers. That’s because higher earners get a 40% tax break while everyone else gets 20%.At the heart of the problem, and why Healey will find it difficult to confront, is the concept of retirement itself, the purpose of which has changed dramatically over the past 80 years.Once a safety net for later life when workers and carers were too infirm or too ill to continue caring or working, it has become something that should involve three, four or five holidays a year, and last for 35 years or more. It’s why many of the people standing outside pubs on a Thursday evening – a ritual Westminster council would ban – are grey heads celebrating their early retirement, and a long one to boot.Someone aged 60 in the UK will live, on average, to 84 and have a 33% chance of living to 90, according to the Office for National Statistics’life expectancy calculator. And that predicted lifespan is longer the more affluent you are.There is a growth industry among consultants who not only plan the finances of those who retire with big pension pots, but also design a life for those who were senior in some way in the latter part of their working life and feel lost without anything to do.While many people will devote their retirement to charity work or looking after children, for too many living the retirement dream is to inhabit a comfortable cocoon. Why? Because those who have saved deserve another entire lifetime of R&R after so much hard graft, they say.Of course, those people who have actually grafted tend to have meagre pension provision. White-collar workers, and especially those in management or aged over 50, have the best of it.The scandal of baby boomers and gen Xers hoarding their pension savings can be seen in the industrial disputes of the 2010s, when almost every strike was called to defend the pensions of older workers.Shop stewards, mostly over the age of 50, would negotiate deals with managers in a similar age bracket to secure guaranteed defined benefit pensions for themselves while younger workers and new joiners were offered the much cheaper, stock market-dependent defined contribution schemes.Over time, these shop stewards and their contemporaries on both sides of the management divide have walked off into the sunset, taking their gold-plated pensions with them.It is damaging to the economy when so many experienced and skilled workers prefer buying an even bigger SUV and a cruise ship holiday to finding a way to contribute into their old age, at least while they have their health. This is especially true in a society like the UK where, since Nigel Lawson’s reforms in the 1980s, pension provision is largely privatised.Global studies of state pensions show they encourage workers to stay employed for longer, either because the payout is too low to sustain a decent standard of living, or because governments have “moved the goalposts” and delayed the state pension age.However, as the state pension has faded into insignificance for many better-off workers, the incentive changes. A defined benefit scheme, more commonly referred to as a final salary pension, has a default retirement age of 60 and anyone who has accrued all their rights has little incentive to carry on.Analysis by the Institute for Fiscal Studies shows that those people with the lowest and highest wealthare least likely to be in work aged 65; the lowest due mainly to ill health and a lack of skills, the better off because they have lucked out with their pensions.Chief among the winners these days – those with guaranteed pensions linked to their salary rather than to the stock market – are public sector workers. They regularly attended retirement parties for colleagues who think it reasonable to retire at 60 after 35 years of office life with a pension lasting another 35, believing the failed economics of this outcome is someone else’s problem.Professional baby boomers may have escaped with their winnings to live the high life, but Healey can stop gen Xers perpetrating the same heist. Of course there will be complaints. But the judges, doctors, marketing executives and company directors who will shout loudest should ask themselves why 40% of their pension pot should be provided by other taxpayers, most of whom are much poorer than they are.Explore more on these topicsPensions industryState pensionsJohn HealeyEconomic policyPensionsSavingsRetirement planningcommentShareReuse this content

title: Lime bikes hurtling around the city: is this the revenge of a priced-out generation? | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: From running red lights to dumping bikes, some Lime users get a bad rap. But many who grumble about them don’t appreciate their own privilege, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: From running red lights to dumping bikes, some Lime users get a bad rap. But many who grumble about them don’t appreciate their own privilege, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: A 2023 report commissioned by Lime found that ‘20% of Lime riders in London had never cycled before’.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/AlamyView image in fullscreenA 2023 report commissioned by Lime found that ‘20% of Lime riders in London had never cycled before’.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/AlamyOpinionEbikesLime bikes hurtling around the city: is this the revenge of a priced-out generation?Andy BeckettFrom running red lights to dumping bikes, some Lime users get a bad rap. But many who grumble about them don’t appreciate their own privilegeSat 8 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 10.48 EDTShareThe night belongs to Lime bikes in the capital this summer. Buses and tube carriages are boiling, cars crawl between low traffic neighbourhoods and Thames Water roadworks, and pedestrians plod through the sticky heat. But Lime riders exist in a different, breezier realm: whirring along, chatting in pairs or blissfully alone, weaving through the city’s tree-lined maze, choosing impulsively between destinations, rarely stopping for anything or anyone.“My favourite part of a night out is Lime biking home,” writesAnnie Lord, a dating columnist and author, in Freewheeling: Essays on Cycling. “As I ride up a hill, the bike’s electrics click … And, for a little while, I’m free.”According to the confidently expansive Californian company that owns Lime, Neutron Holdings Inc, theaverage ageof its London riders is 34. With the capital’s weather becoming warmer and drier, and social media and other online sources making more information about things riders could do instantly available, rented e-bikes seem a perfect tool to unlock the city’s possibilities. Across the globe, they are changing urban life: speeding it up, connecting previously out-of-the-way places, and making many women feel safer at night. Where I live in Hackney, once one of the capital’s more isolated boroughs and now one ofthe busiest Lime markets, many pubs are enjoying a bike-driven boom on summer nights, with the bright green bikes glowing outside like lurid cocktails before their riders wobble home.Yet since Limes became available in London and other British cities in 2018, the narrative has focused on their negative impacts. The way their riders often run red lights and cycle on pavements. How bikes are oftendumped in pedestrian spacesafter use, blocking entrances and vulnerable people’s safe routes. The fact that riders sometimes don’t share space considerately with traditional cyclists, and take over footpaths in parks. The strong sense that some Lime users can barely cycle at all. A2023 reportcommissioned by Lime found that “20% of Lime riders in London had never cycled before”. That is not as straightforwardly positive a statistic as the company likes to think.Other data about Lime usage is hard to come by, as the company considers it commercially sensitive. But information from Transport for London suggests Limes are disproportionately responsible for injuries to pedestrians. It estimates that in 2024 about 12% of the city’s cycling journeys were made on rented e-bikes, of which Lime is by far the biggest provider, yet rented bikes were reportedly responsible foralmost a thirdof cyclist collisions with pedestrians that required police intervention. As anyone who walks much in London knows, Limes have changed the experience of crossing a road.In truth, the Lime phenomenon is both an imposition and a liberation; an improvement to city life, and a sign of its sometimes alienating intensification; an expression of a certain kind of urban privilege (a half-hourLondonride can cost over £10), and evidence of its diminution. It shows how the relationship has changed between mobility and property, especially among the young.In 1975, Peter Ambrose and Bob Colenutt, two far-sighted British analysts of urban places, wrote in their book The Property Machine: “The city is a zone of conflict between competing claims for land.” In today’s London, as in other cities where space is sought-after and expensive, many Lime riders are young professionals, who in the past would have owned or rented homes close to the best public transport. Nowadays, that’s unaffordable for most of them, as is property ownership of any kind – as shown by the fact that the age of the average London first-time buyer has recently overtaken that of the average Lime rider,at 35.E-bike rental, whether for commuting or pleasure, is a solution to the scattering of these people to less-connected suburbs. Young Lime riders in a hurry, you could say, represent the revenge of a generation priced out of living near tube stations. Meanwhile, some of those who complain about Lime users are older Londoners who were able to buy properties in more convenient locations. They say Lime bikes are starting to dominate the city, but late-20th-century homebuyers have a much deeper hold on the capital.Tensions between the two groups can be reduced. This year, Hackney councilsays it has“worked with Lime … to install a high density of dedicated parking bays for the bikes, and compliance [by riders] is generally good”. To discourage riders from running red lights – a practice Lime’s critics claim is encouraged by its policy of charging by the minute – the council has also agreed with Limea flat fee for local residents: £1.75 for trips of up to 25 minutes that start in the borough, the same price as a bus fare, and the lowest Lime rate in London. Amid all the acrimony about rental bikes, it’s often forgotten – deliberately so by the much more powerful motoring lobby – that in polluted cities with unequal public health, more cycling is good.Yet a collaborative, responsible bike rental culture involving Lime, its customers and the overworked local authorities tasked with regulating both is some way off. Partly, this is because of commercial pressures: despite having big investors such as Uber, Lime isheavily in debtand not yet profitable. Meanwhile, as with many tech-enabled enterprises, key aspects of its business model have social costs. “People love the flexibility of being able to start and end their journey anywhere”said oneof Lime’s senior executives, Andrew Savage, last year. What he would not – could not – acknowledge was that absolute convenience for his customers can mean inconvenience for everyone else. As usual last night, despite Hackney’s ban on leaving Lime bikes anywhere but official parking bays, someone left one blocking some of my road.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnless divided, expensive cities such as London build more affordable homes, provide more widely available public transport, and make bicycle ownership less vulnerable to criminals – in other words, make mobility and housing less competitive and hierarchical – the sometimes petty, sometimes dangerous rental bike wars are likely to carry on. But at least we won’t all be stuck in cars.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsEbikesOpinionCycle hire schemesLondonCyclingEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Why Super Furry Animals joined music’s dash to cross over football’s vinyl frontier | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The sponsorship deal between Cwmbran Celtic and the Welsh indie-rockers is part of a trend to monetise ‘adjacent audiences’ as much as it is a nostalgia trip
Author: Emma John
Headline: The sponsorship deal between Cwmbran Celtic and the Welsh indie-rockers is part of a trend to monetise ‘adjacent audiences’ as much as it is a nostalgia trip
Content: ‘In the last couple of years, the relationship between bands and football teams has turned serious.’Illustration: David Lyttleton/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘In the last couple of years, the relationship between bands and football teams has turned serious.’Illustration: David Lyttleton/The GuardianSoccerWhy Super Furry Animals joined music’s dash to cross over football’s vinyl frontierEmma JohnThe sponsorship deal between Cwmbran Celtic and the Welsh indie-rockers is part of a trend to monetise ‘adjacent audiences’ as much as it is a nostalgia tripSat 8 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 16.53 EDTShareAs someone born on the cusp of the gen X-millennial divide, I am the perfect target for today’s 90s nostalgia. I played my modest, teenage part in the Battle of Britpop (verbal skirmisher, Blur division); I fervently sang – and, God help me, believed – thatThings Can Only Get Better. Super Furry Animals were a band I knew only distantly, via the transgressive thrill ofthat song they had with all the swearing in. And yet the news they’ll be shirt sponsor for a Welsh football club this season has managed to whisk me straight back to a time when things seemed simpler, kinder and more hopeful.Nearly three decades have passed sinceSuper Furry Animalslast had their logo on a football kit. Back in 1999, their frontman Gruff Rhys and bassist Guto Pryce, both Cardiff City fans, persuaded their Bangor-born bandmates to lay down their north Wales allegiances for the duration of the Bluebirds’ Welsh Cup run – which was, incidentally, all they could afford. The cup shirts cost them £2,000 and were, according to Rhys, knock-offs made for ice hockey. This year’s beneficiaries are a more modest outfit: Cwmbran Celtic, just relegated from Wales’s second tier. Cwmbran is the town where the band send their stage props for repair, and given the props in question are giant inflatable bears, you wonder whether they could get one installed in goal.Sing when you’re winning: the 20 greatest songs about football – ranked!Read moreSuper Furry Animals aren’t the only 90s band involved: Scottish post-rockersMogwaihave sponsored the men’s away strip, with 10% of the profits from all shirt sales going to a grassroots music charity.There has traditionally been an element of patronage when famous musicians do football, from Elton John’s time as chair of Watford, to Robbie Williams’s 2024 elevation to Port Vale club president. The pattern is a repeating one: local lads (they’re usually lads) make good, and want to give back to the team they’ve followed since they were little. Wet Wet Wet were the first to go down the shirt-sponsorship route with Clydebank in 1993. The team’s shirts turned out to be a more timeless design than the loud, oversized suits that Marti Pellow’s crew wore the day they unveiled them.Slapping your logo on your home side’s shirt was a charitable endeavour, rather than an investment. Nothing underscored this point better than Fatboy Slim’s relationship with Brighton & Hove Albion. The DJ’s record label first sponsored their shirts in the late 90s, back when the team’s financial straits had left them flirting with extinction, and Tony Bloom’s billions were still waiting to be won. It was particularly appropriate back then that Micky Adams’s men should run out on to the field with their chests declaring them SKINT.View image in fullscreenBobby Zamora in Brighton’s home kit sponsored by Fatboy Slim.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesMusical match-ups have tended, therefore, towards the endearing, not the cool. Jake Bugg sponsored Notts County not to market his own music, but to evangelise the Midlands team on his global tours. And it’s even cuter when bands have sponsored kids’ teams. The late Lemmy of Motörhead was tickled by the thought of a Lincolnshire under-10s team sporting his Snaggletooth skull mascot on their fronts; unfortunately the resultant all-black kit too closely resembled referees’ uniforms and the children were banned from wearing it in league matches. Still, the idea had an enduring appeal: the Prodigy, Biffy Clyro, Sleaford Mods and Franz Ferdinand have all paid for youth kits.In the last couple of years, though, the relationship between bands and football teams has turned serious. The move to monetise the “adjacent audiences” of pop and sporting fandom means shirt sponsorship is no longer a way of artists showing their support, but a marketing and merchandising opportunity in its own right.Spotify’s deal with Barcelona got the ball rolling, with Coldplay, Karol G, Rosalía and Travis Scott each briefly appearing on the shirtfront, and limited-edition replicas costing more than £340 a pop. The footie-kit-as-streetwear trend means bands aren’t “sponsors” any more, they’re “collaborators”. Hence Manchester United’s pre-match shirts don’t bear the name of the Stone Roses, just their album artwork. And while that may have baffled a few younger fans – the club’s website ran a post explaining who the Madchester group were for the gen Z-ers – it still reflects a genuine connection. Ian Brown is a lifelong Red, and the team has walked out to This Is the One since Gary Neville first requested it two decades ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenColdplay show off their Barcelona shirts.Photograph: Fc Barcelona Handout/EPAWhereas a year ago, if you’d been asked at a pub quiz what Paris Saint-Germain had in common with a K-pop band, or what Pink Floyd had to do with a Serie A team, you’d have been within your rights to say “nothing”. The answer, now, is clothing ranges – PSG teamed up with the girl group Blackpink to optimise fan engagement in Asia, while Inter marked the 50th anniversary of the album release of Wish You Were Here.All this can be confusing for the simple-minded sports lover like me. What is a culture-forward lifestyle capsule, anyway? It sounds like something Musk and Bezos want to blast to Mars in. Creating a sporting look now involves an advanced understanding of fashion arithmetic: at last year’s Euros it was Admiral x Spice Girls, now it’s the Rolling Stones x England Cricket x Castore. These are powerful equations, as when a 2025 Bohemian FC x Fontaines DC shirt (raised tothe power of Greta Thunbergwhen she wore it on her flotilla to Gaza) = £££££ for charity. Maybe Ed Sheeran’s Mathematics tour top for Ipswich was an omen. Or perhaps this is a fad, and the music industry will soon move on to something new. GQ, which has declared “blokecore” over, says we’ll be wearing classic rugby tops by autumn/winter. Sounds delightfully 90s to me.Explore more on these topicsFootballMogwaiSuper Furry AnimalscommentShareReuse this content

title: Rest assured, the new CDC director thinks ‘abortion surveillance’ is essential | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: An exchange between Dr Erica Schwartz and Senator Josh Hawley during her confirmation hearing is alarming
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: An exchange between Dr Erica Schwartz and Senator Josh Hawley during her confirmation hearing is alarming
Content: ‘Overturning Roe v Wade was just the beginning of the new war on reproductive rights in the US.’Photograph: Mariam Zuhaib/APView image in fullscreen‘Overturning Roe v Wade was just the beginning of the new war on reproductive rights in the US.’Photograph: Mariam Zuhaib/APThe Week in PatriarchyTrump administrationRest assured, the new CDC director thinks ‘abortion surveillance’ is essentialArwa MahdawiAn exchange between Dr Erica Schwartz and Senator Josh Hawley during her confirmation hearing is alarmingSat 8 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 18.03 EDTShareRobert F Kennedy Jr’snew cooking showisn’t the only big news out of the public health world this week. On Wednesday, Dr Erica Schwartzwas confirmedby the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), making her the first Black woman to hold the position. This is the first time in almost a year that the agency has had a permanent leader; the previous director, Susan Monarez, onlylasted 29 daysbefore she was ousted for butting heads with RFK about US vaccine policies. Translation: she was a little too keen on following accepted science for the Trump administration.So is Schwartz an RFK-approved vaccine skeptic who thinks you can cure cancer by praying to trees? Surprisingly: no. Schwartz, who served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first term, actually has government experience and a public health background. During her confirmation hearing in July, she walked acareful tightropewhen asked about her stance towards vaccines. Schwartz said she “will never betray the science” but also dodged questions about how she would handle pressure from Kennedy.But don’t breathe a sigh of relief quite yet. During that same confirmation hearing, Schwartz made some chilling remarks aboutabortion surveillancewhen quizzed on the issue by Missouri senator Josh Hawley, an anti-abortion lawmakerwho wants tobanthe abortion pill mifepristone nationwide.“The CDC collects data on abortions that are committed in the United States of America through a system called the Abortion Reporting System,”Hawley saidwhen asking Schwartz whether she would commit to collecting detailed data on abortions. “This system is voluntary, and so a number of states, not coincidentally large blue states, do not turn over any data, so that it’s difficult to get a picture of just how many abortions and under what circumstances are committed in this country. We do know the numbers are going way up.”“Senator, you have my commitment,” Schwartz replied. “Abortion surveillance is absolutely a critical component of what the CDC is currently doing.”“I also want to make sure that certain states are not conflating emergency services and hiding abortions in that emergency services case definition,” she added. “We need to make sure we’re pulling out true abortions and making sure that we’re really having clear case definitions regarding abortions so the data is actually accurate.”“Tremendous,” Hawley replied. He seemed very happy with her response.If you are concerned about the growingcriminalization of abortionand surveillance of pregnant women in the US, then absolutely nothing about this is tremendous. I’ve quoted the majority of the exchange between Hawley and Schwartz instead of paraphrasing it, because the choice of language is so alarming.
