First, look at the way in which Hawley frames the issue. He talks about abortions beingcommitted:a loaded word which makes you think of murder. (Imagine it in another medical context:I’m having a mammogram committed tomorrow!)Then he insinuates that blue states are hiding abortion data for nefarious reasons. As it is, 44 states plus Washington DC have some form of mandated abortion reporting, according tothe Guttmacher Institute, and there is no evidence that these states are hiding anything. New York is anoutlierin that it only requires abortion reporting when a patient makes a request related to the disposition of the fetus’s remains. Which seems like a sensible policy that protects the privacy of people who have had abortions.Now look at Schwartz’s reply. Why would abortion surveillance be “a critical component” of what the CDC is doing? Data collection around abortions can serve legitimate purposes, sure, but isn’t it rather more important for the CDC to be, I dunno, controlling and preventing diseases? Her reference to “true abortions” (as opposed to fake ones?) and to states “hiding abortions” is also worrying. Pregnant people are already dyingpreventable deathsbecause providers in states with abortion bans are terrified of treating them. This sort of language from the CDC director is going to make the situation even worse.Donald Trump has called Schwartz “a STAR”. If her exchange with Hawley is anything to go by, however, she seems to be yet another stooge: happy to facilitate the Trump administration’s anti-abortion agenda and politicization of public health.“Erica Schwartz’s testimony … should alarm everyone who believes private medical decisions belong to patients, not politicians,” Mini Timmaraju, the president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, said in a statement. She added that, under theTrump administration, “abortion surveillance could be expanded or weaponized to collect more intrusive information, spread disinformation about reproductive health care, and support efforts to investigate or criminalize patients and providers”.As activists and experts have repeatedly said, overturning Roe v Wade was just the beginning of the new war onreproductive rightsin the US – a war facilitated by an unprecedented network of surveillance technology. Theconvicted felonin the White House seems intent on treating every pregnant woman as a potential criminal.Todd Blanche pledged to roll back abortion access nationwideDuring a private call with religious groups, the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche, said effortsto reversethe Biden administration’s efforts to protect abortion were “taking longer than we want”. He seemed to suggest that the administration was working to restrict access toabortion pills and said: “We don’t have complete victory yet, but we will have victory, and victory will be soon, and it will be permanent.” Blanche has faced a rocky road to confirmation as attorney general. The bad news is that the government’s anti-abortion agenda will continue whether he gets the role or not.Arizona clergy who learn of child abuse in confessions aren’t required to report itThat’s according to a new ruling by thestate’s supreme court. No doubt they’ll soon be forced to report abortions, though!skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnya Taylor-Joy has a theory about why method acting is associated with men“If you’ll notice, women don’t method act because we have things to take care of,” Taylor-Joy said in aninterview promotingher new Apple TV show Lucky (which is extremely good, by the way). Back in 2024, Natalie Portmansimilarly describedmethod acting as a “luxury women can’t afford”. She added: “I don’t think that children or partners would be very understanding of, you know, me making everyone call me ‘Jackie Kennedy’ all the time.”Sydney Towle, who shared cancer journey on TikTok, dies aged 26More than a million people watched Towle navigate her cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer of the bile ducts. Sheraised awarenessof the disease and built community. However, because the internet is often toxic, she was alsoaccused by trollsof exaggerating or even faking her cancer. It even got to a point where Towle’s doctor had to confirm to the New York Times that she had stage 4 cancer.Miscarriages are surging in Gaza and births are decliningThis is not someunfortunate byproductof war; it is by design. Last year, a UN report found that Israel’s systemic attacks on women’s healthcare in Gaza amount to “genocidal acts”. The report noted that Israel’s destruction of maternity wards, an IVF clinic and control on essential supplies into Gaza “destroyed in part the reproductive capacity of Palestinians in Gaza as a group”.The week in pawtriarchyA cat called Toast Malonesurvived a firethat destroyed an apartment complex in Utah by hiding in a closet for three days. Toast did not get burned, and has now beenreunitedwith their family. Now they’re the toast of the town.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationThe Week in PatriarchyAbortionHealthWomenVaccines and immunisationUS SenateReproductive rightscommentShareReuse this content

title: Parenting is hard. Should we let AI do it for us? | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: Tech companies offer eye-movement trackers, personalized podcasts and ‘optimized nap predictions’. Who actually needs this?
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: Tech companies offer eye-movement trackers, personalized podcasts and ‘optimized nap predictions’. Who actually needs this?
Content: ‘What about the eight to 10 hours a day when your child has the gift of blissful solitude?’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘What about the eight to 10 hours a day when your child has the gift of blissful solitude?’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionParents and parentingParenting is hard. Should we let AI do it for us?Dave SchillingTech companies offer eye-movement trackers, personalized podcasts and ‘optimized nap predictions’. Who actually needs this?Sat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 08.56 EDTShareWhat job in our world is less lucrative than being a parent? A Hollywood internship? Volunteering at a soup kitchen? Professional writer? Parenting is the only job you have to pay money to do.Lots of money. Lodging, clothes, food, school, Pokémon cards – it really adds up. And it’s getting worse. According to the tech industry, I have to strap my drooling offspring to a computer in order to ensure the baby’s survival.Parents are being offered life-altering advancements in artificial intelligence that purport to make this taxing endeavor a tiny bit easier. OpenAI is suggesting its latest products can make child-rearing more efficient: its boss, Sam Altman, suggestsgenerating a podcast about your kid’s lifethat you can listen to in the morning on the way to school. How entertaining would a podcast “that talks about one kid’s soccer game that afternoon, one kid’s upcoming birthday, some news, etc” actually be? “Jimmy needs to work on his dribbling.” Great. I think he knows already. He’s not going to be the next Messi, so how about we switch back to music?Momfluencers are co-parenting with AI. Is it better than a man? | Arwa MahdawiRead morePresumably, this idea renders the need for conversation moot. The computer already knows everything about our lives and has now regurgitated it into digital mush delivered by a generically cheery voice. But why I would find it helpful to have a machine reiterate information I have at my disposal already is a grand mystery even Philip Marlowe couldn’t solve. I’m a functioning, alive adult human being. This is like giving me an extra tooth with the promise that I can chew my food faster.But what about the eight to 10 hours a day when your child has the gift of blissful solitude? Surely, they can’t be left alone at bedtime, lest they swallow a Hot Wheels car or open your favorite jar of loose razor blades. That’s whereNanitcomes in – a startup that promises the kind of 24-hour surveillance that would make the Department of Homeland Security salivate. Nanit sells a camera and monitor set that observes your kid during sleep, tracking eye movements, “sleep efficiency”, and breathing patterns. Nanit’s rival, a company called Owlet, attaches a pulse oximetry tracker to your child’s foot through a sock. That’s not quite hooking your kid up to a terminal from the novel Neuromancer, but it feels like a decent first step in that direction. An app called Huckleberry offers “optimized nap predictions” and a chatbot assistant.Of course, all of this costs money. A Nanit kit is $474, plus $100 a year in subscription fees. Owlet’s robo-sock is $300. Huckleberry’s app is free, but its nap predictions, like expert sports betting advice, will cost you. For $120, you can be told when your kid might go to sleep. I doubt there’s a money-back guarantee if they get it wrong, and the kid ends up spilling Legos all over the floor instead of going to bed.These services promise to save lives by identifying health issues early in a child’s development. Nanit claims it offers more sleep and peace of mind, so parents can move their babies into their own rooms, thereby giving mom and dad a chance to go back to having regular intercourse. Yes, Nanit has looked intoparents’ sex habits, too. If you went back to when I was married, you’d find there wasn’t much to look into.None of this is anything people actually need to be parents. Babies need food, toys, diapers and a regular bath. Those all cost money. If I have to choose between saving for my son’s college and a spreadsheet with a bunch of biometric data, I’m skipping the spreadsheet. I realize, of course, these products are not for me. I don’t have an unlimited supply of disposable income. I have to prioritize and be practical. These devices are for people who optimize every single shred of their daily lives, thinking it will protect them from the reality of failure, illness and death. I’m sorry to report that a $400 camera isn’t going to fix any of that.Is the promise of AI living up to the hype? | Fiona KatauskasRead moreSociety has been trying to offer solutions to solve the conundrum of parenting for decades: self-help books, classes, the legendary (and expensive)Snoo cribthat shakes your child like it’s a gin martini until it stops crying. In every case, these aids cost money, turning parenting into a lucrative sector of the economy. If you can’t afford these modern “miracles”, where can you turn?Parenting is hard, and we all need help. But there was a time when grandparentslived with their kids and grandkids, or at least lived close enough to help. I grant that the idea of living with my mother is akin to pitching a tent next to a cave filled with grizzly bears, but I’d do that before I got an AI-powered camera system to take a video of my kid sleeping. The best part of extended family childcare is that people can do something an AI can never do. It can teach children about someone besides themselves.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsParents and parentingOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)FamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: Premier League managers have never been less English, title-winning or secure in their jobs | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Huge turnover between seasons means 11 clubs start the 2026-27 campaign led by people with under a year in their dugout
Author: Andrew Beasley
Headline: Huge turnover between seasons means 11 clubs start the 2026-27 campaign led by people with under a year in their dugout
Content: (From left) Frank Lampard, Michael Carrick and Gary O'Neil are the only three English managers currently in charge of Premier League sides.Composite: Getty Images, ReutersView image in fullscreen(From left) Frank Lampard, Michael Carrick and Gary O'Neil are the only three English managers currently in charge of Premier League sides.Composite: Getty Images, ReutersPremier LeaguePremier League managers have never been less English, title-winning or secure in their jobsHuge turnover between seasons means 11 clubs start 2026-27 led by people with under a year in their dugoutAndrew BeasleySat 8 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNine of the 20Premier Leagueclubs will begin the 2026-27 season with a different man in the dugout than the one who ended the last campaign. Opta recently revealed that the only other seasons which started with so many men making their managerial debut for top flight clubs were 1888-89 and 1946-47; the inaugural season of league football and the first following the second world war. Neither occurred under normal circumstances yet the level of turnover this summer does not feel unusual. Job security has never meant less in the Premier League.Adding in the recently appointed pair of Roberto De Zerbi and Michael Carrick – confirmed in March and May respectively – means this season will start with 11 teams led by coaches with less than a year in their hotseat. The median tenure of Premier League managers at the start of each season has never been so low.Chart showing median time in charge for Premier League managers at the start of each seasonThe most recent similar season was 2016-17. Heading into that campaign, 10 clubs had managers with under one year in the role. But with respect to the current Premier League crop, the relatively new head coaches that summer included Antonio Conte, Pep Guardiola, Jürgen Klopp and José Mourinho. All had either already won the Premier League or would go on to do so.With Arsène Wenger still at Arsenal, four of those consideredthe five big beasts of Premier League managementwere competing, with the other (Alex Ferguson) having retired three years earlier. By contrast, Mikel Arteta is the only man who has won the English league who will be starting 2026-27 with the chance to do so again. There was also only one such manager two years ago, albeit it was Guardiola with his bulging trophy cabinet.As Arteta has a single championship win, this season begins with the fewest English league titles on the division’s collective CV in the Premier League era. The previous lowest at the beginning of a campaign was three in 1995-96 (thanks to Ferguson having two and Howard Wilkinson one) and 2019-20 (Guardiola two, Manuel Pellegrini one).This is a natural byproduct of managers being younger and less experienced. The median age of Premier League managers is 46.9 years old. It was the same heading into 2024-25 but was last younger 20 years ago. The drop in age has not led to further opportunities for Englishmen.Chart showing breakdown of Premier League managers by geographical region across seasonsEddie Howe’s departure from Newcastle means there will be three English managers when 2026-27 gets under way. The total was the same at the start of the last two campaigns, though interestingly it will be a different trio this year (Carrick, Frank Lampard and Gary O’Neil) than 12 months ago (Howe, Scott Parker and Graham Potter). The standing of the six clubs led by these men is worth considering. Two of the current coaches are at teams that have just been promoted, while two from last season’s group were with sides that went on to be relegated. Opportunities with even relatively secure Premier League clubs are now rare for English managers, never mind at those with realistic title ambitions.The top end of the division is likely to have a Spanish feel. TheBasque region of Gipuzkoais providing more head coaches to England’s top division than England, with Arsenal, Aston Villa, Chelsea and Liverpool led by men from that relatively small area of Spain. It’s plausible none of them will win the league given the presence of Manchester City (who themselves are under new management after a decade of Guardiola) but Arteta, Xabi Alonso and Andoni Iraola are in charge of three of the leading four clubs in the title betting market, with Unai Emery’s Villa seventh.Managers from overseas lessening opportunities for English coaches in the Premier League is simply following the trend on the pitch. Just 8.6% of available minutes went to players from outside Britain or Ireland in 1992-93 yet a new high of 69.6% was reached last season. It is a truly global competition at every level, including ownership and sporting directors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChart showing percentage of Premier League involvement by players and managers not from UK or Ireland by seasonThe influence of the latter on recruitment decisions has blurred the line between being a head coach and a manager. Liam Rosenior said he was “extremely humbled and honoured to be appointed head coach of Chelsea Football Club” when he was appointed by the Blues in January. “It fills me with immense pride to become manager of this great club,” was Xabi Alonso’s line when he secured essentially the same gig less than six months later. Based on the announcements clubs made to herald news of their appointments, the Premier League currently employs 14 head coaches and six managers.Regardless of what the sign says on Alonso’s office door, he should reflect upon his new club giving him a four-year contract when they haven’t kept a manager for as long as two years since Conte left in 2018, or three years since Mourinho’s first spell in charge over a decade earlier.Rosenior learned this the hard way. He signed a six-and-a-half year deal yet Chelsea previously employed both Rafael Benítez and Guus Hiddink on interim bases for longer than the young Englishman lasted at the club. Head coach or manager, call it what you will. The profession has never offered shorter-term employment, or felt less English, in the Premier League.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France Femmes: Vollering’s late escape for yellow leaves Niewiadoma fuming | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Demi Vollering will take an eight-second lead into the final stage of the Tour de France Femmes after winning the penultimate stage in Nice
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Demi Vollering will take an eight-second lead into the final stage of the Tour de France Femmes after winning the penultimate stage in Nice
Content: Demi Vollering sports the yellow jersey after a blistering attack in the hills near Nice.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemi Vollering sports the yellow jersey after a blistering attack in the hills near Nice.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesTour de France FemmesTour de France Femmes: Vollering’s late escape for yellow leaves Niewiadoma fumingVictory on penultimate stage secures eight-second leadPrevious leader claims she was blocked by rival’s teamJeremy Whittlein NiceSat 8 Aug 2026 13.09 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 16.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDemi Vollering took the overall lead from Kasia Niewiadoma in theTour de France Femmeswith a vicious attack in the hills behind Nice to lead the race by eight seconds from the 2024 winner, with just one stage remaining.“It’s very special to be back in yellow,” Vollering, leader of French team FDJ United-Suez said. “Tomorrow I start in yellow and I will do everything in my power to keep it. So much can happen – it’s still a big fight.”It was Vollering’s fifth stage victory in the Tour Femmes and also her fifth yellow jersey and came after she had regretted failing to mount a meaningful pursuit of Niewiadoma on Friday’s summit finish to Mont Ventoux.Tour de France Femmes 2026: stage eight heads to Nice on penultimate day – liveRead moreVollering took the initiative on the final climb of the Cote de la Ginestière and after a breakneck descent, extended her lead on the long straight road to the finish on the Promenade des Anglais in Nice.But Niewiadoma was critical of the tactics of Vollering’s team. “I was annoyed at the beginning of the climb because Gery, on purpose, just blocked me to the barriers where I had to stop pedalling,” she said of Célia Gery, Vollering’s teammate.“They should compete fair play and not look to block me on the barriers because it is so childish. I lost all the respect for them for that.” Vollering responded by saying she had not seen the incident, which was studied at length by race commissaires after the stage. “I didn’t see anything, I just saw what was in front of me,” she said. “It happened behind me. I don’t have eyes in the back of my head. Celia probably didn’t see Kasia and I’m sure she didn’t do it on purpose. I’m sure Kasia knows deep in her heart that those kinds of things just happen sometimes in racing. It’s the shit part of racing.”While the critical attacks came in the suburbs of Nice, the stage was animated by a two-rider breakaway, featuring Breton rider Maëva Squiban and Loes Adegeest, of the Netherlands.The duo might have hoped to remain clear to the finish, but Squiban, winner of two stages in last year’s race, crashed on a left-hand bend on the descent of the Côte de Colomars and howling in pain, was swallowed up the peloton.That left her former companion riding alone at the front of the Tour, but her escape ended nine kilometres from the finish as Vollering’s team attacked the bends leading to the Cote de la Ginestière.It was there that Vollering attacked, and while Niewiadoma stuck to the task, she lost ground in the final cruel metres of the short steep climb.View image in fullscreenKasia Niewiadoma (second left) relinquished the yellow jersey in Nice.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesNow only eight seconds separate the pair. Every second will count in Sunday’s final stage of the Tour, based around Nice, which takes in four climbs of the Col d’Eze, overlooking the corniche roads of Villefranche-sur-Mer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe rivalry between Vollering and Niewiadoma goes back to the 2024 Tour, when the Dutch rider lost to the Pole by just four seconds, the narrowest margin of defeat in the history of any Tour de France, after an epic duel to Alpe d’Huez.Meanwhile, French favourite Pauline Ferrand-Prévot’s title defence came to a predictable end. From her listless performance in the stage four time trial, to her major losses of time on Mont Brouilly and Mont Ventoux, her performance has been a stark contrast to that of a year ago.The Olympic gold medallist’s exit from the race was sudden and dramatic. Her bike was prepared and readied outside the Visma Lease-a-bike team bus at the start of stage eight in Sisteron, when she was reported by French TV crews to have told team staff “I can’t do it, I can’t do it.”An announcement confirming her withdrawal was made on social media afterwards stating that Ferrand-Prevot “was not feeling well this morning” and adding “in consultation with medical staff, it has been decided that she will not start”.Ferrand-Prévot’s vulnerability was evident as early as stage three, something her trainer, Rutger Tijssen, acknowledged.“When she couldn’t hold on in the fifth stage, the signals were clearer,” he said. “We knew then that it wasn’t realistic to talk about winning the Tour.”Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: West Ham sink Pompey in Carabao Cup as Sullivan ignores advice to stay away | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: West Ham began the season with a 3-1 win over Portsmouth in the Carabao Cup as their former co-chair David Sullivan watched from the stand
Author: John Brewin
Headline: West Ham began the season with a 3-1 win over Portsmouth in the Carabao Cup as their former co-chair David Sullivan watched from the stand
Content: Taty Castellanos heads home West Ham’s third goal early in the second half.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAView image in fullscreenTaty Castellanos heads home West Ham’s third goal early in the second half.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PACarabao CupWest Ham sink Pompey in Carabao Cup as Sullivan ignores advice to stay awayJohn Brewinat the London StadiumSat 8 Aug 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 16.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn an unseasonable black bomber jacket, with heavy duty company beside him, David Sullivan took his seat. Against the advice of the stadium’s operators, unbowed by serious allegations placed against his name and the weight of public opinion, West Ham’s major shareholder, the former co-chair, sat with arms crossed, always conspicuous by his presence.By beating Portsmouth in relative comfort, West Ham, the club where Sullivan’s name is no longer above the door, had secured a hearteningCarabao Cuppassage to the second round. There, they will be reunited with their former Premier League peers. The serious Championship business begins next Sunday at Burnley. Whether Sullivan travels north for that remains to be seen. It cannot be ruled out.Carabao Cup: Preston prevail in Goodison home game, Millwall keeper saves four penaltiesRead more“Neither me nor the players,” said Nuno Espírito Santo when asked about the effect of the uninvited guest’s presence. “We’ll focus on the pitch. The noise that comes from outside cannot distract at all; we’re going to find a lot of noise. We focus on the game, they do their job, they did it well.”Before kick-off, the London Stadium big screen showed a “countdown to walkout”, referring to the players’ arrival rather than to fans deserting the scene in protest. This being West Ham in 2026, any confusion would be understandable. Taking previous mutinies into account, and despite a summer of intrigue and anger, there were surprisingly few audible or visible signs of insurrection as season 2026-27 began, and an extended 90 minutes was played out.Even with Sullivan’s arrival expected, the gate to the directors’ car park did not stage a welcoming committee, the lanes around the London Stadium quiet. Protests there have been a regular sight, targeting Sullivan and his departed associate Karren Brady.Even once Sullivan’s presence was confirmed there was nothing resembling the barracking of last season. Instead, the loudest boos of the first half came at a hydration break at its midway point, with an odd choice of 90s rave musical accompaniment. The legacy of a North American World Cup continues to darken.View image in fullscreenDavid Sullivan takes his seat at the London Stadium just after kick-off.Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty ImagesPerhaps still-searing temperatures and a dose of early optimism had doused the fires raging when theHammers’ drop was confirmed in May. Time-served Irons know plenty about relegation; their club has dropped down each decade since the 1970s; West Ham heritage indeed.The kick-off chorus of I’m Forever Blowing Bubbles drowned out the Pompey Chimes ringing out from 9,000 away fans. As is usual at the London Stadium, the visiting contingent decried their surroundings and the Faustian pact struck for West Ham’s tenancy.Football has rarely been in focus during West Ham’s summer of tumult, boardroom battles after Sullivan’s defenestration. So what of football? Carabao Cup Saturday served as a decent dry run for their attempt at a promotion campaign. The new West Ham closely resembled the former West Ham, though shorn of the £151m worth of player sales that took inMateus Fernandes, Crysencio Summerville and Freddie Potts. Joël Veltman, the sole summer signing so far, came on with three minutes left.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBoardroom struggle deepens gloom as West Ham prepare for life on the outsideRead moreIn midfield, Edson Álvarez, who spent last season on loan to Fenerbahce, lined up alongside Lewis Orford, a 20-year-old it is hoped can follow the path of Frank Lampard, Michael Carrick and Mark Noble, the latter a mentor, into becoming a first-team regular. His was a successful introduction into the first team.“The energy of the young players is really really important for us,” said Nuno. “It’s up to us to develop the young academy players. That’s the vision for the future.”The torpor of a first 30 minutes of little footballing consequence was broken by aPortsmouthgoal, scored by Adrian Segecic, via a deflection off Maximilian Kilman, an expensive purchase far too regularly on the crime scene.It took 10 minutes for West Ham to awaken before Mohamadou Kanté’s pirouetting feint laid up Taty Castellanos to equalise. Mere moments later, Jarrod Bowen, the club captainstaying on to lead his club back up, a rare adult in the room last season, lashed in their second. “Jarrod shows us every day his commitment,” said Nuno.The goals evidenced a quality that ought to guide the club back to the Premier League with some comfort, though nothing should be taken for granted. “If you give them a slight opening they’re going to take it,” said the Portsmouth manager, John Mousinho.Sullivan kept any celebrations to himself and returned for a second half that began with Castellanos nodding in Bowen’s cross. An afternoon that might have descended into a familiar seething pit of rage and resentment now offered grounds for optimism. Though just beyond the hour, a chorus of “Stand up if you hate the board”.If Sullivan is no longer a board member he was its undoubted target. He has turned many a deaf ear down the years and continues to do so.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupWest Ham UnitedPortsmouthmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Versatile Bruno Guimarães gives Mikel Arteta options to shuffle midfield pack  | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: While able to play deeper, the onus will also be on Arsenal’s £75m signing to provide creativity in an attack that has struggled to break down the low block
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: While able to play deeper, the onus will also be on Arsenal’s £75m signing to provide creativity in an attack that has struggled to break down the low block
Content: While emotional over his Newcastle departure, Bruno Guimarães knew that at 28, the chance to join Arsenal might never come again.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWhile emotional over his Newcastle departure, Bruno Guimarães knew that at 28, the chance to join Arsenal might never come again.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesArsenalAnalysisVersatile Bruno Guimarães gives Mikel Arteta options to shuffle midfield packEd AaronsWhile able to play deeper, the onus will also be on Arsenal’s £75m signing to provide creativity in an attack that has struggled to break down the low blockData shows deal could be another set-piece masterstrokeSat 8 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTShareIf there was one of his many assets Newcastle supporters grew to love above all about Bruno Guimarães then it was best summed up by the man himself after being unveiled asArsenal’s new £75m signing. “That’s a tough one,” said the Brazil midfielder when asked what fans in north London can expect from him. “I would say I can pass the ball, run a lot and play like a warrior. I’ll never give up.”After more than four years on Tyneside and having seen Alexander Isak, Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali precede Eddie Howe’s departure, Guimarães – who was devastated after missing a penalty for theSeleçãoin their defeat against Norway in the last 16 of the World Cup – was determined to seize his opportunity.Data shows Bruno Guimarães deal could be another Arsenal set-piece masterstrokeRead moreWhile his emotional statement released by Newcastle as his move toArsenalwas confirmed on Saturday said they “did everything they could to keep me”, at the age of 28 he clearly felt it may never come again.Andrea Berta’s pursuit of Vinícius Júnior came up short this week after the Brazil forward signed an improved six-year deal with Real Madrid. But at least Arsenal’s sporting director was finally able to bring in a player who was first courted by the club in the early days of Mikel Arteta’s reign, and who will add to the outstanding crop of central midfielders at his disposal.Edu Gaspar, Berta’s predecessor, is understood to have first enquired about Guimarães when he was still at Athletico Paranaense in Brazil before he joined Lyon in the January 2020 transfer window – a few weeks after Arteta’s arrival at the Emirates.They were also interested when Newcastle won the race to sign him in January 2022 for €40m, which came back to haunt Arsenal when he scored in a 2-0 win that went a long way to them missing out on Champions League qualification that season.That first of nine appearances is the only time he scored against Arsenal, but Guimarães always impressed in a variety of roles whenever he came up against them, including in the Carabao Cup semi-final Newcastle won 4-0 on aggregate in 2025. He has covered more distance, won more duels and committed more fouls against Arsenal than any other side since making his Premier League debut.It was no surprise that Declan Rice – the only player in the division to have covered more distance than Guimarães in that period and who enjoyed their fair share of battles – was one of the first to welcome him to Arsenal with a message that said “come here and please no more fights, now we’re friends”.It is hard to argue with Guimarães that Arsenal have “one of the best midfields” in Europe because last season proved it. Yet having gone all the way to the Champions League final before spending the summer with England, after suffering with neural pain in his hamstring and lower back since December, Rice must be treated with the utmost care in the coming months. Guimarães can provide cover for him in a box-to-box role and gives Arteta options to rotate his other midfielders more frequently.View image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães will provide box-to-box cover for Declan Rice, rather than engage him in midfield combat.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesHe did not seem to trust Christian Nørgaard, who has joined Everton, to deputise for Martín Zubimendi in the Premier League last year, and that led to the Spain midfielder running out of steam in the spring.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt was telling that the teenager Myles Lewis-Skelly started in his preferred position at the base of midfield during the title run-in, and against Paris Saint-Germain in Budapest for the Champions League final, having begun the campaign as a left-back. Guimarães showed at Newcastle he is capable of playing in a deeper role as well and Arteta must decide how to balance his plethora of options in a crucial part of the pitch.While he could not match Mikel Merino’s goalscoring exploits for Spain,Martin Ødegaard showed signs that he is back to his best during the World Cup after another disappointing season for Arsenal that was again interrupted by injury.Having missed out on Morgan Rogers, the onus will be on the Norway captain, Guimarães and last summer’s big signing, Eberechi Eze, to provide some creativity to an attack that struggled to break down the low block at times last season.Arsenal are still in the market for a defender to cover the absence of William Saliba for an extended period, while they would like to bring in another forward to add to the signing of Christos Tzolis. Atlético Madrid’s Julián Alvarez or Bradley Barcola of Paris Saint-Germain would fit the bill, although it remains to be seen if they will bring in a marquee player without offloading Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus – who has interest from Napoli. Even if they do depart, the presence of another familiar face in the Brazil centre-back Gabriel should also help Guimarães settle into his new home.“Big Gabi was very excited,” he told Arsenal’s website. “Every time he sent me the message: ‘We’ll wait for you, when will you come?’ I’m so excited to join them, not only the Brazilians, we have an amazing squad here. I’m so excited to meet the other players, to start training. I just want to give my best.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Jorge Messi, father and agent of Argentina great, dies aged 68  | Lionel Messi | The Guardian
description: Lionel Messi’s father and agent Jorge has died at the age of 68 at a medical clinic in the ⁠Argentinian city of ⁠Rosario after ​a long illness, the family have announced
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Lionel Messi’s father and agent Jorge has died at the age of 68 at a medical clinic in the ⁠Argentinian city of ⁠Rosario after ​a long illness, the family have announced
Content: Jorge Messi, father and agent of Lionel Messi, holding his son's Golden Ball World Cup trophy in 2022.Photograph: Jean Catuffe/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJorge Messi, father and agent of Lionel Messi, holding his son's Golden Ball World Cup trophy in 2022.Photograph: Jean Catuffe/Getty ImagesLionel MessiJorge Messi, father and agent of Argentina great, dies aged 68Messi family report death at medical clinic in RosarioInter Miami are due to play Monterrey on Saturday nightGuardian sportSat 8 Aug 2026 10.49 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLionel Messi’s father and agent, Jorge, has died aged 68 at a medical clinic in the ⁠Argentinian city of ⁠Rosario after ​a long illness, the family have announced. Jorge Messi spent his final months ⁠alternating between a medical centre in Rosario and his home, accompanied by his wife, Celia, and his ⁠children Rodrigo, Matías and María Sol.Lionel Messi ​spent time with his ‌father after the World ‌Cup before rejoining his club,Inter Miami, for whom he ‌returned to action a week ago. Inter Miami are due to play Monterrey on Saturday at home in the 2026 Leagues Cup, but the MLS club have yet to announce whether he will feature.Newell’s Old Boys announced the death in a social media post that said he had undergone treatment in recent months for an unspecified illness. The post described him as “the pillar and the person who, with vision, rigour and affection, supported the career of the best player of all time, alongside his wife, Celia Cuccittini”. The Argentinian FA also expressed its ⁠condolences in a statement, saying: “From here, we stand in solidarity ​with the entire family ​during this difficult time and send ​the most heartfelt, warm, and affectionate embrace. Strength to you all.”View image in fullscreenLionel Messi poses with his brother Rodrigo, sister María Sol, father Jorge, mother Celia, nephew Tomás and brother Matías in Rosario, Argentina, in 2003.Photograph: El Grafico/Getty ImagesAt the World Cup, Lionel Messi said afterArgentina’s 3-0 victory over Algeria– when he broke down in ​tears while celebrating ​his first goal in the team’s opening match – that he was going through a difficult personal situation. Later, he explained his tears ​were due ‌to “something unrelated to ​football” after ​going through “a few difficult, complicated days”.There was speculation that the player’s emotional reaction toArgentina’s last-16 victory over Egyptwas due in part to his father’s deteriorating condition. A few days later, the family issued a statement regarding Jorge Messi’s “health situation”, informing the public that he was undergoing medical treatment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJorge Messi closely accompanied his son throughout his career, beginning with his early years at Barcelona. He acted as a crucial pillar of support and, for several years, served as his representative. “I always ‌needed my dad’s approval, ever since I was a kid. After every match, I’d ask him ​what he thought of how I played,” said Lionel Messi.Explore more on these topicsLionel MessiInter MiamiArgentinaUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sky’s DiJonai Carrington posts ‘white privilege’ after ejection for hard foul on Sophie Cunningham | WNBA | The Guardian
description: Chicago’s DiJonai Carrington tagged Indiana in a post saying ‘WHITE PRIVILEGE’ after she was tossed for a hard foul on Sophie Cunningham
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Chicago’s DiJonai Carrington tagged Indiana in a post saying ‘WHITE PRIVILEGE’ after she was tossed for a hard foul on Sophie Cunningham
Content: Indiana’s Sophie Cunningham is fouled by Chicago’s DiJonai Carrington during the first half of Saturday’s game at the United Center in Chicago.Photograph: Michael Reaves/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIndiana’s Sophie Cunningham is fouled by Chicago’s DiJonai Carrington during the first half of Saturday’s game at the United Center in Chicago.Photograph: Michael Reaves/Getty ImagesWNBASky’s DiJonai Carrington posts ‘white privilege’ after ejection for hard foul on Sophie CunninghamCarrington tossed for Flagrant 2 on CunninghamChicago player tags Fever in social media postClark’s eighth technical triggers one-game banAgenciesSat 8 Aug 2026 17.26 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 19.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDiJonai Carrington of the Chicago Sky was ejected Saturday after being called for a Flagrant 2 foul on Sophie Cunningham of theIndiana Fever. Minutes later, Carrington posted on social media the words “WHITE PRIVILEGE” and tagged the Fever.Sophie Cunningham isn’t rejecting politics. She’s cashing in on themRead moreCunningham, who is white, was shooting a fast-break layup in the first quarter when Carrington, who is Black, came from behind and hit her in the head and neck, knocking her to the court as the shot went in.Cunningham said she thought the foul in the 90-86 Indiana win was “absolutely” intentional.“Clearly I think it was unnecessary,” Cunningham said. “I’ve never really spoken to her and I have no beef with her, but I guess she has some pent up stuff.”Fever coach Stephanie White had a different view of the play.“It was a hard foul,” White said. “I don’t think that Dijonai intentionally came out to get her across the neck like she did, but it did happen, and I thought it was the right call.”Cunningham got up immediately, charged toward Carrington and pushed her as she was held back by a teammate.“I popped up,” Cunningham said. “I’m not going to let anyone just do that to me. I think everyone knows that. I think that’s why she did it because she wants attention.”The play was reviewed and upgraded to a Flagrant 2 after the referee said there was windup, impact and follow-through on the foul.Sky coach Tyler Marsh said he hadn’t seen a replay of the play, but that seeing it live, he thought Carrington was making a play on the ball and that he didn’t believe it warranted a Flagrant 2 foul.“I haven’t looked at that play since, so I really don’t know if it was justified or not,” he said. “But, that’s what I thought in the moment.”Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onthreads.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueMarsh was then asked about Carrington’s social media post.“I have to get back to you on that because I’m just now hearing about that,” he said. “So yeah, we’ll handle that.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut Cunningham had plenty to say about the post.“I think the league is taking care of that,” she said. “This has nothing to do with race. Last year, I did the same thing and I got kicked out. And I deserved to be kicked out. There’s no reason even to play that card.”View image in fullscreenIndiana’s Sophie Cunningham (center) reacts to DiJonai Carrington’s hard foul during Saturday’s game.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesIn the third quarter, Fever starCaitlin Clarkwas assessed a technical foul after she made contact with a referee when she was forced out of bounds. The technical was Clark’s eighth of the season, triggering a one-game suspension for Indiana’s next game.After the game, Clark said the contact was inadvertent and that no words were exchanged. She was hopeful theWNBAwould rescind the foul.“She said I ran into her,” Clark said of the referee. “I have already watched it on the tape. So, we’ll let the league decide. But, it wasn’t anything intentional or anything. So, I hope it gets rescinded. And, nothing was said.”Fever coach Fever coach Stephanie White said it was “a bad call”.Cunningham has frequently come to Clark’s defense after physical play by opponents and has become one of the higher-profile players in the league this season. In an ESPN article published last month, she voiced support for barring transgender girls and women from girls’ and women’s sports, which led to small protests and rallies outside Fever games in Seattle and Portland.In a memo to teams on Friday, WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert said the leaguewould have ongoing discussionsabout the issue of transgender participation in women’s basketball.Explore more on these topicsWNBAIndiana FeverChicago SkyCaitlin ClarkShareReuse this content

title: A tale of two Murrays: when Ewan met Ewen to talk Tiger Woods, stiff gins and 15 years of mistaken identity | Golf | The Guardian
description: Guardian journalist Ewan Murray and Sky Sports Golf commentator Ewen Murray on being mixed up by irate fans and ‘canteen commandos’
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Guardian journalist Ewan Murray and Sky Sports Golf commentator Ewen Murray on being mixed up by irate fans and ‘canteen commandos’
Content: The Guardian’s Ewan Murray (left) with Sky Sports Golf commentator Ewen Murray at Royal Birkdale.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Guardian’s Ewan Murray (left) with Sky Sports Golf commentator Ewen Murray at Royal Birkdale.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianGolfInterviewA tale of two Murrays: when Ewan met Ewen to talk Tiger Woods, stiff gins and 15 years of mistaken identityEwan MurrayGuardian journalist Ewan Murray and Sky Sports Golf commentator Ewen Murray on being mixed up by irate fans and ‘canteen commandos’Sat 8 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt started with an email in early 2011. “I don’t know what it is like in your country, sir,” wrote angry of Arizona. “But here in America we SPIT!!!”The penny eventually dropped. Ewen Murray’s commentary on Sky Sports about Tiger Woods emptying his mouth on a putting surface in Dubai triggered a reaction fired directly towards Ewan Murray of the Guardian. Murray of Sky fame can still recall it.“Tiger spat on the green with three groups playing behind him,” Ewen says. “I remember my words. ‘For a person who is an inspiration, not just to golfers but to everyone, there are times when he is arrogant and disrespectful.’ I switched the mic off straight away. I knew there would be trouble. But if I don’t say anything, people close to me are going to ask why I didn’t comment.Maguire survives missed cuts and controversy to headline Solheim Cup wildcard picksRead more“There was no bigger supporter of Tiger than me but the email you got, I got an awful lot more of ‘Who the hell are you to tell …’ I wasn’t telling, I was only saying it wasn’t acceptable.”Months later, at the Scottish Open, I explained the email episode to Ewen. He was concerned at the impact of this tirade on me. My response related to my ongoing coverage of Scottish football, a domain where even mild opinion fuels abuse. Water, duck’s back.Fast forward to 2026 and we are together again, this time in the Open Championship’s media centre. “If only we knew,” says Ewen. Indeed. If only we knew.It is coincidental enough for two individuals whose names are one letter apart to work in media coverage of the same sport. Freakish in this instance is that we both joined Twitter in October 2010. Before long, confusion reigned. We may be almost three decades apart in age and of totally different stock – Ewen a former professional golfer who competed in the Open, me an erratic amateur – but social media criticism (plus the odd element of praise) intended for Sky’s esteemed commentator flew this way. Lots and lots of it.My response was to fight fire with fire in an alter ego; to take on the canteen commandos in a manner that is considerably more pretentious than Ewen in reality. The man himself soon roared with approval.“I think if you don’t have humour in life; and let’s face it, there isn’t much nowadays … ” he says. “Laughter is the best medicine. I have found it all very funny and everyone I have spoken to about it is the same. What I should have been doing is answering some more of the messages meant for you but the trouble was the language was so bad. People just Google the name. ‘That’s him, there he is, Ewan Murray!’View image in fullscreen‘Laughter is the best medicine’: Ewen Murray (left) chats to Ewan Murray at Royal Birkdale.Photograph: Gary Calton/The Guardian“Some of your answers are very, very funny. Darren Clarke had tears coming out of his eyes when I showed him a few of them. He used to collapse with laughter. ‘Look what he has written now.’ Something about buggers upstairs not paying you properly, sinking stiff gins and dancing on the table. People started looking forward to the next one. I certainly do.”Just for clarity: “I don’t drink stiff gin any more. And I found dancing on tables was bad for the hamstrings.”Quick GuideIn characterShowWhen the Guardian's Ewan masquerades as Sky's Ewen"Ewan - do you like everyone in your @SkySportsGolf team? Does that impact your ability to be a good broadcaster?"Ryder Cup, 2021The buggers upstairs get on my wick sometimes – lack of a pay rise, lack of appropriate air time – but the majority of the riff raff are fine. I am, however, a GREAT broadcaster because of ME. Yours in golf."Contrary to your comments - I think you will find that Dubai have now moved weekends to Saturday/Sunday from previously Friday/Saturday as mentioned. Good move too I think."Jan 2022Gary, if I want to know the days of the week, I’ll consult a calendar. Not a backseat driver on Twitter. If you want lifestyle chatter, take out a Hello subscription. Yours in golf"Are you not commentating at the Phoenix Open this week? Missing your lovely Scottish voice."Feb 2023Alas, Syl … I’m at the bottom of a Tanqueray 10 bottle in deepest Sussex. Pringle sweater on, Dire Straits playing. Lamb madras demolished. Take it up with The Buggers Upstairs … Yours in golf"The lads need to sort out the delay that’s going on between the broadcast and the commentary. Rich Beem] asking a ball to stop when it’s already gone into the water."Players Championship, 2023When you have a problem with your ears, do you phone your podiatrist? Production types – common lackeys – are nothing to do with me. Take it up with them. Yours in golf"Matthew Jordan's home town is West Kirby not Liverpool ....for the avoidance of doubt the city of Liverpool is some 11 miles away from Hoylake on the other side of the River Mersey!"The Open, 2023Tell you what, George: why don't you pitch up at my booth with a map of Liverpool in your hand? You'll discover I can ram it into a place that doesn't have a postcode. Yours in golf"Why oh why were we subjected to 4 hours of Faldo droning on? Presumably yourself and Coltart were face down in the members bar?!"The Masters, 2024What goes on tour, stays on tour, my friend. I can however safely assure you that a gentleman's measure at Augusta would knock out a horse"Good to hear you on commentary, hopefully we will see @ShaneLowryGolf in green tonight."The Masters, 2026Niall, you are a fine man. Perhaps 24 hours early but I was atop the piano in Surrey Tavern at 1am, belting out "When Irish eyes are smiling."  Enjoy the finaleWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.There have been high-profile victims. Mick Fitzgerald, the famed jockey, praisedmytelevision commentary on a recent major. Rory McIlroy sought me out mid-round at the 2018 Open having been so tickled that a multiple world champion in another sport (who shall remain nameless) asserted, “you’re not Ewen Murray” when we first met.Other moments have flirted with danger. One punter threatened to seek me out in a public house close to Hoylake after some Ewan/Ewen antics during the Open of 2023. “He was going to findme,”Ewen says. “If people don’t find it funny, if people take offence to that, I think they have a major problem. It’s actually quite lucky to have this because so many people are involved; the players, the fans, the press, the TV. Because it is funny.“If I say something wrong on air, I know what is coming to you. You get the brunt of it but you also get the joy of answering them. ‘Do you know how many Opens I have played in? I have played with Arnold Palmer, you know.’” He is spurting with laughter once more.View image in fullscreen‘You get the brunt of it but you also get the joy of answering them,’ says the Sky Sports Golf commentator Ewen Murray.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianThis frivolity is a mere footnote on Ewen’s rich career. He combines commentary skill with an unrivalled, intense knowledge of golf and its courses. Now 71, he is still going strong in the booth and intends to do so for some time.Ewen’s time in broadcasting began almost by accident in 1990, after an executive at Emirates airlines called a professional’s shop in Sussex looking to offer Brian Barnes the gig at the second edition of the Desert Classic. “I said, ‘I’ll do it,’” Ewen says. “That was the start, a two-minute phone call. They sent me an air ticket and £500. I was lucky in that I had just finished playing so I knew all the players. I knew their strengths, their weaknesses and their characters. I still have the tapes.”He had lost his European Tour card a year earlier. Ewen’s confidence, primarily on the greens, had left him. “Too much negativity,” he says of his mindset. “When I was a kid, it was the other way round. I would dream then about hitting shots and they were all good shots. As I got older, that changed. I could see the end coming; then there was a big problem. What do you do now?”He left home in Edinburgh at 18 for an assistant professional’s job at Walton Heath. “I sat on the bed and thought ‘What the hell have I done?’ I had no car. My wage was £5 a week, my digs was £5 for the week.” Teaching, playing, commentating. A life in golf was colourful enough before online mischief-making. Not that all condemnation is swatted aside.“I ignore it unless I think they might be right,” Ewen says. “Constructive criticism is vital in life. I haven’t had it too bad, though. Nowhere near as bad as you.” Long may it continue.Explore more on these topicsGolfinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: US accused of meddling in British politics with $500,000 grant for ‘public education’ courses | US news | The Guardian
description: Documents published on US embassy’s website prompt claims of attempt to export Maga propaganda to UK
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Documents published on US embassy’s website prompt claims of attempt to export Maga propaganda to UK
Content: A funding notice on the US embassy website talks of fostering a ‘national conversation’ about ‘shared civilizational values’.Photograph: Andrew De Thabrew-HuttonView image in fullscreenA funding notice on the US embassy website talks of fostering a ‘national conversation’ about ‘shared civilizational values’.Photograph: Andrew De Thabrew-HuttonUS newsUS accused of meddling in British politics with $500,000 grant for ‘public education’ coursesDocuments published on US embassy’s website prompt claims of attempt to export Maga propaganda to UKBen QuinnandAisha DownSat 8 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 04.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US embassy in London is offering grants of up to half a million dollars for new “public education” programmes in what has been criticised as interference in British domestic politics.Using language that the pro-Trump Maga movement has sought to appropriate, a funding notice identifies a goal of fostering a “national conversation” about “shared civilizational values” underpinning US-UK ties. Priority will go to applicants aiming to celebrate “freedom of speech” and “limited government”.It comes after senior Trump officials voiced sharp criticism of British authorities and repeated misinformation on a range of fronts includingabortionanddigital regulation, andallied with European far-right movementsin attacks on hate speech and immigration policies.The grants appear to be separate from other grants of $12m whichthe US state department is planningto allocate to organisations in the UKfounded by the prominent Conservatives Jacob Rees-Mogg and Toby Young.Those intended grants, revealed in US government documents leaked to the Guardian, are part of a package of support for European groups viewed favourably by the Trump administration.However, the US government has now been accused of “meddling in British democracy” after documents published on the US embassy’s website invited charities, non-profit organisations and others to apply for grants under a scheme labelled “Liberty Under Law: The Shared Anglo-American Tradition”.It seeks “innovative, high-visibility public education and civic-engagement programs” that “deepen public understanding of the shared Anglo-American common law tradition” and to commemorate the 70th anniversary next year of the American Bar Association (ABA)’s unveiling of the Magna Carta memorial in Runnymede.The ABA – which is not involved in the grant scheme – is suing the Trump administration over alleged intimidation of lawyers and legal firms. European counterparts including the Law Society and the Bar Association in Britain have voiced support for US lawyers claiming that the US president’s attacks on law firms bearsimilarities to events in Nazi Germany.A notice offering the funding states: “Priority will be given to ambitious initiatives that connect foundational principles, such as freedom of speech, due process, trial by jury, limited government, rule of law, property rights, taxation by consent, and ordered liberty to contemporary civic life.”Proposed projects must meet one or more of a number of objectives, including the need to “demonstrate measurable impact on public discourse, media coverage, and civic engagement regarding the rule of law and democratic norms”.Lisa Smart, a Liberal Democrat MP and the party’s Cabinet Office spokesperson, said: “Magna Carta aimed to limit the powers of tyrants and said everyone was subject to the rule of law, something for which Trump has repeatedly shown utter contempt.“We have a proud tradition of liberty and freedom of speech in this country and we don’t need Trump’s Maga money meddling in our democracy.”There is also deep unease among serving and recently departed US state department officials. One told the Guardian: “While it’s not unusual to support public diplomacy efforts to showcase the special relationship between the US and UK, to specifically fund topics related to a narrow vision of America First is highly unusual.”The same person accused the US government of trying to “create UK-originated narratives to support Maga propaganda”.The notice states that the funding is not intended to support partisan political activity or lobbying.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA spokesperson at the US embassy in London said the funding initiative aimed to strengthen US-UK ties “and deepen public understanding of the constitutional principles, rule of law, and democratic norms that underpin both nations”.Responding to Smart’s allegation of “meddling”, they added: “The Embassy is mindful of such concerns, and has discontinued Biden-era public diplomacy spending on divisive ideological projects such as ‘climate justice,’ LGBTQ activism, and race-based hiring initiatives – none of which, to our recollection, raised such complaints from officials.”Eyebrows have also been raised by veteran former state department officials at some language used in a second grant opportunity being offered by the US embassy’s website under its Public Diplomacy Section program, an annual grant scheme.Applications, including those intending to run “Educational and public awareness initiatives”, are invited to submit proposals for goals including strengthening US prosperity and UK economic resilience, securing UK support for US policy including “ensuring support for Israel’s right to defend itself” and countering competition from China.A former state department official said: “In the past the language for this stuff would be more like ‘increase understanding of US policy’. This is very openly saying more ‘persuade people to agree with US policy’.”“Increasing support for Israel in a third country is weird. Can’t say if it’s ever been done, but it’s weird.”Get in touchContact Ben Quinn about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Ben using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’. When asked to choose a recipient please switch to the Journalists list and select Ben Quinn.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailben.quinn@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsUS newsDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nicola Sturgeon ‘has not spoken to’ estranged husband, Peter Murrell, since he was jailed | Nicola Sturgeon | The Guardian
description: Scotland’s former first minister says she will not visit Murrell in prison, where he is serving five-year sentence for embezzling SNP funds
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Scotland’s former first minister says she will not visit Murrell in prison, where he is serving five-year sentence for embezzling SNP funds
Content: Nicola Sturgeon’s comments came during a podcast recording at the Edinburgh festival fringe.Photograph: Claudia savage/PAView image in fullscreenNicola Sturgeon’s comments came during a podcast recording at the Edinburgh festival fringe.Photograph: Claudia savage/PANicola SturgeonNicola Sturgeon ‘has not spoken to’ estranged husband, Peter Murrell, since he was jailedScotland’s former first minister says she will not visit Murrell in prison, where he is serving five-year sentence for embezzling SNP fundsDonna FergusonSat 8 Aug 2026 10.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNicola Surgeon has said she will not visit her estranged husband, Peter Murrell, in prison, has stopped speaking to him and views herself as a “mug” for worrying about his wellbeing and mental health earlier this year.During a podcast recording at the Edinburgh festival fringe, Scotland’s former first minister said Murrell had lied to her until the day he pleaded guilty to embezzling more than £400,000 from the Scottish National party.He was imprisoned for five years in June, and Sturgeon revealed she had not spoken to him since then. She told the broadcaster Iain Dale she had only discovered Murrell was due to plead guilty a week before he appeared in court.She later found out he had been negotiating his plea for months.“[That] hit me like a tonne of bricks,” she said. “He was still lying to me right up until the day he pled guilty.”She added: “He was very isolated over that period, he very rarely left the house, he wasn’t communicative, I was a bit worried about his wellbeing and his mental health.“And then, now I think: ‘What a mug, why were you worried about him?’ He didn’t worry about me. He didn’t worry at all about what he was doing.“What he has subjected me to is beyond anything I could ever have comprehended. I don’t understand why he did it, he had no need to do it. I don’t think I will ever understand his motivations.“But whatever that motivation was, he could not have stopped and ever thought about me. But I was, until recently, still worrying about him.”Asked if she would visit him in prison, Sturgeon replied: “No. I’m not going to speak to him, I’m not going to visit him.”The former first minister said that when Murrell was in court she was still finding out details of the purchases he had made using party funds.“Over the years, he never really levelled with me,” she said. “The day he pled guilty, I was still learning about some of the detail of what he had done for the first time. I suddenly realised I had been living with somebody that I never really knew properly.“That’s something for me to come to terms with, and I don’t think I’m there yet, but also for my family to come to terms with. It’s a really difficult process.”Murrell, 61, spent the money on items including a motorhome, a Jaguar SUV and a VW Golf, boutique cosmetics, iPads and a pair of Lalique Feuilles salt and pepper grinders worth £2,618.Sturgeon, 55, has consistently denied knowledge of his crimes, which spanned the years 2010 to 2022, and was not charged after a police investigation.She has previously said she made an error of judgment by keeping Murrell on as SNP chief executive when she became party leader in November 2014, but refused to apologise for his crimes and denied ever “consciously” seeing the motorhome he bought and stored at her mother-in-law’s house.Explore more on these topicsNicola SturgeonScotlandScottish National party (SNP)Scottish politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Old racist wine in a new bottle’: Black academics respond to Jason Arday affair | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Figures in higher education feel double standards are being used to delegitimise work of minority groups
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Figures in higher education feel double standards are being used to delegitimise work of minority groups
Content: Jason Arday resigned from his role as a professor at the University of Cambridge this week.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Arday resigned from his role as a professor at the University of Cambridge this week.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianJason Arday‘Old racist wine in a new bottle’: Black academics respond to Jason Arday affairFigures in higher education feel double standards are being used to delegitimise work of minority groupsChris OsuhCommunity affairs correspondentSat 8 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Jason has to take responsibility for what he did. But when a white person makes mistakes, it’s just a story about them as an individual. When a Black person makes a mistake, it’s treated as collective – and used to undermine the very principle that Black people should be in these spaces,” one Black academic said this week, describing the impact of Jason Arday’s case on his peers.Arday, who was the University of Cambridge’s youngest Black professor when appointed in 2023, stepped down this week amid allegations of plagiarism and embellishing his CV.As well as allegations about his academic credentials, therehave been questionsraised about his claimed sporting achievements, his charity work and some of the abuse he says he received. Arday, 41, has admitted “mistakes”, but says he has been falsely framed as “this kind of liar and fantasist”.Whatever the truth of the claims, days of reporting describing sociologist Arday as a “diversity poster boy” have had a chilling effect on the UK’sBlack academics, already demoralised by the impact of cuts on Black scholarship. Many compared the response to the academic criticism with accusations against white academics that have passed with little fanfare.While views among Arday’s peers vary on the gravity of the accusations about his academic work – no formal investigation to date has found him guilty of plagiarism – opinion is united that Arday’s story has provoked a rightwing backlash against Black progress in academia and public life.“I think there’s a real question about whether these spaces are safe for us and whether we just have to start doing this outside universities,” says Kehinde Andrews, who was the first Black Studies professor in the UK but was recently made redundant from Birmingham City University.View image in fullscreenKehinde Andrews says the coverage of the Arday case is a ‘dedicated, coordinated smear campaign’.Photograph: Sonja Horsman/The ObserverAndrews added: “No matter how many cracks have appeared in [Arday’s] CV, it doesn’t change the fact that this is a dedicated, coordinated smear campaign from the right, based on the premise that Black people should not be at Cambridge. There’s so many other things that happen in higher education that are never discussed.”Andrews believes there were “problems with some of [Arday’s] scholarship,” but that they stopped short of plagiarism.For theeminent sociologist Paul Gilroy, responsibility for the row lies with the “culture warriors” who appointed Arday, as well as “racist critics” – and comes at a critical time for the sector.“Reckoning with Jason Arday and his impact-chasing enablers should not be allowed to obscure the vicious, irrationalcuts to humanitiesthat are wrecking UK universities,” Gilroy added.“The unthinking culture warriors who have supported [Arday] unconditionally share responsibility with his racist critics for making life harder for Black academics and dragging UK higher education deeper into the mire.”Few black academics are happy to speak about Arday’s case publicly. One academic said: “I can’t say anything on the record or I’ll be the right’s next target. The [right] have set their sights on pushing Black people out from all these institutions.“There’s awhite Cambridge academic who was accused of plagiarising a student’s work, kept his job and didn’t receive the same amount of media attention.”The row erupted this month after another academic – self-defined “race realist” Nathan Cofnas, who wassacked from his Cambridge role in 2024– alleged he had found plagiarism in Arday’s work. Cofnas had previously suggested in a blogpost that, in a meritocracy, there would be “close to zero” Black professors at Harvard.“It’s not just about Black people – any minoritised group, our success is generally seen as not being genuine,” said one academic, speaking anonymously.“[The row] will make the small number of Black people in the field feel much more vulnerable. It will give licence for a while to people who don’t want Black people in the academic space and it may give pause to people who want to redress the massive [racial] imbalance in academia.“But it’s a mistake to think of any of this as a meritocracy – there’s lots of people in academia who don’t deserve to be where they are, and there’s lots of people who should be more advanced in their careers than they are.”The takedown of Jason Arday has overjoyed the right, and must be a wake-up call for the left | Jason OkundayeRead moreAndrews said he was setting up an independent Black Studies centre, describing the university sector as “toxic”.“Academia is set up so that there’s these few places and we’re all fighting over scraps to get into these places,” he said. “It might just be time to say, let’s do it ourselves and let’s not keep relying on these institutions.”But while Arday’s case – and cuts to the humanities – negatively affect morale, many academics emphasised the proud history of Black scholarship, insisting the Arday affair must not be allowed to tarnish it.“Black British academics – likeStuart Hall, Paul Gilroy, Hazel Carby and Isaac Julien – punch way above their weight globally. The idea that this one incident in some way reflects Black British academia in general is bonkers,” one academic said.“There’s a bunch of people out there who think Black people are less intelligent than white people, and that the only way they can get anywhere is by being forced into situations that they are unqualified for. For those people, being Black is the definition of being unqualified. It’s an old racist wine in a new bottle.”Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayHigher educationAcademicsRacefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Can’t stop smiling!’ The wait is over for epic Game of Thrones prequel The Mad King  | Theatre | The Guardian
description: New play, which has been a decade in the works, opens at the Royal Shakespeare theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon after five previews were cancelled
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: New play, which has been a decade in the works, opens at the Royal Shakespeare theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon after five previews were cancelled
Content: Tanisha Spring, Elizabeth Ayodele, Mariah Gale, Callum Woodhouse, Michael Shaeffer, Harmony Rose-Bremner, Luke Brady, Noah Ritter and Michael Abubakar, the cast of Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Seamus Ryan © RSCView image in fullscreenTanisha Spring, Elizabeth Ayodele, Mariah Gale, Callum Woodhouse, Michael Shaeffer, Harmony Rose-Bremner, Luke Brady, Noah Ritter and Michael Abubakar, the cast of Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Seamus Ryan © RSCTheatre‘Can’t stop smiling!’ The wait is over for epic Game of Thrones prequel The Mad KingNew play, which has been a decade in the works, opens at the Royal Shakespeare theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon after five previews were cancelledChris WiegandStage editorSat 8 Aug 2026 06.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 06.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA winter of discontent is anticipated by the embattled characters in Game of Thrones, but the Royal Shakespeare Company is banking on a glorious summer with itsworld premiereof a prequel to the hit TV series based on George RR Martin’s fantasy novels.The new play,The Mad King, arrives 30 years to the month after the original publication of A Game of Thrones, the first novel in Martin’s series A Song of Ice and Fire. It has a gala performance in Stratford-upon-Avon on Saturday evening in a reconfigured Royal Shakespeare theatre with a capacity of 870. Tickets for the entire run, priced from £10 to £95, have already sold out.The RSC’s co-artistic directors,Daniel Evans and Tamara Harvey, have said that the epic play – which lasts 225 minutes including an interval – “thrillingly imagines events teased in the books” and they trumpet it as the “first-ever stage production arising from the canon of George RR Martin”. The Mad King bookmarks, handy for all those doorstop novels, are on sale in the RSC gift shop – although scripts for the play are not currently purchasable, leading to heated discussions on message boards about its plot, which involves familiar characters from the houses of Targaryen, Stark, Lannister, Baratheon and Martell. To “protect the magic” of the play, theatregoers with cameraphones are asked to cover them with stickers labelled “sworn shield”, a reference to a dutiful oath in Game of Thrones.View image in fullscreenNoah Ritter as Prince Rhaegar Targaryen and Harmony Rose-Bremner as Lyanna Stark in The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonThe play is adapted by Duncan Macmillan, who has worked on it for almost a decade. In the programme, Macmillan writes that its focus is a jousting tournament at Harrenhal – “a major event in Game of Thrones lore that has never been depicted on the page or on screen”. Macmillan added that he and director Dominic Cooke wanted to make a play “for fans and novices alike, a piece of theatre that sits inside the wider history but is also complete in its own right”. Macmillan and Cooke werefirst announcedin 2021 as collaborating on a Game of Thrones project for an unspecified venue.The Mad King – which unfolds on a cross-shaped stage with the audience all around and has a cast of three dozen – weathered a challenging period of previews. Five early performances were cancelled, with an announcement that “the actors, creative and technical teams [were taking] the additional time necessary to progress and refine the work in real time, owing to the ambitious and epic nature of the production and, as a knock-on effect of unforeseen delays to the fit-up process”. (A spokesperson for the RSC said that affected audiences were contacted to arrange refunds or to rebook their tickets.)The demand for tickets, alongside a sold out run ofThe Cherry Orchard(starringHelen Huntand Kenneth Branagh) in its Swan theatre, will help fill the company’s coffers after what Evans described last year as a“perilous situation”. A recent restructure has enabled the company to reduce its cost base by £2.8m a year. The RSC said the process was “not solely based on reducing our financial overheads” but also to help it “work as effectively and efficiently as possible and to position us to generate additional income to invest in the creation of theatre and learning through theatre, which is our founding purpose”.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Daniel Evans, Duncan Macmillan, George RR Martin, Tamara Harvey and Dominic Cooke.Photograph: Seamus Ryan © RSCBy transforming its stage into the world of Westeros for The Mad King, the RSC hopes to welcome audiences who are new to either its Stratford venue or to theatre more generally. In recent years, it has drawn upon existing IP with considerable success, including an adaptation of the Studio Ghibli filmMy Neighbour Totoro, also powered by imaginative puppetry like The Mad King. My Neighbour Totoro opened at the Barbican in London in 2022 andtransferred to the West End, where it will end its run in January.Among the audience at the Royal Shakespeare theatre on Friday night wasGame of Thronesfan Edward, 29, from Dudley, who said he had visited Birmingham Hippodrome and Wolverhampton Grand but it was his first time at the RSC. “I just can’t stop smiling – it’s so fun,” he said of the production, despite initially being “shocked when I saw the run time”. Another newcomer to the building was Aisha, 28, who had travelled from London.
