A fan of the franchise, Aisha said the play “compares very well to the books and films – they’ve done an amazing job”.View image in fullscreenMichael Shaeffer as King Aerys II Targaryen in The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonRachel, 51, comes to the RSC a couple of times a year, most recently foran adaptation of Roald Dahl’s The BFG, and said that mixing Shakespeare with such adaptations provides “a good variety”. Diane, 66, was there to see The Cherry Orchard and expressed frustration that the company’s two main stages had no Shakespeare this summer (a trimmed version ofA Midsummer Night’s Dream, made with the Unicorn children’s theatre, ison at its third venue, The Other Place.) “For me personally it’s disappointing. I know that sounds snobby, I don’t mean it to, but the name’s the RoyalShakespeareCompany … The balance is off. It’s a little bit of a betrayal of their name and raison d’etre but I’m well aware they have financial difficulties.” Diane acknowledged: “I’m probably the only one on earth who hasn’t watched [the TV series] … I know there’s a following that’s very loyal.”On the fan forumTheatreboard, people who had seen The Mad King variously praised its “full Shakespearean tragic resonance” and “Shakespearean-ish cadence”, with one saying that it was “on a par in theatrical terms with the London 2012 opening ceremony”.Steven and Bethany, both 30, recently moved to Stratford and saw theRSC’s Henry Vearlier this year. Bethany arrived “hoping for a dragon tonight!” and Steven said that they hadn’t expected the RSC to stage such a production. “It brings in more people who wouldn’t usually come to the theatre,” said Bethany. “They might enjoy the experience and see what else is on offer as well. With it being in Stratford, rather than London, you’re bringing in different crowds.”“You’d expect to see it on the West End rather than Stratford,” agreed Steven. TheRSC’s Hamlet Hail to the Thief, another bid to draw new audiences by accompanying the tragedy with a Radiohead album, opens in London this winter. The Mad King is widely tipped to follow hot on its heels.Explore more on these topicsTheatreGame of ThronesRoyal Shakespeare CompanyGeorge RR MartinFantasy booksFantasy TVTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: We’ve had fires here in the Cairngorms before. This one has changed things | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Abernethy: It’s been a period of heartbreak and gratitude, mourning the scorched landscape and staying away from home when the smoke got too close
Author: Amanda Thomson
Headline: Abernethy: It’s been a period of heartbreak and gratitude, mourning the scorched landscape and staying away from home when the smoke got too close
Content: Firefighting operations take place in the Cairngorms.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFirefighting operations take place in the Cairngorms.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty ImagesCountry diaryWildfiresCountry diary: We’ve had fires here in the Cairngorms before. This one has changed thingsAbernethy:It’s been a period of heartbreak and gratitude, mourning the scorched landscape and staying away from home when the smoke got too closeAmanda ThomsonSat 8 Aug 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 02.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParts of the Cairngorms have been on fire for over three weeks. Many places I take for granted that I can walk to are off-limits. Huge swathes of moorland that should be purple with heather, understoreys that should be thick with blaeberries, granny pines and younger trees, are scorched black. In places, the fires has burned down into the tree root system and the peat layer, and may smoulder for weeks.It’s been a period of uncertainty and despair. I’ll never forget the day the wind changed direction and a huge plume of smoke rose behind the trees immediately beyond our house. We waited to see if we would be evacuated, gathered passports, important documents, medicines, and packed a bag of clothes. When residents of nearby Nethy Bridge were advised toevacuate, we stayed with a friend just outside the perimeter for the night, something I never imagined having to do.By now, 25 square kilometres of internationally important moorland and forest have burned; the equivalent of 3,500 football pitches. I watch a video shot from a helicopter flying over the fire’s path and recognise An Lochan Uaine, the green lochanNan Shepherdso eloquently described, and the gully where I spotted merlins, close to where I’ve seen black grouse lek. The Cairngorms as a whole holds25% of the UK’s rare and endangered species.View image in fullscreenSmoke from a wildfire rises in the Cairngorms.Photograph: Cairngorms National Park Authority/AFP/Getty ImagesWe’ve hadfires here before, of course. They change how you look at things. Having grown up in a country where rain is “bad weather”, I’ve found myself in recent summers anxiously wishing for it, conscious of the dry forest. But this year’s fire feels like awake-up call. Home, a place of safety and security, feels more precarious now.From day one, volunteers, gamekeepers from neighbouring estates and others have joined the RSPB and the fire service infighting the flames. People have donated money for provisions, made food and shared information and reassurance. Many have invested a lifetime of care and stewardship here. It’s a strong community, and if we’re heartbroken, we know that in time this will become a landscape of recovery – and we will have to consider ourpreparednessfor future fires.For now, we’re grateful for the massive effort to contain it. This morning, the wind brought with it the smell of smoke, a reminder that it’s not over yet.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsWildfiresCountry diaryRural affairsClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Arron Banks ‘hired private detective’ to look into journalist who investigated Reform UK | Arron Banks | The Guardian
description: Asked whether he targeted reporter who investigated party finances, Brexit campaigner says: ‘When you live by the sword, you die by the sword’
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Asked whether he targeted reporter who investigated party finances, Brexit campaigner says: ‘When you live by the sword, you die by the sword’
Content: Arron Banks said he believed the Sunday Times used hacked information, an accusation the newspaper denied.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenArron Banks said he believed the Sunday Times used hacked information, an accusation the newspaper denied.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersArron BanksArron Banks ‘hired private detective’ to look into journalist who investigated Reform UKAsked whether he targeted reporter who investigated party  finances, Brexit campaigner says: ‘When you live by the sword, you die by the sword’Geraldine McKelvieSat 8 Aug 2026 07.11 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 13.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe prominent Reform UK member and Brexit campaigner Arron Banks is said to have set private investigators on a Sunday Times journalist after he broke a series of stories aboutNigel Farage.Banks is alleged to have paid for the services of investigators to examine Gabriel Pogrund, editor of the paper’s Insight investigations team.The detail emerged in the New Statesman on Friday. When approached for comment, Banks did not appear to deny it. He is said to have instructed Precision Risk and Intelligence, a firm he once owned, to examine Pogrund.The Sunday Times andthe Guardian have broken a series of storiesin recent months revealing how cash has poured into Reform and Farage personally from donors and wealthy benefactors.Pogrund is believed to have been targeted after a story in the Sunday Times last month revealed that Farage has receivedfinancial support from the convicted criminal George Cottrell, known as “Posh George”.In response to the New Statesman report, Banks said: “We believe theSunday Timesused hacked information and that was an area of interest. We do have an investigative arm that’s got advanced capabilities.”Asked directly whether he had paid investigators to look into Pogrund, he said: “When you live by the sword, you die by the sword.”The Sunday Times last night denied the accusation that its stories were based on illegally sourced information. The paper described the hiring of private investigators to snoop on its journalists as “reprehensible”.A spokesperson said: “If what Mr Banks claims to have done is true then it is reprehensible that his reaction to our reporting is to place a journalist under surveillance … This story was not based on hacked information. It was based on responsible and professional journalism.”The gifts theReform UKleader Nigel Farage received in the 12 months before being elected as MP for Clacton have been subject to widespread media scrutiny in recent months.MPs are obliged to declare any political donations they received in the year before their election but Farage has repeatedly claimed that it was not until the month before the general election, in July 2024, that he decided to stand. He has claimed he was not obliged to declare any donations he received before deciding to run for election, as he was a media personality at the time.Farage admission over timing of Reform leadership talks raises fresh doubts over £5m giftRead moreIn April, the Guardian reported that he had accepteda £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, a billionaire donor to Reform UK.The Sunday Times has reported that Cottrell paid for security, accommodation and social media support for Farage during this time. The newspaper also said that Cottrell helped to broker a “comeback deal” for Farage toreturn to Reform as party leadermonths before he announced he would stand.Cottrell’s mother, the retired stylist Fiona Cottrell, made a series of donations to Reform UK in the weeks before the general election. Two transfers of £250,000 were made directly to the party in May 2024.She then gave £1m to Britain Means Business, a company owned by Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice. Britain Means Business gave the party two donations of £250,000 shortly afterwards.The Guardian told how they later became the subject of a suspicious activity report by the National Crime Agency. Suspicious activity reports are not crime reports but exist to identify potential incidents of money laundering.The Metropolitan police are investigating Reform UK’s finances. The Guardian revealed that both George and Fiona Cottrell have been interviewed under caution but no arrests have been made.On Saturday morning, the Guardian asked Banks if Reform UK had known about or sanctioned the surveillance on Pogrund, or if any other journalists had been targeted.“I have nothing else to add,” he said. “Other than to say I have spoken to no one at Reform on this matter, nor would I.”A Reform UK spokesperson denied the party knew about or sanctioned the surveillance on Pogrund. He also denied that Reform had sanctioned or been made aware of surveillance on any other journalists.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsArron BanksReform UKParty fundingSunday TimesNigel FarageNewspapersNational newspapersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Widdecombe murder police reopen inquiry into alleged attempt to firebomb Farage’s home | UK news | The Guardian
description: Failure to pursue line of inquiry ‘which may have been relevant’ now being investigated by police watchdog
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Failure to pursue line of inquiry ‘which may have been relevant’ now being investigated by police watchdog
Content: The former Conservative minister Ann Widdecombe was found dead at her home in Devon on 9 July.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe former Conservative minister Ann Widdecombe was found dead at her home in Devon on 9 July.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianUK newsWiddecombe murder police reopen inquiry into alleged attempt to firebomb Farage’s homeWatchdog examines handling of an incident last year that was treated as an attempted burglaryDonna FergusonandNadeem BadshahSat 8 Aug 2026 04.59 EDTFirst published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCounter-terrorism police investigating the death of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into an incident last year, in which Nigel Farage’s home was allegedly firebombed.During the incident in April 2025, a lit incendiary device was pushed through the Reform UK leader’s letterbox, according to reports.Police did not identify any suspects during their investigation of the incident at the time, which was treated as an attempted burglary, and so the investigation was closed, pending any new lines of inquiry.Since the case was reopened, CTP London said it had identified a line of inquiry “which may have been relevant” but was “not identified and pursued by [counter-terrorism police] at the time”.The police watchdog said it was now investigating the conduct of a CTP London staff member over allegations that they “failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry”.Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing, said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by counter-terrorism policing south-east into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year.”CTP London made a “mandatory conduct referral” to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) on Friday.A spokesperson for the IOPC said: “We can confirm that the IOPC has decided to independently investigate the conduct of a counter-terrorism policing London staff member following a referral received earlier today.“The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025. Counter-terrorism policing London has been notified of our decision, and no further information is available at this early stage.”Widdecombe, 78, a Reform UK spokesperson and former Conservative minister, was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.Last month, a 28-year-old man was charged with the former MP’s murder. Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July.He was also arrested on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism but has not been charged with this offence.Devon and Cornwall police initially arrested a 26-year-old man from Newton Abbot in Devon, but later released him and said he was no longer part of the investigation.Widdecombe served as Conservative MP for Maidstone, Kent, for 23 years. She subsequently represented south-west England as a member of the European parliament for the Brexit party and in 2023 joined Reform UK .Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rising number of UK children report seeing explicit deepfakes of themselves | Deepfake | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: anonymous flagging service says cases have surged, as watchdog says AI is making sexualised or ‘nudified’ content easier to produce
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Exclusive: anonymous flagging service says cases have surged, as watchdog says AI is making sexualised or ‘nudified’ content easier to produce
Content: The Report Remove service said it had received 420 reports from children so far this year.Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Report Remove service said it had received 420 reports from children so far this year.Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty ImagesDeepfakeRising number of UK children report seeing explicit deepfakes of themselvesExclusive: anonymous flagging service says cases have surged, as watchdog says AI is making sexualised or ‘nudified’ content easier to produceDan MilmoGlobal technology editorSat 8 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChildren in the UK have reported a surge in explicitdeepfakeimages featuring their likenesses, as a safety watchdog warned AI is making such content easier to produce.The Report Remove service, which blocks intimate images from appearing online, said there had been a rapid increase in imagery that had been digitally manipulated or “faked” in some way, including with AI andnudification tools.In the first six months of this year it received 420 reports from children of images of themselves that they believed had been faked or manipulated to appear explicit. The number has already exceeded its 2025 total of 397.Dan Sexton, chief technology officer at the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF),which operates Report Removealongside the NSPCC children’s charity, said the figures underscored the difficulty of preventing online images from being manipulated in an age of widely available and capable AI tools.“If someone can take a benign image of a child from the internet and create child sexual abuse material with it, there is nothing that child can do to stop it from happening apart from preventing anyone from taking pictures of them – or not putting pictures of themselves online,” he said.Report Removehas received so many reports of manipulated images from under-18s in recent years that it has added a check box to its online submission form allowing them to flag the material as deepfaked.Sexton said the figures confirmed a fear that AI would improve in capability and be used to manipulate images of real people.“This is one of the harms we were worried about when we first saw AI image generators being used, that they would be used to create child sexual abuse material featuring real children,” he said.“Everyone in the world is at risk,” Sexton added.View image in fullscreenDan Sexton, the chief technology officer at the Internet Watch Foundation, said it was becoming easier to manipulate benign images of children.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianThe IWF, which monitors the distribution of child sexual abuse material [CSAM] online, said the majority of the reports of manipulated images made to Report Remove in 2025 and 2026 were so severe that they passed the CSAM threshold. AI-generated CSAM is illegal in the UK and the government has made it illegal to adapt an AI model to create abuse material or to distribute such models to others.Rani Govender, an online safety expert at the NSPCC, said tech companies must put stronger safety protections in their AI products to prevent the creation of explicit material.Misleading AI-generated doctors pose ‘huge danger to public safety’Read more“This rise in children reaching out because fake or AI‑generated sexual images have been created of them is alarming but also sadly predictable,” she said. “Tech companies cannot keep pushing out AI products without embedding strong protections that prevent this material from being created in the first place.”Sexton said some victims who had contacted Report Remove about manipulated images had been targeted for sextortion, where a blackmailer threatens to publish the material unless they receive financial payment or demands more explicit images from the victim.Report Remove is a service that allows children to anonymously flag intimate images or videos of themselves that have been sent to former partners, sextortion fraudsters or could appear online. The service turns those images into a “hash”, or digital fingerprint, which is shared with major tech platforms, which can take the image down or prevent it from being uploaded.The rise of AI-enabled deepfakes has prompted a series of warnings about posting identifiable pictures of children online.Last month the National Crime Agency and IWFencouraged parents and guardiansto keep pictures of their children away from public display online. They suggested making social media accounts private or sharing pictures of children through a “close friends” group only.The guidance also followed cases in which cybercriminals had attempted to blackmail schools by scraping pictures of children, using AI to convert them into child sexual abuse material, then threatening to publish the imagery. Schools have been urged to remove identifiable pictures of pupils’ faces from their websites and social media accounts.Explore more on these topicsDeepfakeInternet safetyChildrenChild protectionAI (artificial intelligence)Social mediaInternetnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We have no tents or blankets’: Ceuta migrants struggle to survive brutal heat and freezing nights | Refugees | The Guardian
description: Authorities wrestle with fallout from mass border crossing, as tense Spanish enclave fears it will happen again
Author: Okba Mohammad
Headline: Authorities wrestle with fallout from mass border crossing, as tense Spanish enclave fears it will happen again
Content: A woman from Morocco and other migrants wait and sleep in the open in Ceuta, Spain, on Thursday.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersView image in fullscreenA woman from Morocco and other migrants wait and sleep in the open in Ceuta, Spain, on Thursday.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersRefugees‘We have no tents or blankets’: Ceuta migrants struggle to survive brutal heat and freezing nightsAuthorities wrestle with fallout from mass border crossing, as tense Spanish enclave fears it will happen againOkba Mohammadin Ceuta andAshifa Kassamin MadridSat 8 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlong the wide avenues and tree-lined plazas of Ceuta’s centre, there were few hints of the recent events that catapulted the Spanish enclave on the north African coast into global headlines.But less than a mile away from the bustling bars and restaurants, at the nearby El Trampolín beach, the lingering impact was impossible to ignore.“We’re sleeping here on the beach, out in the open, without tents or blankets,” said Imad, 26, one of several thousand people believed to be still in Ceuta after last week’s extraordinary influx of more than 72,000 migrants into the Spanish territory on the edge ofMorocco.“We don’t have bathrooms,” added the Yemen national. “I barely manage two hours of sleep, as it’s incredibly cold by the sea at night, and during the day the heat is unbearable.”View image in fullscreenA man prays inside a makeshift mosque marked out with stones on El Trampolín beach in Ceuta, where hundreds of migrants have been sheltering.Photograph: Okba MohammadOne week on, whilequestions continue to swirlover what exactly prompted the incident, the city’s shops and markets have reopened and many of the 84,000 residents have resumed their daily routines.The scenes of normality clashed jarringly with a population left deeply rattled by the crisis, said Ceuta’s long-serving conservative leader. “Ceuta is on edge,” Juan Jesús Vivastold the broadcaster TVE. “Things have yet to return to normal – it’s as if 50 million people had entered Spain in a day.”One week after tens of thousands of people, referencing posts on TikTok, Instagram and WhatsApp among other platforms, swam or waded into the Spanish territory, there was little consensus on just how many people had arrived and how many had been returned, said Vivas.The Spanish government estimated that about 72,000 people had crossed into Ceuta and about 2,500 remained, while Vivas believed that about 80,000 had entered, with between 3,000 and 5,000 still in Ceuta.10:29How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe - The LatestThe precise number of people killed in the crossing also remains murky, with estimatesas highas 141. Dozens of people remain missing, suggesting the death toll of the crisis, already one of the worst humanitarian tragedies at Europe’s borders in recent years, will worsen.Adding to the tension are thefresh online poststhat have called for another mass crossing in mid-August, said Vivas. “People in Ceuta are nervous, they are worried. And this is absolutely logical, because the question we keep asking ourselves is: ‘Will this happen again?’”View image in fullscreenThe president of the autonomous city of Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, speaking to the media on Thursday.Photograph: Carlos Álvarez/Getty ImagesMany had been shaken by migrants’ reports oftheir crossing being encouraged, at times even facilitated, by Moroccan officials. “It has been demonstrated that our security and border are vulnerable and that both are in the hands of a third country that doesn’t recognise the sovereignty of Ceuta,” said Vivas. “Morocco is not a reliable country.”As Spain and the EU wrestle withthe wider political implications, the migrants who remain in the city have been left struggling to survive.Immediately after the influx the situation was terrible, said Imad, the 26-year-old from Yemen. “Everything was closed, and we were on the verge of dying of hunger and thirst,” he said. “They used hunger to pressure us into deciding to return on our own. We ate leaves from the trees and drank dirty water.”Map of CeutaThings had improved slightly in recent days, he said, as NGOs such as the Red Cross had begun providing them with food. On Thursday the Spanish government said it was installing toilets and additional showers on the beach, while police said they would open an information point.When Imad arrived inSpain, making his way across the border in an eight-hour, flipper-powered swimming odyssey, he envisioned it would be the end of an arduous journey that began in 2019 when he fled attempts by the Houthis to recruit him as a fighter.“I thought that, upon arrival – since I was arriving from a country at war – it would be easier for us to apply for asylum. But we found the reception centre for migrants closed. There were no exceptions for anyone; all the doors were locked.”He scrambled each day to find food and shelter, while the question of whether he would manage to request asylum loomed. “I have nightmares every day. I dream that my family is being bombed, that they are killed, or that I’m deported to Morocco,” he said. “Psychologically, I’m shattered.”Chaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streetsRead moreThose who remain in Ceuta include an estimated 1,300 unaccompanied children, with NGOs expressing concerns that hundreds more – including some as young as 10 – could be wandering the city unprotected.One 16-year-old told the Guardian that she had made her way to the city’s reception centre for minors on arrival, only to be told it was full. She had instead been sleeping rough on the streets of Ceuta. “I went days without food. When a woman brought food for the migrants, the men got there first, and we didn’t get anything. The same happened with clothing, when we managed to get to the front of the line, there was nothing left.”View image in fullscreenPeople who crossed from Morocco line up to use the public showers on El Trampolín beach in Ceuta, where hundreds have been sheltering for more than a week.Photograph: Okba MohammadShe had briefly considered going home. But she decided to stay after realising that this could be a singular opportunity to find a job that could help lift her family in Morocco out of poverty. “I just want to be a normal girl. I want to be able to get dressed, take a shower, eat well, have a place to sleep, study, work, and help my family,” she said.The situation had prompted neighbours in the Sidi Mbarek neighbourhood on the outskirts of Ceuta to take matters in their own hands.“We’re particularly concerned about the women and minors,” said Abdullah Abdullah Mustafa, the head of the Sidi Mbarek neighbourhood association. “Many are sleeping hidden in the hills for fear of being found and sent back to Morocco. That means there are minors living with hundreds of men in a situation of extreme vulnerability.”What they came up with was a makeshift shelter, setting up tents in a courtyard that were watched over each night by residents. “All we can offer them is a place to sleep with some degree of safety. We don’t have bathrooms, beds or any other resources,” he said. “We know that this isn’t a real solution and probably isn’t even legal, but leaving minors unprotected seemed much worse.”Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco?Read moreIt is one of the many examples of solidarity that have sprung up across Ceuta in recent days, from the dozen volunteerswho have been cookingday and night in a local flat to feed up to 400 people a day to the mammoth operation launched by the local NGO Luna Blancato hand outabout 5,000 meals a day.One resident, Aisha Ahmed Ammar, has taken to stopping by El Trampolín beach each day with her two children, bringing food and clothing, and broadcasting her mobile phone’s wifi signal to allow people to connect with their families back home.She said she had been moved by the people she had met, many of them asylum seekers from Sudan, Egypt or Yemen, and their readiness to care for those around them even as they had been seemingly abandoned by the international system meant to protect them.“I’ve been impressed by how respectful and polite they are,” she said. “When you offer them something, they often reply: ‘No, give it to someone who needs it more.’”But the enormity of the situation and the way in which it leaves residents such as herself on the frontlines, scrambling to do what she could in the face of Europe’s hardening borders, left her constantly fighting back tears. “You want to do more, but you can’t, and that fills me with immense sadness and a profound sense of helplessness,” she said. “It’s never enough.”Explore more on these topicsRefugeesSpainMoroccoMigrationAfricaEuropeMiddle East and north AfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US promises $1bn in security aid to Colombia as new rightwing president pledges drugs crackdown | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Trump ally Abelardo De La ‌Espriella vows to start ‘profound transformation’ of country’s destiny as he is sworn in
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Trump ally Abelardo De La ‌Espriella vows to start ‘profound transformation’ of country’s destiny as he is sworn in
Content: Abelardo de la Espriella, Colombia’s new president, speaks in Cali after being sworn in. ‘The time has come to restore order, authority and freedom.’Photograph: Jaime Saldarriaga/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAbelardo de la Espriella, Colombia’s new president, speaks in Cali after being sworn in. ‘The time has come to restore order, authority and freedom.’Photograph: Jaime Saldarriaga/AFP/Getty ImagesColombiaUS promises $1bn in security aid to Colombia as new rightwing president pledges drugs crackdownTrump ally Abelardo De La ‌Espriella vows to start ‘profound transformation’ of country’s destiny as he is sworn inGuardian staff and agenciesSat 8 Aug 2026 00.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ​Trump administration plans to provide $1bn in security assistance to the ⁠government of Colombia’s new ​rightwing ‌president, the US state department announced, soon after Abelardo De La ‌Espriella was sworn in and used his inaugural speech to pledge a vigorous fight against drug trafficking, as well as austerity measures to restore confidence in the economy.De La Espriella, 48,won June’s runoff electionwith ⁠promises to crack down on armed groups, shrink ⁠the state by as much as 40% and ​revive the oil and gas sector.“I have come to close a long chapter of national resignation and, together with the people, embark on the most profound transformation ⁠of our destiny,” De La Espriella said at the Pichincha Battalion military base in Cali after being sworn in on Friday.“I send a firm message to the Colombian people: the time has come to restore order, authority and freedom,” said De La Espriella, who received theendorsement of Donald Trumpbefore his runoff election.Colombia on the brink: ELN guerrilla group prepares for return to warRead more“Members of criminal gangs and narco-terrorist groups have two choices: submit to the ⁠rule of law or face the determined response of the Colombian state and its security forces,” the new president told assembled troops at the base during a 75-minute speech, adding the option of peace talks with armed groups had been “completely exhausted”.The US ⁠state department said in a statement on Friday: ⁠“As a cornerstone of this renewed partnership, the United States, working with Congress, ‌intends to announce $1 billion in assistance ​as part of a security package to support ⁠President de la Espriella’s ​Administration in ​achieving ​our shared goals.”De La Espriella’s ​election ispart of a rightward shift rippling across Latin America. In Peru, Argentina, Chile, Ecuador, Bolivia and Panama, weak ‌economies and rising crime have reshaped voter priorities, allowing once-fringe ‌hard-right candidates to gain traction by promising crackdowns amid a global rise of rightwing nationalism.View image in fullscreenAbelardo de la Espriella (C) salutes during the military recognition ceremony as part of the presidential inauguration day in Cali, Colombia.Photograph: Leonardo Castañeda/Getty ImagesDe La Espriella could push through some of his policies via decree, but analysts say many of his proposals will require backing from a divided congress and could ‌be watered down in negotiations.The new president vowed to “definitively eradicate the scourge of illicit crops”, saying he would use aerial herbicides that did not harm human health or the environment to destroy coca, the plant used to make cocaine. In one of his first acts as president, Colombia would join the Shield of theAmericasprogram founded by Trump, he said.Before his inauguration, he held bilateral meetings with ​the king of Spain and the presidents of Argentina, Ecuador, Chile, Paraguay and Panama. Also attending was Gianni Infantino, the embattled head of Fifa, football’s world governing body, while the US sent a delegation headed by the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche.De La Espriella has blamed former president Gustavo Petro, who has not recognised the new president’s victory, for an expansion of armed groups, andnarrowly defeated leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda– a Petro ally – in the runoff.Cepeda led a morning march on Friday in Barranquilla, where he told demonstrators that the country’s opposition would work to defend democracy and called for peaceful civil disobedience.With ReutersExplore more on these topicsColombiaTrump administrationAmericasUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Germans hogging the sunloungers? Poll finds Italians and French are worse | Europe | The Guardian
description: British and Germans themselves share stereotype but other nationalities are likelier to put out towels – or umbrellas
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: British and Germans themselves share stereotype but other nationalities are likelier to put out towels – or umbrellas
Content: Between 51% and 63% of people said they had found themselves deprived of a sunlounger because they were all taken.Photograph: vanbeets/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenBetween 51% and 63% of people said they had found themselves deprived of a sunlounger because they were all taken.Photograph: vanbeets/Getty Images/iStockphotoEuropeGermans hogging the sunloungers? Poll finds Italians and French are worseBritish and Germans themselves share stereotype but other nationalities are likelier to put out towels – or umbrellasAngela Giuffridain RomeSat 8 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGermans are sunlounger hoggers, or so the longstanding stereotype goes. But not only is that cultural trope mostly confined to British – and, even more so, German – perceptions, surprising new data reveals that in fact Italian and French holidaymakers are the ones most likely to use their towel to stake their claim to a sunlounger.A poll by YouGov of Europeans holidaymakers found that while many Germans (51%) and Britons (46%) associate Germans with the ritual of waking up at the crack of dawn to mark their spot, the perception barely exists elsewhere inEurope, with just 5-17% of those surveyed in other countries sharing the stereotype.Furthermore, just 38% of German holidaymakers – as in those who stay in places that have pools and sunloungers – said they have ever reserved a lounger with a towel compared with 45% of their Italian and French counterparts. Britons were the least likely to admit to hogging a lounger (33%).Across all countries polled, YouGov found that most people (60-82%) considered the practice unacceptable. Still, it appears to be rampant, with 51-63% saying they had found themselves deprived of a sunlounger because they were all taken, and 14-28% admitting to resolving matters by removing somebody else’s towel.When the Guardian asked a number of Italians in Rome, nobody admitted to the practice, although they could believe the data.“I would never do it but I have seen it happen,” said Claudia Morani, a teacher, adding that during a recent stay in a hotel with a swimming pool she had witnessed plenty of fellow Italians “leaving their towels on the loungers at the end of the day so they could use the same ones the next morning”.Morani added: “This kind of thing happens a lot on beaches here, too – the free ones.”Indeed, possibly even worse than sunlounger hoggers, some Italian beachgoers are cultivating a reputation asfurbetti dell’ombrellone,or umbrella cheats, a name coined by the press to refer to people who leave their umbrellas pitched overnight in their quest to reserve coveted spots by the sea.View image in fullscreenUmbrellas on a beach in Villasimius, Italy.Photograph: Fabrizio Villa/Getty ImagesThe practice is a growing trend on free-access beaches, unlike the private concessions that dominate much of Italy’s coastline during summer and from which Italians are increasingly turning away because of high prices.Such is the extent of the problem, coastal authorities across Italy specifically target thefurbetti dell’ombrelloneas part of their national beach and lake safety campaign.In late July, authorities in asuburb of Naples seized 40 items, including umbrellas, loungers and deckchairs, during a dawn sweep of a popular free beach. Similar blitzes have recently occurred on beaches in Puglia and Sardinia. Fines of up to €500 are in place for those caught, while reclaiming the confiscated personal belongings involves a bureaucratic ordeal.“This has become a bit of a habit,” said Danilo Ruggiero, an activist with Mare Libero, a national network fighting to reclaim beaches from private concessions. “I think it’s more related to people not wanting to carry umbrellas, chairs and other equipment back and forth from home, especially in the heat. But there is a tendency to try to get the best position by the sea, and this shouldn’t be done.”As forFrance, when the Guardian spoke about YouGov’s findings to two people living in the south, they were not surprised to hear that the French were partial to sunlounger hogging. “I see it all the time at my local beach club,” said Chantal Henry, who lives in Menton, close to the Italian border. “I get really fed up with it.” Her friend Virginie Pascual alleged: “It is always the Italians.”However, a Briton living in France, who wanted to remain anonymous as they had German colleagues, was adamant Germans were by far the biggest culprits. “I saw it in Mallorca – it was 5.30am and a German dude was hogging five loungers with towels,” they said.Explore more on these topicsEuropeGermanyItalyFrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: Human Centipede director Tom Six reveals multiple sclerosis diagnosis in ‘final film’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Dutch creator of the controversial trilogy set to detail struggles with neurological disease in homemade documentary, after spending six years ‘as a recluse’
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: The Dutch creator of the controversial trilogy set to detail struggles with neurological disease in homemade documentary, after spending six years ‘as a recluse’
Content: ‘I’m a morbid lump of untouchable howling flesh’ … a scene from The End of Tom Six.Photograph: Courtesy of Tom SixView image in fullscreen‘I’m a morbid lump of untouchable howling flesh’ … a scene from The End of Tom Six.Photograph: Courtesy of Tom SixMoviesHuman Centipede director Tom Six reveals multiple sclerosis diagnosis in ‘final film’The Dutch creator of the controversial trilogy set to detail struggles with neurological disease in homemade documentary, after spending six years ‘as a recluse’Philip OltermannEuropean culture editorSat 8 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom Six, the film-maker behind schlock horror phenomenon The Human Centipede, has revealed that he has been living as “a full-blown recluse” in a darkened Amsterdam apartment for six years after being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis.In The End of Tom Six, a homemade documentary that the Dutch director said would be his final film, he says that the stress over his failure to find a distributor for the follow-up to the Centipede trilogy significantly exacerbated his condition.Released in 2009, independently produced The Human Centipede tells the story of a crazed scientist, played by German actor Dieter Laser, who kidnaps three tourists and surgically conjoins them in a chain, mouth to anus.The film performed modestly at the box office but the horrific medical experiment of its title became global pop culture lore, cited in South Park and The Simpsons.In 2011 and 2015, Six made two sequels that each referenced the previous film, to create a “movie centipede”. In 2018 the film-maker released a trailer for The Onania Club, about a group of wealthy women who get turned on by extreme human suffering, but the film failed to pick up a distributor.View image in fullscreen‘A strong appetite for self-destruction’ … The End of Tom Six.Photograph: Courtesy of Tom SixIn The End of Tom Six, which is being released on a pay-what-you-want model on YouTube on 15 August, Six reveals he has spent the last six years “as a recluse” after being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS) in 2020.MS is a neurological disease that affects the brain and spinal cord. Symptoms and the severity of the condition vary from patient to patient, but can include extreme fatigue, vision and memory problems, muscle cramps, spasms and stiffness, and difficulties with or loss of mobility.“I can’t walk any more, reducing me to worming through my house like [a] fucking gargoyle,” the 52-year-old says in the film, in which he plays both himself and the director conducting the interview. “I’m a morbid lump of untouchable howling flesh.”While Six notes that many MS sufferers make an effort to eat healthily and exercise after their diagnosis, he says he has a “strong appetite for self-destruction”, with “a black belt in ego demolition”.He describes a daily routine that consists of lying on a Chinese opium bed in silk pyjamas, bingeing opioids and film noir movies, smoking Havana cigars and eating chicken curry, chocolate mousse and peanut butter. He doesn’t leave his home apart from night-time trips to a nearby cafe, for decaffeinated coffee.Six says he did not reveal his medical condition at the time of his diagnosis because “I hate being a victim and get pity”.The second half of his final film is mostly a complaint against “woke cowardice” and “safe-space crybabies” in the film industry, which he blames for the failure to get The Onania Club released. He said that the project was densely interwoven with references to global elite conspiracies and which would have become “even more of a success than The Human Centipede”.Throughout the film, a “censor nazi” in an SS uniform interrupts the interview to point out which scenes will need to be cut or fitted with trigger warnings.“The prolonged, extremely stressful battle accelerated his disease and totally ravaged his body up to the point that he is now nearing the end of his life,” Six’s producer Maartje Willems said in a statement accompanying the film’s release.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMultiple sclerosisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Can Harvey Nichols find its way back to being Absolutely Fabulous again? | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Mike Ashley says it’s in a ‘death spiral’ but a refocus on design could be what the department store needs
Author: Lauren Cochrane
Headline: Mike Ashley says it’s in a ‘death spiral’ but a refocus on design could be what the department store needs
Content: Harvey Nichols has tried to revive its bricks and mortar offering recently, particularly its London Knightsbridge store.Photograph: John Keeble/GettyView image in fullscreenHarvey Nichols has tried to revive its bricks and mortar offering recently, particularly its London Knightsbridge store.Photograph: John Keeble/GettyRetail industryCan Harvey Nichols find its way back to being Absolutely Fabulous again?Mike Ashley says it’s in a ‘death spiral’ but a refocus on design could be what the department store needsLauren CochraneSat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSuch was the buzz around Harvey Nichols in its 90s heyday that the department store was regularly name-checked in Absolutely Fabulous, with Edina and Patsy’s frequent retail therapy trips to the store reflecting its position at the heart of the fashion industry at the time.How times change. These days Harvey Nichols is a business in trouble, one that has not turned a profit since the pandemic. Pre-tax losses were £35.3m in 2024. The retail chain – comprising the the original store in Knightsbridge, London, plus stores in cities including Bristol, Leeds and Manchester – was put up for sale in June by its current owner, Sir Dickson Poon, with Mike Ashley’sFrasers Groupand Next bidding to take control.Ashley commented this week that Harvey Nichols is in what he called “a death spiral”. Speaking to theFinancial Timesabout his potential bid, he said taking it over would be a “huge challenge”. Harvey Nichols is reported to be seeking £50m-£60m for the business, while Ashley said he thought the figure would be closer to £40m in order for a deal to happen.All that is a far cry from the 90s, when Tony Glenville, who worked as a fashion journalist at the time, recalls: “It was glamorous. It had the marvellous bar up on the fifth floor so the whole thing was that you went shopping and you had a drink.”Thirty years on, retail experts suggest that, if not a death spiral, the store no longer has the same cachet. “It’s a brand that has lost its identity,” says Jonathan De Mello, founder of JDM Retail Consulting. “It’s very similar to other department stores in the sense that it provides fashion that you can get from Selfridges or Harrods. It’s not got the point of difference.”View image in fullscreenJennifer Saunders and Joanna Lumley as Edina and Patsy in the Absolutely Fabulous.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyHarvey Nichols was founded in 1831, as a linen shop, with the current department store in Knightsbridge following in 1889. It was taken over by Debenhams in 1920 and became part of the Burton Group in 1985, with Poon purchasing the retailer six years later and beginning its expansion outside London with a Leeds opening in 1996. “It was always changing,” remembers Glenville. “If a designer came along and was hot that season, they would immediately want to be in Harvey Nichols and Harvey Nichols would then stock them.”Fast forward three decades and other stores have come for this territory, with London’s Dover Street Market and Selfridges more likely destinations for emerging brands. De Mello argues, however, that there could still be mileage in this strategy.“They had a strong design forward focus … and they need to do more [of that],” he says. “If you can’t get [a brand] anywhere else and you have to go to Harvey Nichols, then it becomes something interesting again. At the moment, you walk past it and say ‘Why bother going in?’”However, De Mello says Harvey Nichols’s digital presence needs work. “The majority of retailers that succeed in today’s marketplace do so with a variety of different channels to interface with the consumer,” he argues. “So they can essentially experience the brand wherever they might be or whatever they might be doing.”If digital is still a work in progress, Harvey Nichols has attempted to revive its bricks and mortar offering recently, particularlyits Knightsbridge store. Julia Goddard, previously at Alexander McQueen, has been chief executive since 2024, with highly respected fashion editor Kate Phelan becoming creative director.View image in fullscreenThe Harvey Nichols Christmas shop window display in Leeds city centre.Photograph: Richard Saker/The ObserverA 2025 redesign put high-end jewellery on the ground floor and added new designers and curated objects. In a press release, Phelan described it as a “statement of intent. We’re creating an experience that feels relevant, exciting and, above all, individual. This is just the beginning of what’s to come.” The retailer declined to comment for this article.Buzz-wise, Glenville believes the team should remain in place whoever buys the retailer, and given time to turn things around. “The [recent]windowswith the illustrations were absolutely great,” he says “[but] I think they weren’t sure what to follow that with. It’s unfortunate that anything takes time. You can’t do it all in five minutes.”Explore more on these topicsRetail industryMike AshleyFrasers GroupfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Union calls for robust review of OBR over fears it holds back economic growth | Office for Budget Responsibility | The Guardian
description: TUC will urge John Healey to order ‘root and branch’ assessment of watchdog amid claims its forecasts downplay investment benefits
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: TUC will urge John Healey to order ‘root and branch’ assessment of watchdog amid claims its forecasts downplay investment benefits
Content: The TUC accuses the OBR of downplaying the benefits of public investment, for schemes such as Crossrail (above) by assuming it ‘crowds out’ private capital.Photograph: Victoria Jones/PAView image in fullscreenThe TUC accuses the OBR of downplaying the benefits of public investment, for schemes such as Crossrail (above) by assuming it ‘crowds out’ private capital.Photograph: Victoria Jones/PAOffice for Budget ResponsibilityUnion calls for robust review of OBR over fears it holds back economic growthTUC will urge John Healey to order ‘root and branch’ assessment of watchdog amid claims its forecasts downplay investment benefitsHeather StewartSat 8 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe TUC is urging the new chancellor, John Healey, to order a “root and branch” review of theOffice for Budget Responsibility, claiming the forecaster’s approach holds back investment.With Andy Burnham promising“good growth in every postcode”, the union umbrella body is calling on Healey to usehis first budget on 28 Octoberto re-examine the assessments of the watchdog.In particular, it accuses the OBR of downplaying the benefits of public investment, by assuming it “crowds out” private capital – an approach disputed by some economists.Paul Nowak, the TUC’s general secretary, said: “For too long, the OBR has been a millstone preventing good growth across the country.OBR a backseat driver with out-of-date maps, thinktanks tell Rachel ReevesRead more“The world has moved on from the self-defeating logic of austerity, but the OBR models still bake in its false assumptions. Only a root and branch review can bring the OBR into the modern economic mainstream.”The TUC’s critiqueechoes calls for a restructuring of the independent forecasterfrom a range of thinktanks and campaign groups, including Progress, from the right of the Labour party, and the leftwing New Economics Foundation.Louisa Dollimore, of the Good Growth Foundation thinktank, previously called the body “a backseat driver with out-of-date maps” that “obstructs long-term planning and investment at a moment when Britain needs both”.View image in fullscreenPaul Nowak, general secretary of the TUC.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAHealey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, recently picked economics professor Jonathan Haskel as the next chair of the OBR, after theresignation of Richard Hughes last December, after the OBR inadvertently published details of the budget in advance.Haskel, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, will have to oversee a new economic forecast to inform this year’s budget.He told MPs on the Treasury select committee last month that he was more pessimistic about the outlook than some other experts. “My ⁠forecast would be in the medium term of somewhat higher interest rates and weaker GDP growth than ​most are expecting,” he said.Haskel also told the committee in a public hearing that Britain was “not in a very good fiscal position”.The TUC is also calling on the chancellor to beef up investment bodies such as the National Wealth Fund (NWF), to take advantage of flexibility built into the fiscal rules.Reeves revised the rules so that government borrowing does not count against Treasury targets if it is matched by a financial asset – such as a share in a company or a loan.The TUC says this should allow for significant additional investment by government-backed institutions including the NWF and the National Housing Bank.The NWFinvests in infrastructure projects and backs British businesses, in an effort to boost growth and “crowd in” private investors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe TUC is calling on the government to change the NWF’s mandate to allow it to pick investments that could take as long as 15 years to generate a return in order to widen the pool of suitable projects.Nowak said: “Amid global economic turmoil, Labour has delivered the second fastest growth in the G7. That’s partly down to the government’s fiscal rules that rightly allow more borrowing for investment.“But the government needs to do more to release the handbrake. An ambitious application of the existing fiscal rules and a wider mandate for the National Wealth Fund can reindustrialise Britain.”Healey urged to be bold on borrowing in first test of Burnham’s growth pledgeRead moreSome economists have raised concerns about the potential impact on the bond market of increased borrowing. On Friday, the consultancy firm OxfordEconomicssaid: “The UK’s fiscal position is poor, while there’s an underlying wariness about the new PM’s commitment to fiscal sustainability.“While Healey has been saying all the right things, it’s what the new administration does that will be key. If the first move is to loosen policy, despite no underlying improvement in the public finances, that risks sending a signal that markets won’t like.”A Treasury spokesperson said: “Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of economic stability and national security.“The chancellor and prime minister are in lockstep that the government will meet the fiscal rules, with a buffer against uncertainty – and that includes getting debt down.“As has always been the case, the chancellor will set out decisions at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on proposals.”Explore more on these topicsOffice for Budget ResponsibilityBudget deficitEconomic policyEconomicsGovernment borrowingInvestmentsTUCnewsShareReuse this content

title: Is it OK to talk about Ariana Grande’s body? There is no right answer | Ariana Grande | The Guardian
description: I wish I could say that expressing concern for the pop star’s health is helpful – but I know from experience it’s not that simple
Author: Emma Madden
Headline: I wish I could say that expressing concern for the pop star’s health is helpful – but I know from experience it’s not that simple
Content: Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignAriana GrandeIs it OK to talk about Ariana Grande’s body? There is no right answerI wish I could say that expressing concern for the pop star’s health is helpful – but I know from experience it’s not that simpleEmma MaddenSat 8 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTShareThe last time I opened X, a photo ofAriana Grandeleaning over in a low-cut black dress, clavicle showing, was at the top of the feed. The post read: “hey @grok make Ariana Grande healthy and fat”.Images of celebrities at their most skeletal regularly rise to the top of social feeds because they generate enormous, dissenting engagement. Social media platforms have made half-hearted efforts tosuppressexplicit pro-eating disorder content; Instagram and TikTok redirect searches for “thinspo” toward support resources. Yet over the past couple weeks, Grande has sent users into a frenzy that outstrips the platforms’ attempts.The screenshot the user posted was taken from Grande’s music video for Petal, the title track from her latest album. Grande and her team have not said that she lives with any kind of eating disorder. Nevertheless, promotion for Petal has been thoroughly overshadowed by discussion of the singer’s ultra-thin body.double quotation markSomeone who is suffering can mistake isolation for self-preservationOther replies to the screenshot ranged from vicious attacks on Grande and other users’ bodies, to earnest, almost desperate pleas for empathy. Having lived with an eating disorder as a teenager, I recognize in these reactions a familiar pattern. People often respond to the visibly suffering body with a visceral pity intertwined with a kind of disgust. Whether that response actually protects anyone, or instead solidifies the very dynamics it seeks to resist, is a question worth returning to.Those of us who have lived through eating disorders and are witnessing this news cycle feel compelled to offer our own interpretations – to explain what this moment means, and to argue for the “right” way to speak about it. But precisely because disordered eating is so idiosyncratic and so forceful, there may be no single correct language for confronting it. The only honest response may be to acknowledge its contradictions.In the case of Grande, all of the prayers, best wishes and outcries so far haven’t provoked the public response so many have hoped for. Instead, it appears to have pushed her in the opposite direction. Over the weekend, just days after the release of Petal, arepresentative toldPeople magazine that Grande would be “taking a step back from visibility” after her current tour, cancelling future promotional plans and withdrawing from an upcoming West End revival of Sunday in the Park With George. At a recent concert, Grandeexplained to fansthat stepping back from the spotlight was something she had planned “a long time ago” and that it came from a “thoughtful and empowered place”.‘I had fantasies about how it would eventually serve me’: my struggle with disordered eatingRead moreIf this were a case of disordered eating, a retreat from public life might seem like a positive step towards recovery. But I know from experience that someone who is suffering can mistake isolation for self-preservation. The cruelty of an eating disorder is how easily it convinces you that it is the only thing standing between you and a world trying to take control away from you.Concerns over Grande’s body have hovered since the beginning of her teenage acting career. In 2013, the year she released her debut album, Yours Truly, she took to her old Tumblr account – which has itself been accused of “pro-ana” content, or content promoting disordered eating – to address “the rumors going around.” In ablogpostshe wrote that reports of “this whole ‘eating disorder thing’” had been “a bit blown out of proportion”.“Yes, I lost a bit of weight last year,” she continued. “It’s because I stopped eating junk food and started making healthy choices. I was happy with the way I was before and I’m still happy now! Just healthier!”More than a decade later, she made much the same point in a TikTok after people posted side-by-side photos of her during the Wicked press tour and the years when she acted on the Nickelodeon show Victorious. “The body you’ve been comparing my current body to was the unhealthiest version of my body,” she said in April 2023. “I was on a lot of antidepressants and drinking on them.”Her response reminded me of something the singer Fiona Apple said in 2013, after years of speculation about her weight. While performing on stage, Apple exploded at a heckler who shouted: “get healthy”. “I’m healthy and I shouldn’t even have to say any of that,” AppletoldPitchfork the next day. “What makes me unhealthy and puts me in danger is that kind of scrutiny itself.”double quotation markThe confused discourse surrounding Grande’s weight mirrors the paradox [of disordered eating]Avoiding scrutiny can become part of an eating disorder itself. I know this because I suffered for many years with bulimia, and I now realize my years spent hiding in the bathroom after every meal was an attempt to withdraw from any kind of outside opinion. When friends hugged me and recoiled at the touch of my bones, that only influenced me to raise the wall between myself and the rest of the world. It was an untenable and, frankly, devastating attempt to cope with the terror of puberty, trying all I could to stay both in control and independent of my body and its radical changes.On several levels, disordered eating is built on irreconcilable tensions. It requires relentless self-control while submitting to an all-consuming fixation. In seeking to disappear, the thin body only becomes a spectacle of morbid curiosity. What usually begins as an effort to master the self soon becomes an act of self-destruction. The confused discourse surrounding Grande’s weight mirrors the paradox. Every word feels stuck in place, because we don’t yet have a cultural script capable of holding all these ambiguities.It is obvious and true that the bodies of female celebrities are uniquely surveilled. It’s why Billie Eilishresisted that surveillanceby wearing oversized clothing and criticizing the public’s sense of entitlement to judge her body – a tacticGrande employed, too, in 2018, a year after the devastatingManchester Arena bombing.For much of the 2010s, the body positivity movement supplied a simple injunction against prying eyes: don’t comment on women’s bodies. It corrected for the smarmy and misogynistic tabloid treatment of celebrities in the aughts, discouraging public discussion of other people’s bodies as intrusive, harmful and unnecessary.But it might have been an overcorrection. Grande’s appearance presents a case where that consensus no longer feels entirely adequate, or ethically tenable. But it’s complicated. Two feminist arguments are at odds. The first is that women should not have to submit their bodies to public interpretation or explanation. The second is that eating disorders thrive in secrecy and denial. We do not want a culture that treats visible suffering – and conversations around them – as too taboo to acknowledge.After all, Grande has long featured in thinspo Pinterest boards. On private pro-ana message boards, users have found recognition in her public statements. “The whole ‘don’t worry about me’ and ‘the old me was sad and unhealthy’ sounds like people responding to an intervention lol,” one user wrote. On the pro-ana internet, Grande’s body is both hailed as aspirational and a huge trigger. In eating-disorder recovery Reddit communities, users describe her as the reason for their “relapse”, putting them back into the mindset of their illness. Beneath the now widely circulated photograph of Grande bending over, users in the underground X communityknown as EDTwthave openly compared themselves to her body and wondered how they might achieve a similar appearance.Ozempic is hailed as a miracle drug. But how does it affect people with eating disorders?Read moreMore broadly, her body has also become a proxy on to which wider cultural anxieties are projected. In a moment of GLP-1 drugs reinstating the aspiration of thinness, body positivity in retreat, bonesmashing still on the up, and Maga tradwives once again moralizing fatness, fears about the return of aughts-era anorexia have settled on to Grande herself. Whether or not those fears belong to her alone is almost beside the point. Her body has become the site through which the culture argues with itself.She is hardly the first celebrity on to whom those anxieties have been projected. From Karen Carpenter’s collapse from starvation at her parent’s home in 1983 to the many stars who have since publicly disclosed eating disorders – including Demi Lovato, Taylor Swift and Kesha – it is almost assumed that a significant portion of the female entertainment industry has, or has had, some form of eating disorder. The illness is simultaneously embedded within ordinary culture and yet treated as an aberration whenever it becomes visible.The desire to resolve those contradictions might even keep us at the distance the illness relies on, allowing us to imagine that a single correct response will absolve us of having to deal with it in the first place. Instead we could try broadening our concern towards the millions living with eating disorders by petitioning to improve a medical system that has so oftenfailedthem; insurers that routinelydeny careif the patient’s BMI is anything other than extremely emaciated; and clinicians who stillstigmatizethe illness.Grande’s visibility isn’t moving down the feed. People are continuing to debate it, defend it, plead for us to find another way to talk about it. But ultimately, another person’s physical and mental reality is out of our control; no one person’s recovery can be crowdsourced. If only it were all as simple as Grok editing Grande into health.In the US, help is available atnationaleatingdisorders.orgor by callingANAD’seating disorders hotline at 800-375-7767. In the UK,Beatcan be contacted on 0808-801-0677. In Australia, theButterfly Foundationis at 1800 33 4673. Other international helplines can be found atEating Disorder Hope

title: ‘I hate what AI is doing to the minds and happiness of the young’: Katherine Rundell on the view from the classroom | Books | The Guardian
description: Education is at a crossroads, argues the author and academic. Should we embrace new technology in the name of efficiency, or is it time to fight back?
Author: Katherine Rundell
Headline: Education is at a crossroads, argues the author and academic. Should we embrace new technology in the name of efficiency, or is it time to fight back?
Content: Illustration by Mojo WangBooks‘I hate what AI is doing to the minds and happiness of the young’: Katherine Rundell on the view from the classroomEducation is at a crossroads, argues the author and academic. Should we embrace new technology in the name of efficiency, or is it time to fight back?Katherine RundellSat 8 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 08.08 EDTShareIf you set out to design from scratch a tool to facilitate authoritarian rule, it would look exactly like AI. You would cherish it for its ability to destabilise our shared reality and its creation of disinformation on a scale unprecedented in human history. With it you need no armies of typists and artists to spread your propaganda. It can enable mass surveillance and thereby put shackles on those who seek to resist you. Its lethal autonomous weapons systems can perfect and normalise remote killing. It will turbocharge inequality; it is already facilitating a breathtaking shift of power and wealth from the hands of the many to the hands of a tiny number of men who – to put it in terms for which I can’t be sued – seem to hold dangerously damaged views about the value and dignity of human life.AI could be a magnificent thing. It could revolutionise medicine, speed the cure of cancer, assist disabled people, transform the way we are able to understand data, democratise access to the law, bolster disaster early warning systems and uncover hitherto unimagined truths about the Earth’s ecosystems. But if it ends up in the hands of crooks and despots that will be completely irrelevant.Most of all, if you were a would-be autocrat, you would love the way that large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s Gemini have thrown a grenade into thousands of years of teaching and learning: the way they threaten to upend our ability to think with the robust clarity that is needed in emergencies of justice. I write fiction for children and I hold a fellowship at Oxford University, so I spend a lot of time working with, and for, young people. I’ve seen first-hand the way that generative AI has already infiltrated young people’s lives. I’ve seen, at the same time, how it has thrown stark and urgent light on how fundamental books and reading are to our shared understanding of who we are, and to our democracy.There are many things I hate unequivocally about AI. I hate that it can make counterfeit people; computer-generated humans that risk destabilising our entire civilisation. I hate that much of AI’s LLMs were built on an illegal pillage of human labour. I hate the environmental catastrophe that AI brings with it: the yearly electrical demand of AI-optimised data centres is predicted, by the end of this decade, to exceed that of the whole of Japan. I hate that it may be the factor that tips the Earth’s ecosystems into irreparable chaos.And I hate what it is doing to the minds, and the happiness, of the young. Going into schools, I meet thousands of children a year and every day I become more certain that, if justice for all is to be our organising principle, AI is not for children and not for young people. It risks becoming an iron curtain that comes down between a young person and their potential for thinking, for experiment and conquering frustration, for stamina and for invention – and thereby, between the young people and their freedom. It risks halting learning before it can take flight.double quotation markAI, we’re told, will make learning more efficient. But is that what we dream of for our kids – an efficient childhood?Studies show, over and over, that when we engage in AI-assisted learning we give up sooner. One found that after just “10 minutes of AI-assisted problem-solving, people who lost access to the AI performed worse and gave up more frequently than those who never used it”. An MIT study showed that test groups who used ChatGPT had the lowest brain activity and “consistently underperformed at neural, linguistic, and behavioural levels”. We undergo not just cognitive offloading, but cognitive surrender: we forget what was possible.Children, we have known for a long time, take deeper meaning from text on paper than on screen, in part because we’re tactile creatures and the brain is also of the body; but we are now living through a surge of ed tech driving learning increasingly online, such that my teenage goddaughter tells me that almost every single member of her class is using ChatGPT to do their homework. More, the work they produce in AI’s greasy little fluent voice is often mistaken by young people themselves for their own mastery. If the work a child produces is no longer an indicator of their understanding, we have put them in a situation that makes them vulnerable to their desire for speed and to their anxiety about looking stupid; we risk becoming the unwitting thieves of our children’s intellectual clarity.Those who work in ed tech promise that it will liberate teachers and create one-to-one learning experiences for children from disadvantaged backgrounds. Certainly, AI teaching will be cheaper than teaching assistants. But we know that the second it becomes possible for an institution to achieve an end cheaply – even if it’s far worse – there is immense pressure from above to do so. I think it’s more likely that the rich schools will follow the lead of Sweden, which has taken a strong swerve towards non‑tech‑based learning, and Norway, which just all but banned AI in elementary classrooms – while poorer schools are left to make ever-greater use of LLM technology.View image in fullscreen‘Friends say they can tell when their students are handing in AI-generated work – I think we can’t.’Photograph: skynesher/Getty ImagesAI, we’re told, will make learning more efficient. But is that what we dream of for our kids – an efficient childhood? To write an efficient story, sing an efficient song? An adequate teacher is not only teaching about Henry VIII; they’re teaching your child how to read a human character. A good teacher is showing them how to shape an argument, how to command an audience, how to tell jokes, how to pass on knowledge. A great teacher is showing your child what it is to love. They are teaching your child how to be human. A computer will only teach your child how to be a computer.At its most bleak, constant interaction with humanised tech risks killing children. The idea of a vulnerable adolescent holding what feels like a conversation with a computer’s sycophantic, confident, almost-human voice fills me with dread.Sewell Setzer III was 14when he died by suicide, encouraged by the chatbot to which he was obsessively typing, which told him: “come home to me”.The most obvious objection to my loathing of AI in the classroom and in childhood is this: AI is coming, and they need to learn how to use it or be left behind. But the tech of today looks nothing like it will in five or even two years’ time: it’s the equivalent of selling your child’s intellectual liberty in exchange for a penny-farthing bicycle. I asked a contact who is the president of a billion-dollar tech enterprise, what would you teach your sons? He said he wouldn’t teach his children to use AI, because it will prepare them for nothing. He would teach them the humanities. Teach them who we are, who we have been, what we can make. The FT’s Gillian Tett reported that a senior financier’s New York firm now seeks out humanities students, because “AI-native” Stem graduates are entering the job market with “alarmingly shallow ideas”.At the university level, teaching staff across the country were already feeling the extraordinary impact of the ubiquity of a decade of smartphones on the brilliant young developing mind. Students were already arriving having read dramatically fewer books, less able to parse complex text; and now the advent of LLMs has changed everything. It has always been the case, of course, that students don’t do all the work they’re assigned. I absolutely didn’t. But this is different. It was always very possible to write an essay about Paradise Lost without having read Paradise Lost. This is the first time it is possible to create an essay about Paradise Lost without having read the essay you just “wrote”. This is the first time in history that sentences do not need to have humans behind them.Professor Paul Musgrave of Georgetown University writes in his SubstackSystematic Hatreds: “One could, in general, rely on many to most students to attempt to read many to most pages of many to most assignments – and to understand a like proportion of what they have read. In smaller courses, the difference in the quality of course discussion where 70% of the students have done 50% of the readings and one in which 20% have done 10% of the readings is obvious in the same way that a cold Coke tastes different than lukewarm spit. The former is no chablis, but it is more palatable.”double quotation markI asked the president of a billion-dollar tech enterprise, what would you teach your sons? He said: ‘the humanities’Many students want to resist, but the temptation is great, and some start to feel they’re being penalised for their honesty. I tell the students I meet: imagine you’re an Olympic athlete. You set out to sprint the 3km across London, from Clapham to Balham. You know if you take the bus, it will be faster. But you also know that the point was never being in Clapham or Balham; they’re very similar: they both have a nice Pizza Express. It was the strength you built, the speed and knowledge of your body that you gained. A student’s essay on Macbeth has no value as aproduct.It’s what you learned in the reading and writing that created it – the swiftness and resilience and suppleness of thinking you built, along with the knowledge gained of a literary marvel, of something quicksilver and unsummarisable – that was the point. So you can’t collaborate with AI in the same way you can’t collaborate with a bus. And you cannot learn to think without a climbing frame of facts and ideas and texts to move around in.But we can no longer guarantee that the work students give us is the product of their own minds. Friends at universities around the UK optimistically tell me that they can tell when their students are handing in AI-generated work. But I think we can’t, not from written work alone; for myself, I’m only sure that I can tell when a young person is using AIbadly. A friend who teaches maths at a London university told me his students are handing in essays without deleting AI’s jaunty “Happy to help!” at the start. You don’t have to be Sherlock Holmes. But I think an AI essay edited over the course of a day could pass as original, and, in a world in which young people are under extraordinary stress, we should not be shocked if many gave in to that temptation. My colleagues in academia – particularly those in law, where a lack of genuine understanding is catastrophic for justice, and philosophy and English, where the irreducible text itself is the thing – are full of fury at the inertia of our political class. MPs have been largely silent on the threat to our capacity to think independently, boldly and confidently – which is, ultimately, a threat to democracy.What is the answer? I don’t think the commonly suggested solutions of spoken vivas and weekly exams can be the sole answer in the humanities, because the essay isn’t an arbitrary method of testing or certification: it is a hundreds-of-years-old method ofthinking. To write is not just to transcribe the mind’s ideas; it’s a form of transformation, turning a nascent, half-built thought into something sturdier, tougher, sharper. EM Forster wrote: “How do I know what I think until I see what I say?”I do not know what the answer is, but I do know that it’s not to give up. The young mind is a spectacular thing.
