To waste its beauty and strength would be a dereliction of the trust the young are asked to put in the old. To wrap AI into the art of learning when we have overwhelming proof of the harm it does to developing minds is feeding snake oil to the people we should cherish most. We already have counterfeit AI people infiltrating our media: we must not risk sending out young people into a hard world armed only with counterfeit knowledge. We should treat it with the same urgency with which we would treat a wildfire.There are many young people who are furious at the influx of AI slop and tech chaos into their lives, who have asked me over the last year,how do we resist? I tell them that I think, for the young, knowledge and imagination are together the first site of resistance. And that by reading books (and talking about what they have loved reading so that it becomes a community, rather than purely private, act) they can begin their fight.I talk a great deal about reading for pleasure; I’ve written elsewhere about the necessity of pleasure in the classroom, and why it is not an optional extra but the hallmark of true education. We must find ways to show children that reading gives you access to an inexhaustible source of delight. But I worry, too, that we are limiting the meaning of the word pleasure. Learning is a strange and discomfiting experience; it’s a struggle and a frustration, and epiphanies are rare. It is not always pleasure in its easiest sense.So I think we also need to talk to young people about reading to outrun and outfight injustice. Reading to get faster, swifter and tougher; to develop powers of scrutiny and criticism and huge creative imagination. Reading human work to insist that we are human. Reading for liberation and emancipation; reading for intellectual freedom, and to have the strength to fight in the arenas of the mind, because when we let a computer think for us, we put a gun to the head of civilisation.There are dark days ahead. If we are to fight against those with untold financial wealth, we will need untold intellectual wealth. We will need tough-minded people; people with stamina, a huge range of knowledge, and an ability to see wide and far enough to understand in real time what is being done to us.Reading for pleasure and delight are vital – but alongside that and even more urgently: reading for power.Katherine Rundell’s latest children’s book, Impossible Creatures: The Neverfear, will be published by Bloomsbury on 27 August

title: TV tonight: a joyous night of live music with Paul Heaton  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: A hugely fun performance of all the Beautiful South and Housemartins hits. Plus: how deep were Elvis Presley’s connections to organised crime? Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: A hugely fun performance of all the Beautiful South and Housemartins hits. Plus: how deep were Elvis Presley’s connections to organised crime? Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: It’s happy hour again! … Paul Heaton: Live at Bramall Lane on BBC Two.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyView image in fullscreenIt’s happy hour again! … Paul Heaton: Live at Bramall Lane on BBC Two.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a joyous night of live music with Paul HeatonA hugely fun performance of all the Beautiful South and Housemartins hits. Plus: how deep were Elvis Presley’s connections to organised crime? Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Graeme Virtue,Jack SealeandSimon WardellSat 8 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePaul Heaton: Live at Bramall Lane10.10pm, BBC TwoThe Sheffield United fan and maker of some of pop’s most fun melodies performed at Bramall Lane last year – and it was 90 minutes packed with joy. In this recording, he is joined by Rianne Downey as they perform all the Housemartins, Beautiful South and solo hits to a lively crowd. The opening half-hour alone boasts Bell Bottomed Tear, Old Red Eyes Is Back, Song for Whoever and I’ll Sail This Ship Alone.Hollie RichardsonSandi Toksvig’s Hidden Wonders7pm, Channel 4Before launching her TV career, Sandi Toksvig earned a degree in archaeology. This fascinating series sees her returning to her academic roots, joining a dig in Dorset. There’s an iron age cemetery to be unearthed and, somewhat troublingly, some secrets about human sacrifice to be revealed.PHBettany Hughes’ Lost Worlds: Dawn of Civilisations8pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenAdventure time … Bettany Hughes’ Lost Worlds : Dawn of Civilisations.Photograph: Channel 4For her latest historical adventure Hughes heads to Turkey to explore the legacy of ancient Anatolia, a region that “left its mark on every era of human history”. Highlights include the otherworldly Cappadocia and the spectacular architecture of a 13th-century mosque.Graeme VirtueElvis, the Colonel and the Mob10pm, Channel 4Blame it on Colonel Tom Parker but Elvis Presley’s links to organised crime were, according to this two-part documentary, surprisingly strong. Parker was a denizen of Las Vegas and, along with taking care of Elvis’s business, he forged a few shady connections. Eventually, as this film shows, this court became a mixed blessing for the King.Phil HarrisnThe Staircase10.20pm, ITV1Colin Firth continues to excel in the drama about murder suspect Michael Peterson, despite the production being less essential than the original documentary. In 2003, the Petersons’ son Clayton makes an important discovery; in 2017, Michael’s new partner Sophie considers how meeting him changed her life.Jack SealeGhosts Australia10.50pm, BBC ThreeThe genius of the Ghosts premise is its adaptability to any cultural context. This Australian version is a case in point, this week touching on issues around colonisation but with the lightest and wittiest of touches. In the present, Kate and Sean handle an invasion of their own as the odious neighbours turn up.PHFilm choiceParallel Mothers, 11.10pm, BBC FourView image in fullscreenBumps in the road … Parallel Mothers on BBC Four.Photograph: Sony/AllstarJust before his latest twisty film, Bitter Christmas, hits cinemas, here’s another chance to see Pedro Almodóvar’s equally knotty 2021 drama, which explores family secrets in the domestic and national spheres. It features a standout performance from Penélope Cruz as photographer Janis, who gets pregnant by a forensic anthropologist investigating the forgotten civil war victims of Franco – including her ancestors. When her newborn gets swapped with that of the young Ana (Milena Smit), fate intertwines their lives. A forceful experience.Simon WardellLive sportWomen’s Hundred Cricket: MI London v Trent Rockets, 11am, Sky Sports Main EventFrom Kia Oval in London.Cycling: Tour de France Femmes, 2.30pm, TNT Sports 1Stage eight from Sisteron to Nice.EFL Cup Football: Colchester v Southampton, 5pm, Sky Sports Main EventOn Sunday, Mansfield v Sheffield Utd is at 3.45pm. title: Supposing: review – only ancient Greek rage will suffice in our exasperating times | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A modern, secular woman is transformed into a Hellenic heroine as she sees visions of the future in Zinnie Harris’s minimalist drama
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: A modern, secular woman is transformed into a Hellenic heroine as she sees visions of the future in Zinnie Harris’s minimalist drama
Content: She is getting intense … Nicole Cooper in Supposing:.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicView image in fullscreenShe is getting intense … Nicole Cooper in Supposing:.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewSupposing: review – only ancient Greek rage will suffice in our exasperating timesTraverse theatre, EdinburghA modern, secular woman is transformed into a Hellenic heroine as she sees visions of the future in Zinnie Harris’s minimalist dramaMark FisherSat 8 Aug 2026 12.09 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you found Christopher Nolan’sThe Odysseytoo bombastic, you might prefer your Greek drama filtered like this. Written and directed by Zinnie Harris, Supposing: could scarcely be staged more simply. Designer Alisa Kalyanova outlines a white-edged circle on the floor of an otherwise empty space. It could be the hole on the high street that Sally trips into for want of a protective bollard. Or it could be the kitchen where she tells her husband, Richard, about her strange concern. “I think I’ve been cursed,” she says, imagining him react in a hundred different ways – incredulous, mocking, shocked – none of them good.Either way, the circle defines the relationship between actors Nicole Cooper and Richard Conlon – both excellent as they revolve around each other, desiring to get close but so often repelled, twisting apart because of the import of Sally’s revelation. Is this modern day secular woman, who does not believe in gods but in concrete facts, suffering some kind of mental collapse, or does her curse mean she can she really see the future? And if she can, what to do with the prophecies?With a 17-strong Greek chorus in her head, nagging her like a guilty conscience, she reads up about satyrs and tragedies, portents and sacrifices, in case they have something to do with her. She even tries a bit of libation, with water, salt and wine, to make it all stop. Like Greek antecedents such as Medea, Clytemnestra and Penelope, she is getting intense.View image in fullscreenTroubled times … Nicole Cooper and Richard Conlon in Supposing:.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicShe admits as much and, delivered in a tone of helpless irony by Cooper, it is one of this elliptical play’s funnier observations. The ancient heroines are a comically imperfect fit for Sally, an ordinary wife and mother, yet something in our own troubled times calls for the kind of full-blooded response that only the Greeks can provide.In the Black review – rewarding drama about the Faustian pact of big businessRead moreSally’s frequent references to pregnancies and miscarriages suggest there is a future, but an uncertain one. In a society beset by political extremism, she sees visions of a racist neighbour and an unknown refugee housed in accommodation targeted by rightwing protesters. In such exasperating times, perhaps only ancient rage will suffice. Or perhaps, as the play’s closing moments hint at, there is still a possibility of healing the fractures.AtTraverse theatre, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: [seagull] review – silence proves golden in innovative if puzzling shot at Chekhov | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Magnificently expressive performances make this ambitious sign-language production feel viscerally new. But what’s with the square brackets?
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Magnificently expressive performances make this ambitious sign-language production feel viscerally new. But what’s with the square brackets?
Content: Startling … [seagull].Photograph: Kurt van der Elst/Kvde.beView image in fullscreenStartling … [seagull].Photograph: Kurt van der Elst/Kvde.beEdinburgh festival 2026Review[seagull] review – silence proves golden in innovative if puzzling shot at ChekhovStudio theatre, EdinburghMagnificently expressive performances make this ambitious sign-language production feel viscerally new. But what’s with the square brackets?Arifa AkbarSat 8 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 10.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe silence in this adaptation “after” Anton Chekhov’s The Seagull is startling. Performed straight through at two and a half hours, the intakes of breath, tears, screams of anguish and, of course, the gunshots when they come arrest the senses. So do the intermittent spoken words, which sound almost like an intrusion, and occasional lines of music.Directed by Stijn Van Opstal, this is a sharp, ambitious, modern-dress chamber piece at the Edinburgh international festival by Belgian theatre companies Toneelhuis and Olympique Dramatique, with numerous translators and adapters. For the first 30 minutes, there is just signing on stage (Flemish Sign Language translated into British Sign Language), with screens translating dialogue.The story is the same but appears new and visceral. Konstantin (Yana Wuytjens) is an aspiring writer intent on discovering innovative forms of storytelling, but is overshadowed by his grand actor-mother, Arkadina (Sofie Decleir), who comes back to the family’s country estate with her lover, Trigorin (Serge Vlerick), in tow. He is a distinguished novelist and his presence gives rise to a love triangle involving Konstantin’s companion, Nina (Yousra Boukantar), who is an aspiring actor.Performers are a mix of D/deaf and hearing, magnificently expressive across the board – though Lobke Leirens, as ancillary character Masja, has a particularly formidable presence. Arkadina is a good blend of thespy self-importance, charm and maternal concern. Konstantin is performed by a woman, which makes his relationship with Nina somehow more tender and intimate, while Wuytjens brings a good blend of anger, tantrum and earnestness to the part.View image in fullscreenFormidable … [seagull].Photograph: Kurt van der Elst/Kvde.beCharacters swill in boredom and sometimes seem ridiculous. Humour sits close to anguish. Sound clangs. Damiaan De Schrijver and Van Opstal’s set design on a traverse stage exposes the construction of its effects. A host of techniques amplify the sense of overt theatricality.A Trial: After An Enemy of the People review – Wagner Moura upends Ibsen and keeps us guessingRead moreActors bring on the props, sometimes create sound effects and take up the wooden boards towards the end, which brings a plaintive, packed-up, autumnal quality to both the summer home and the drama. But the production is hampered by too many of these techniques; they come to seem like tricks, there for the sake of clever contrivance. Why, for instance, is there a seemingly random freezing of some scenes? Why do the surtitles become non-grammatical and seemingly a literal translation before returning back to standardised English? What, for that matter, is the point of the square brackets of the title? These questions are frustratingly unanswered.Then again, at its best, this play dazzles and contains a fresh, dangerous quality, as physical as a gut-punch in its climatic moments. Silence has never sounded louder or more loaded.AtStudio theatre, Edinburgh, until 11 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalAnton ChekhovDeafness and hearing lossBelgiumreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Trial: After An Enemy of the People review – Wagner Moura upends Ibsen and keeps us guessing | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: At the Edinburgh international festival, the Narcos star and director Christiane Jatahy transform the 1882 classic into a resonant, fourth wall-breaking event
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: At the Edinburgh international festival, the Narcos star and director Christiane Jatahy transform the 1882 classic into a resonant, fourth wall-breaking event
Content: Original … Wagner Moura in A Trial: After An Enemy of the People.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOriginal … Wagner Moura in A Trial: After An Enemy of the People.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewA Trial: After An Enemy of the People review – Wagner Moura upends Ibsen and keeps us guessingLyceum theatre, EdinburghAt the Edinburgh international festival, the Narcos star and director Christiane Jatahy transform the 1882 classic into a resonant, fourth wall-breaking eventArifa AkbarSat 8 Aug 2026 08.25 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis dramatised trial takes Henrik Ibsen’s 1882 play about a man’s campaign to expose the secret scandal of contaminated water in his town and turns it into a modern day interrogation: of speaking out versus remaining silent, of a family at war and of fiction and reality itself.In fact, is this a drama at all? It starts off as such but minutes later, the celebrated Brazilian screen actorWagner Moura, playing Ibsen’s Thomas Stockmann, seemingly breaks character to talk to us directly. Stockmann still sits invisibly on stage and we as an audience are here to judge him, he says, before returning to inhabit him.View image in fullscreenFamily drama … A Trial: After An Enemy of the People.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianSo Stockmann’s trial begins. Here he is: a family man living in contemporary Brazil, in a spa town whose tourism is dependent on the water that he insists is poisoning people. Is he a heroic truth-teller, belligerent anti-hero or self-serving villain? A 12-strong jury made up of audience members (have actors infiltrated this lineup? We don’t know, it is all uncertain ground) are called to sit on stage for most of the play before leaving to deliberate their verdict.Christiane Jatahy, who has conceived the show and written it with Moura and Lucas Paraizo, knows how to reinvent a classic. Often using post-dramatic techniques and incorporating screens on stage, she has repurposed the works of Anton Chekhov and August Strindberg, and three years ago broughtDusk, her documentary-style adaptation of Lars von Trier’s film Dogville, to the Edinburgh international festival.A blend of documentary and drama forms, it dismantles the fourth wall, at times, in a similar vein toThomas Ostermeier’s version of the play, staged in London two years ago. But this is more radical in its ambitions. Its central scandal certainly chimes in our world, too – as shown in the recent docudramaDirty Business– but also resonates with the“forever chemicals” investigationsin the US. Jatahy has taken an old story and turned it into a tale of our time.Despite this resonance, there is just not enough force in the moral debate at the heart of this production. The question of whether Thomas was right to reveal the truth is a foregone conclusion, with not enough to mitigate it. That his truth-telling affects the town’s tourism seems like an inadequate argument in the face of mass water poisoning.You wish for greater complexity or more skin in the game.View image in fullscreenUncertain ground … the jury of A Trial: After An Enemy of the People.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianIn the Black review – rewarding drama about the Faustian pact of big businessRead moreStill, it is gripping and original. Moura is an immensely charismatic force on stage, at ease with his fissured role – as Thomas and an observing commentator of Thomas. Everyone around him gives powerful performances, too. There are two young sons off stage and a wife who has died – partly, it is implied, from the stress of Thomas’s campaigning. We see these characters on screen, in videos that bring grief and betrayal to the storyline. His daughter Petra (Julia Bernat) sits on stage with him, presenting evidence and conducting cross-examinations opposite his brother, Peter (Danilo Grangheia), who is Thomas’s most vocal adversary. They bring raised passions, fights and tears. Ultimately, it is this traditional element, of turbulent family drama, that grips the most.At theLyceum theatre, Edinburgh, until 10 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreHenrik IbsenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sex, drugs and washing dishes: inside Anthony Bourdain’s unruly younger years  | Biopics | The Guardian
description: In the acclaimed new drama Tony, the early career of the late food writer and chef is brought to life, and those who knew him best are now also looking back
Author: David Smith
Headline: In the acclaimed new drama Tony, the early career of the late food writer and chef is brought to life, and those who knew him best are now also looking back
Content: Dominic Sessa as a young Anthony Bourdain in the film Tony.Photograph: Bob Gruen/A24View image in fullscreenDominic Sessa as a young Anthony Bourdain in the film Tony.Photograph: Bob Gruen/A24BiopicsSex, drugs and washing dishes: inside Anthony Bourdain’s unruly younger yearsIn the acclaimed new drama Tony, the early career of the late food writer and chef is brought to life, and those who knew him best are now also looking backDavid SmithWashington bureau chiefSat 8 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 06.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe novelist Michael Cunninghamhas described Provincetown, on the tip of Cape Cod, as “the only small town I know of where those who live unconventionally seem to outnumber those who live within the prescribed bounds of home and licensed marriage, respectable job, and biological children. It is one of the places in the world you can disappear into.”‘These cooks ripped each other apart’: Dominic Sessa on playing Anthony Bourdain, kitchen bullies and the joys of being a 70s barflyRead moreThis idiosyncratic bohemia has attracted the likes of Edward Hopper, Eugene O’Neill, Mark Rothko and Tennessee Williams along with poets, dropouts, drag queens and drifters. In the summer of 1975 came a lanky, restless 19-year-old from New Jersey with no job and no money, sleeping on the floor of a shared cottage while his roommates worked to pay the rent. His name wasAnthony Bourdain, who would later become a celebrity chef, author and television globetrotter.Half a century later, that coming-of-age has been mythologised by Hollywood. Matt Johnson’s new film, Tony, starringDominic Sessaas the adolescent dishwasher, imagines the origin story of the man before he rewrote the rules of food writing with his 2000 memoir, Kitchen Confidential.For those who knew Bourdain best, the film’s release – eight years after his death by suicide – has been a difficult one to sit with. “I have a very strong emotional relationship to Tony and yeah, it’s hard,” saysJoel Rose, 78, a novelist and editor who was arguably Bourdain’s closest literary confidant for 35 years.“This has been a difficult period for me. There’s a lot going on with Tony’s memory and the memories that I have, and how in so many ways I feel cheated and confused. I had a very different relationship with Tony than his TV persona and all that. I wasn’t in that world with him, and I’m not sure that it was a favorite place for Tony to be.”Bourdain described his time in Provincetown in Kitchen Confidential: “We all went to the beaches and ponds each morning, smoked pot, sniffed a little coke, dropped acid and sunbathed nude, as well as indulging in other healthy teenage activities.”After getting a job as a dishwasher in the kitchen of local restaurant Flagship – later fictionalised as the Dreadnaught in Kitchen Confidential – he discovered a structure he’d never known before: something with real stakes, real hierarchy and an odd, brutal kind of belonging. He worked his way up from the dish pit to the salad station, then to the fryer, and eventually earned a shift or two at the broiler.He put it this wayto the Observer in 2017: “I only became happy – in fact, intensely satisfied – as a dishwasher at a restaurant in Provincetown in Cape Cod, my first job. I was a shy, goofy, awkward teenager. But in this blue-collar, factory-like environment, there was no blurred line, no grey area, no philosophical question to fret over.“Dishes had to go in the washer and come out taintless, and doing this swiftly and competently meant I was acknowledged as a human being by colleagues I wanted to be like. The day they promoted me to dunking fries I was overjoyed.”It was also that first summer at the Flagship that Bourdain saw the moment he would later credit with making him want to become a chef. He and the rest of the kitchen crew crowded around a window overlooking the restaurant’s trash-bin corral to watch their chef in the middle of a sexual encounter with a customer who, still in her wedding dress, was minutes from sitting down to dinner with her own wedding party.Whether the marriage survived is not recorded anywhere. What is clear is the effect the scene had on a teenage Bourdain: the kitchen staff, he decided, were like pirates, answerable to nobody, living entirely by their own rules.Michael Ruhlman, 63, a food writer who became one of Bourdain’s closest friends in later years, said he once asked Bourdain directly whether the bridal-gown story was true. “He said: yeah, it happened, the guy was a total fucking pig,” Ruhlman recalls. “He said he was the kind of chef who would make servers give him blowjobs while he was prepping his station. He was always hanging out with an interesting crowd.”That romantic image of the kitchen pirate cut both ways. As the restaurant industry later reckoned with its long history of physical and sexual abuse,Bourdain said he regrettedhaving glamorised a culture that was, underneath the swagger, often exploitative.Tony review – knives out in tasty reheat of Anthony Bourdain’s memoirRead moreHe also grew more clear-eyed about the drug use that hollowed out so many of the Provincetown kitchens he had worked in. In a 2014 episode ofAnthony Bourdain: Parts Unknownhe said simply: “Many of our friends from those days didn’t make it.”None of that was visible to him yet in 1975. Riding the confidence of his first Flagship summer, Bourdain came back to Provincetown the next spring hoping to land the broiler position outright. But the Flagship had new ownership, and he ended up trying out instead at Ciro’s, an Italian restaurant run byCiriaco Cozzithat turned out hundreds of dinners a night on a kitchen that ran with near-military precision.The cooks at Ciro’s unsettled him – they moved as a unit and talked in what he later called a “lush, intimidating, sardonic secret language”, part 18th-century literary allusion, part marine drill sergeant. They were not impressed with him in return. During a tryout at the broiler, an overconfident Bourdain badly burned himself on a hot pan and was immediately bumped back down to salads.The humiliation stung Bourdain, prompting him to enroll at the Culinary Institute of America in February 1977 in an effort to prove himself. If Provincetown was where Bourdain discovered the kitchen, it was the grimy streets of New York’s East Village in the early 1980s that forged him as a writer.View image in fullscreenAntonio Banderas and Dominic Sessa in Tony.Photograph: A24/APIn 1983 Rose and his then wife, the French novelistCatherine Texier, were running a radical, highly influential literary magazine called Between C & D. Produced on a dot matrix printer using fanfold paper, the magazine was sold in big, plastic Ziploc bags – a cheeky nod to the heavy heroin trade that dominated their neighborhood.One afternoon, Rose’s fourth-floor apartment buzzer rang. “I went downstairs and there was a very tall guy, never seen him before, in chef whites, and he introduced himself,” Rose recalls by phone from the mountains in Kerhonkson, New York. “He said he had submitted a comic that he had drawn to the magazine and that I had rejected it, but I’d written something very nice. And he wondered, could he talk to me?“So I invited him up to my apartment on the fourth floor. I’d written back that his drawing sort of sucked, but that his writing was good. He said he didn’t know any writers, that he wanted to be a writer and he just wanted to talk.”The two men sat in the apartment for hours, talking about their lives. They discovered a shared suburban background, a love of literature and a mutual history with the restaurant business. Rose’s father had been a career waiter at New York spots like theStage DeliandCarnegie Deli.“I didn’t influence his writing one iota,” Rose says. “He was a good writer right from the start. He was a natural writer. If you’re young and unsure and don’t even have a voice yet, wow, it’s terrifying. And he was terrified because he was already looking ahead. He was barely established and, as much as he loved what he was doing, he could see the wear and tear that it took on a person in the long term.”Bourdain was still living on the margins, balancing intense double-shifts in Manhattan kitchens with a heavy drug habit.Rose continues:“When Tony came up to the apartment that day, he was pinned. He had just gotten high and I called him on it right away because I knew. I’ve been there myself. I wasn’t doing drugs then. I had a hard time and almost gotten killed, and I didn’t need to go back there. I know he was doing more coke than heroin but he was coming around my house quite a bit. I lived on 7th Street and he was getting drugs on 2nd and 3rd. I saw him quite a bit in those days.”View image in fullscreenBourdain pictured in 2000.Photograph: David Rentas/Rex/ShutterstockIn the late 1990s, Bourdain was in a Tokyo hotel room, looking out over the city after a visit to the fish market, when he sent a long, incredibly vivid email to Rose, who was living with Karen Rinaldi, an editor at Bloomsbury who had recently given birth to their son, Rocco.“She was in the living room breastfeeding the baby, and I came in with this email and I said to Karen, ‘I’ve got to read you this.’ She said, ‘Joel, get the fuck away from me, do you see what I’m doing?’ I said, ‘No, no, no, no, let me read it to you.’ I read it to her and she knew Tony through me a little bit, and she said, ‘Does Tony have any other stories?’ I said, ‘Are you kidding me? He has so many!’”Rinaldi contacted Bourdain’s agent, made an offer and bought the book. When it was published in 2000, Kitchen Confidential shattered the genteel, recipe-driven world of food publishing, ushering in an era that would lead to TV dramas such asThe Bear.Dianne Jacob, 71, a food writer and editor, comments: “First of all, the writing is incredible. He has a very strong voice. He’s an excellent storyteller. He understands pacing and candour, and he was almost like an investigative reporter. It made food writing sexy … More than anything else, it was real bad-boy persona and he was such a beautiful writer.”Yet when Jacob met Bourdain in person during a book promotional tour in San Francisco, she encountered a man who seemed profoundly uncomfortable with the sudden glare of global fame.She recalls: “There was an older woman in the bathroom applying blush to her cleavage. There were all these men who were chefs who were full of tattoos and in love with him. When I got in line to have him sign my book, there were women passing him notes, maybe with their phone numbers. It was an incredible scene.“He was charismatic, but he was also a little awkward and shy. I saw him afterwards, outside, smoking a cigarette, and I just thought I’m not going to bother him, you know? He wasn’t all in on the glamorous part of being a celebrity. He was kind of like a deer in the headlights with all these people admiring him. They all wanted to sleep with him, I think, everyone in the audience. Even straight men who are chefs.”José Andrés, a Spanish American chef and restaurateur, and founder of the food aid charity World Central Kitchen, first met Bourdain 20 years ago and became a close friend.Andrés and Bourdain watched each other’s children grow up and for years would holiday together for a week in the Cayman Islands. They also travelled – and ate – far and wide in countries ranging from Spain to Haiti.“He gave joints a lot of value in ways other shows never did,” Andrés recalls. “As much as he loved high-end cooking and great wines and three-star Michelin, he loved the people doing the impossible hole-in-the-walls, and that was beautiful.“I remember we ate in the streets of Port-au-Prince [in Haiti] in places nobody would eat. That was Tony. He could be eating in the best restaurants in the world but he would go to the hole-in-the-walls, and many of them, because he made them famous, sometimes moved to better places.”The Bourdain AI furore shouldn’t overshadow an effective, complicated film | Adrian HortonRead moreYet as the travel shows grew more successful, the TV crews bigger and the global adoration more intense, Bourdain’s private world was fracturing. His 20-year marriage dissolved in 2005, unable to withstand the constant strain of his travel schedule.View image in fullscreenA still from Roadrunner.Photograph: Capital Pictures/AlamyThe final, tragic chapter of his life began when he met the Italian actorAsia Argento. To those who had known him for decades, the change in his personality was abrupt and alarming.Ruhlman says: “He was a completely different person after Asia. After he met her, I got an email. I had invited him to my wedding reception in New York City and he says, ‘Can’t do it. I’m in Italy shooting. I’m in love too. Love abounds. Nothing but happiness.’ And a year later he’d killed himself.”For Rose, who was in text and email contact with Bourdain just a day before his death, finishing work on their graphic novel Hungry Ghosts, the suicide in a French hotel room in June 2018 remains an open wound.He says: “He was not one who shied away from talking about suicide and killing himself and throwing himself in a meat grinder or a wood chipper or whatever he said. But from the day that I learned of his passing, I always felt that Tony probably put that noose around his neck and then at the last moment said, ‘What the fuck am I doing now?’”Up in the quiet mountains of New York, Rose watches the hummingbird at his bird feeder and looks out at the vast, green vista of the Catskills. He has just watched the first footage ofGet Jiro!, an upcoming TV adaptation of the graphic novel he wrote with Bourdain.“Tony would be in heaven,” he says, with a bittersweet note in his voice. “I know it’s just what he envisioned, blood spatter and all the stuff that he loved. I have warm feelings about this as a long project and to see it through and then I also feel like, fuck, man, why aren’t you here? This would be so much better ifyouwerehere.”Tony is out now in US cinemas and in the UK on 14 August and Australia on 20 AugustExplore more on these topicsBiopicsAnthony BourdainFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A kids’ film taught me the power of delusion – and helped me chase my standup dreams | Comedy | The Guardian
description: The protagonist of A Little Princess wills reality to bend to her desires. Comedians need that same idiot confidence when we’re starting out, or else we’d all give up
Author: Olivia Ladanyi
Headline: The protagonist of A Little Princess wills reality to bend to her desires. Comedians need that same idiot confidence when we’re starting out, or else we’d all give up
Content: Illustration: Martin O’NeillView image in fullscreenIllustration: Martin O’NeillMy cultural awakeningComedyA kids’ film taught me the power of delusion – and helped me chase my standup dreamsThe protagonist of A Little Princess wills reality to bend to her desires. Comedians need that same idiot confidence when we’re starting out, or else we’d all give upExplore the rest of our coverage of the Edinburgh festival 2026Sarah Roberts; as told toOlivia LadanyiSat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwas 28 the first time I did standup. It was an open-mic competition where the audience decided the winner. As I held the tiny gold trophy, I decided to quit my job the next day. Some people might call that crazy, and it probably was. But I’d been honing that delusional self-belief since I was eight when I first watched the film adaptation of Frances Hodgson Burnett’s story A Little Princess.I already almost had the same name as its protagonist, Sara, a young girl who is sent off to boarding school while her father fights in the war. I wanted to be exactly like her. She was so sure of herself, and believed so completely in the worlds she created, that all the other girls at school wanted to be her friend. My favourite scene is the one where the girls sit on Sara’s bed, forming a circle round her as she tells fantastical stories. I would watch it and think: I want to tell stories that make people gather round me.But unlike Sara, I was shy and making friends didn’t come easily. I did, however, understand how to use my inner world to escape my reality. My imagination became my most powerful asset. It’s why I told everyone the reason I didn’t get into S Club Juniors was because I would overshadow the other members, when the reality was that I couldn’t sing or dance and hadn’t even got through the first round of auditions.double quotation markYou have to believe in what you’re doing, even after bombing to a room full of stag dos“Don’t you ever do that? Believe in something just to make it seem real?” Sara says in the film. At the boarding school, Sara’s belief that she’s a princess – “All girls are! Even if they live in tiny old attics, even if they dress in rags, even if they aren’t pretty, or smart or young” – helps her to stand up against the cruel headteacher, Miss Minchin.As a teenager, I wrote poems and short stories about boys I fancied, imagining they fancied me back. As an adult, I would fantasise about being anywhere else to escape my meaningless nine-to-five that largely involved sending emails. Those fantasies were a refusal to believe that this was my fate. It was as if by having them, I was preparing myself for a bigger, more exciting life.As a standup comedian, delusion is your greatest asset: you have to believe in what you’re doing more than anyone else. When it’s 2am and you’re at a service station on the M6 after bombing to a room full of stag dos, knowing you have to do it all again tomorrow, you tell yourself that it’s just one show, and you’re building towards something bigger.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEuphoria gave me the courage to come out to my friend – now we’re togetherRead moreSara never loses her resolve. Even after everyone believes her father has died and left her penniless, and she’s forced to live in the attic as a servant girl, she still insists she’s a princess. One day, when Miss Minchin locks her in with no breakfast, lunch or dinner, Sara imagines a feast with candles and trays of good things to eat, and there, laid out in the morning, are platters of sausages, muffins and fresh fruit. Her imagination helps her to survive her reality until her fantasy becomes her reality. That’s the thing about delusion: you have to believe it’s real until it becomes real. Fantasy isn’t just escapism, it’s strategy.I have been doing standup consistently for five years now. The longer you do it, the more you embrace failing: you don’t get better if you don’t bomb. You need delusion, resilience and persistence, the same qualities I admired in Sara all those years ago. You have to believe in your version of reality even when everything around you seems to prove the opposite.Every time I do standup now, I want to feel exactly like Sara, enchanting her classmates at her boarding school. I didn’t realise until I rewatched A Little Princess as an adult that she’s not just a fantasist – she’s a standup comedian.Sarah Roberts: Scary Movie 7is at theMonkey Barrel 2,Edinburgh, to 30 August.Did a cultural moment prompt you to make a major life change? title: Martin & Roman’s Irish Road Trip: the choice of presenters for this travelogue is utterly baffling | Television | The Guardian
description: Spandau Ballet bassist Martin Kemp and his son Roman embark on a journey around the Emerald Isle. For what reason, nobody really knows
Author: Frances Ryan
Headline: Spandau Ballet bassist Martin Kemp and his son Roman embark on a journey around the Emerald Isle. For what reason, nobody really knows
Content: Driven … the Kemps star in Martin & Roman’s Irish Road Trip.Photograph: Sphere AbacusView image in fullscreenDriven … the Kemps star in Martin & Roman’s Irish Road Trip.Photograph: Sphere AbacusThe watcherTelevisionMartin & Roman’s Irish Road Trip: the choice of presenters for this travelogue is utterly bafflingSpandau Ballet bassist Martin Kemp and his son Roman embark on a journey around the Emerald Isle. For what reason, nobody really knowsFrances RyanSat 8 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you’re someone who believes the celebrity travelogue genre has been pushed too far, Martin & Roman’s Irish Road Trip (Monday, 8pm, Channel 4) is here to push you to the edge. Then continue pushing until you’re falling off a cliff into the Irish Sea.It is unclear why exactly the producers choseMartin Kempand his son, Roman, to take viewers on a tour of Ireland. Which to be fair, the two men address in the first three minutes. Martin lived in the country briefly in the 80s during his Spandau Ballet era, we’re told. His mum “always said” she was half Irish but – as Roman points out – the family did an ancestral DNA test and they’re actually Germanic.Still, they’re keen for a rare chance to spend time together away without the rest of the family. “We’ve never done it before!” Martin says with excitement. “For good reason,” Roman replies.The series is essentially the television equivalent of English people applying for an Irish passport post-Brexit to avoid the large queues at the airport. Did your great-grandmother twice removed once sleep with a man named Seamus? Who cares, I just want to go on my holidays!Accept that premise and you’re in for a perfectly reasonable time. Part father-and-son buddy movie, part exploration of Irish folklore and landscapes, Irish Road Trip is a love letter to both people and place, albeit one that doesn’t quite know what tone to land on.There’s humour, most successfully when Roman – clearly thoughtful and witty – finds opportunities to poke fun at his dad. When they explore keening – the traditional Irish vocal lament for the dead – and Martin does a double take on the word, Roman quips he should know all about “cleaners” as he has about 12 back home to look after his mansion. The jaunty Irish folk music that pops up every 10 minutes reassures the viewer we’re all here to have a lovely time.View image in fullscreenPrison break … Martin and Roman take a boat over to Spike Island.Photograph: Sphere AbacusAnd yet a fair portion of the content is melancholic. At one point, Roman touchingly admits he’s thinking about his own mortality – and the future death of his parents – more as he gets older, to the extent it sometimes keeps him awake at night.Other sections are outright distressing, especially the tour around Spike Island in Cork Harbour – known as “Ireland’s Alcatraz” for its on/off use as a prison for 1,300 years. A tour guide shows the Kemps the seventh-century version of solitary confinement: an isolation room used for punishment where prisoners, including children, were chained to the wall by their neck for weeks. It doesn’t help when the tour guide declares that she sometimes sees a ghost. On the ferry ride back, Roman tells Martin that’s the first time he’s ever been somewhere without hope.But don’t worry, the upbeat fiddle has started playing! No wait, Roman is talking about death again. Does his dad believe that you can see your family from above when you die? He hopes not because he’d just be seeing Roman taking the keys to his car.On paper, I’m the target audience for the series. I’m English-Irish: my grandfather was a jockey in the Grand National; I inherited a Waterford crystal whiskey glass from my Nan; I’ve never set foot farther west than Birmingham. But two Englishmen learning about Irish folklore is a hard thing to sell, even when they are so earnestly engaged with the locals and experts they meet along the way.The best moments come when the father-and-son relationship is at the forefront. The tour around the ancient tomb in the second episode is visually striking but my favourite part comes before they even enter. When they’re told that a local has a key to get in the tomb (yes, really), Roman encourages his dad to go to her house to ask for it. “He doesn’t like meeting new people,” Roman says to the camera as he proudly watches Martin knock at the front door.That, I suppose, is why celebrity travelogues keep getting commissioned: they are a chance for viewers to get up close and personal with both another country and family.What’s next for the Kemps? A German road trip? I’ve heard they’ve got suitable DNA.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherMartin KempfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #255: The great front‑row backlash ignores what makes films feel truly colossal | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: You’re all wrong about the most maligned seats in the house, which offer the purest form of moviegoing
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: You’re all wrong about the most maligned seats in the house, which offer the purest form of moviegoing
Content: A question of perspective … The Odyssey.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenA question of perspective … The Odyssey.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #255: The great front‑row backlash ignores what makes films feel truly colossalIn this week’s newsletter: You’re all wrong about the most maligned seats in the house, which offer the purest form of moviegoingDon’t get The Guide delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereGwilym MumfordSat 8 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter so many years of doomy predictions about their coming demise, these are suddenly boom times for cinemas. A clutch of massive releases – most recently theall-time-record-breakingSpider-Man: Brand New Day – along with a heatwave thathas transformed Britain’s parksinto the Oklahoma dust bowl, has sent the nation sprinting (or at least fast-walking) to the air-conditioned environs of their local picture houses. In fact so packed are cinemas that, in order to find a free seat for Imax screenings of Spider-Man and the Odyssey, punters are having to resort to quite literally the lowest of the low: the front row.Not that those same people are happy about it. Social media is full of grumblings from those lumbered with seats situated directly in front of the screen, often accompanied by pictures showing how vertiginous their views are:Agamemnon’s distended, helmeted headlooming threateningly above them, say. I’m pretty sure a lot of these pictures are AI-generated fakes – mainly a chance togive Robert Pattinson a massive chin– but they are still spooking cinemagoers: Reddit is full of threads of panicked patrons asking just how painful their neck is going to feel after craning up at a screen for three hours.This, I think, is a fairly recent phenomenon; I can’t remember such vitriol directed towards the front row of the cinema when I was a teenager, though then again there wasn’t social media then to share and amplify that sentiment. Regardless, you are all wrong about the front row. It’s nowhere near as bad as many pretend it is – in fact it’s often pretty great.View image in fullscreenHe might betooclose … Cillian Murphy in Oppenheimer.Photograph: BFA/AlamyThe front row is the place where a movie feels most like amovie. Watch one back in those nosebleed seats you all seem to covet so much, and often you might as well have viewed it from an iPhone on the end of a selfie stick, so tiddly are its relative dimensions. No such problems in row A, where the screen dominates your eyeline, drenching you in light and colour. Gawp at the sheer scale of the atomic explosion inOppenheimer. Luxuriate in the cosmic Technicolor wash ofProject Hail Mary’sspace scenes. Marvel at being able to see in extreme close up every last perfect pore on Tom Holland’s shimmering forehead. This iscinema, not the glorified inflight entertainment the seats at the back are experiencing.What’s more, it is an entirely unobstructed view. That means no frustration at the bored teen scrolling away on their 100-percent-brightness phone screen somewhere in your peripheral vision, or the person reclining their seat back to its full extension right against your kneecaps, or the patron getting up in front of you for their sixth bathroom break of the film. Oh and if you have to get up for the loo yourself, you’ll be able to do so without having to squeeze past half a dozen irritated filmgoers, all of whom (and this is a semi-related gripe) have inexplicably decided to swing their legs to the side while staying seated instead of doing the best thing for everyone and standing up to let you pass. As for your own legs: stretch them out! There’s no seat in the way – a pleasure not granted to the squeezed middle, back in rows B to Z.It’s cheap too: thanks to years of anti-front row bias, some cinemas have been forced to reduce the price of those seats to get them filled. And there’s the extra bonus of being able to leave promptly, rather than being stuck in a slow-moving trudge down a narrow set of stairs.Granted, I’m not going to pretend there aren’t drawbacks to the front row. Cinema firms’ eagerness to squeeze every last penny out of their punters has led, in some cases, to seats being squeezed right up to the screen. There’s no sugar-coating it: in such front row seats, the view will be pretty sheer. Neck pain in those cases will be a serious concern. I’d argue those are minority cases and at most cinemas row A is far enough back to make for an enjoyable viewing experience, particularly with the widespread adoption of those reclining seats.So, don’t be afraid: if you do spot a couple of spare front row seats at that otherwise fully booked 70mm screening ofThe Odyssey(every showing of Nolan’s film at London’s BFI Imax is sold out until late September, staggeringly), take the leap. You will be rewarded with an immersive, transporting, eyeball-frying cinematic experience – and if not, well at least you’ll get back to the car quicker than everyone else.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletterThe OdysseySpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DayOppenheimerImaxnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Blind date: ‘I asked him to compliment my outfit and he said he didn’t really like it’ | Dating | The Guardian
description: Imogen, 31, a doctor, meets Andy, 36, founder of a consultancy firm
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Imogen, 31, a doctor, meets Andy, 36, founder of a consultancy firm
Content:
Composite: Linda Nylind & Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenComposite: Linda Nylind & Antonio Olmos/The GuardianBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘I asked him to compliment my outfit and he said he didn’t really like it’Imogen, 31, a doctor, meets Andy, 36, founder of a consultancy firmSat 8 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleImogen on AndyView image in fullscreenWhat were you hoping for?Something to tell the group chat that would elicit more :o reactions than usual.First impressions?Polite, nice hands, early.What did you talk about?We covered most of the world’s topics, my favourite being whether having an AI boyfriend is functionally the same as being in a long-distance relationship (I admit that was slight rage bait).Most awkward moment?I jokingly asked for a compliment on my outfit and he said he didn’t really like it. I told him white lies exist for a reason …Good table manners?Excellent – my water glass was never empty and our food was always perfectly shared down the middle. (By the way, best roast of my life.)Best thing about Andy?An unparalleled debate partner who called me out when he disagreed with me (which I appreciated).Would you introduce Andy to your friends?My single ones would love him.Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Describe Andy in three wordsWitty, self-aware, circumspect.What do you think Andy made of you?He swore he wasn’t, but I felt as if he might have been a bit overwhelmed by me – especially when I asked what his dream wedding would look like.Did you go on somewhere?We went to the pub, then threw sticks for his dog Bella in the park (11/10 for her).And … did you kiss?Cheek only.If you could change one thing about the evening what would it be?Make it 5C cooler so I didn’t have to fan myself like an aghast Victorian maiden.Marks out of 10?6.6.Would you meet again?To debate, or to dog-walk.View image in fullscreenImogen and Andy on their dateAndy on ImogenView image in fullscreenWhat were you hoping for?To be able to say, “You’ll never guess how we met.”First impressions?What a whirlwind.What did you talk about?Living abroad and learning languages. Tarot cards. The joy of dancing. The insufficiency of men. Autism.Most awkward moment?When Imogen asked why I hadn’t complimented her outfit.Good table manners?Flawless – glasses were attended at all times, swear words used only at appropriate points, all waiting staff were treated with admiration.Best thing about Imogen?Her openness and love of all things strange and interesting.Would you introduce Imogen to your friends?Yes.Describe Imogen in three wordsCharismatic, intelligent, direct.Blind date: ‘We were chatting as soon as we sat down’Read moreWhat do you think Imogen made of you?She told me I was a nerd, and we related in our passion for various things novel and brave – so an adventurous nerd?Did you go on somewhere?We did – to a pub, and then for a walk.And … did you kiss?On the cheek.If you could change one thing about the evening what would it be?I’d have complimented her outfit.Marks out of 10?8.Would you meet again?I think Imogen could probably make anything a party, so yes.Imogen andAndy ateatWilson’s, London, SE13.Fancy a blind date? Author: Rosanna Greenstreet
Headline: The actor on being told she was no Ingrid Bergman, forgetting her lines on stage, and not caring about getting older
Content: Stockard Channing: ‘Who would play me in the film of my life? Miriam Margolyes.’Photograph: Alan Chapman/Dave Benett/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStockard Channing: ‘Who would play me in the film of my life? Miriam Margolyes.’Photograph: Alan Chapman/Dave Benett/Getty ImagesThe Q&ALife and styleInterviewStockard Channing: ‘I cried at the election of Joe Biden, thinking we were out of the woods. Wrong!’Rosanna GreenstreetThe actor on being told she was no Ingrid Bergman, forgetting her lines on stage, and not caring about getting olderSat 8 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBorn in New York City, Stockard Channing, 82, played Rizzo in the 1978 film Grease. In 1985, she received a Tony for her performance in A Day in the Death of Joe Egg, and in 1994 was Oscar-nominated for her role in the film Six Degrees of Separation. She has three Emmys for her TV work, which includesThe West Wing. She makes her directorial debut at the Edinburgh festival with Krapp’s Last Tape, in aid of the Wembley to Soweto Foundation, Upstairs at the Roxy until 31 August. Her latest film is Practical Magic 2. She lives in London.What is your greatest fear?Climate change.What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?Pedantry.What is the trait you most deplore in others?Ignorance.Paula Wilcox: ‘More sex, money or fame? How sad to have to choose. Let’s have it all’Read moreWhat was your most embarrassing moment?Fifteen years ago, I totally forgot my lines on stage and was mortified. We skipped two pages of dialogue and took three minutes off the play – to the delight of the audience!What makes you unhappy?The loss of moral compass.If you could bring something extinct back to life, what would you choose?A vibrant political culture.Who would play you in the film of your life?Miriam Margolyes.What scares you about getting older?I’m over that.What did you want to be when you were growing up?A dress designer.What is the worst thing anyone’ssaid to you?“Let’s face it, you’re not Ingrid Bergman.” I was 19 and he was a potential boyfriend. My only thought at the time was: “I’m not?”What do you most dislike about your appearance?My nose.What do you owe your parents?An apology.What does love feel like?Coming home.Which living person do you most despise?Guess …When did you last cryand why?At the election of Joe Biden, thinking we were out of the woods. Wrong.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat has been your biggest disappointment?Not keeping off the last 5lbs.If not yourself, who would you most like to be?Miriam Margolyes.What do you consider your greatest achievement?Still working.What keeps you awake at night?Insomnia.Would you rather have more sex, money or fame?Money – so I could give it away.How would you like to be remembered?Accurately.What is the most important lesson life has taught you?Don’t answer every question you’re asked.What happens when we die?God knows.Tell us a jokeA man goes to the doctor and takes off his hat to reveal a huge toad on the top of his head. “When did you notice that?” asked the doctor.
