title: Bar fight: Hugo cocktail takes aim at Aperol in UK summer of spritz | Food & drink industry | The Guardian
description: The elderflower drink is enjoying explosive growth, with Campari, Sarti Rosa and limoncello varieties also taking off
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: The elderflower drink is enjoying explosive growth, with Campari, Sarti Rosa and limoncello varieties also taking off
Content: The Hugo spritz is made with prosecco, elderflower liqueur, soda, mint and lemon slices.Photograph: Maren Winter/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Hugo spritz is made with prosecco, elderflower liqueur, soda, mint and lemon slices.Photograph: Maren Winter/AlamyFood & drink industryBar fight: Hugo cocktail takes aim at Aperol in UK summer of spritzThe elderflower drink is enjoying explosive growth, with Campari, Sarti Rosa and limoncello varieties also taking offZoe WoodSat 8 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s the summer of spritz as British sales figures show the Hugo elderflower cocktail snapping at the heels of the market-leader Aperol to be this year’s favourite drink.The number of Hugos ordered in bars nearly tripled in the three months to the end of June while demand for the vibrant red Campari spritz surged 52%.A limoncello version has also taken off, with sales up 31%, according to the payments company Square.The Hugo “has absolutely blown up,” said Steve Young, business unit director for Bacardi in the UK (the group’s St-Germain liqueur is the drink’s signature ingredient). He agreed that the Hugo spritz could be the drink of summer.Young said sales of St-Germain are growing faster in the UK than in any other country, with the elderflower liqueur “outselling some of our major spritz competitors across a lot of our customers. It has doubled in size over the last 12 months.”Created in Italy, and very popular in France, theHugo is sweeter than an Aperol spritzand is made with elderflower liqueur, prosecco, soda water and mint.View image in fullscreenThe Hugo may be on the rise, but Aperol spritz is still a UK market leader.Photograph: Kateryna Sheviakova/AlamyThe spritz sales data, gleaned from bar, cafe and restaurant till receipts, showed a 196% uplift for the Hugo in Great Britain in the three months to the end of June compared with a year ago. For the same period, Aperol spritz sales climbed 13%.The phenomenon is driven in part by the rise of the “daycap” – a replacement for the traditional nightcap with a longer, lighter-tasting drink in the late afternoon. This coincides with a shift in drinking patterns as late-afternoon – as opposed to late-night – drinking has become popular with millennials and gen Z.But it is gen Z that has put a rocket under the spritz business. For this age group (18-29) it is the number one cocktail, despite ranking sixth overall, according to Bacardi’s annual cocktail trends report.The popularity of the spritz means the choice on bar menus is increasing. This has been good news for Campari, which owns a drinks cabinet full of brands suitable for making colourful, Instagram-friendly spritzes.In the UK, sales of the group’s aperitif brands – which include Aperol, Campari, Sarti Rosa and the non-alcoholic Crodino – were up more than 10% in the first six months of this year. With its notes of “blood orange, mango and passion fruit”, the hot pink Sarti spritz is tipped as the next big thing, with Google searches up 341% on 2025.View image in fullscreenThe Sarti spritz may well become the next big thing in summer daycaps.Photograph: Sarti Aperitivo“The spritz has taken the UK by storm,” said Young. “Two years ago it did not make the top 10 in our annual survey and now it is the number one choice for gen-Zers.”But it is not just on a night out that Britons are enjoying a spritz, as supermarket and high street sales data suggests they have been added to the drinks cabinets of those socialising at home.“Spritzes are having their moment this summer,” said Tom Oakton, analyst at the data company NielsenIQ, adding that sales of this type of cocktail were growing much faster than the alcohol market as a whole in the UK.“Aperol remains the most popular, but St-Germain saw triple-digit growth from the rising popularity of the Hugo spritz,” said Oakton. While Aperol sales were up 32.4% by value in the 12 weeks to 1 August – boosted by the launch of Aperol-in-a-tin – St-Germain grew 135.5%.Global food prices at three-year high as heatwaves and wars push up crop costsRead moreFrancesca Parker-Partridge, spirits buyer at Ocado Retail, confirmed that spritzes are “dominating this summer’s drink scene. Total liqueur sales are up 19% year on year, driven by a massive 122% spike for St-Germain.”The Hugo may be elbowing its way on to drinks menus, but it still has a way to go to steal Aperol’s crown, with St-Germain becoming the David to the bright orange Goliath. Industry data suggests that about eight Aperols are sold for every St-Germain mixed Hugo.“It’s great to see new brands joining the space and growing the category, but scale tells the real story, with 8.8m cases sold globally last year alone,” said Francesco Cruciani, the managing director of Campari Group UK.“The Campari group remains the undisputed trailblazer leading the spritz movement into its next era,” he added, in comments underlining that – for the time being at least – Aperol is still king of the spritzes.Explore more on these topicsFood & drink industryAlcoholItalyCocktailsFoodShareReuse this content

title: ‘Never had anything like it’: Meera Sodha’s recipe for Marseille-style apple cake | Cake | The Guardian
description: With its sweet, caramelised edge and soft, creamy apple centre, you’ll be thinking about this cake for months after the first bite
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: With its sweet, caramelised edge and soft, creamy apple centre, you’ll be thinking about this cake for months after the first bite
Content: Meera Sodha’s apple cake, in homage to the team at Limmat restaurant in Marseille, France.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence. Photo assistant: Sophie Bronze.View image in fullscreenMeera Sodha’s apple cake, in homage to the team at Limmat restaurant in Marseille, France.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence. Photo assistant: Sophie Bronze.Meera Sodha recipesCake‘Never had anything like it’: Meera Sodha’s recipe for Marseille-style apple cakeWith its sweet, caramelised edge and soft, creamy apple centre, you’ll be thinking about this cake for months after the first biteMeera SodhaSat 8 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor better or for worse (definitely for worse), this column is one-way. If we could talk, I’d ask you about the most mindblowing things you’ve eaten in your wild and precious life (feel free to use the comments). This year, for me, it was chef Lili’s apple cake at her restaurant,Limmatin Marseille. I’ve never had anything like it: a cake of pure apple – one and a half kilos – sliced and bound together with a breath of flour, a trickle of cream, a spoonful of sugar, a couple of eggs and a lot of time (in the oven). The result is a caramelised edge and a heavenly, scoopable, custard-like apple centre. Heavenly.Limmat’s apple cakeWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appYou’ll need a 23cm springform tin and a food processor with a 2mm slicing disc to cut the apples thinly enough. Alternatively, do this by hand with a mandoline or knife, though you’ll need to take your time to make sure the apples are thin enough.Prep15 minCook2 hrChill4 hr+Makes1 x 23cm cake, to serve 8-101½kg braeburn apples(about 12), peeled, cored and halved2 large eggs100ml double cream130g soft light brown sugar¾ tsp baking powder75g plain flourCreme fraiche, or more double cream, to serveHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4, and line a 23cm springform cake tin with baking paper, making sure there are no gaps for liquid to escape through later.Using a food processor with a slicing disc, finely slice the apples into 2mm-thick half-moons, then layer them horizontally in the cake tin, making sure there are no big gaps and pressing down each layer as you go.Break the eggs into a large bowl, add the double cream and sugar, and whisk well. Evenly sprinkle the baking powder and flour on top and whisk again. Slowly pour this batter over the sliced apples, then give the tin a gentle shimmy so it falls into and fills any gaps in the apples, if need be.Bake for an hour and 40 minutes (if need be, turn the tin around in the oven halfway through), until the cake is evenly golden brown on top and there are lots of browned apple slices showing through. Remove from the oven, leave to cool to room temperature, then chill in the fridge for at least four hours, or overnight.Unmould the cake from its tin, peel off the paper and place on a serving plate. Slice with a sharp knife and serve with big spoonfuls of creme fraiche alongside.Explore more on these topicsCakeMeera Sodha recipesDessertFruitSummer food and drinkVegetablesBakingFoodrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Going bananas for bandanas: the latest fashion trend that goes back centuries | Accessories | The Guardian
description: From Dua Lipa to Zendaya, the kerchief worn by gang members, presidents and pirates has become ‘mad-glamorous’
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: From Dua Lipa to Zendaya, the kerchief worn by gang members, presidents and pirates has become ‘mad-glamorous’
Content: Karen Blanchard wearing a turquoise bandana at the Malene Birger show at Copenhagen fashion week on Tuesday.Photograph: Raimonda Kulikauskienė/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKaren Blanchard wearing a turquoise bandana at the Malene Birger show at Copenhagen fashion week on Tuesday.Photograph: Raimonda Kulikauskienė/Getty ImagesAccessoriesGoing bananas for bandanas: the latest fashion trend that goes back centuriesFrom Dua Lipa to Zendaya, the kerchief worn by gang members, presidents and pirates has become ‘mad-glamorous’Ellie Violet BramleySat 8 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBaseball caps have been keeping the heads of fashion folk covered and shaded for the past few years. But there’s a new accessory to be seen everywhere this summer: the bandana.They are as common as cinnamon buns at Copenhagen fashion week, which is taking place in the Danish capital this week. They have also recently been worn by Dua Lipa to the beach, Zendaya to shop for books and Priyanka Chopra Jonas to watch the tennis at Wimbledon.Toast offers them blockprinted by artisans in India, they come in broderie Anglaise at Asos and embroidered at Next. The singer Gracie Abrams, who wore one last summer to play Glastonbury, has sincereleased bandanas as part of her merchandise.View image in fullscreenStreet style … Laura Schulte wearing a bandana during Copenhagen fashion week on Tuesday.Photograph: Moritz Scholz/Getty ImagesOn the secondhand site Depop, which offers bandanas in gingham, with skulls and crossbones, and crocheted, searches have gone up 152% in the past three months. Social media is, unsurprisingly,rich in tutorialson how to style them, whether on dayswhen hair is waiting for a washorusing an elastic headbandto keep slippy silk styles in place.Grazia’s fashion commerce editor, Daisy Murray, “started wearing bandanas last summer as a little Jackie O homage”.“They offer a little vintage – 60s/70s and 90s – feel to every look,” she says, adding how practical they are. “I live in Brighton and have two small children, so it’s a great way to manage curly hair on a windy beach.”Bella Webb, sustainability editor at Vogue Business, has been wearing one to the shows in Copenhagen. “I love multi-functional items that can make my outfits feel fresh and playful without buying something new,” she says.The history goes back far further than Felicity Kendal in a pair of dungarees. Invented in India (the Sanskrit wordbandhmeans “to tie”),according to the Smithsonian magazine, “textile makers employed a millennium-old tie-dyeing technique calledbandhanito create colourful silk and cotton kerchiefs covered in lively patterns”.View image in fullscreenGracie Abrams performing on the Other Stage at Glastonbury in 2025.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAFrom south Asia they were imported to England by the Dutch and English East India Companies, where snuff-takers, used to leaving unsightly tobacco stains on their plain hankies, apparently “embraced them to make their habit more discreet”. Paisley, a pattern named after the Scottish townbut which originated in Kashmir, is the classic bandana pattern.With a rich and global lineage, bandanas can signal drastically different things. Throughout history they have been associated with cowboys and robbers,linked to gang affiliationand becomea symbol for workers’ rights.They alsofit quietly into Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy’s 90s minimalism. They have been worn by hip-hop stars such as Tupac Shakur, and by Rosie the Riveter, who professed on wartime women’s behalf: “We can do it!”, wearing a red polka dot bandana. In 2003,Missy Elliott matched a pink onewith her velour Adidas tracksuit to accept a Grammy. Carrie Bradshaw wore them with abandon in Sex and the City.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMissy Elliot after winning best female rap solo performance at the 2003 Grammy awards in New York City.Photograph: Scott Gries/Getty ImagesPolitical campaigners have long understood the potential power of a bandana. Martha Washington is thought to have commissioned a bandana design, featuring George on a horse, around 1775, during the revolutionary war, and they have been popular presidential campaign items since at least the 1840s. A red bandanawas created for Theodore Roosevelt’s presidential campaign in 1912(he famously wore one while fighting during the Spanish-American war) and in 1952 Dwight Eisenhower’s campaign emblazoned one with: “Win with Ike for President”.Are slogan hats the new slogan T-shirts?Read moreBridget Dalton, a semiotician and cultural analyst at Truth Consulting, says: “There is a subtext around race when it comes to headscarves. Black communities have long worn them, obviously hijabi people cover their heads, as do [married women in] Haredi communities.” For many people they serve a specific purpose. “For Black people with natural hair, they protect them, they cover them, they keep [their hair] protected at night. For people with religious beliefs, they’re part of their spiritual life. And for people who wear them for work, then they’re to keep their hair clean and safe.”All of these references, meanings and iterations are loaded on to what is, on the surface, a simple square of fabric. But for many people this summer, they have become an adornment. As Dalton says, “bandanas are also mad-glamorous”.Explore more on these topicsAccessoriesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I haven’t felt this present for months’: sail back in time on a Thames barge in Essex | Sailing holidays | The Guardian
description: You don’t have to be a sailor to cruise the estuaries of Essex on this historic craft. The skipper will show you the ropes – or just sit back and enjoy the ride
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: You don’t have to be a sailor to cruise the estuaries of Essex on this historic craft. The skipper will show you the ropes – or just sit back and enjoy the ride
Content: Tollesbury Saltings, a natural tidal marina and saltmarsh ecosystem at the mouth of the River Blackwater.Photograph: Geoffrey Robinson/AlamyView image in fullscreenTollesbury Saltings, a natural tidal marina and saltmarsh ecosystem at the mouth of the River Blackwater.Photograph: Geoffrey Robinson/AlamySailing holidays‘I haven’t felt this present for months’: sail back in time on a Thames barge in EssexYou don’t have to be a sailor to cruise the estuaries of Essex on this historic craft. The skipper will show you the ropes – or just sit back and enjoy the rideImogen LepereSat 8 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 06.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a darkened room in Maldon, Essex, a ship’s lantern illuminates the laundry drying on a web of ropes suspended from the ceiling. Between piles of sailing memorabilia, 86-year-old Barry Pearce is flipping through a yellowing logbook, watched by his mongrel, Winkle. It feels more like a ship’s cabin than a terrace house. Pearce is one of a handful of surviving skippers who delivered freight on the Thames by sailing barge, the flat-bottomed trading boats famous for their striking red sails that were endemic to the river’s estuary until the 1960s. He remembers the names of every vessel he worked on – Remercie, Edith May, Colonia.In the 19th century, the ochre sails of thousands of Thames sailing barges pierced the skyline as the craft carried cargo from the Thames estuary and beyond in and out of London. Their shallow draft allowed them to snake far upriver in as little as a metre of water (bargemen would boast that they could sail anywhere there had been a heavy dew). Their ingenious rig, with sails that could be set and stowed with the help of winches, meant around 150tonnes of cargo could be shifted by just a skipper and mate – often accompanied by a guard dog. This efficiency allowed them to outlive all other commercial sailing vessels, surviving until the 1960s, when Pearce himself took the helm.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian GraphicsToday, only about 30 Thames barges are still sailing, either as private homes or leisure cruisers. Two of them – Pudge and Centaur – lie like beached krakens on the oozing mud of Maldon’s Blackwater estuary. Both are owned by theThames Sailing Barge Trust, a charity run entirely by volunteers, including Pearce. Every summer, both vessels can be hired asprivate chartersfor groups of up to 12, or you can book a berth on one of their one- to three-daypublic sailing cruises. They also offer events such aschildren’s art daysthroughout the year.I’m here on a scorching evening at Hythe quay to spend the weekend exploring the River Blackwater and Essex coast aboard Centaur, a barge built in 1895. Itineraries are flexible and based on passengers’ interests. For us it involves sailing up the Blackwater, a Pimm’s at Tollesbury Marina, and a swim off Shingle Point and wander around West Mersea on Mersea Island. Our motley crew consists of three trainees overseen by skipper Chris Martin, who teaches boatbuilding at vocational training organisationCircles Alternative Education.View image in fullscreenCentaur in the Blackwater estuary.Photograph: Chris BourneThere are also six passengers, ranging in age from 18 to 76, in five cabins, which are basic but comfortable (each has a wash basin). Although I am the only one who is not a competent sailor, Martin makes it clear that helping to handle the barge is optional.Unwisely, given our 3am departure to catch high tide, I sink several pints with the two youngest members of Pudge’s crew in the Little Ship Club on the quay. A behemothic man wielding a squeezebox sings sea shanties as salty couples slow dance nearby. “I only know of one or two people my age who are into barging, and I find that disturbing,” yells 25-year-old Charlie Francis over strains of Bound for South Australia. “Barging was the lifeblood of the east coast. We should be proud of our heritage and celebrate the communities working to preserve it.”double quotation markSailing barges can teach us the value of slowing down, doing things with our hands and spending time in natureAfter a few hours in my bunk, I make it on to deck at 4.15am. The moon is a slice of radish in a lilac sky. We’re bearing away from the wind and, having set the sails, the crew is already on their second round of tea and custard creams.As dawn paints its peachy palette, Martin turns the great wheel. He points out Blackwater landmarks that only a local would know: the green buoy known as the Doctor, where early 20th-century fishers left spirits for the alcoholics supposedly drying out at Osea Island’s temperance resort; the pub where, as recently as 20 years ago, Martin witnessed a smuggler wordlessly deliver two dripping bags while regulars stared determinedly into their pints; the hulking trawler, Ross Revenge, which is still home to Radio Caroline, the former pirate station – another relic kept alive by volunteers of the Blackwater.View image in fullscreenThe writer on the deck of the Centaur.Photograph: Laura Lewis/The GuardianWhere the river opens into the silvery sea, the wind picks up and the barge rocks gently against the tide. My eyelids are heavy and the slowness of the whole experience is working its magic on my screen-frazzled brain. Martin calls for the staysail to be unfurled, a 20-minute task that rewards the barge with another knot and a half of speed. “This life is the antithesis of the digital age’s obsession with instant gratification,” he says. “Sailing barges may not be able to teach us much about cargo any more, but they can teach us the value of slowing down, doing things with our hands and spending time in nature.”As we make our stately, seven-knot progress, 370 sq metres of rust-red canvas billows above and fingers of salt marsh slide by. With so little distraction, the coffee tastes lip-curlingly bitter, the bacon sandwiches as saline as the deep. I settle on a coil of rope to scan the horizon for porpoises, but soon drift into sleep.A swim from a sandbank near Tollesbury is followed by a meander through West Mersea at golden hour. Clapboard cottages framed by hollyhocks sit beside sailmakers and chandleries converted into trendy cafes. We drop anchor in the Blackwater estuary and beneath a blazing sunset tuck into lasagne on deck. I haven’t felt this present for months. It’s all such a delight I begin to feel concerned about the trust’s future. Sailing barges cost between £30,000 and £100,000 a year to keep afloat. The trip I’m on costs just £220 including meals, while the Trust’s annual membership is only £37.50.Although the trust offers training in many of the skills needed to maintain the barges, sourcing the timber is becoming increasingly difficult – and expensive. “Centaur’s exterior planking is pitch pine from the Mississippi basin, which is incredibly durable, but has been virtually exhausted,” says Martin. “And so much of the timber trade has been replaced by plastic.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markSailing may be associated with privilege, but we are a seafaring nation and this inheritance belongs to all of usThe trust also offers free training for future skippers, including the mate on our trip, 18-year-old Ben Weldon, the son of a local shipwright. However, it typically takes 2,000 hours – or 10 years – and the dropout rate is high.While the trust has recently been awarded £28,090 from the National Lottery Heritage Fund to develop a bid for the £4m needed to restore Centaur, it seems wrong that responsibility for keeping this thread of Britain’s maritime story from unravelling rests on so few shoulders. Sailing may be associated with privilege, but we are a seafaring nation and this inheritance belongs to all of us.View image in fullscreenSkipper Chris Martin, on the left, on board Centaur.Photograph: Imogen LepereOn Sunday morning, our last on board, a westerly fills the sails, and the tea-coloured Blackwater wrinkles beneath the bow as we beat our way back towards Maldon. “Lee ho,” Martin calls, showing me how to spin the wheel to help the crew tack. “So far we’ve used less than a gallon of fuel to do 50 miles. Pretty extraordinary, given that a family car does about 30 miles to the gallon.”When I asked Pearce at the start of the trip why keeping Thames sailing barges afloat is worth the fight, he looked blank, as if such a question had never occurred to him. He showed me a pencil sketch of a barge he had drawn at the age of 15 in Greenwich, left half-finished when his skipper had poked his head through the hatch and invited him below for dinner. Now, more than 70 years later, he bends once more over that drawing as though no time has passed.Eventually, he half-whispers: “Well, they’re just lovely, ain’t they?” He glances toward the window. Nearby, Centaur waits on the mud for the returning tide.The trip was provided by theThames Sailing Barge Trust. The next weekend aboardCentaurdepartson 14August, £220for two nights’ full board; three-night trips depart on3 September(£350on Pudge, £320 onCentaur)and 18 September(£290 on Centaur). A variety of one-day sailings are also availablefrom £55 to £125ppExplore more on these topicsSailing holidaysEngland holidaysUnited Kingdom holidaysShort breaksDay tripsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: how many electricians does it take to install an electric car charger? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: ‘Can’t you just plug it in?’ asks our garage mechanic neighbour. If only it were that simple
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: ‘Can’t you just plug it in?’ asks our garage mechanic neighbour. If only it were that simple
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnLife and styleTim Dowling: how many electricians does it take to install an electric car charger?‘Can’t you just plug it in?’ asks our garage mechanic neighbour. If only it were that simpleTim DowlingSat 8 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 16.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a Wednesday morning the doorbell rings while I’m working in the kitchen. My wife, who is expecting a delivery, opens the door. “No, I don’t want brake pads,” she says. I don’t hear the reply. “Because I’m not a garage,” my wife says. “Do I look like a garage?”There actually is a small garage just beyond the end of our back garden. Only a brick wall separates it from my office shed – my working days are punctuated by the bright ring of dropped wrenches and the grating whine of power tools.double quotation markWe get a lot of the mechanic’s deliveries. Sometimes it’s brake pads or a headlamp unit. Once I was asked to sign for a smashed-up BMW on a low-loader at 11pmBecause of this proximity, we get a lot of the mechanic’s post, and many of his deliveries come to us first. Sometimes it’s brake pads; sometimes it’s a headlamp unit for an Audi A3. Once I was asked to sign for a smashed-up BMW on a low-loader at 11pm.We’re on friendly terms with the mechanic – he has parking spaces we sometimes borrow – so it’s in a spirit of neighbourly diplomacy that I walk round to his premises with the two shock absorbers I found leaning against my front door when I arrived home on Friday afternoon.“I was just thinking of ringing your bell,” he says.“I don’t know how long they’ve been there,” I say.We chat for a bit about the weather, pausing while someone inside uses an angle grinder.“So,” he says. “I see you’ve got an electric car now.”“Yeah,” I say.“How’s that working out for you?”I hesitate, because I know he probably doesn’t want my full answer. The problem, I explain anyway, is not the car – I like the car – but the fast charging point that still hasn’t been installed on my drive.“You can’t just use a regular plug?” he says.“You can,” I say, “but then a full charge takes 36 hours.”“OK,” he says, in a tone that does not suggest he can’t wait to hear more.The electrician who came to install the charger, I explain anyway, fell into immediate despair on seeing the proposed route between the fuse box and the installation site. After some passive-aggressive wheedling on my part, he reluctantly agreed to help me lift some floorboards to run the cable. Only then did he inform me I needed remedial electrical work done – bonding, he called it – before he could continue. Then he left.“Sounds crazy,” says the mechanic, his voice carefully stripped of encouragement.It took three days, I continue anyway, to negotiate a price for the bonding, and another three to secure a second appointment. I changed my plans to ensure I would be home on the day, only for the appointment to be suddenly postponed for a further week, to a date in the middle of my holiday. Finally, with very little remaining goodwill on my part, a fourth installation date was agreed upon.“And that date,” I say, “is next Monday. It’s taken two months so far.”“Well, good luck with it,” says the mechanic, waving me off with a raised shock absorber.double quotation markOnce the new electrician has examined the fuse box, I show him where the laid cable runs and wait for him to tell me what’s wrong with itThat evening a new electrician rings to confirm our Monday appointment. He adds that he’s very concerned about the proposed cable route from the fuse box to the installation site.“The cable’s already laid,” I tell him. “The other guy did it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“What other guy?” he says.“You don’t know about the other guy?” I say. “Do you know about the bonding?”“It’s not on my worksheet,” he says.“I have a story to tell you,” I say. “A long story.”Tim Dowling: our new electric car has a mind all of its ownRead moreAt 8am on Monday my wife lets the new electrician in, and promptly leaves with the dog. Once he’s examined the fuse box, I show him where the laid cable runs – under the living room floor, out through the wall and along the side of the house – and wait for him to tell me what’s wrong with it.“No, that’s fine,” he says.“What about the bonding?” I say.“You don’t need bonding,” he says. “I tested it, and it’s all working.”“I don’t need bonding?” I say.When my wife comes home an hour later the electrician is gone, and the charging point is installed. I show her how to control it via the app.“How do I get the app?” she says.“I don’t know, he did it for me,” I say. “In, like, 10 seconds.” My phone pings in my hand: an automated message from the charger company, saying that a qualified electrician will be arriving that afternoon.“Christ,” I say.When the doorbell rings at five I’m half expecting a third electrician with no knowledge of the previous two, but it’s just a delivery driver holding an intake manifold.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘You can feel the warmth of the sun’: Bertram Greenhough’s best phone picture | Photography | The Guardian
description: The Brighton-based photographer was walking along a crowded beach looking for ice-cream when he spotted this calm, minimalist scene
Author: Grace Holliday
Headline: The Brighton-based photographer was walking along a crowded beach looking for ice-cream when he spotted this calm, minimalist scene
Content: Lifeguard, 2023, shot on iPhone 13 Pro.Photograph: Bertram GreenhoughView image in fullscreenLifeguard, 2023, shot on iPhone 13 Pro.Photograph: Bertram GreenhoughSmart shotPhotography‘You can feel the warmth of the sun’: Bertram Greenhough’s best phone pictureThe Brighton-based photographer was walking along a crowded beach looking for ice-cream when he spotted this calm, minimalist sceneGrace HollidaySat 8 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBertram Greenhough had promised his six-year-old daughter Audrey an ice-cream. It was a warm June day in Brighton and the pair were playing tourists in their own city, having just visitedan upside-down housenear the i360 observation tower. The beach was packed, and they were heading in the direction of the Palace Pier so that Greenhough could stay true to his word. Along the way, they passed this lifeguard shelter.‘The children were delighted to see themselves in such bright colours’: Moe Wai’s best phone pictureRead more“I often walk around Brighton with my SLR film camera – very hipster of me. However, that day I only had my phone,” Greenhough recalls. “But, as the adage goes, the best camera is the one you have with you. I saw this calm, minimalist scene suspended above thousands of people and I remember saying to my daughter, ‘Oh, look at that, I need to take a picture!’ She had no idea what I was talking about!”A second later, the lifeguard moved and the composition and harmony had gone. It was, for Greenhough, “a decisive moment”.Later that evening – Mr Whippy with a flake secured and devoured – he used one of the presets in Lightroom to make some edits. “I tend to use them as a starting point,” he says. “I often find how I see a scene and what the camera actually records can be quite different, so I increased the vibrancy of the yellows and reds, and adjusted the hue of the blue sky to complement the other two colours.“I hope it gives people a sense of peace and security,” Greenhough adds. “Perhaps, like me, they can feel the warmth of the sun.”Explore more on these topicsPhotographySmart shotArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I couldn’t breathe’: the deadly health burden of wildfire smoke | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Scientists race to untangle complex links between exposure and mortality as fire weather grows more prevalent
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: Scientists race to untangle complex links between exposure and mortality as fire weather grows more prevalent
Content: People look toward the downtown skyline from the Toronto Islands as forest fires cause poor air quality over the city.Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople look toward the downtown skyline from the Toronto Islands as forest fires cause poor air quality over the city.Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty ImagesThe Saturday readWildfires‘I couldn’t breathe’: the deadly health burden of wildfire smokeScientists race to untangle complex links between exposure and mortality as fire weather grows more prevalentAjit NiranjanSat 8 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 08.07 EDTShareA thousand kilometres from the infernos gorging on northern Ontario’s boreal forests, Erin O’Connor watched the sky above Canada’s biggest city turn an “almost post-apocalyptic” orange as it filled with light-scattering particles of soot and ash. Stepping outside the halls of Toronto General hospital, where air filters were keeping patients safe from the worst of the fumes, she was struck by a smell so strong it felt like standing by a campfire.“It really hit you in the face as soon as you walked outside,” said O’Connor, who runs UniversityHealthNetwork’s emergency department and saw a rise in patients presenting with allergies and shortness of breath. “As the days progressed, it was like that everywhere. It seemed even inside you could smell that burning.”Far more than the flames that have engulfed southern Europe and North America in recent weeks, it is the smoke that dominates the astonishing death toll from combusting nature. Thick with toxic gases that inflame the airways and tiny particulates that breach the lungs and ride the bloodstream to hit every organ in the body, fumes from landscape fires kill 1.5 million people each year, astudyin the Lancet found in 2024 – more than floods, flames, storms and heat combined.So damaging are the lung-scarring effects of charred plant matter that people far from the fires may still perish. The plumes spewed by wildfires in Canada in 2023 caused 82,000 early deaths, astudyin Nature found last year, with unfavourable winds pushing a third of the mortality burden into the US and another quarter into Europe. About 10% of the UK’s fine particulate pollution (PM2.5) comes from biomass burned abroad, researchersfoundin March.View image in fullscreenThe Quilpituk Creek wildfire in British Columbia, seen here across Okanagan Lake.Photograph: Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press/APYet while scientists agree the health burden of wildfire smoke is jaw droppingly large, they are only beginning to untangle the complex links between exposure and mortality. The open research questions are growing more pressing as climate breakdown makes fire weather more severe. What if hotter infernos cause pollution to peak at even more extreme levels? What if bad air lasts several days or weeks? What if a severe episode hits before a person has fully recovered from the last bout of smoke?Whims of the windThe lack of answers in the existing research makes it hard to get a handle on how brutal the fallout from this furious fire season will be. Early signs are troubling, with vast tracts of vegetation torched close to big European cities and, after a late but explosive start to the North American fire season, smoke choking major population centres such as Chicago and New York City. In Toronto, which briefly had theworst air qualityof any major metropolis in the world last month – a title claimed by Portland in the US on Wednesday – O’Connor said she could not remember the pollution ever having been so bad, with such a sudden onset that took so long to clear up.“I had never looked outside and had the sky seem orange in the middle of the day,” said O’Connor, who amid treating patients and fielding media requests rushed to pull her son from summer camp. “Certainly, we have had other wildfire smoke, but in more of a transient way.”Graphs of hazardous peaks in air pollution in Bordeaux, Angoulême and Limoges caused by Gironde wildfiresPerhaps surprisingly, the death toll from a fire season can depend on the whims of the wind as much as the size of the fire. Wildfires in France spewed record amounts of pollution in the first half of the year and in Spain emissions have so far fallen just shy of the worst it has known. But even though monster infernos were halted alarmingly close toMadridandBordeaux, the smoke was mostly blown away from where people live. Daily particulate pollution levels still worsened across southern Europe and peaked at a staggering 342 micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic metre (μg/m³) in Bordeaux on 24 July – and 486 μg/m³ in Limoges, 180km (112 miles) away, the following day – but other big cities in southern Europe were spared the extremes that doctors fear.View image in fullscreenWildfires across France, such as this one near Carcassonne, have been burning for weeks.Photograph: Pablo Cozzaglio/AFP/Getty ImagesNorth America has not been so lucky. As winds blew south and south-east from scarcely populated forests in Ontario and the Northwest Territories, at least 36 million people across the continent were breathing air fouled by “very unhealthy” concentrations of PM2.5 that exceeded 125.5μg/m³ on 16 July, preliminary analysis conducted for the Guardian shows. At least 10 million people were exposed to more than 250μg/m³, according to the estimates, a level of daily pollution that smog-choked New Delhi saw no more than eight times last year.Scientists say the hit to air quality in some big cities is reminiscent of the megafires in 2023 that came with vast death tolls. “As soon as we have massive population centres exposed, we’re going to see those increases,” said Stephanie Cleland, a wildfire health scientist at Simon Fraser University, who considered only people living within 25km of a measuring station in her calculations for the Guardian and said the figures are therefore conservative. “I would be concerned by the fact that it’s only been three years since this last happened and now we’re having it again.”‘It felt like working in a war zone’In a quiet suburb of Duluth, in north-east Minnesota, the worst of the smoke was seen, smelled and tasted on 16 July. Jae Jeon and Dan McClelland, a married couple who grow flowers for weddings and subscription deliveries, were looking forward to opening the windows after days baking in oppressive heat. Instead, they woke up to a fog that they soon realised was made up of something much worse. By late morning, their local hardware store had sold out of masks and air purifiers. People resorted to attaching furnace filters to box fans instead.Map of wildfires smoke spreading across North AmericaThe McClellands were among 12,000 people in west Duluth exposed to an average of 541μg/m³ of fine particulate pollution, the analysis shows, higher than anywhere else in North America. They sent their sole farmworker home early after she complained of a headache but, with two weddings coming up on the weekend and little chance of cancellation, they still had plenty of flowers to pick and arrange. The couple got to work harvesting roses, yarrows, clematises and sweet peas, surrounded by a dystopian haze the likes of which they had never experienced.“It felt like working in a war zone,” said Jae Jeon. “When I went outside, I couldn’t breathe, so I had to wear a mask, but it was still painful. After just a couple of minutes you started to get a headache.”View image in fullscreenPeople look out at the smog caused by wildfire smoke from the CN Tower in Ontario last month. yellowish-grey in Canada’s largest city.Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty ImagesClimate breakdown made last month’s fire weather twice as likely in Canada and France, and 20 times more likely in Spain, recentrapid analyseshave found, the result of planet-heating emissions that have made it easier for vegetation to dry out. As plants and trees combust, they spew a host of harmful particles that also trigger damaging inflammatory responses as the body seeks to purge foreign objects.Scientists have relied on general air pollution relations to model the smoke’s chronic health effects, which make up the bulk of the death toll, because they lack long-term studies specific to wildfires. “The reason we don’t have them for wildfire smoke is because we haven’t had to deal with this as kind of a repeated ongoing problem,” said Michael Brauer, a wildfire health scientist at the University of British Columbia and co-author of the study onCanada’s 2023 fires. He first experienced wildfire smoke when he was about 40 years old, he said, while a 10-year-old child where he lives in British Columbia would have breathed it every summer of their life.Compounding climate eventsBut the analogy to regular pollution is imperfect. Compared with other sources of PM2.5, such as factories or cars, wildfire smoke contains a greater share of organic compounds that increase inflammation and a higher concentration of ultra-fine particles that penetrate the deepest recesses of the lungs. PM2.5 from wildfire smoke is up to 10 times more harmful in the short-term, astudyin Nature Communications found in 2021, and factoring this into epidemiological models suggests death tolls from short-term exposure to wildfire smoke have been greatly underestimated, astudyin the Lancet Planetary Health found last year.Some researchers suggest high peak exposure during serious smoke episodes better explains why wildfire particulates do more damage than regular ones. “It may be that it’s because the smoke is chemically more toxic, or it may be – what I think is more likely – that it’s basically overwhelming your defences,” said Brauer, who compared it to having one drink a day for a year rather than bingeing 365 in 24 hours. “That’s clearly going to have different impacts.”When wildfire smoke gets bad, experts recommend wearing masks, closing windows and checking in on vulnerable neighbours, particularly old people with chronic disease who live alone. They also recommend checking air quality monitors in the morning and moving activities indoors when the pollution is too high.In some cases, actions to keep the air clean may conflict with efforts to stay cool, according to areportfrom the BC Lung Foundation published last month. “The issue is we have a lot of compound climate exposure events where you have heat and wildfire,” said Cathryn Tonne, an environmental epidemiologist at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health and co-author of the study modelling wildfire-specific PM2.5. “Being home with the windows closed can be very bad – if you don’t have air conditioning – if it’s also hot.”Can the fires behind the smoke at least be prevented? At the Fifa World Cup final, which barely avoided disruption from bad air, the US president, Donald Trump,asked his Canadian counterpart, Mark Carney, to “stop these fires from coming in and poisoning our air”. The demand was accompanied by threats of sanctions and came as Republican senators blamed Canada’s fires on poor forest management. Scientists countered that the blazes had little to do with land management – most of what has burned is boreal forest in unpopulated areas – and a lot to do with the rise in temperatures caused by burning fossil fuels, which Republicans have expanded.View image in fullscreenA view of Manhattan, New York from Brooklyn Bridge park as wildfire smoke from Canada causes smoggy conditions last month.Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty ImagesInEurope, though, changes in land use have alarmed firefighters and wildfire experts about as much as global heating. Rural regions across the Mediterranean have hollowed out, resulting in more overgrown vegetation that dries out and allows fires to spread more easily during the hotter heatwaves that climate breakdown has brought. The combination of the two factors has led Spanish wildfire scientists to warn that we have “entered an era of fires we cannot extinguish”.It is a problem that other parts of the world, from the western US to Australia, already know well. Adding to the climatic burden in the coming months is the arrival of a strongEl Niño, a cyclical warming weather pattern, along with a related natural phenomenon in the Indian Ocean, which is priming countries across south-east Asia to burn.The McClellands said that – even though they still had their homes and their health – the episode had given them a taste of the suffering that climate breakdown has long caused in other countries. “I know that people all around the world are feeling a kind of helplessness because of climate disasters,” said Dan McClelland. “I feel like this opened my eyes to understand just a sliver of what other people are feeling.”

title: Google DeepMind enters a new era as co-founder Demis Hassabis shifts AI role | DeepMind | The Guardian
description: Observers express concern that the division has lost its independence and commercial reality has taken over
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Observers express concern that the division has lost its independence and commercial reality has taken over
Content: Demis Hassabis at Google's offices in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDemis Hassabis at Google's offices in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianDeepMindGoogle DeepMind enters a new era as co-founder Demis Hassabis shifts AI roleObservers express concern that the division has lost its independence and commercial reality has taken overDan MilmoandAisha DownSat 8 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenSir Demis Hassabissaid AI had brought the world to a “pivotal moment in human history” last month, he knew another big change was imminent.This shift was closer to home. TheNobel prize-winninghead of Google DeepMind, Google’s AI unit, announced this week he wasrelinquishing his day-to-day duties as chief executiveand becoming chair. He is also taking on the role of chief scientist at DeepMind’s parent, Alphabet.Hassabis andDeepMindhave been key players in AI’s breakthrough era. The 50-year-old co-founded DeepMind and sold it to Google in 2014, which gave him the resources to oversee a number of advances.These included building the AlphaGo system that mastered theChinese board game Goand developing AlphaFold, a programme that predicts the 3D structure of proteins. The latter resulted in Hassabis being jointly awarded the 2024 Nobel prize in chemistry.A formerGoogleexecutive said the leadership overhaul showed London-based DeepMind being brought firmly into the orbit of its parent in Mountain View, California. DeepMind will now be run by Hassabis’s longstanding colleague, the US-based Koray Kavukcuoglu, who will take the non-CEO role of senior vice-president of DeepMind.“The era of DeepMind as an independent actor is over and the obvious sign of that is you have gone from a charismatic founder-leader to appointing Koray in a non-CEO leadership role. Koray is a technical character, not an inspirational figure like Demis,” said the former executive.The ex-Google employee added that it would be “galling” for Google and Hassabis that the latest iterations of Google’s flagship AI model series, Gemini, have lost ground to rival models developed by its US rivals Anthropic and OpenAI.Hassabis has said he was looking forward to focusing more on the “big picture” for AI and believed he was handing over operational management of a unit that was well placed for the competitive battles ahead.View image in fullscreenThe London DeepMind office will be brought into the orbit of its parent in Mountain View, California, a former Google executive said.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesInternally, DeepMind is a workplace where there have been political tensions. Employees who spoke to the Guardian said there was internal disquiet over the company’s work with the Pentagon. Earlier this year, a former Google DeepMind employee launched a legal challenge against Google, claiming they wereunfairly dismissedfor their views on Gaza.That employee was involved in unionisation efforts at Google DeepMind, which have taken place against a backdrop of concern that Google’s AI could assist militaries, including the Israel Defense Forces. Another Google DeepMind employeeresignedfrom the company in mid-July, citing Google’s work with the Pentagon and the US Department of Homeland Security.One said to the Guardian that Hassabis’s departure was the “end of an era”.“Now the person we were supposed to trust to get the right outcomes for humanity has stepped away,” they said. Google DeepMind “has become just another subdivision of Google”, they added.Rosa Curling, the executive director of Foxglove, a campaign group that supported the Google DeepMind employee in their legal challenge, said: “The departure of the co-founder of a company that once prided itself on its ethical credentials is likely to cause further concern among its frontier AI staff about how their work will end up being used in the real world.”Google has said it is committed to the “private and public sector consensus” that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without “appropriate human oversight”. While Google has declined a voluntary union recognition agreement in London, it has said it valued “the constructive and direct dialogue that we have with our employees about building a positive and successful workplace”.View image in fullscreenSome Google staff have been uncomfortable about its work with the Pentagon.Photograph: Joshua Roberts/ReutersOn the commercial side, a new cutting-edge model, Gemini 3.5 Pro, has yet to be released amid reports it has been delayed owing to attempts to improve its code-writing abilities – a core part of the appeal of Anthropic and OpenAI’s best products.Google’s two AI labs, London-based DeepMind and California-based Google Brain, were merged into Google DeepMind under Hassabis’s leadership three years ago. Control now appears to be moving back to the US, where Google’s co-founder Sergey Brin is reportedly playing a bigger role in AI development.Citing the departure of the leading AI researcher Yann LeCun from Meta and Geoffrey Hinton from Google as another example of “the end of an era in the AI ecosystem”, the former executive added: “This is very clearly a sign that the science-driven agenda of leadership in these labs has given way to cold, hard commercial reality that all of these companies want to make a return on the hundreds of billions of dollars they have invested in AI.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe source added, however, that Google still had the benefit of being able to combine its Gemini models with an impressive suite of products, from its all-conquering search product to its cloud platform and YouTube. Thanks to its search business it also has the money to continue investing heavily in AI, having generated net income – a US measure of profit – of $132bn (£98bn) last year.View image in fullscreenHassabis has called for a US safety body to assess cutting-edge AI models.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersHassabis has also taken on a more statesman-like role in recent years. The reference to a “pivotal moment” came in a blogpost in which he called for a US safety body to assess cutting-edge models, with the hope it would lead to the establishment of global standards.The need for such a body, Hassabis argued, was pressing because the tech industry was approaching the “pivotal” point of achieving AGI, the term for a theoretical state of AI where a system can perform any human cognitive task – which also means being capable of performing white collar jobs in sectors such as law, finance and health.A Google spokesperson said: “This is a move Demis has been thinking about for a while. He is very excited, and this will give him more time to focus on AI-driven scientific breakthroughs.” They disputed that the changes had anything to do with the performance of Gemini.Hassabis’s move was announced alongside the departure of Jeff Dean, a veteran Google engineer and DeepMind’s chief scientist, who is leaving along with three other top researchers to form an AI startup called Discovery Loop.According to one former Google employee, Dean’s departure could augur further personnel losses. Dean’s move also follows OpenAI’s poaching in June of Google’s Noam Shazeer, a leading figure in the field as co-author of the2017 research paperAttention is All You Need, a crucial step in developing chatbots.“It’s hugely problematic for Google,” said Jeremy Nixon, a former AI researcher at Google and founder of Infinity Artificial Intelligence Institute, a startup. “It’s problematic because of who Jeff will hire and because the primary reason people want to work at Google is because of him and Noam Shazeer and all these other phenomenal researchers. It’s no longer true to say that if you want to work with the greatest researchers on the planet, you go to Google DeepMind.”Nixon added that Dean was an “angelic diplomat” who could “deal with these complex political organisations”.Google denies it faces a post-Dean talent crisis, pointing to attrition rates for AI talent for the first half of this year being lower than they were at this time last year.If AI is indeed facing a pivotal moment, Google has just had one.Explore more on these topicsDeepMindGoogleAI (artificial intelligence)AlphabetComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Fearless and quietly astonishing’: the dragonfly that migrates further than any other insect | Environment | The Guardian
description: Wandering gliders are descended from some of the earliest known insects – and breed as one global population
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: Wandering gliders are descended from some of the earliest known insects – and breed as one global population
Content: Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianInvertebrate of the year 2026Environment‘Fearless and quietly astonishing’: the dragonfly that migrates further than any other insectWandering gliders are descended from some of the earliest known insects – and breed as one global populationRevealed: the top 10 invertebrates of the yearPatrick BarkhamSat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll hail the wandering glider, a citizen of the globe, an insect for all of us.Whenever we see a dragonfly zipping through the airspace and devouring tiny insects with aplomb, we can appreciate they are so timelessly effective that they have barely needed to tweak their way of life in 200m years. Odonates are directly descended from some of the earliest winged insects, known as griffin flies, which evolved around 317m years ago.And if you were a mobile predator who had evolved when the continents were completely different to the world we know today, why would you settle down in a single country?Wherever we live in the world, we can probably glance up and see one of these sleek, darting dragonflies, which have transparent wings and a yellow or golden-coloured thorax marked with a dark line.The wandering glider is found on every continent except Antarctica, and from sea level to more than 6,000 metres above it in the Himalayas. It even finds lodgings on the remotest oceanic islands.Unlike other dragonfly species, whose water-dwelling larvae may slowly grow in ponds over several years, the wandering glider larvae can develop as rapidly as within 38 days, enabling females, which lay up to 2,000 eggs, to take advantage of ephemeral waters and even swimming pools.View image in fullscreenA wandering glider dragonfly (Pantala flavescens)in Gambia.Photograph: blickwinkel/AlamyIts ubiquity and ability to quickly produce a new generation point to its truly awesome power: this 4.5cm-long insect weighing a fraction of a gram migrates further than any other known insect. Across generations, it completes a route of up to 18,000km between India and east Africa. Some individuals even cross 3,500km of open water – the Indian Ocean – riding high-altitude monsoon winds.Ben Price, principal curator of entomology at the Natural History Museum in London, said this miraculous migration had been discovered only this century. It was proposed by the marine biologist Charles Anderson in 2009. Anderson, who lives in the Maldives, observed the dragonflies arriving on the islands with the October monsoons, and then continuing on to Seychelles. Travelling on, they arrive in eastern Africa to take advantage of the monsoon rains there, which enable them to reproduce again, and send the next generation onwards.This migration was confirmed by isotope evidence in 2012. In 2016, a genetic study discovered that wandering gliders interbreed as one global population.Price said: “That a common, familiar insect could hide the greatest migration on the planet until our own century is a perfect reminder that the natural world is still full of discoveries. Ubiquitous, fearless, and quietly astonishing. My vote goes to the wandering glider.”It’sinvertebrate of the year again! From August 3-12, every day we’ll be profiling one of the thousands of amazing invertebrates that our readers have nominated, and then, when you’ve got to hear about all of them, we’ll open the voting so you can choose your favourites. Don’t hesitate to get in touch with thoughts and ideas: email us at environment.desk@theguardian.com with Invertebrate in the subject line.This article was amended on 8 August 2026. The image was changed because an earlier one, due to a captioning error in an agency-supplied image, did not show a wandering glider dragonfly.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentInvertebrate of the year 2026ShareReuse this content

Wildfires in France spewed record amounts of pollution in the first half of the year and in Spain emissions have so far fallen just shy of the worst it has known. But even though monster infernos were halted alarmingly close toMadridandBordeaux, the smoke was mostly blown away from where people live. Daily particulate pollution levels still worsened across southern Europe and peaked at a staggering 342 micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic metre (μg/m³) in Bordeaux on 24 July – and 486 μg/m³ in Limoges, 180km (112 miles) away, the following day – but other big cities in southern Europe were spared the extremes that doctors fear.View image in fullscreenWildfires across France, such as this one near Carcassonne, have been burning for weeks.Photograph: Pablo Cozzaglio/AFP/Getty ImagesNorth America has not been so lucky. As winds blew south and south-east from scarcely populated forests in Ontario and the Northwest Territories, at least 36 million people across the continent were breathing air fouled by “very unhealthy” concentrations of PM2.5 that exceeded 125.5μg/m³ on 16 July, preliminary analysis conducted for the Guardian shows. At least 10 million people were exposed to more than 250μg/m³, according to the estimates, a level of daily pollution that smog-choked New Delhi saw no more than eight times last year.Scientists say the hit to air quality in some big cities is reminiscent of the megafires in 2023 that came with vast death tolls. “As soon as we have massive population centres exposed, we’re going to see those increases,” said Stephanie Cleland, a wildfire health scientist at Simon Fraser University, who considered only people living within 25km of a measuring station in her calculations for the Guardian and said the figures are therefore conservative. “I would be concerned by the fact that it’s only been three years since this last happened and now we’re having it again.”‘It felt like working in a war zone’In a quiet suburb of Duluth, in north-east Minnesota, the worst of the smoke was seen, smelled and tasted on 16 July. Jae Jeon and Dan McClelland, a married couple who grow flowers for weddings and subscription deliveries, were looking forward to opening the windows after days baking in oppressive heat. Instead, they woke up to a fog that they soon realised was made up of something much worse. By late morning, their local hardware store had sold out of masks and air purifiers. People resorted to attaching furnace filters to box fans instead.Map of wildfires smoke spreading across North AmericaThe McClellands were among 12,000 people in west Duluth exposed to an average of 541μg/m³ of fine particulate pollution, the analysis shows, higher than anywhere else in North America. They sent their sole farmworker home early after she complained of a headache but, with two weddings coming up on the weekend and little chance of cancellation, they still had plenty of flowers to pick and arrange. The couple got to work harvesting roses, yarrows, clematises and sweet peas, surrounded by a dystopian haze the likes of which they had never experienced.“It felt like working in a war zone,” said Jae Jeon. “When I went outside, I couldn’t breathe, so I had to wear a mask, but it was still painful. After just a couple of minutes you started to get a headache.”View image in fullscreenPeople look out at the smog caused by wildfire smoke from the CN Tower in Ontario last month. yellowish-grey in Canada’s largest city.Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty ImagesClimate breakdown made last month’s fire weather twice as likely in Canada and France, and 20 times more likely in Spain, recentrapid analyseshave found, the result of planet-heating emissions that have made it easier for vegetation to dry out. As plants and trees combust, they spew a host of harmful particles that also trigger damaging inflammatory responses as the body seeks to purge foreign objects.Scientists have relied on general air pollution relations to model the smoke’s chronic health effects, which make up the bulk of the death toll, because they lack long-term studies specific to wildfires. “The reason we don’t have them for wildfire smoke is because we haven’t had to deal with this as kind of a repeated ongoing problem,” said Michael Brauer, a wildfire health scientist at the University of British Columbia and co-author of the study onCanada’s 2023 fires. He first experienced wildfire smoke when he was about 40 years old, he said, while a 10-year-old child where he lives in British Columbia would have breathed it every summer of their life.Compounding climate eventsBut the analogy to regular pollution is imperfect. Compared with other sources of PM2.5, such as factories or cars, wildfire smoke contains a greater share of organic compounds that increase inflammation and a higher concentration of ultra-fine particles that penetrate the deepest recesses of the lungs. PM2.5 from wildfire smoke is up to 10 times more harmful in the short-term, astudyin Nature Communications found in 2021, and factoring this into epidemiological models suggests death tolls from short-term exposure to wildfire smoke have been greatly underestimated, astudyin the Lancet Planetary Health found last year.Some researchers suggest high peak exposure during serious smoke episodes better explains why wildfire particulates do more damage than regular ones. “It may be that it’s because the smoke is chemically more toxic, or it may be – what I think is more likely – that it’s basically overwhelming your defences,” said Brauer, who compared it to having one drink a day for a year rather than bingeing 365 in 24 hours. “That’s clearly going to have different impacts.”When wildfire smoke gets bad, experts recommend wearing masks, closing windows and checking in on vulnerable neighbours, particularly old people with chronic disease who live alone. They also recommend checking air quality monitors in the morning and moving activities indoors when the pollution is too high.In some cases, actions to keep the air clean may conflict with efforts to stay cool, according to areportfrom the BC Lung Foundation published last month. “The issue is we have a lot of compound climate exposure events where you have heat and wildfire,” said Cathryn Tonne, an environmental epidemiologist at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health and co-author of the study modelling wildfire-specific PM2.5. “Being home with the windows closed can be very bad – if you don’t have air conditioning – if it’s also hot.”Can the fires behind the smoke at least be prevented? At the Fifa World Cup final, which barely avoided disruption from bad air, the US president, Donald Trump,asked his Canadian counterpart, Mark Carney, to “stop these fires from coming in and poisoning our air”. The demand was accompanied by threats of sanctions and came as Republican senators blamed Canada’s fires on poor forest management. Scientists countered that the blazes had little to do with land management – most of what has burned is boreal forest in unpopulated areas – and a lot to do with the rise in temperatures caused by burning fossil fuels, which Republicans have expanded.View image in fullscreenA view of Manhattan, New York from Brooklyn Bridge park as wildfire smoke from Canada causes smoggy conditions last month.Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty ImagesInEurope, though, changes in land use have alarmed firefighters and wildfire experts about as much as global heating. Rural regions across the Mediterranean have hollowed out, resulting in more overgrown vegetation that dries out and allows fires to spread more easily during the hotter heatwaves that climate breakdown has brought. The combination of the two factors has led Spanish wildfire scientists to warn that we have “entered an era of fires we cannot extinguish”.It is a problem that other parts of the world, from the western US to Australia, already know well. Adding to the climatic burden in the coming months is the arrival of a strongEl Niño, a cyclical warming weather pattern, along with a related natural phenomenon in the Indian Ocean, which is priming countries across south-east Asia to burn.The McClellands said that – even though they still had their homes and their health – the episode had given them a taste of the suffering that climate breakdown has long caused in other countries. “I know that people all around the world are feeling a kind of helplessness because of climate disasters,” said Dan McClelland. “I feel like this opened my eyes to understand just a sliver of what other people are feeling.”

title: US promises $1bn in security aid to Colombia as new rightwing president pledges drugs crackdown | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Trump ally Abelardo De La ‌Espriella vows to start ‘profound transformation’ of country’s destiny as he is sworn in
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Trump ally Abelardo De La ‌Espriella vows to start ‘profound transformation’ of country’s destiny as he is sworn in
Content: Abelardo de la Espriella, Colombia’s new president, speaks in Cali after being sworn in. ‘The time has come to restore order, authority and freedom.’Photograph: Jaime Saldarriaga/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAbelardo de la Espriella, Colombia’s new president, speaks in Cali after being sworn in. ‘The time has come to restore order, authority and freedom.’Photograph: Jaime Saldarriaga/AFP/Getty ImagesColombiaUS promises $1bn in security aid to Colombia as new rightwing president pledges drugs crackdownTrump ally Abelardo De La ‌Espriella vows to start ‘profound transformation’ of country’s destiny as he is sworn inGuardian staff and agenciesSat 8 Aug 2026 00.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ​Trump administration plans to provide $1bn in security assistance to the ⁠government of Colombia’s new ​rightwing ‌president, the US state department announced, soon after Abelardo De La ‌Espriella was sworn in and used his inaugural speech to pledge a vigorous fight against drug trafficking, as well as austerity measures to restore confidence in the economy.De La Espriella, 48,won June’s runoff electionwith ⁠promises to crack down on armed groups, shrink ⁠the state by as much as 40% and ​revive the oil and gas sector.“I have come to close a long chapter of national resignation and, together with the people, embark on the most profound transformation ⁠of our destiny,” De La Espriella said at the Pichincha Battalion military base in Cali after being sworn in on Friday.“I send a firm message to the Colombian people: the time has come to restore order, authority and freedom,” said De La Espriella, who received theendorsement of Donald Trumpbefore his runoff election.Colombia on the brink: ELN guerrilla group prepares for return to warRead more“Members of criminal gangs and narco-terrorist groups have two choices: submit to the ⁠rule of law or face the determined response of the Colombian state and its security forces,” the new president told assembled troops at the base during a 75-minute speech, adding the option of peace talks with armed groups had been “completely exhausted”.The US ⁠state department said in a statement on Friday: ⁠“As a cornerstone of this renewed partnership, the United States, working with Congress, ‌intends to announce $1 billion in assistance ​as part of a security package to support ⁠President de la Espriella’s ​Administration in ​achieving ​our shared goals.”De La Espriella’s ​election ispart of a rightward shift rippling across Latin America. In Peru, Argentina, Chile, Ecuador, Bolivia and Panama, weak ‌economies and rising crime have reshaped voter priorities, allowing once-fringe ‌hard-right candidates to gain traction by promising crackdowns amid a global rise of rightwing nationalism.View image in fullscreenAbelardo de la Espriella (C) salutes during the military recognition ceremony as part of the presidential inauguration day in Cali, Colombia.Photograph: Leonardo Castañeda/Getty ImagesDe La Espriella could push through some of his policies via decree, but analysts say many of his proposals will require backing from a divided congress and could ‌be watered down in negotiations.The new president vowed to “definitively eradicate the scourge of illicit crops”, saying he would use aerial herbicides that did not harm human health or the environment to destroy coca, the plant used to make cocaine. In one of his first acts as president, Colombia would join the Shield of theAmericasprogram founded by Trump, he said.Before his inauguration, he held bilateral meetings with ​the king of Spain and the presidents of Argentina, Ecuador, Chile, Paraguay and Panama. Also attending was Gianni Infantino, the embattled head of Fifa, football’s world governing body, while the US sent a delegation headed by the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche.De La Espriella has blamed former president Gustavo Petro, who has not recognised the new president’s victory, for an expansion of armed groups, andnarrowly defeated leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda– a Petro ally – in the runoff.Cepeda led a morning march on Friday in Barranquilla, where he told demonstrators that the country’s opposition would work to defend democracy and called for peaceful civil disobedience.With ReutersExplore more on these topicsColombiaTrump administrationAmericasUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: National Indigenous Music awards 2026: Baker Boy wins big, including album and song of the year | National Indigenous Music awards | The Guardian
description: Yolŋu hip-hop artist dominates, while Butchulla duo and cousins Birdz and Fred Leone win artist of the year and Drifting Clouds takes home best new talent
Author: Ima Caldwell
Headline: Yolŋu hip-hop artist dominates, while Butchulla duo and cousins Birdz and Fred Leone win artist of the year and Drifting Clouds takes home best new talent
Content: Musician Baker Boy, who won album, song and film clip of the year at the National Indigenous Music Awards on Saturday.Photograph: Michelle Grace Hunder/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMusician Baker Boy, who won album, song and film clip of the year at the National Indigenous Music Awards on Saturday.Photograph: Michelle Grace Hunder/The GuardianNational Indigenous Music awardsNational Indigenous Music awards 2026: Baker Boy wins big, including album and song of the yearYolŋu hip-hop artist dominates, while Butchulla duo and cousins Birdz and Fred Leone win artist of the year and Drifting Clouds takes home best new talentIma CaldwellSat 8 Aug 2026 18.06 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 22.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBaker Boy has won album, song and film clip of the year at the 2026National Indigenous music awards (Nimas), paying tribute to his late grandmother who his sophomore album,Djandjay, is named for.The Yolŋu hip-hop artist, whose name is Danzal Baker, won three awards for Djandjay, including song of the year and film clip of the year for its hit single Thick Skin, which features Indigenous artists Thelma Plum, Emma Donovan, Kee’ahn and Jada Weazel.Baker Boy on naming his album for his grandmother: ‘She was the reason that I fell in love with hip-hop’Read moreDjandjay marks an evolution from Baker’s 2021 debut, Gela, delivering deeper lyrical themes and a heavier sound.“[Djandjay] has the lyricism, the play on words, the whole thing,” he told Guardian Australia backstage at the Nimas. “I would say the persona and the whole Blak look has a very staunch feel, and that vulnerability as well.”Accepting album of the year, Baker dedicated the honour to his late grandmother, whom he credits with bringing hip-hop to Arnhem Land after returning from a Los Angeles honeymoon with vinyl records and VHS tapes. These inspired his father and uncle to form 1980s dance duo the Baker Boys.“She was the reason that I have confidence and have no shame to be able to get out there and express my feelings, and who I am and where I come from,” Baker said.Baker told Guardian Australia he wrote Thick Skin, which won song and film clip of the year, following the voice to parliament referendum.“I was in the middle of working on the album and there was like a brick wall that was happening right in front of me … I had to speak my voice,” he said.The music video was filmed at the colonial-era Werribee Mansion in Victoria. “Filming somewhere with that colonialism, taking back that authority and giving a ‘this is my house’ vibe,” Baker told Guardian Australia. “It’s about POC [people of colour] and Blak excellence – having white butlers and flipping that sort of feel.”View image in fullscreenNational Indigenous Music Awards 2026: Birdz and Fred Leone (left and second from R) celebrate after winning artist of the year.Photograph: Leicolhn McKellarArtist of the year was awarded to Butchulla duo Birdz and Fred Leone. The cousins – rapper Birdz and songman Leone – released a joint six-track EP titled Gira in 2025.“I grew up in Katherine and this territory really shaped me and inspires me still today. So, thank you, thank you, thank you,” Birdz said, accepting the award with Leone by his side.Yolŋu musician Drifting Clouds, whose name is Terry Guyula, took home best new talent. Known for his synth-driven tracks with Yolŋu Matha lyrics, Guyula accepted the award alongside producer and bandmate Zac Terry, whom Guyula thanked for “bringing me out from the bush to the city.”View image in fullscreenTerry Guyula of Drifting Clouds wins best new talent.Photograph: Leicolhn McKellarGuguyelandji and Woppaburra jazz and blues musician Marlene Cummins and Galiwin’ku’s Saltwater Band were inducted into the Nimas Hall of Fame, joining the likes of Jessica Mauboy and Yothu Yindi.Baker Boy told Guardian Australia he was “very proud” to see Saltwater Band inducted, having grown up listening to them, saying: “When I was a kid on [Milingimbi] island, they would come perform and I’d be up there dancing.”Mauboy presented Saltwater Band with their award, praising their three-decade legacy of blending traditional Yolŋu song with reggae, ska and contemporary music.“It fills me with pride to celebrate music from theNorthern Territory,” Mauboy said. “Saltwater Band created a sound that was completely their own … they showed artists like me and so many young people watching that you never have to leave your culture to chase your dreams. You can carry it with you.”Full list of 2026 Nima winnersArtist of the year:Birdz and Fred LeoneBest new talent:Drifting CloudsAlbum of the year:Baker Boy – DjandjaySong of the year:Baker Boy – Thick Skin (feat. Thelma Plum, Emma Donovan, Kee’ahn & Jada Weazel)Film clip of the year:Baker Boy – Thick Skin (feat. Thelma Plum, Emma Donovan, Kee’ahn & Jada Weazel)Community clip of the year:Northern Peninsula Area – All The Way From The NPAIndigenous language award:Bulman School & Community – Lok Lok Mah Burarr (Lizard & Goanna)Hall of fame inductions:Marlene Cummins and Saltwater BandGuardian Australia travelled toDarwincourtesy of Tourism NTExplore more on these topicsNational Indigenous Music awardsAustralian musicIndigenous AustraliansDarwinNorthern TerritoryRapHip-hopnewsShareReuse this content

title: Centrelink pursuing debts that are more than 40 years old despite agreeing to waive old arrears | Centrelink | The Guardian
description: Advocates and legal bodies want the debt to be made ‘out of bounds’ given how hard it is to determine its accuracy
Author: Cait Kelly
Headline: Advocates and legal bodies want the debt to be made ‘out of bounds’ given how hard it is to determine its accuracy
