Content: There are 1.34m outstanding Centrelink debts, data shows, with around 600 of these over 30 years old.Photograph: Darren England/AAPView image in fullscreenThere are 1.34m outstanding Centrelink debts, data shows, with around 600 of these over 30 years old.Photograph: Darren England/AAPCentrelinkCentrelink pursuing debts that are more than 40 years old despite agreeing to waive old arrearsAdvocates and legal bodies want the debt to be made ‘out of bounds’ given how hard it is to determine its accuracyFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastCait KellySat 8 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 19.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCentrelink is pursuing $4.93bn in unpaid debts, with the oldest dating back more than 40 years, despite the government agreeing to implement a six-year statute of limitations on debt recovery.A growing list of advocates, including peak legal body Economic Justice Australia, want the debts wiped, while Australia’s leading welfare expert has warned it is impossible to trust whether the huge amount of debt is accurate.Services Australia’sdebt collection system has been in chaos, with the government announcing last year it would provide resolution payments of up to $600 for people affected byunlawful income apportionment. Around the same time, it was also revealed that about 44,000 Australians have overpaid their Centrelink debts, some by $20,000 or more.Now, data from Services Australia shows there are 1.34m outstanding Centrelink debts, amounting to $4.93bn in debt. Approximately 645,000 have a repayment arrangement in place.‘Like battery hens’: ATO’s outsourced debt collectors face much worse conditions than those in public service, former staff sayRead moreAbout 600 of the outstanding debts are over 30 years old, with the median amount for those sitting at $5,451.49.There are76,800 debts between 15 and 30 years old, with a median amount of $2,197.64.The oldest outstanding debt was raised over 40 years ago and is now under a repayment arrangement, but the department would not say how much it was because of privacy.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailInterest is also applied to some outstanding debts owed by former recipients who have not repaid the debt or maintained an acceptable repayment arrangement.The Australian government had agreed in principle to theRobodebt royal commission’srecommendation to reinstate the limitation of six years on debt recovery but has not said when that will be implemented or if it will apply to current debts.Christopher Rudge, a welfare expert and academic at the University of Sydney, said the debt’s “calculations cannot be trusted to be correct. For those debts already admitted to be wrong via the income apportionment resolution scheme, they are being ‘corrected’ on a likelihood test.“And for most debts under $2,000, no manual review will occur; instead, a computer program will determine whether it is ‘likely’ correct or not,” he said.“For all other remaining historical debts, many are decades old and were calculated long ago by systems incompatible with today’s auditing tools.”He said the in-principle acceptance from the government should mean any debt more than six years old should “be out of bounds” – and that the cost of trying to administer older debt could be greater than the debt itself.“In many circumstances where people have held debts for a decade or longer, it is likely that they are in financial circumstances that are prohibitive,” he said.“You could hear multiple narratives about this. One would be, well, this needs to be cracked down on harder,” Rudge said. “But I would not agree with that.“When you have these huge numbers and the economic circumstances have changed so much in the last few decades, you need to consider whether these debts should be waived.”Last year Services Australia undertook two investigations, finding 147,773 debts that may have been unlawfully calculated with income apportionment, though FoI records showed about 3 million Australians could have had a debt calculated that way.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNew data from the department shows 78,000 of the suspected 3 million Australians who were given an illegal debt by Centrelink have made a claim to the Income Apportionment Resolution Scheme. The applications relate to more than 201,000 debts, with $92,000 in resolution payments paid so far.Economic Justice Australia’s CEO, Kate Allingham, said up until 2017 the government had a time limit that prevented the recovery of a social security debt more than six years after a Centrelink officer knew or could reasonably have been expected to know about the circumstances that caused it.“This time limit was in place in recognition of the fact it is near impossible for someone who allegedly owes a debt to not only remember the specific circumstances they were in, but to pull together evidence from that time to defend themselves,” she said.In the 1990s, for example, payslips were in paper form. “How is it fair for the government to expect you to have held on to a paper payslip for decades?” she said.Allingham said in most states in Australia, limitation periods apply to most debt categories mean they can only be recovered within six years.“If government systems aren’t robust enough to identify and raise issues within a six-year time frame, that is an issue with the government system,” she said. “And not one that should be passed on as financial hardship to individuals.”A spokesperson for the Department of Social Services said the government believed “the recovery of social security related debts must always be legal, fair, and done so with compassion towards Australians who are doing it tough”.“Since 2022, we’ve delivered a suite of reforms to strengthen the social security system and ensure the injustices of past debt collection practices like Robodebt will never happen again,” the spokesperson said.This included a $300m package to increase the small debt waiver threshold for the first time in 30 years, expanding the special circumstances waiver and introducing the Income Apportionment Resolution Scheme.”More than 1.1m debts were waived or no longer need to be raised in 2025-26, with the small debt reform waiving “more debts than reintroducing the original six-year limit”, the spokesperson said.Explore more on these topicsCentrelinkCentrelink debt recoveryDebt collectionDebt reliefnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hospitality recruitment app Supp calls gig-workers contractors. Some users say it leads to casual work without entitlements | Gig economy | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Workers’ rights experts raise ‘alarm bells’ over app requiring ABNs for jobs they say lack worker autonomy
Author: Stephanie Convery
Headline: Exclusive: Workers’ rights experts raise ‘alarm bells’ over app requiring ABNs for jobs they say lack worker autonomy
Content: Supp describes itself as a ‘jobs marketplace’, where hospitality businesses can advertise available shifts to potential workers at an hourly rate, and where workers can secure ad-hoc employment.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSupp describes itself as a ‘jobs marketplace’, where hospitality businesses can advertise available shifts to potential workers at an hourly rate, and where workers can secure ad-hoc employment.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianGig economyHospitality recruitment app Supp calls gig-workers contractors. Some users say it leads to casual work without entitlementsExclusive: Workers’ rights experts raise ‘alarm bells’ over app requiring ABNs for jobs they say lack worker autonomyFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastStephanie ConverySat 8 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConcerns have been raised that workers using an increasingly popular Australian hospitality gig-work app may be missing out on entitlements such as superannuation by being hired as “independent contractors”, similar to delivery riders.Launched in Melbourne in 2017, Supp describes itself as a “jobs marketplace”, where hospitality businesses can advertise available shifts to potential workers at an hourly rate, and where workers can secure ad-hoc employment. It was created by Kate and Cameron Reid, the owners of Lune Croissanterie, who maintain a financial stake in the company but are no longer on its board.It has since expanded across Australia and the US, with the company claiming it was used by about 15,000 venues and 200,000 workers.Businesses pay workers through the app, with Supp adding a 12% surcharge as its service fee and sending workers payment advice and summaries at the end of the financial year.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailBut Supp requires workers to have their own ABN, and describes them as individual contractors – not casual employees – to the hospitality businesses that hire them through the platform.Supp has rejected any suggestion that it has misrepresented the working relationship facilitated through the app.But concerns have been raised by a worker, Daniel McBurnie, who began investigating whether he was entitled to superannuation for shifts obtained through the app from 2021.Those shifts – including bartending, popcorn-selling, front-of-house and table-waiting – involved the same kinds of labour McBurnie said he had previously performed in hospitality.McBurnie said he was hired as an individual contractor – rather than a casual employee – for 15 different companies through Supp.He said he was never paid superannuation for any of those shifts, and that there was no mechanism within the app for businesses to collect that information or for him to provide it.“Hospitality workers coming in to do a barista shift – they don’t have autonomy,” McBurnie said.“They’re not setting their [pay] rate, they’re not setting their hours. They are reporting to a supervisor, they’re carrying out the tasks delegated to them.”Supp rejects ‘sham contracting’ allegationsCasual employees have more workplace entitlements than independent contractors, including minimum rates of pay and casual loading, penalty rates, rest breaks, superannuation, and protection from unfair dismissal.There are also more obligations on employers, such as record-keeping requirements.Independent contractors who are paid mainly for their labour are also entitled to receive superannuation,according to the Australian Tax Office. There have also been moves to provide other entitlements for gig-workers, such as inthe food delivery sector.McBurnie was worried the app could enable widespread misclassification of casual workers as independent contractors, and that hundreds of thousands of workers may be missing out on workplace entitlements and protections as a result.Misrepresenting an employment relationship as an independent contracting relationship – known as “sham contracting” – is unlawful under the Fair Work Act and can attract penalties of up to $546,000 for large businesses. Third parties involved in contraventions can also be liable.Supp’s chief executive, Jordan Murray, said the company rejected and denied “any suggestions and/or allegations made or raised in relation to misrepresentation of the working relationship arranged through Supp” and “any sham contracting allegations.”“Supp engages constructively with regulators and supports clear, workable standards for independent work on digital platforms,” Murray said.“As the law evolves we will keep adapting the platform with it, including tools that help businesses meet obligations where they apply.”The app’s co-founder, Cameron Reid, said: “Lune regularly uses Supp, and is confident to do so due to Supp’s regular legal compliance reviews, its diligent work with regulators, and the insurance and support offered to both sides of the marketplace.”‘Deserves close scrutiny’Imogen Szumer, a senior associate at law firm Maurice Blackburn, said the way Supp described the workplace relationship was “peculiar, looking at the type of work that this is”.“Just because the website or the app is saying that it’s an individual contractor relationship, doesn’t mean that it is. How the parties describe the relationship is one factor, but it is not determinative. And that’s obviously important in the employment relationship, which is inherently an unequal one,” Szumer said.“​​We have strict rules in this country governing the employment relationship and which provide important protections for employees. Where you have the business or the app provider saying that their arrangement falls outside the remit of our employment laws, that deserves close scrutiny.”Szumer said if workers showed up to shifts at times set by the business, used its tools and equipment, were subject to its control and direction the entire time, including complying with its policies, procedures and dress standard, “looking at all the circumstances, a court might find that, in actuality, the hospitality business is employing these workers on a casual basis.”double quotation markHospo work is largely the same everywhere you go – with similar procedures and tasks.Bartender Miranda RoopThree other Supp users who spoke to Guardian Australia said they had not received superannuation or other entitlements.A Melbourne bartender, Fred Siggins, said he had taken on bartending work at events with a company that used Supp as a payment platform for ad-hoc roles. He did not receive superannuation for those shifts, but said it had not concerned him as he had been in a position to negotiate a high rate for the work.Miranda Roop used Supp to pick up bartending and front-of-house shifts after moving to Australia in November.The work was no different to roles she obtained through word-of-mouth or other means, she said, but in other circumstances she was usually brought on as a casual employee.“Hospo work is largely the same everywhere you go – with similar procedures and tasks,” she said.Another worker, who spoke to the Guardian on condition that his name not be published, said he had used Supp to find extra shifts intermittently between 2022 and 2025, mainly bartending and occasionally as a barista or server. He had not been paid superannuation for those shifts and assumed he would have to pay it himself.‘Growing gigification’McBurnie said the app was becoming “the new go-to” in hospitality.“You’ll see some venues that have used it literally thousands of times,” he said.But Pat O’Donnell, director of casino, pubs and clubs at the United Workers Union, said convenience for employers should not come at the expense of workers’ rights, security or fair treatment.“Alarm bells should ring whenever workers are told they need an ABN, or they must become a sole trader, to pick up a shift in a hospitality venue,” O’Donnell said.“United Workers Union is concerned by the growing gigification of hospitality work. Workers deserve secure jobs, fair pay and the protections that come with proper employment, not arrangements that shift risk on to workers to maximise flexibility for businesses.”McBurnie has called for the Fair Work Ombudsman to independently audit the platform and its use by businesses to source labour, saying many workers lacked the knowledge and confidence to take it on.“That is a more fair way to go about it rather than getting a really vulnerable section of the workforce to dispute their claims individually,” he said.The Fair Work Ombudsman refused to comment on Supp specifically, and encouraged workers with concerns to contact them or their union directly.Do you have a story? Contact: stephanie.convery@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsGig economyHospitality industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Senior managers at St Basil’s aged care, where 50 died from Covid, can’t remember it all. Grieving loved ones can’t forget | Coronavirus | The Guardian
description: Konstantin Kontis and Vicky Kos were compelled to testify at a coronial inquest resuming on the sixth anniversary of the tragedy
Author: Melissa Davey
Headline: Konstantin Kontis and Vicky Kos were compelled to testify at a coronial inquest resuming on the sixth anniversary of the tragedy
Content: Almost a quarter of the 188 residents at St Basil’s aged care home died from Covid-19 or neglect during July and August 2020.Photograph: James Ross/AAPView image in fullscreenAlmost a quarter of the 188 residents at St Basil’s aged care home died from Covid-19 or neglect during July and August 2020.Photograph: James Ross/AAPCoronavirusSenior managers at St Basil’s aged care, where 50 died from Covid, can’t remember it all. Grieving loved ones can’t forgetKonstantin Kontis and Vicky Kos were compelled to testify at a coronial inquest resuming on the sixth anniversary of the tragedyGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMelissa DaveyMedical editorFri 7 Aug 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 20.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQuiet sobs could be heard in Melbourne’s coroner’s court, as several families attended to finally hear from the pair who were the most senior managers when, throughout July and August 2020, almost a quarter of the 188 residents at St Basil’s aged care homedied from Covid-19 or neglect.Following multiple failed legal bids to avoid giving evidence after 50 residents died in the Victorian aged care home they managed, Konstantin Kontis and Vicky Kos were compelled to testify at a coronial inquest resuming on the sixth anniversary of the tragedy.During his evidence on Friday, Kontis said that the board of St Basil’s, operating under the auspice of the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia, never signed off on the facility’s Covid-19 management policy and that he believed, as chair, he had the delegated authority to approve it without them.Counsel assisting the coroner, Naomi Hodgson, told the court the policy contained no strong guidance on close contacts of Covid cases, and that the main guidance on symptoms was to follow the directives of the state and federal governments.The policy document was not updated as new directives came in from the government, the court heard. Instead this information was printed and put into a yellow folder for staff to keep up-to-date with.Kontis accepted under questioning that there was no delegation of authority that allowed him to approve “such a significant document” without input from the board.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailKontis was also questioned about why he did not convene board meetings as the outbreak grew, especially once testing of 116 residents and 95 staff on 15 July 2020 – as organised by the federal department of health – revealed 28 positive cases.“My communication then had switched to the archbishop direct,” Kontis said.“I don’t want to put tickets on myself, but he had full confidence that I would handle the matter in the most appropriate way.”St Basil’s Covid tragedy: ‘We are still finding out things that we weren’t aware of and it makes us angry’Read moreHodgson put it to Kontis that regardless of whether an approved aged care provider was a not-for-profit, for-profit, or religiously run, the leadership had obligations under the aged care and corporate laws to inform the board.She suggested Kontis was wrong in some of his understanding of these obligations, which he accepted.Kontis said a board meeting was held in April 2020 before the outbreak at the home and after Covid was spreading through aged care elsewhere. Discussions would have occurred then, he said, about what to do if a significant portion of the workforce became infected.The court heard that no minutes from that meeting had been found in about 10,000 pages of briefing evidence provided to the coroner. It prompted the inquest – due to close its questioning of witnesses on Friday – to be delayed to allow St Basil’s representatives to conduct a search.Kontis’ evidence is due to resume on 16 November.View image in fullscreenMedical waste is removed from St Basil's on 27 July 2020.Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty ImagesThe yellow folderEarlier in the week, the court heard that no cohort plan for separating Covid positive residents from uninfected ones could be found in documents provided to the court.Kos, who was director of nursing and facility manager at the time, said this plan was placed in the yellow folder. Some documents from that folder had gone missing, she said.‘In one fell swoop they’re gone’: how Covid tore through Melbourne’s St Basil’sRead moreShe gave evidence that many documents from the state and federal government were being added to this folder, and that staff were expected to keep up-to-date with it when starting shifts. Information was also shared during handovers, she said.Following this evidence, a search on Monday night of electronic and hard-file repositories of documents, including those previously seized by Victoria police, did not reveal such a cohort plan, the court heard on Tuesday from St Basil’s barrister, Conor O’Bryan.O’Bryan said because some files had been lost it could not be proven that a cohort plan never existed.‘I didn’t attend’During his evidence, Kontis was pressed on why he did not attend key meetings, organised by senior management of the home and attended by health officials, once it became clear the outbreak was significant and the entire workforce needed to be stood down.Kontis said he disagreed with a directive from the chief health officer at the time, Prof Brett Sutton,to furlough the entire workforceand replace them with agency staff to prevent further spread. Kontis said he did not trust the staff would be competent and Covid-free.“You’ve just received the news that your entire staff is going to be stood down,” Hodgson said. “Why didn’t you attend [meetings] as the only person on the board with vision of what was happening here?”Kontis responded: “I can’t answer that. I didn’t attend.” He said he was informed about what happened at meetings immediately afterwards by attenders.Kontis said there were also some meetings he did not believe he was invited to.Hodgson said that St Basil’s, as an approved aged care provider, had a duty under law to implement policies and procedures to manage risk and ensure care for consumers.View image in fullscreenSpiros Vasilakis’ mother died at St Basil’s during the outbreak and he has attended the inquest every day.  ‘It still hurts for all of us families here,’ he says.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianAsked why he did not convene a meeting of the risk and audit committee before or throughout the outbreak, Kontis said, “I couldn’t get anybody to attend a meeting because of Covid.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHodgson responded this was “an improbable answer in circumstances where you’ve already told me you can get people on the phone”.The court previously heard that agency staff brought in to take over struggled to find the information they needed to run the facility, from passwords and logins for computers, to notes about the clinical care of residents.Kontis said this information could be found in folders. “We had folders in the kitchen, folders with the cleaners, folders with the maintenance people,” he said.Hodgson put it to Kontis that, as an approved aged care provider and chairman, he had responsibility for the agency staff and to assist them to fulfil their duties.“Well, that’s your interpretation,” Kontis said.Hodgson replied: “I’d suggest to you … that it’s not my interpretation, it was your responsibility as an approved provider.”“That’s that’s your assertion,” Kontis said.Signs in ‘simple language’Kos had earlier told the court that English was a second language for 95% of the original St Basil’s staff, and the majority did not have laptops or computers. Asked how critical and sometimes complicated Covid information was then communicated, she said signs in “simple language” were placed around the facility and information was shared during shift handovers.Kos disagreed under cross-examination that the process of adding documents constantly to folders and expecting staff with English as a second language to keep across these during shifts was a complex task for them.Aged care worker living with relatives who had Covid symptoms cleared to work at St Basil’s, inquest hearsRead moreShe agreed that having a clear Covid plan in place would make it less likely that people would die.The inquest had previously heard from staff and family members in 2021 that infected residents were mingling with those who had not tested positive to the virus, and that infection control procedures throughout the home were poor.Kos told the court that on 9 July 2020, when the first case in a staff member was identified, she began to follow a Covid-19 aged care checklist issued by the federal government about what to do in the first 24 hours.Kos told the court she did not complete the step that said to alert the commonwealth department of health at a dedicated aged care email address within 30 minutes.She said she spoke with the state public health hotline as the document required, and because she was told to wait to hear about next steps, she did not proceed to the next step on the checklist, which was to email the commonwealth.The checklist said the commonwealth could connect aged care homes with resources to manage the outbreak including testing, additional PPE and a surge workforce, the court heard.Delays in the commonwealth learning of the case meantstaff and residents were not mass-tested until days later. The inquest previously heard this was a root cause of the outbreak.Kontis said he did not believe it was his role to email the commonwealth as he trusted facility staff to do so and to follow procedures in place.‘I don’t remember’Throughout the five days, Kontis had to be reminded several times not to interject during questioning, and to listen before responding. With years having passed since the tragedy, Kos’ response to many questions throughout the week was, “I don’t remember”.Both Kontis and Kos refused to testify, only doing so after a certificate was granted by the coroner, Liberty Sanger – meaning their evidence can not be used against them in criminal or civil litigation.Spiros Vasilakis, whose mother, Maria, died at the home during the outbreak, attended each day.“It still hurts for all of us families here,” Vasilakis said.“It hurts to hear anyone say that because it’s been six years, they can’t remember. I can tell you that families remember, detail by detail, what occurred. I haven’t forgotten anything.”The inquest continues.Explore more on these topicsCoronavirusVictoriaHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Navy says it is spending 25% more time monitoring Russian vessels around UK waters | Royal Navy | The Guardian
description: Warning of increased activity as patrols spent 21 days in July shadowing Moscow’s ships in Dover Strait and North Sea
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Warning of increased activity as patrols spent 21 days in July shadowing Moscow’s ships in Dover Strait and North Sea
Content: HMS Mersey tracking the Russian Admiral Grigorovich frigate.Photograph: UK MOD Crown copyright/Royal Navy/ReutersView image in fullscreenHMS Mersey tracking the Russian Admiral Grigorovich frigate.Photograph: UK MOD Crown copyright/Royal Navy/ReutersRoyal NavyNavy says it is spending 25% more time monitoring Russian vessels around UK watersWarning of increased activity as patrols spent 21 days in July shadowing Moscow’s ships in Dover Strait and North SeaNadeem Badshahand PA MediaSat 8 Aug 2026 16.03 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 16.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheRoyal Navyhas warned of increasing Russian activity around the UK’s waters after it spent 21 days in July monitoring Moscow’s ships.Naval operations to monitor Russian vessels increased by 25% last month compared with the previous year, with warships making repeated voyages through the strait of Dover and the North Sea.Offshore patrol vessels HMS Tyne, HMS Mersey and HMS Severn, alongside Wildcat helicopters from 815 Naval Air Squadron and Merlin submarine-hunting aircraft, were deployed throughout the month to shadow Russian frigates Neustrashimy and Admiral Grigorovich, which are tasked with escorting so-called “shadow fleet” tankers.Last month, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in its annual report that Royal Navy vessels had been “activated” 116 times in the year to March 2026, shadowing 61 Russian warships and 28 merchant vessels around the UK’s waters.This reflected a 30% increase in Russian naval activity over the previous two years and included operations to deter the spy ship Yantar, which was spotted near undersea cables off Scotland last November.Vladimir Putin has been accused of using the Kremlin’s shadow fleet of ageing vessels to evade international sanctions on its oil and fund the war in Ukraine.The increase in Russian naval activity follows theseizure of the tanker Smyrtosby Royal Marines in June, the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel.The MoD said the diversion of ships from Russia to escort shadow fleet vessels meant the country was “using up valuable operational capacity to constantly guard cargo”.The UK has already imposed sanctions on more than 500 vessels, and Russia’s oil and gas revenues fell by 24% year on year in 2025.HMS Tyne was also tasked with monitoring the Neustrashimy as it carried out a live-firing exercise outside British and French waters on 20 July.Another ship, the frigate HMS Somerset, has been involved in monitoring Russian activity in the North Atlantic as part of a four-month Nato deployment searching for submarines, alongside helicopters from the Navy’s Fleet Air Arm.Somerset’s commanding officer, Cmdr Matt Millyard, said on Saturday: “This deployment demonstrates exactly what the Royal Navy exists to do: protect the UK and our allies from wherever our interests are threatened.“I am immensely proud of every single member of the ship’s company for what we have achieved over the past four months.”Explore more on these topicsRoyal NavyMilitaryRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: The Bond effect? How MI6 fascinates spy watchers around the world | Espionage | The Guardian
description: Britain’s spooks take quiet satisfaction from survey ranking Secret Intelligence Service Europe’s top espionage agency
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Britain’s spooks take quiet satisfaction from survey ranking Secret Intelligence Service Europe’s top espionage agency
Content: Roger Moore as MI6’s James Bond in the 1983 film Octopussy.Photograph: Danjaq/Eon/Ua/Kobal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRoger Moore as MI6’s James Bond in the 1983 film Octopussy.Photograph: Danjaq/Eon/Ua/Kobal/ShutterstockEspionageThe Bond effect? How MI6 fascinates spy watchers around the worldBritain’s spooks take quiet satisfaction from survey ranking Secret Intelligence Service Europe’s top espionage agencyDan SabbaghDefence and security editorSat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 08.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMI6 has the swagger of James Bond; its French equivalent, DGSE, the complexities of the television drama Le Bureau. The film and TV shows may be fictional, but a survey run by a French magazine that placed the British spy agency above the French as No 1 across all of Europe this week is not.L’Express, a news weekly, conducted a Eurovision-style poll of 60 current and former spies from across the continent, plus the CIA and Israel’s Mossad. Each was asked to rank their top five foreign intelligence agencies, in secret, naturally enough. MI6 was first with 251 points ahead of DGSE on 169, with other agencies trailing behind.The result did not surprise Alexandra Saviana, a deputy editor at the publication, specialising in defence and intelligence, but the margin of victory did. “It is a huge point gap,” she said, reflecting the opinions of insiders and allies, 17 of whom are or were agency chiefs in a interconnected, covert ecosystem.At MI6’s headquarters in Vauxhall, London, there has been no sign of a public reaction from its chief,Blaise Metreweli. But there is a quiet satisfaction at the unexpected verdict, not least because the agency values how it is perceived by both allies and adversaries. “Reputation matters a lot in the espionage game,” said a former Whitehall insider.View image in fullscreenMI6’s headquarters in London.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images“British spies fascinateEurope, and beyond,” L’Express explained in its cover story. Saviana added that MI6’s success in the poll was principally down to its record in recruiting and running high-level human sources over generations: a focus on human intelligence in an era dominated by technology, intercepts and satellite monitoring.“The British have the ability to play the long game, to bet on sources over 10 years, a bit like the Russians,” a former French DGSE spy told the magazine, adding “and they have a penchant for underhand tactics” without revealing what they meant.One ex-spy voiced scepticism about the survey and added that a human intelligence service such as MI6 was only as good as the high-value agents on its books. UnderRichard Moore, MI6’s previous chief, there were worries that it no longer had enough. Others, including Saviana, accept that greater credit might have been given to MI6’s sister agency, the signals intelligence experts at GCHQ, but it was not in the poll.MI6’s reputation among its peers, the French publication said, was built on “long standing tradition”, including recruiting cold war assets, most notably the KGB’sOleg Gordievsky, a double agent through late 1970s and early 80s, who helped convince Margaret Thatcher to take Mikhail Gorbachev seriously before he had to be dramatically smuggled into Finland in 1985, his cover finally blown.View image in fullscreenRonald Reagan meeting Oleg Gordievsky, an MI6 cold war asset, in the White House, 1987.Photograph: Eraza Collection/AlamyNot every mole evaded capture. Alireza Akbari, a former Iranian deputy defence minister who had become a British citizen, was arrested on a return to Iran in 2019 and executed in 2023. Prior to his death, he confessed to being an MI6 agent. Though the confessions appeared coerced, spies from a number of countries indicated he was the person who had passed on the existence of theFordow nuclear enrichmentsite in 2008.In the run-up to the 2003 Iraq war, MI6 was accused of simplistically supporting the case for war, promoting what turned out to be false sources, claiming that Iraq’s leader, Saddam Hussein, could attack UK targets within “45 minutes”, and relied on one source who described supposed chemical weapons devices that were remarkably similar to one inthe Hollywood movie The Rock. It was a low point.L’Express argued that MI6 had rehabilitated itself in the run-up to the Ukraine war in February 2022,correctly warningin conjunction with the CIA that Russia was about to invade, while French and German counterparts were sceptical up until the last minute, having misjudged the situation. The chief of the German BND agency even flew into Kyiv the day before the invasion, seemingly unprepared.It reflects MI6’s close and longstanding relationship with the CIA, part of the wider Five Eyes arrangements for intelligence sharing, between the US, UK, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, that are the envy of continental Europe, even allowing for the complexities posed by Donald Trump’s chaotic presidency. “Every other country wants to say they are the sixth eye,” Saviana said.Fiction also has its advantages. Gordon Corera, a co-presenter of The Rest is Classified podcast, recalled that a former MI6 chief once told him a story of a young officer going somewhere far flung, not knowing whether the person he was trying to cultivate spoke English. “As he walked into the room the contact extended his hand and said: ‘Hello, Mr Bond.’ The former chief remarked: ‘I doubt if he would have received such a warm welcome if he’d been from the Belgian secret service.’”Explore more on these topicsEspionageMI6EuropeUK security and counter-terrorismJames BondnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nazi shipwrecks emerge from the depths as Europe’s Danube dries up | Drought | The Guardian
description: Unexploded ordnance and a military motorcycle also recovered following record heat and drought conditions
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Unexploded ordnance and a military motorcycle also recovered following record heat and drought conditions
Content: The wreckage of a Nazi warship has become visible above the exceptionally low water line on the Danube near Prahovo in Serbia this week.Photograph: Darko Vojinović/APView image in fullscreenThe wreckage of a Nazi warship has become visible above the exceptionally low water line on the Danube near Prahovo in Serbia this week.Photograph: Darko Vojinović/APDroughtNazi shipwrecks emerge from the depths as Europe’s Danube dries upUnexploded ordnance and a military motorcycle also recovered following record heat and drought conditionsOliver HolmesSat 8 Aug 2026 06.55 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 08.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRecord-low water levels in the Danube have exposed remnants of Europe’s Nazi past, with dozens of second world war ships emerging from the riverbed during an intense drought.In the middle of the river on the Serbian and Romanian border, a broken-up hull was visible on a sandbank that is normally underwater. Other vessels were partly submerged, some still believed to be laden with weapons.View image in fullscreenThe wreckage of a second world war German warship near Prahovo, Serbia on Tuesday.Photograph: Darko Vojinović/APThe ships were part of Adolf Hitler’s Black Sea fleet that the German military deliberately sank towards the end of the war to slow down the Soviet advance. Historians say up to 200 German warships were scuttled in this way in September 1944. But Nazi Germany did not surrender until the following year in May 1945.Sunken WWII era ships appear as Danube levels go down amid droughtThe ships have been revealed during previous droughts only to disappear again as water levels rose along the second-longest river in Europe. The Serbian government has tried in the past to remove the wrecks, but most remain in place owing to the explosives they carried.View image in fullscreenThe Serbian government has previously tried to remove wrecks such as the one pictured here near Prahovo.Photograph: Darko Vojinović/APOther second world war remnants have been found in other parts of the river, including a German military motorcycle in Budapest,Hungary.In Slovakia, police recoveredan unexploded British 1,543lb (700kg) bomb. Police said authorities loaded it on to a “specially modified firefighter vehicle with a sand bed, which ensured its safe transport” and took it to a 5-metre deep pit to detonate it.View image in fullscreenA second world war German military motorcycle is displayed at the defence ministry museum in Budapest, Hungary on Wednesday.Photograph: Tamas Purger/EPAIn 1944, Britain’s Royal Air Force mined the river to disrupt enemy troops.The Danube, which flows through 10 countries, has become increasingly difficult to navigate as low water levels create dangerous conditions. Prolonged droughts have left major European rivers at significantly lower water levels than is typical for the time of year, creating an energy crisis as many power plants rely on their natural water supply for cooling.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion1:51Europe hit by wildfires and severe drought – videoIntense summer heat and continuing drought conditions arebeing supercharged by the escalating human-caused climate crisis.Temperature records have been brokenin several countries across central and eastern Europeas the extreme weather that has caused wildfires and droughts across the continent continues.View image in fullscreenThe head of mechanised military equipment at the defence ministry museum, József Bakondi, attends to the German motorcycle.Photograph: Tamas Purger/EPASlovakia, Austria and Hungary registered record temperatures this week. On Thursday, the Slovakian hydrometeorological agency said a new national record of 42C (108F) had been reached in the village of Dolné Plachtince.The Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsDroughtEuropeClimate crisisExtreme heatHungarySlovakiaSecond world warnewsShareReuse this content

title: High divers take the plunge in Paris for a new test of reclaimed Seine’s water | Diving | The Guardian
description: Paris is staging its first high-diving competition in the Seine, with athletes launching themselves from a 20-metre platform in front of the Eiffel Tower
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Paris is staging its first high-diving competition in the Seine, with athletes launching themselves from a 20-metre platform in front of the Eiffel Tower
Content: Germany’s Maike Elena Halbisch competes in the women’s 20m high diving event during the European Aquatics Championships, alongside the Seine, with the Eiffel Tower in the background.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGermany’s Maike Elena Halbisch competes in the women’s 20m high diving event during the European Aquatics Championships, alongside the Seine, with the Eiffel Tower in the background.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty ImagesDivingHigh divers take the plunge in Paris for a new test of reclaimed Seine’s waterEuropean Aquatics Championships taking place in cityThreat to water quality tested two years after GamesAssociated PressSat 8 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParis is staging its first high-diving competition in the Seine, with athletes launching themselves from a 20-metre platform in front of the Eiffel Tower – a spectacular new test of the city’s effort to reclaim its river for sport. The event on the Pont de Bir-Hakeim has also exposed the fragility of that ambition.Organisers suspended training on Thursday when traces of hydrocarbons were detected upstream. By Friday, the FrenchSwimmingFederation said the affected area had been treated, allowing athletes to return to the water and the event to proceed as planned. High diving concludes on Saturday with the final two rounds and medal events, while the broader European Aquatics Championships run through to 16 August.View image in fullscreenFrance’s Gary Hunt in the men’s 20m high diving event.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty Images“There are things that are within our control and there are uncertainties that are inevitably linked to any outdoor activity,” said Maxime Sauvage, the Paris deputy mayor in charge of sports, sports facilities and equal access to sport. Among the things within the city’s control, he said, are the massive investments made before the 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Gamesto make the river safe for swimming, such as work to prevent sewage from flowing directly into the Seine to improvements in stormwater management.“There is always a small risk, but that is also part of what makes outdoor events special,” he said. “When they work, it is magical.”Hundreds of people gathered along the banks on Friday to watch the divers. Some stopped during their lunch break, while others stumbled across the competition by chance. Among them was Rebecca Kapogiannis, a 45-year-old visitor from London, Ontario, who was visiting Paris with her daughter to celebrate her graduation. Her daughter had even packed a bathing suit in case she got the chance to swim in the Seine.View image in fullscreenA diver during practice with the Eiffel Tower in the background.Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/AP“We just headed down to the [Eiffel] Tower today and thought we would walk along the Seine and stumbled upon this and thought it was a really cool activity to watch,” she said. “I was not expecting a competition to take place in the Seine, but it’s such a cool use of this water that runs right through the city.”For Cynthia Matz, who was visiting with her husband, Sean, the setting was part of the draw. She said they probably would not have sought out the competition had it been held inside. “Anybody can go. I don’t have to know anything about diving. I can just say: ‘This is really cool to see’. Having it out in public, people will just stop and go, ‘huh, what’s going on?’ and stop and spend some time and enjoy it.”View image in fullscreenSpectators watch the action from the riverbank.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty ImagesThat ability to stumble across elite sport in the middle of the city reflects a broader transformation Paris officials have been pushing for years: turning the Seine from a river associated largely with commerce, transport and tourism into a place where people can also swim, play and compete.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe 38th European Aquatics Championships mark the centenary of the inaugural championships, held in Budapest. For Paris, they are a return of another kind: the capital last hosted the event in 1931. More than 1,000 athletes are competing in five disciplines: swimming, diving, artistic swimming, open-water swimming and high diving.The Seine is hosting the open-water swimming and high diving, placing the river back at the centre of a major international sporting event two years after the Paris Oympics. Swimming in the Seine was banned in 1923 because of pollution and the dangers of river traffic. Public swimming returned in 2025, after Paris and its partners mobilised €1.4bn to make the river swimmable, an effort accelerated by the Olympics.View image in fullscreenSwimmers compete in the men’s 10km open-water event.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty ImagesFor many French people, making the Seine clean enough for swimming again seemed a distant dream. But images of athletes competing – and now residents swimming – in the river have become almost familiar. “Paris is not just a postcard image, it is also a magnificent sporting venue,” said Sauvage.Explore more on these topicsDivingSwimmingParisFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Spanish mountain village braces for astrotourists lured by total solar eclipse | Europe | The Guardian
description: Somosierra will be prime spot to view celestial alignment on 12 August, an event that poses logistical challenges
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Somosierra will be prime spot to view celestial alignment on 12 August, an event that poses logistical challenges
Content: Somosierra, Spain village to view solar eclipseEuropeSpanish mountain village braces for astrotourists lured by total solar eclipseSomosierra will be prime spot to view celestial alignment on 12 August, an event that poses logistical challengesSam Jonesin SomosierraSat 8 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 05.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLittle stirs in the mountains above Somosierra beyond the wind that lashes the flat peaks, the cows that graze on parched grass and the sun that beats down on the abandoned aerodrome where generations of glider pilots learned to ride air currents alongside squadrons of vultures and red kites.But all this stillness will disappear, albeit temporarily, on the evening of 12 August, whenswathes of northern and eastern Spainand the Balearic islands experiencea total solar eclipse, the likes of which has not been seen here for more than 120 years.View image in fullscreenIrma López Muñoz, Somosierra’s tourism manager, tests a pair of protective eclipse glases in the mountain meadows above the village.Photograph: Ben Roberts/Panos PicturesThe rare celestial alignment has suddenly turned Somosierra – a small village that sits at an altitude of 1,440 metres where the northernmost reaches of the Madrid region fade into neighbouring Castilla y León and Castilla-La Mancha – into a prime astrotourist destination. No site as close to the Spanish capital will enjoy what Somosierra will: one minute and 29 seconds of pure, clear-skied total eclipse.Awe-inspiring as the event promises to be, however, it has thrown up all sorts of unexpected but pressing questions for the village and its 93 inhabitants.With as many as 2,000 visitors expected, where will everyone park? Will there be enough water? And, last but not least, how many batches of paella will the local restaurant need to prepare for the invasion of hungry sky-gazers?“The fact that we’ve been selected as the best place in the Madrid region to watch the eclipse has led to a huge amount of media and social media coverage,” said Somosierra council’s tourism manager, Irma López Muñoz, as she looked out across the eclipse observation site, a 10-minute drive up past the village.View image in fullscreenSomosierra village council has offered 400 official registration slots but believes five times as many people could turn up on the day.Photograph: Ben Roberts/Panos Pictures“That’s generated a lot of interest among people in Madrid – and some from abroad. So we’re anticipating a large influx of visitors because it is a unique event that hasn’t been seen for over 100 years.”Even before the recentmassive wildfires broke out to the west of Madrid, Somosierra council was thinking about how to minimise risk factors on the day of the eclipse and has been coordinating its efforts with police and civil protection authorities.Although the village council has offered 400 official registration slots, it believes five times as many people could turn up on the day.“We’re very close to a major European capital with a huge population, and many people are going to come without seeking out information beforehand,” added López. “That’s beyond our control. We can’t predict that someone might be watching television and say, ‘Well, I’m going to make some sandwiches and go see the eclipse with my children.’”mapWith that in mind, the council is scrambling to recruit and educate volunteers to help steward events on 12 August. It recently hired El Nocturnario, a company of astrotourism experts, to deliver a day’s training to the volunteers who had gathered in Somosierra’s tiny cultural centre to learn about the joys and dangers of eclipses.One of the volunteers, María Gradaille, said she was delighted to help out with what she called “a once-in-a-lifetime event and a historic scientific milestone”. She was also grateful for the knowledge and the tips she had picked up at the training session.“I’ve learned so much about the eclipse,” she said. “I didn’t know it could burn your eyes so badly or just how dangerous it can be.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenVolunteers from the village gather to plan for the eclipse, which will take place on 12 August.Photograph: Ben Roberts/Panos PicturesAccording to Sarai de la Hoz, one of El Nocturnario’s co-founders, local and regional authorities aroundSpainare belatedly beginning to wake up the potential benefits of all things astronomical. The looming total solar eclipse will be followed by a six-minute-long “eclipse of the century” in August next year, and by a spectacular “ring of fire eclipse” in January 2028.Little wonder, then, that the Spanish government has set upa special committee to oversee the trio of eclipses. As the government spokesperson Elma Saiz Delgado pointed out on Tuesday, the events will put Spain “at the centre of global astronomical observation and astrotourism”. This first eclipse alone is expected to attract 446,000 additional visitors in a year whentourist numbers in Spain could pass the 100-million mark for the first time. The event is also forecast to bring in an extra €342m (£292m) in tourist revenue.“When we started talking about the eclipse a year ago, people kind of thought we were mad. They were like: ‘It’s not going to be that big a deal’ and: ‘Not that many people will come,’” said De la Hoz, “But as time’s gone by and the authorities have realised what’s to come, we’re been getting calls from people who need our help.”View image in fullscreenOne hour’s drive north of Madrid, Somosierra has a population of 93.Photograph: Ben Roberts/Panos PicturesWhile much of the training she and her colleagues provide is about eclipses and how to watch one safely, the classes also involve a lot of logistics and organisation: “How’s the event going to be organised; who’s going to liaise with the local police and the civil protection authorities, and how will you deal with parking and people at the venue?”Authorities in the Balearics, which are bracing for huge numbers of extra visitors, have already announced thatrestrictions will be introduced on 20 main roads across Mallorca, Ibiza, Menorca and Formenterafrom 3pm until 9pm on the day of the eclipse to prevent gridlock.Practicalities of a rather different nature are on the mind of Yolanda Cerezo, who has run the Hotel Restaurante El Puerto de Somosierra for the past 26 years. Sitting on the shady terrace of the hotel and restaurant, Cerezo pondered the possibility of a tenfold increase in the 200 to 300 customers she would normally serve on a busy day.View image in fullscreenYolanda Cerezo, owner of the Hotel Restaurante El Puerto de Somosierra, hopes to get licences to set up a stall and bar at the observation site.Photograph: Ben Roberts/Panos Pictures“We’ve had some big one-day events and parties, but we’ve never seen this kind of volume,” she said. “The eclipse is going to be a long day, but we have to make the most of it. We’re not going to see another day like it, are we? It’ll be unique.”Cerezo, who also caters events, is hoping to get the necessary licences to set up a stall and a bar at the observation site. If she succeeds, she will need to hire another eight or nine people to supplement the restaurant’s regular workforce of nine people. Menu-wise, she’s thinking lamb stew, paella and an assortment of hot and cold sandwiches, all of which can be prepared in the hotel kitchen and driven up the mountain.“If I do a massive paella and it runs out, I’ll ring down to my people in the kitchen here and they’ll prepare another one and bring it up,” she said. “We can’t leave people stuck halfway up a mountain with nothing to eat.”Explore more on these topicsEuropeSolar eclipsesSpainSpaceAstronomynewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz as deal still out of reach | Strait of Hormuz | The Guardian
description: Tehran urges US to ‘correct its behaviour’ as UAE says one of its ships targeted by Iranian missile
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tehran urges US to ‘correct its behaviour’ as UAE says one of its ships targeted by Iranian missile
Content: Tehran, Iran. An Iranian statement said the US must never threaten the country again.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTehran, Iran. An Iranian statement said the US must never threaten the country again.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesStrait of HormuzIran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz as deal still out of reachTehran urges US to ‘correct its behaviour’ as UAE says one of its ships targeted by Iranian missileGuardian staff and agenciesSat 8 Aug 2026 17.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 20.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, while theUnited Arab Emiratessaid one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile, as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach on Saturday.Iran’s politburo-like body known as the supreme national security council said the strait of Hormuz will not open until the United States “corrects its behaviour”, and its state broadcaster published a statement from the council’s secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who is also a commander in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).The US must never threaten Iran again, the statement said, and must permanently end the war with Iran and its armed allies in the region. The US must lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area. It also must “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets.Iran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in warRead moreThere was no immediate comment from the US, which has wanted an acceptable deal on the strait before ending the blockade. According to the interim deal signed in June, a schedule to end sanctions and a plan for compensation would be part of the final deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets.The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said on Saturday that they were close to reaching anagreement on navigation, “specifically the determination of a transit route”. But the waterway’s reopening is contingent on other conditions, he said, in remarks shared on social media, and blamed the situation on what he called the US violation of the interim deal.Oman, which is mediating and has made relatively few comments on the talks, said in a statement on Saturday that the discussions were continuing “in a positive and constructive atmosphere”, and condemned attacks on ships on the strait.Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait and wants to charge users for passage, repeatedly attacking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route.The US opposes any Iranian tolls in the strait, though the June deal allows Tehran to hammer out arrangements for the “future administration” of Hormuz in conjunction with fellow coastal state Oman.The 60-day period to negotiate a final deal will end in just over a week but could be extended.Iran has said it was close to reaching a separate deal with Oman to manage the strait, which runs between the two countries.Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian, a relative moderate, said he believed now was the best time for an agreement.“There is cohesion, strength, and unity in the country, and as far as I know, Iran is considered victorious and powerful in this war,” Iranian news agencies quoted him as saying.Continued attacks in the strait, which was free to sail through before the war, led to the collapse of an April ceasefire, and mediators have since urged both sides to return to the terms of the June memorandum.The strait, which is crucial to global supplies of oil and natural gas, had been considered an international waterway before the war. Ship transits remain low.Meanwhile, a vessel owned by Abu Dhabi’s state-owned Adnoc oil and gas company was attacked while sailing through the strait of Hormuz, Emirati authorities said earlier on Saturday. The foreign ministry said Iran fired the missile as part of attacks on commercial shipping.Adnoc said in a statement that there were no casualties following the attack early on Saturday. The company said more than a dozen of its vessels have been attacked by missiles and drones while using the strait since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. One crew member has been killed and 20 others wounded, it said.Adnoc did not elaborate on the location of the attack or any damage.Later, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre said a vessel east of the town of Khasab, Oman had been struck by a projectile that caused a fire that was put out, and the vessel and crew were safe. It was not clear whether this was the Adnoc incident.Explore more on these topicsStrait of HormuzIranOmanUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricaUnited Arab EmiratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bluster and backdown have turned Iran war into Trump’s own Groundhog Day | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: The US president’s profound ignorance of his enemy has led to an impotent cycle of empty threats, analysts say
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: The US president’s profound ignorance of his enemy has led to an impotent cycle of empty threats, analysts say
Content: Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignUS-Israel war on IranBluster and backdown have turned Iran war into Trump’s own Groundhog DayThe US president’s profound ignorance of his enemy has led to an impotent cycle of empty threats, analysts sayRobert Taitin WashingtonSat 8 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTShareBeing the subject of mockery may be the most intense of allDonald Trump’sknown aversions.Yet more than five months after embarking on a war of choice againstIran, the US president risks attracting ridicule as he struggles to secure a military victory – while repeatedly threatening devastating bombardment against the Tehran regime, only to back down on the pretext of renewed negotiations.Critics suggest the ultimatum-climbdown sequence has acquired aGroundhog Dayquality. By one count, he has adopted the same tacticseven timessince launching the war in tandem with Israel on 28 February.Last weekend saw the latest episode, as Trump told reporters onboard Air Force One that he had suddenly called off “a massive” attack that he said would have been “the biggest since world war two” after an appeal from US allies and because “I think there’s a deal”.Iran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in warRead moreDespite negotiations between Iran and Oman over shipping in the strait of Hormuz, no deal has thus far materialized, and the strategically vital waterway – conduit to a fifth of the world’s oil supply before the war – remains closed.The pattern resembled one that unfolded on a string of other occasions – including Trump’s memorably dire threat in April that Iranian“civilization will die tonight”unless Tehran capitulated to his demands only to retreat at the 11th hour and agree to a ceasefire.The US president has also claimed multiple times that the US has “virtually” won the war and that Iran’s regime was clamoring for a deal.Increasingly, such claims are prompting ridicule.A recent CNN montage showed 14 separate pieces of footage dating back to March, with Trump insisting peace was at hand because Iran’s leaders “want to make a deal” after being supposedly rendered militarily impotent – assertions belied by a continuing Iranian ability to inflict damage on US and allied targets in the Middle East.The veteran British journalist and commentator Andrew Neil pilloried Trump’s boasts as worthy of the Nobel peace prize he is known to covet.“He, in the past five months, has brought peace to the Iran war eight times,” Neilsaid sarcastically on Times Radio. “What more do you have to do to merit a Nobel peace prize?”He added: “We waste our time even analyzing it, because it’s either meaningless, or he’s done a U-turn on it within 24 hours … You might as well read the shipping forecasts.”Trump’s wildly zigzagging messaging on the war betrays an absence of strategy and a profound ignorance of his enemy, analysts say – and threatens to deliver an electoral disaster in November’s US congressional midterms.Mehrzad Boroujerdi, vice-provost and a political scientist at Missouri Science and Technology University, believes the US president’s failure to understand the individuals leading Iran’s authoritarian Islamic system has misled him into a dead end of ineffective and counterproductive threats.“One of the most terrible mistakes that Trump made was invoking this type of a language,” said Boroujerdi, who argued that regimes who come into being through mass revolutions such as the one in 1979 that swept Iranian revolutionaries to power are much harder to topple than other governments.“First, these are not people who are going to bend the knee,” he said. “Second, you have just killed the top of their leadership (including the former supreme leader,Ayatollah Ali Khamenei). Their psychology is only an invitation for Trump to become more aggressive.”Understanding TehranBoroujerdi made it his life’s mission to understand the motivations of the men inside the Islamic regime after his father, Malek-Mohammad Boroujerdi, a senior executive with the national oil company,was assassinatedby an Islamist guerrilla group in December 1978, on the eve of the revolution that overthrew the western-backed monarch, Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.He kept his personal stake in scrutinizing the regime under wraps, lest it be seen as impairing the impartiality of his academic studiesNearly half a century later, key members of the group, the Mansouroun, occupy some of the regime’s most sensitive military posts. They includeMohammad Baqer Zolqadr, secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, andMohsen Rezaei, the founding commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, who is now military adviser to the present supreme leader,Mojtaba Khamenei, whose father was killed in an Israeli military strike at the start of the war.Having compiled over two decades a vast database of about 2,700 members of the country’s elite, Boroujerdi has co-authored a 900-page book,Post Revolutionary Iran: A Political Handbook, that puts its political leadership under the microscope.Understanding it helps to explain how the outwardly ramshackle regime has withstood US hostility, international sanctions, diplomatic isolation and periods of war over 47 years all while staying resilient, he argued.“I have looked at their nepotism ties, who is connected to whom,” said Boroujerdi. “These are folks who came from very modest backgrounds. They are predominantly the sons of farmers, peasants. And then secondly, clerics, who basically enjoyed social mobility thanks to the revolution.“These were mister nobodies who became mister somebodies thanks to the revolution. And therefore, their attachment to this system and wanting to defend this system makes absolute sense because they owe everything they have currently, their whole career, to what this revolution has given them.View image in fullscreenA man holds a flag with a picture of the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and Mojtaba Khamenei, all supreme leaders of Iran’s Islamic Republic, during a rally in Tehran on 29 April 2026.Photograph: Majid-Asgaripour/Reuters“If we want to understand Iran’s resilience, its performance, we need to better understand the psychology and upbringing of these individuals. But that requires serious work that the political class in Washington isn’t necessarily interested in.”Having not undertaken such work, Trump has been reduced torailing in frustrationat a regime whose defiance is a source of confusion and bewilderment to him.After a ceasefire agreed in June collapsed over differing interpretations of a memorandum of understanding Trump had signed in the Palace of Versailles, he shocked fellow attenders at last month’s Nato summit in Ankara bycalling Iran’s leaders “scum”.“All they do is make me angry,” he told reporters, while also calling their behavior “unbelievably duplicitous”.Such incomprehension means Trump’s pattern of ultimately unfulfilled blood-curdling threats is likely to continue, according to Boroujerdi. Other seasoned Iran observers agree.Ali Vaez, the International Crisis Group’s deputy program director for the Middle East and north Africa, called explaining Trump’s approach in strategic terms “an impossible task” and lamented what he called the lack of a clear policy process in the current administration.View image in fullscreenA woman walks by a mural in Tehran on Thursday. The Iranian regime has shown resilience since the death of its supreme leader on the war’s first day.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesBut he also said Iran’s leaders had strengthened their negotiating position in the strait of Hormuz since the collapse of the June ceasefire, while triggering a painful debate in Washington about military choices after recent strikes on a US base in Jordan that killed three US service personnel.The possibilities for a renewed military onslaught against Iranian targets are believed to be limited because ofconcerns that US missile and interceptor stockpiles have become depleted.Trump’s approach “boils down to his frustration that he really doesn’t have any good military options in front of him”, suggested Vaez. “A lot of it is emotional reactions, like when he does a deal with Iran that produces a political backlash, even among Republicans.“That criticism gets under his skin, so he tries to extract better terms from Iran by bombing them. But when he ends up in an even worse position, he returns to the negotiating table and tries to pursue a diplomatic solution.“This war started based on a lot of misguided assumptions, which are a clear reminder that half the battle is understanding your enemy – and clearly, President Trump and his administration didn’t understand the enemy.”

title: One of UK’s best fossil collections sold overseas in ‘loss to the nation’ | Fossils | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Lack of funds left British museums unable pay eight-figure sum for collection, which went to Abu Dhabi institution
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Exclusive: Lack of funds left British museums unable pay eight-figure sum for collection, which went to Abu Dhabi institution
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesFossilsOne of UK’s best fossil collections sold overseas in ‘loss to the nation’Exclusive: Lack of funds left British museums unable pay eight-figure sum for collection, which went to Abu Dhabi institutionNicola DavisScience correspondentSat 8 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.02 EDTShareOne of the most important collections of UK Jurassic fossils ever compiled has been sold to a museum in Abu Dhabi, the Guardian can reveal, in what British experts have described as a loss for the nation.The collection, which was amassed by a private fossil collector, consisted of 318 specimens, including ichthyosaurs, fish and crustaceans among other creatures, some of which could be new species.The fossils were initially offered for purchase to the Natural History Museum (NHM) in London and to Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales) for what was described by one source as an “eight-figure sum”.Neither institution bought the collection, with both citing a lack of funding. An email seen by the Guardian suggested the NHM had “no money at all” for acquisitions.One curator said that while there had long been a hope that the collection could be kept in the UK, it also posed issues around storage space, curatorial time and packaging materials.“I don’t blame the collectors at all. That’s all they can do. They can’t sit on these things forever,” the curator said, adding that the issue was expected to occur again and again as collectors get older and look for a suitable home for their life’s work.“Whose responsibility is it to fund our heritage and the preservation of our heritage? Because otherwise it could get lost,” they added.The extensive collection is understood to come from a sequence of rocks known as the Lower Lias, from Lyme Regis, Charmouth, and the south-west of the UK.It was compiled by Chris Moore, a private Dorset-based collector with experience ofhunting fossils in the area. In emails seen by the Guardian the collection is described as “stunning”.View image in fullscreenIchthyosaur fossil.Photograph: Martin Shields/AlamySome countries, including Mongolia and Brazil, consider all fossils found in those countries in recent decades to be property of the state – a situation thathas led to international disputesover repatriation of fossils housed abroad. However, this is not the case in the UK.Richard Butler, a professor of palaebiology at the University of Birmingham who was not involved in the sale, said the collection was of national significance. “This is one of the most important collections of fossils ever made on the world-famous Jurassic Coast of Dorset. It would have been wonderful to see these fossils on display and engaging the public in a UK museum.”He added: “This sale raises important questions about whether more should be done to preserve important and irreplaceable natural heritage such as this for the benefit of the UK public.”Britain’s Jurassic gold rush: the fossil hunters chasing fortunes on Dorset’s beachesRead moreIn theUnited Arab Emirates, the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi confirmed it had bought a collection from Moore, which went on display in November 2025. A spokesperson for the museum said the Lower Jurassic rocks of the UK preserved some of the best examples of marine life from when what is now the Dorset coast was roughly at the same latitude as north Africa.“All natural history museums around the world tell this story, often using fossils from multiple countries to help narrate their journey through time. If we are to tell a 4.2bn-year story of the evolution of life on Earth, all museums must travel both spatially and temporally with their collections,” the spokesperson said.“A large majority of the Chris Moore collection is already on public display in the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi in the Mesozoic Gallery (Age of Dinosaurs Gallery).”Lyme Regis is part of theJurassic Coast, a Unesco world heritage site, that is rich with fossilsthat date back to between 200m and 145m years ago. The area has a long history of private fossil collecting, with notable figures including Mary Anning – a pioneering palaeontologist and fossil dealer whose triumphs included the discovery of the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaurusin 1823.While approaches vary across the UK nations, modern fossil collectors along England’s Jurassic Coast are encouraged to follow the west Dorset fossil collecting code and the Undercliffs national nature reservefossil collecting code.Fossils initially belong to the owner of the land on which they are found, legal ownership is typical transferred to collectors who adhere to such codes and recording schemes – a situation that reflects the valuable role collectors are deemed to have in finding fossils that might otherwise never be recovered.View image in fullscreenSunset at Durdle Door in Dorset’s Jurassic coast.Photograph: Loop Images/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesBut whilehighly valuable archeological findsturned up by activities such as metal detecting can be classified as treasure – and therefore must be reported to the relevant authorities within 14 days of discovery – the same is not true for fossils, even those deemed to be key scientifically important fossils, known as category 1.According to the west Dorset fossil collecting code of conduct, collectors “who intend to sell or otherwise dispose of their category 1 specimens must first offer them to UK registered museums for a period of six months. If no purchase has been agreed by this time, the collector will be free to offer the specimen elsewhere.”However, such codes are not legally binding and even if followed, as Moore did, fossils found in the UK can be sold by collectors to private individuals, museums or other buyers – including those overseas. Moore was approached for comment.According to the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DDCMS), only objects that are over 50 years old and are manufactured or produced require an individual cultural property export licence, and there are no export requirements specific to the sale of fossils.A quick search of online marketplaces reveals a plethora of fossils, with small ammonites selling for as little as a few pounds.But some fossils can also fetch colossal sums: in 2020, Stan the T rex, now also housed atthe Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, was sold for a then record-breaking $31.8m (£23.6m), while in July this year another T rex skeleton nicknamed Guswas sold at Sotheby’s for $50.1m.These figures are far beyond the budget of most museums, with such specimens instead snapped up by private buyers – including business people and celebrities. Among those known to have bought dinosaur fossils are the actors Leonardo DiCaprio, Nicolas Cage andRussell Crowe– although Cage later returned the rare dinosaur skull he had bought to Mongolia, after it emerged it hadbeen illegally removed from the country.View image in fullscreenA Tyrannosaurus Rex dinosaur skeleton that was auctioned by Christie’s in New York in 2020.Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesFossils have also become popular on social media, with hunters using platforms such as TikTok to share videos of themselves cracking open rocks in a “fossil or no fossil?” reveal. Some accounts have several million followers.Finding a fossil is only the first step on the road to a sale: as the NHM in London notes,painstaking mechanical and chemical preparation is neededto turn it one into a museum-grade exhibit. Only dedicated fossil hunters have the tools and skills to prepare fossils –and Moore is among them.Many experts support the status quo for fossil collecting and sales, arguing that a ban on collecting would mean many important specimens would remain undiscovered and could result in a black-market for fossils – rather than allowing collectors to work with academics.View image in fullscreenAn ammonite at the fossil graveyard at Lyme Regis in Dorset.Photograph: Loop Images/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesThere is no suggestion the sale of the Moore collection to the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi has broken any rules.Yet Dr Erin Maxwell, an expert in Early Jurassic marine vertebrates based at the State Museum of Natural History in Stuttgart said the sale was a blow. “Such a sale in my opinion represents a loss to the UK, as fossils represent part of the natural [or] cultural heritage of the region and country from which they originate.“The loss is somewhat offset by the fact that these fossils are going to a museum rather than into the collection of a wealthy individual.”Maxwell added that there were other options for countries such as the UK where fossils are not automatically considered property of the state.“I think it is important for the state to have the right of first refusal on acquiring the collection on an at-cost basis prior to export – rather than the currently grossly inflated market price,” she said. “However, if the state declines, then sale to a foreign museum is a best-case scenario.”Phil Davidson, a palaeontologist at Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre in Dorset, said the priority was that fossil specimens of key scientific interest were in public collections, such as museums, so they could be described by teams of international experts, noting most scientific journals did not allow specimens to be described if they were within a private collection.“All the researchers I have talked to have said the same thing:
