the location of where the museum collection is housed is secondary,” Davidson said.“Countless specimens of scientific importance are housed outside their country of origin. Often this was because the specific researchers are based in other countries, or that they do not have the capacity or need to focus on other pressing priorities”.Davidson also stressed the importance of keeping the Moore collection together, adding the specimens come from a world heritage site “and this heritage is for everyone and not limited to lines on a map”.

title: Where in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse? | Solar eclipses | The Guardian
description: When, where and how to get the optimal view of the first solar eclipse to be visible across the country this century
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: When, where and how to get the optimal view of the first solar eclipse to be visible across the country this century
Content: Planetarium astronomer Carys Herbert demonstrates wearing Celestron solar eclipse glasses at the Royal Observatory Greenwich, south-east London, before the solar eclipse on 12 August.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenPlanetarium astronomer Carys Herbert demonstrates wearing Celestron solar eclipse glasses at the Royal Observatory Greenwich, south-east London, before the solar eclipse on 12 August.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PASolar eclipsesWhere in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse?When, where and how to get the optimal view of the first solar eclipse to be visible across the country this centuryRachel HallSat 8 Aug 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the first time this century, people across the UK will be able to see an almost total solar eclipse in the evening sky on Wednesday.A solar eclipse occurs when the moon moves between the sun and the Earth, blocking the sun’s light either partly or fully. This year, people in the UK and Ireland will see 90-96% of the sun covered by the moon for the first time since 1999 – and it’s their last chance until 2081.Across north-western Europe, people will see about 88-95% coverage, while spectators in parts of Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain will see a total eclipse for up to two minutes and 18 seconds in duration.In the UK, viewers in the west will see the most of the sun obscured: 95% in Plymouth, 93.2% in Cardiff and 93.1% in Belfast. Spectators in Manchester will see 91.9% and Londoners will catch 91.4%. Farther north and east people will see smaller proportions, with Edinburgh at 90.7%, Newcastle at 90.2%. Shetland will have the lowest coverage at 88%.Map of the best locations in UK to view the solar eclipseRoyal Observatory Greenwich astronomer Jess Lee said that these are small differences, and all “will still be impressive sights”. She recommended finding hills with clear views to the west, for example Parliament Hill, Alexandra Palace or Primrose Hill in London, or rooftop venues.Because the eclipse takes place in August, there’s a stronger chance of clear skies. Tom Morgan, a Met Office meteorologist, said it was too early to be confident, but “given the summer we’ve had a lot of the UK will have reasonable viewing conditions”.At present, there is a higher risk of thick cloud and rain in Scotland and Northern Ireland, while the clearest skies are likely to be towards the south and the east of the UK. “For many it’ll be quite a spectacular and rare event,” he said.For Scotland’s astronomer royal, Catherine Heymans, keeping an eye on the clouds is the secret to scoring the best view, since these could partly or entirely obscure the eclipse.“I plan to check the Met Office’s fantastic online cloud cover forecast as we get closer to the day. I’m ready to hop on a train north, south, east or west to find some cloud-free skies,” she said.Spanish mountain village braces for astrotourists lured by total solar eclipseRead moreGetting to a high point with a clear view of the horizon also helps. “I’d recommend a dress rehearsal in the days before. If you can’t see the sun from your planned viewing spot at 7.30pm because your view is blocked by a hill or a house, then you’ll want to find yourself a different location for the real event,” Heymans added.The most important thing, she stressed, is to wear eclipse glasses and avoid looking directly at the sun.During an eclipse, the sun appears dimmer, making it easier to look at directly. However, solar radiation can still reach and damage the retina, often without causing any pain, so viewers may not realise harm is occurring until it’s too late.Following the 1999 total solar eclipse, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists reportedabout 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems after watching the eclipse.The UK Health Security Agency advises that there are two safe approaches: specialist eclipse viewers or indirect viewing methods.Eclipse glasses or handheld solar viewers must be genuine and sold by a reputable retailer, and should have specially designed filters that meet the international safety standard ISO 12312-2:2015(E), and no scratches, tearing or damage to the lens. Old pairs may not be reusable and sunglasses should never be used.Indirect view methods include viewing the sun’s image projected through a colander or the gaps between tree leaves on to white paper, or using a pinhole pierced in one sheet of card and projected on to another.Sarah Crowther, an astronomer at the University of Manchester, said it was important to remember that the solar eclipse would take place at different times across the UK.It starts at about 6.08pm in Edinburgh and Glasgow, 6.10pm in Belfast, 6.13pm in Manchester and Liverpool, 6.15pm in Birmingham, 6.17pm in London and 6.18pm in Cornwall. Maximum eclipse follows roughly an hour later, ending about 8pm.People might observe the surrounding area going quiet during the solar eclipse, “when animals think it is night because it is darker, which gives a sense of calm. And then there’s an awakening as it gets light again, birds think it is dawn so there could be a dawn chorus,” said Crowther.She added: “I think many people feel a sense of awe when they see an eclipse. It can put the vast scales of the solar system into some kind of perspective.”Explore more on these topicsSolar eclipsesAstronomySpacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Nicola Sturgeon ‘has not spoken to’ estranged husband, Peter Murrell, since he was jailed | Nicola Sturgeon | The Guardian
description: Scotland’s former first minister says she will not visit Murrell in prison, where he is serving five-year sentence for embezzling SNP funds
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Scotland’s former first minister says she will not visit Murrell in prison, where he is serving five-year sentence for embezzling SNP funds
Content: Nicola Sturgeon’s comments came during a podcast recording at the Edinburgh festival fringe.Photograph: Claudia savage/PAView image in fullscreenNicola Sturgeon’s comments came during a podcast recording at the Edinburgh festival fringe.Photograph: Claudia savage/PANicola SturgeonNicola Sturgeon ‘has not spoken to’ estranged husband, Peter Murrell, since he was jailedScotland’s former first minister says she will not visit Murrell in prison, where he is serving five-year sentence for embezzling SNP fundsDonna FergusonSat 8 Aug 2026 10.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNicola Surgeon has said she will not visit her estranged husband, Peter Murrell, in prison, has stopped speaking to him and views herself as a “mug” for worrying about his wellbeing and mental health earlier this year.During a podcast recording at the Edinburgh festival fringe, Scotland’s former first minister said Murrell had lied to her until the day he pleaded guilty to embezzling more than £400,000 from the Scottish National party.He was imprisoned for five years in June, and Sturgeon revealed she had not spoken to him since then. She told the broadcaster Iain Dale she had only discovered Murrell was due to plead guilty a week before he appeared in court.She later found out he had been negotiating his plea for months.“[That] hit me like a tonne of bricks,” she said. “He was still lying to me right up until the day he pled guilty.”She added: “He was very isolated over that period, he very rarely left the house, he wasn’t communicative, I was a bit worried about his wellbeing and his mental health.“And then, now I think: ‘What a mug, why were you worried about him?’ He didn’t worry about me. He didn’t worry at all about what he was doing.“What he has subjected me to is beyond anything I could ever have comprehended. I don’t understand why he did it, he had no need to do it. I don’t think I will ever understand his motivations.“But whatever that motivation was, he could not have stopped and ever thought about me. But I was, until recently, still worrying about him.”Asked if she would visit him in prison, Sturgeon replied: “No. I’m not going to speak to him, I’m not going to visit him.”The former first minister said that when Murrell was in court she was still finding out details of the purchases he had made using party funds.“Over the years, he never really levelled with me,” she said. “The day he pled guilty, I was still learning about some of the detail of what he had done for the first time. I suddenly realised I had been living with somebody that I never really knew properly.“That’s something for me to come to terms with, and I don’t think I’m there yet, but also for my family to come to terms with. It’s a really difficult process.”Murrell, 61, spent the money on items including a motorhome, a Jaguar SUV and a VW Golf, boutique cosmetics, iPads and a pair of Lalique Feuilles salt and pepper grinders worth £2,618.Sturgeon, 55, has consistently denied knowledge of his crimes, which spanned the years 2010 to 2022, and was not charged after a police investigation.She has previously said she made an error of judgment by keeping Murrell on as SNP chief executive when she became party leader in November 2014, but refused to apologise for his crimes and denied ever “consciously” seeing the motorhome he bought and stored at her mother-in-law’s house.Explore more on these topicsNicola SturgeonScotlandScottish National party (SNP)Scottish politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Google DeepMind enters a new era as co-founder Demis Hassabis shifts AI role | DeepMind | The Guardian
description: Observers express concern that the division has lost its independence and commercial reality has taken over
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Observers express concern that the division has lost its independence and commercial reality has taken over
Content: Demis Hassabis at Google's offices in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDemis Hassabis at Google's offices in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianDeepMindGoogle DeepMind enters a new era as co-founder Demis Hassabis shifts AI roleObservers express concern that the division has lost its independence and commercial reality has taken overDan MilmoandAisha DownSat 8 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenSir Demis Hassabissaid AI had brought the world to a “pivotal moment in human history” last month, he knew another big change was imminent.This shift was closer to home. TheNobel prize-winninghead of Google DeepMind, Google’s AI unit, announced this week he wasrelinquishing his day-to-day duties as chief executiveand becoming chair. He is also taking on the role of chief scientist at DeepMind’s parent, Alphabet.Hassabis andDeepMindhave been key players in AI’s breakthrough era. The 50-year-old co-founded DeepMind and sold it to Google in 2014, which gave him the resources to oversee a number of advances.These included building the AlphaGo system that mastered theChinese board game Goand developing AlphaFold, a programme that predicts the 3D structure of proteins. The latter resulted in Hassabis being jointly awarded the 2024 Nobel prize in chemistry.A formerGoogleexecutive said the leadership overhaul showed London-based DeepMind being brought firmly into the orbit of its parent in Mountain View, California. DeepMind will now be run by Hassabis’s longstanding colleague, the US-based Koray Kavukcuoglu, who will take the non-CEO role of senior vice-president of DeepMind.“The era of DeepMind as an independent actor is over and the obvious sign of that is you have gone from a charismatic founder-leader to appointing Koray in a non-CEO leadership role. Koray is a technical character, not an inspirational figure like Demis,” said the former executive.The ex-Google employee added that it would be “galling” for Google and Hassabis that the latest iterations of Google’s flagship AI model series, Gemini, have lost ground to rival models developed by its US rivals Anthropic and OpenAI.Hassabis has said he was looking forward to focusing more on the “big picture” for AI and believed he was handing over operational management of a unit that was well placed for the competitive battles ahead.View image in fullscreenThe London DeepMind office will be brought into the orbit of its parent in Mountain View, California, a former Google executive said.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesInternally, DeepMind is a workplace where there have been political tensions. Employees who spoke to the Guardian said there was internal disquiet over the company’s work with the Pentagon. Earlier this year, a former Google DeepMind employee launched a legal challenge against Google, claiming they wereunfairly dismissedfor their views on Gaza.That employee was involved in unionisation efforts at Google DeepMind, which have taken place against a backdrop of concern that Google’s AI could assist militaries, including the Israel Defense Forces. Another Google DeepMind employeeresignedfrom the company in mid-July, citing Google’s work with the Pentagon and the US Department of Homeland Security.One said to the Guardian that Hassabis’s departure was the “end of an era”.“Now the person we were supposed to trust to get the right outcomes for humanity has stepped away,” they said. Google DeepMind “has become just another subdivision of Google”, they added.Rosa Curling, the executive director of Foxglove, a campaign group that supported the Google DeepMind employee in their legal challenge, said: “The departure of the co-founder of a company that once prided itself on its ethical credentials is likely to cause further concern among its frontier AI staff about how their work will end up being used in the real world.”Google has said it is committed to the “private and public sector consensus” that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without “appropriate human oversight”. While Google has declined a voluntary union recognition agreement in London, it has said it valued “the constructive and direct dialogue that we have with our employees about building a positive and successful workplace”.View image in fullscreenSome Google staff have been uncomfortable about its work with the Pentagon.Photograph: Joshua Roberts/ReutersOn the commercial side, a new cutting-edge model, Gemini 3.5 Pro, has yet to be released amid reports it has been delayed owing to attempts to improve its code-writing abilities – a core part of the appeal of Anthropic and OpenAI’s best products.Google’s two AI labs, London-based DeepMind and California-based Google Brain, were merged into Google DeepMind under Hassabis’s leadership three years ago. Control now appears to be moving back to the US, where Google’s co-founder Sergey Brin is reportedly playing a bigger role in AI development.Citing the departure of the leading AI researcher Yann LeCun from Meta and Geoffrey Hinton from Google as another example of “the end of an era in the AI ecosystem”, the former executive added: “This is very clearly a sign that the science-driven agenda of leadership in these labs has given way to cold, hard commercial reality that all of these companies want to make a return on the hundreds of billions of dollars they have invested in AI.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe source added, however, that Google still had the benefit of being able to combine its Gemini models with an impressive suite of products, from its all-conquering search product to its cloud platform and YouTube. Thanks to its search business it also has the money to continue investing heavily in AI, having generated net income – a US measure of profit – of $132bn (£98bn) last year.View image in fullscreenHassabis has called for a US safety body to assess cutting-edge AI models.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersHassabis has also taken on a more statesman-like role in recent years. The reference to a “pivotal moment” came in a blogpost in which he called for a US safety body to assess cutting-edge models, with the hope it would lead to the establishment of global standards.The need for such a body, Hassabis argued, was pressing because the tech industry was approaching the “pivotal” point of achieving AGI, the term for a theoretical state of AI where a system can perform any human cognitive task – which also means being capable of performing white collar jobs in sectors such as law, finance and health.A Google spokesperson said: “This is a move Demis has been thinking about for a while. He is very excited, and this will give him more time to focus on AI-driven scientific breakthroughs.” They disputed that the changes had anything to do with the performance of Gemini.Hassabis’s move was announced alongside the departure of Jeff Dean, a veteran Google engineer and DeepMind’s chief scientist, who is leaving along with three other top researchers to form an AI startup called Discovery Loop.According to one former Google employee, Dean’s departure could augur further personnel losses. Dean’s move also follows OpenAI’s poaching in June of Google’s Noam Shazeer, a leading figure in the field as co-author of the2017 research paperAttention is All You Need, a crucial step in developing chatbots.“It’s hugely problematic for Google,” said Jeremy Nixon, a former AI researcher at Google and founder of Infinity Artificial Intelligence Institute, a startup. “It’s problematic because of who Jeff will hire and because the primary reason people want to work at Google is because of him and Noam Shazeer and all these other phenomenal researchers. It’s no longer true to say that if you want to work with the greatest researchers on the planet, you go to Google DeepMind.”Nixon added that Dean was an “angelic diplomat” who could “deal with these complex political organisations”.Google denies it faces a post-Dean talent crisis, pointing to attrition rates for AI talent for the first half of this year being lower than they were at this time last year.If AI is indeed facing a pivotal moment, Google has just had one.Explore more on these topicsDeepMindGoogleAI (artificial intelligence)AlphabetComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Arron Banks ‘hired private detective’ to look into journalist who investigated Reform UK | Arron Banks | The Guardian
description: Asked whether he targeted reporter who investigated party finances, Brexit campaigner says: ‘When you live by the sword, you die by the sword’
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Asked whether he targeted reporter who investigated party finances, Brexit campaigner says: ‘When you live by the sword, you die by the sword’
Content: Arron Banks said he believed the Sunday Times used hacked information, an accusation the newspaper denied.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenArron Banks said he believed the Sunday Times used hacked information, an accusation the newspaper denied.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersArron BanksArron Banks ‘hired private detective’ to look into journalist who investigated Reform UKAsked whether he targeted reporter who investigated party  finances, Brexit campaigner says: ‘When you live by the sword, you die by the sword’Geraldine McKelvieSat 8 Aug 2026 07.11 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 13.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe prominent Reform UK member and Brexit campaigner Arron Banks is said to have set private investigators on a Sunday Times journalist after he broke a series of stories aboutNigel Farage.Banks is alleged to have paid for the services of investigators to examine Gabriel Pogrund, editor of the paper’s Insight investigations team.The detail emerged in the New Statesman on Friday. When approached for comment, Banks did not appear to deny it. He is said to have instructed Precision Risk and Intelligence, a firm he once owned, to examine Pogrund.The Sunday Times andthe Guardian have broken a series of storiesin recent months revealing how cash has poured into Reform and Farage personally from donors and wealthy benefactors.Pogrund is believed to have been targeted after a story in the Sunday Times last month revealed that Farage has receivedfinancial support from the convicted criminal George Cottrell, known as “Posh George”.In response to the New Statesman report, Banks said: “We believe theSunday Timesused hacked information and that was an area of interest. We do have an investigative arm that’s got advanced capabilities.”Asked directly whether he had paid investigators to look into Pogrund, he said: “When you live by the sword, you die by the sword.”The Sunday Times last night denied the accusation that its stories were based on illegally sourced information. The paper described the hiring of private investigators to snoop on its journalists as “reprehensible”.A spokesperson said: “If what Mr Banks claims to have done is true then it is reprehensible that his reaction to our reporting is to place a journalist under surveillance … This story was not based on hacked information. It was based on responsible and professional journalism.”The gifts theReform UKleader Nigel Farage received in the 12 months before being elected as MP for Clacton have been subject to widespread media scrutiny in recent months.MPs are obliged to declare any political donations they received in the year before their election but Farage has repeatedly claimed that it was not until the month before the general election, in July 2024, that he decided to stand. He has claimed he was not obliged to declare any donations he received before deciding to run for election, as he was a media personality at the time.Farage admission over timing of Reform leadership talks raises fresh doubts over £5m giftRead moreIn April, the Guardian reported that he had accepteda £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, a billionaire donor to Reform UK.The Sunday Times has reported that Cottrell paid for security, accommodation and social media support for Farage during this time. The newspaper also said that Cottrell helped to broker a “comeback deal” for Farage toreturn to Reform as party leadermonths before he announced he would stand.Cottrell’s mother, the retired stylist Fiona Cottrell, made a series of donations to Reform UK in the weeks before the general election. Two transfers of £250,000 were made directly to the party in May 2024.She then gave £1m to Britain Means Business, a company owned by Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice. Britain Means Business gave the party two donations of £250,000 shortly afterwards.The Guardian told how they later became the subject of a suspicious activity report by the National Crime Agency. Suspicious activity reports are not crime reports but exist to identify potential incidents of money laundering.The Metropolitan police are investigating Reform UK’s finances. The Guardian revealed that both George and Fiona Cottrell have been interviewed under caution but no arrests have been made.On Saturday morning, the Guardian asked Banks if Reform UK had known about or sanctioned the surveillance on Pogrund, or if any other journalists had been targeted.“I have nothing else to add,” he said. “Other than to say I have spoken to no one at Reform on this matter, nor would I.”A Reform UK spokesperson denied the party knew about or sanctioned the surveillance on Pogrund. He also denied that Reform had sanctioned or been made aware of surveillance on any other journalists.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsArron BanksReform UKParty fundingSunday TimesNigel FarageNewspapersNational newspapersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Utah wildfire blocks rescuers from reaching firefighting helicopter crash site | Utah | The Guardian
description: Fate of two passengers onboard helicopter that went down Friday morning remains unknown after more than 24 hours
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Fate of two passengers onboard helicopter that went down Friday morning remains unknown after more than 24 hours
Content: A Sikorsky Skycrane rises after refilling during efforts to fight the Widemouth 2 fire east of Fillmore, Utah, on 4 August, before it crashed on 7 August.Photograph: Scott G Winterton/The Deseret News/APView image in fullscreenA Sikorsky Skycrane rises after refilling during efforts to fight the Widemouth 2 fire east of Fillmore, Utah, on 4 August, before it crashed on 7 August.Photograph: Scott G Winterton/The Deseret News/APUtahUtah wildfire blocks rescuers from reaching firefighting helicopter crash siteFate of two passengers onboard helicopter that went down Friday morning remains unknown after more than 24 hoursUwa Ede-OsifoSat 8 Aug 2026 19.43 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 19.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe fate of two passengersonboarda firefighting helicopter that crashed Friday morning in Utah remains unknown after more than 24 hours, as one of the country’s largest wildfires continues to grow, preventing authorities from safely reaching the accident site.The Sikorsky S-64 helicopter, contracted by the US Forest Service, was responding on Friday to the Widemouth 2 fire, a blaze sparked in late July by lightning, when it crashed in a remote area of centralUtah.Widemouth 2 hasswept through more than 114,600 acres(46,400 hectares) and is 24% contained, as of Saturday. That figure marked a jump from early on Friday, where the fire’s scope was reported as reaching more than 105,000 acres, according to state data.The chopper’s crash ignited a new blaze, state authorities said at a news conference on Friday evening. The accident site is within the fire’s perimeter.“Ground resources attempted to respond immediately, but access to the scene was compromised by the emergent fire,” the US Forest Servicewrotein a Saturday statement. “Without a safety zone, the Incident Management Team determined not to place lives at risk until the area is deemed safe.”Federal officials have advised the public to refrain from speculating on the nature of the crash, as search-and-rescue teams wait for fire conditions to subside to safer levels.In a Saturday daily report, however, the US National Interagency Fire Center, a coalition of state and federal agencies, said the helicopter’s “pilot and one crewmember were fatally injured”. At a Saturday morning briefing,a moment of silence was observedto honor the passengers.The US Forest Service has declined to confirm their status.“There have already been many false reports and rumors, and the victims deserve the highest level of respect and avoidance of speculation,” the agency wrote.Investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) were en route to Richfield, a city roughly 160 miles (250km) south of Salt Lake City, as of Friday. When they are able to reach the crash site, they will document the scene, before retrieving the aircraft.The western US states have faced a deadly wildfire season. In June, three firefighters died, as they battled a blaze along the Colorado-Utah border. A fourth firefighter later died from burn injuries sustained during the emergency response.Explore more on these topicsUtahHelicopter crashesFirefightersWildfiresnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Super El Niño’ could bring wet winter and flooding to western US, climate scientists warn | US weather | The Guardian
description: Weather system tied to warming sea surface expected to intensify in fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Weather system tied to warming sea surface expected to intensify in fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027
Content: El Niño-generated storm waves crash onto seaside houses at Mondos Beach, California, on 12 January 2016.Photograph: Mark Ralston/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEl Niño-generated storm waves crash onto seaside houses at Mondos Beach, California, on 12 January 2016.Photograph: Mark Ralston/AFP/Getty ImagesUS weather‘Super El Niño’ could bring wet winter and flooding to western US, climate scientists warnWeather system tied to warming sea surface expected to intensify in fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027Uwa Ede-OsifoSat 8 Aug 2026 15.21 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 15.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEl Niño, a recurring climate phenomenon marked by above-average sea surface temperatures, when changes in wind patterns allow warmer water to spread across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, could spell a wet winter for portions of the western and south-eastern US, climate models show. Coastal areas may be at elevated risk of flooding, experts warn.Climate scientists predict this year’s “super” El Niño, a label assigned when sea surface temperaturesclimb by at least 2C, will be the strongest of the century. The weather system is expected to intensify in the fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027,according tothe US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa).El Niño could push 50m people into acute hunger before end of next yearRead moreCalifornia has a 70%-100% chance of experiencing above-average rainfall along its coast, according to a model from the European center for medium-range forecasts.“El Niño is never going to guarantee any particular outcome in any California winter,” Daniel Swain, the UCLA climate scientist, noted ata virtual El Niño town hallhosted by the California state senator Mike McGuire this week. But, he added, a weather event as strong as the one being currently predicted shifts the odds in favor of a wet winter: “That will likely affect and increase the likelihood of coastal flooding, particularly during strong storm events or during king tide events.”California has been devastated by El Niños in the past.A 1982-83 weather system destroyed 33 oceanfront homes and damaged 3,000 other residences,according to the California coastal commission. In a 1997-98 El Niño, California experiencedmassive flooding and 17 storm-related deaths. In more recent history, during the El Niño winter of 2015-16, state officials reportedrecord coastal erosionon California beaches.“With less beach in front of the coastline, the waves will have even greater impact on the shoreline with more likelihood of flooding and undercutting of cliffs,” said Mark Merrifield of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, at McGuire’s town hall.El Niño is not expected to completely erase drought in the US south-west, where some reservoirs are at an all-time low. “It would have to be exceptionally wet,” Dr Joel Lisonbee, senior associate scientist at the Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences at the University of Colorado Boulder,toldthe Guardian in June. “That would also mean flooding, and the destruction and potential loss of life that comes along with that.”Swathes of the US Gulf coast and east coast, stretching from Florida up to the mid-Atlantic region, are facing similar high odds of increased precipitation.During El Niño years, central and south Florida has historically experienced more severe weather with more tornadoes and flood events,according to Noaa. In a 1998 El Niño winter, an outbreak of unusually strong tornadoes in that region led to 42 deaths and more than $100m in damage.Experts warn that not every El Niño behaves the same, nor does it affect different geographical regions in the same way. Some have fueled hurricanes and heavy precipitation, while others have triggered extreme heat and drought.While this is “a natural cycle”, Merrifield said at the town hall, the potential effects of a temporary sea-level rise in California from the super El Niño also “gives us a bit of a stress test of what the state is likely to experience with future climate change”.“The El Niño, I think, is a good opportunity to sort of see where our vulnerabilities are throughout the state and what we can do to prepare,” Merrifield added, “and it also is a sobering look at what we can expect with climate change.”Explore more on these topicsUS weatherEl Niño southern oscillationClimate crisis in the American westExtreme weatherClimate crisisCaliforniaWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hunter Biden talks about how his father’s cancer has spread and is causing him pain | Joe Biden | The Guardian
description: Joe Biden’s prostate cancer is reportedly ‘debilitating’, even as ex-president continues to speak out on public issues
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Joe Biden’s prostate cancer is reportedly ‘debilitating’, even as ex-president continues to speak out on public issues
Content: Then president Joe Biden and his son Hunter embrace in the Oval Office of the White House on 24 July 2024.Photograph: Evan Vucci/EPAView image in fullscreenThen president Joe Biden and his son Hunter embrace in the Oval Office of the White House on 24 July 2024.Photograph: Evan Vucci/EPAJoe BidenHunter Biden talks about how his father’s cancer has spread and is causing him painJoe Biden’s prostate cancer is reportedly ‘debilitating’, even as ex-president continues to speak out on public issuesStaff and agenciesSat 8 Aug 2026 15.17 EDTFirst published on Sat 8 Aug 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormer US presidentJoe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread to other parts of his body and is causing him pain, even as he continues to speak out on public issues, his sonHuntersaid in an interview.In a wide-ranging interview with the BBC broadcast late on Friday,Hunter Bidengrew emotional as he discussed his father’s condition, describing it as very sad to watch.“The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further,” he said. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects.”Joe Biden appears to discuss sensitive information on tape with ghostwriterRead moreJoe Biden, 83, was the oldest man to serve as US president and his age was a source of concern for much of his four years in office. He and his White House advisers have faced intense criticism for allegedly concealing the extent of his health issues, especially after he was forced to abandon his bid for re-election after a disastrous debate with his eventual successor, Donald Trump.The former president revealed his cancer diagnosis in May of last year, less than four months after he left the White House.Hunter Biden said the diagnosis had been tough on the family.“It’s really sad to watch,” Biden said. “The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good.”But Biden said his father remains “out there”, speaking publicly about the issues that are important to him.“He’s still doing his thing,” he said. “He so believes in this country.”Biden also expressed gratitude for the pardon his father granted him because if he had not, Trump would have sought retribution against him, he said. But he also acknowledged that it was not good for the former president’s legacy or the American people.“It is something that is easily criticized and for good reason,” Biden said. “All I know is that I’m grateful he did it for me, and all I can say to anybody out there is, what would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me?”Joe Biden will publish a memoir, Promise Me, America, after the midterm elections.The Associated Press contributedreportingExplore more on these topicsJoe BidenHunter BidenCancerUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Blanche confirmation allows Trump to continue ‘pervasive, breathtaking corruption’, says Schumer – as it happened | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Senate minority leader condemns Republicans after Donald Trump’s former defense lawyer confirmed by 50 votes to 49 early on Saturday morning. This blog is now closed.
Author: Yohannes Lowe
Headline: Senate minority leader condemns Republicans after Donald Trump’s former defense lawyer confirmed by 50 votes to 49 early on Saturday morning. This blog is now closed.
Content: 06.49 EDTBlanche confirmation gives Trump 'excuse' to continue his 'breathtaking corruption', Schumer saysThe Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, has said SenateRepublicanshave “handed Trump an excuse on a silver platter” to continue his “pervasive, breathtaking corruption” by confirming Todd Blanche as attorney general“If you want to wipe out corruption, you can’t have the president’s personal attorney as the attorney general. You don’t need a PhD in political science to know that,”he wrote in a post on X.“Todd Blanche has no intention of stopping Trump’s corruption. He advanced his career enabling it. Every senator who voted to confirm him has now branded themselves as an enabler, too.”Schumer said Senate Democrats will continue to resist the Trump administration’s “assault on the rule of law and undermining of democratic values”.All Democrats voted against Blanche’s nomination to lead the Justice Department on a permanent basis, with a wide spectrum of lawmakers saying he was unfit for the role and would do the president’s bidding.Chuck Schumer speaking at a press conference with Jeffrey Epstein Survivors in the Capitol Building on 15 July 2026 in Washington DC.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/Getty ImagesShare

title: OpenAI to pause some work on AI model Astra due to security concerns | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Agent found to be able to find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, and to carry out cyber-attacks
Author: Eric Berger
Headline: Agent found to be able to find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, and to carry out cyber-attacks
Content: ‘The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them.’Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them.’Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAI to pause some work on AI model Astra due to security concernsAgent found to be able to find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, and to carry out cyber-attacksEric BergerSat 8 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTFirst published on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI will pausesomework on an artificial intelligence model because of security concerns, the company stated on Friday, following a series of incidents in which AI agents have escaped containment.The company had evaluated the agent, Astra, and found “significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity”, which had moved to a “critical” threshold where it can find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, or devise and execute cyber-attacks when given only a “high level desired goal”.OpenAI stated that the model was not involved in an incident in which one of its AI agentswent rogueduring a test, accessed the open web and hacked a startup, Hugging Face. The company discovered other instances in which autonomous agents had escaped containment,Reuters reportedin July.Google DeepMind enters a new era as co-founder Demis Hassabis shifts AI roleRead moreThe reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them. Still, critics of the AI industryhave warnedthat such disclosures from OpenAI and its competitors Anthropic and Meta could be designed to generate hype about the technology’s power and thus spur additional interest from investors.To prevent potential rogue behavior from AI agents,OpenAIis “implementing stricter security controls for higher-capability models and associated activities, including isolated testing environments, restricted network and tool access”, the company’s blogpost stated. It will also install “enhanced model weight protections and encryption, additional monitoring and detection capabilities”.The company will pause internal activities involving Astra that do not meet these new requirements.“We’re committed to working alongside governments, safety institutes, and civil society to ensure that the frontier capabilities of models like Astra, and those that follow, are deployed responsibly and broadly for the benefit of all humanity,” the company stated.Metaalso disclosedthis week that one of its models hacked another company during cybersecurity testing. And the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) announced on 4 August that agents powered by OpenAI and Anthropic had senttargeted emailsto software developers in an attempt to pass a cyber challenge.“These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world,” theinstitute statedin a blogpost.The organisation cautioned that the models’ sending of harmful software was not a case of a “model escaping its secure test environment” but rather that the group had intentionally permitted internet access to “best assess the maximum capability of models”.Still, the “behaviour was possible, sustained and new; that alone warrants attention”, the AISI said.The reports emerged while the Trump administrationwas finalizinga framework on how to test AI models for safety and cybersecurity risks. OpenAI and Anthropic, which have increased competition from China and other tech firms, have argued that open-source models, meaning those that allow anyone to see and modify the underlying program code, pose asecurity riskand pushed for additional federal regulations on them.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAInewsShareReuse this content

title: Sky’s DiJonai Carrington posts ‘white privilege’ after ejection for hard foul on Sophie Cunningham | WNBA | The Guardian
description: Chicago’s DiJonai Carrington tagged Indiana in a post saying ‘WHITE PRIVILEGE’ after she was tossed for a hard foul on Sophie Cunningham
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Chicago’s DiJonai Carrington tagged Indiana in a post saying ‘WHITE PRIVILEGE’ after she was tossed for a hard foul on Sophie Cunningham
Content: Indiana’s Sophie Cunningham is fouled by Chicago’s DiJonai Carrington during the first half of Saturday’s game at the United Center in Chicago.Photograph: Michael Reaves/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIndiana’s Sophie Cunningham is fouled by Chicago’s DiJonai Carrington during the first half of Saturday’s game at the United Center in Chicago.Photograph: Michael Reaves/Getty ImagesWNBASky’s DiJonai Carrington posts ‘white privilege’ after ejection for hard foul on Sophie CunninghamCarrington tossed for Flagrant 2 on CunninghamChicago player tags Fever in social media postClark’s eighth technical triggers one-game banAgenciesSat 8 Aug 2026 17.26 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 19.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDiJonai Carrington of the Chicago Sky was ejected Saturday after being called for a Flagrant 2 foul on Sophie Cunningham of theIndiana Fever. Minutes later, Carrington posted on social media the words “WHITE PRIVILEGE” and tagged the Fever.Sophie Cunningham isn’t rejecting politics. She’s cashing in on themRead moreCunningham, who is white, was shooting a fast-break layup in the first quarter when Carrington, who is Black, came from behind and hit her in the head and neck, knocking her to the court as the shot went in.Cunningham said she thought the foul in the 90-86 Indiana win was “absolutely” intentional.“Clearly I think it was unnecessary,” Cunningham said. “I’ve never really spoken to her and I have no beef with her, but I guess she has some pent up stuff.”Fever coach Stephanie White had a different view of the play.“It was a hard foul,” White said. “I don’t think that Dijonai intentionally came out to get her across the neck like she did, but it did happen, and I thought it was the right call.”Cunningham got up immediately, charged toward Carrington and pushed her as she was held back by a teammate.“I popped up,” Cunningham said. “I’m not going to let anyone just do that to me. I think everyone knows that. I think that’s why she did it because she wants attention.”The play was reviewed and upgraded to a Flagrant 2 after the referee said there was windup, impact and follow-through on the foul.Sky coach Tyler Marsh said he hadn’t seen a replay of the play, but that seeing it live, he thought Carrington was making a play on the ball and that he didn’t believe it warranted a Flagrant 2 foul.“I haven’t looked at that play since, so I really don’t know if it was justified or not,” he said. “But, that’s what I thought in the moment.”Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onthreads.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueMarsh was then asked about Carrington’s social media post.“I have to get back to you on that because I’m just now hearing about that,” he said. “So yeah, we’ll handle that.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut Cunningham had plenty to say about the post.“I think the league is taking care of that,” she said. “This has nothing to do with race. Last year, I did the same thing and I got kicked out. And I deserved to be kicked out. There’s no reason even to play that card.”View image in fullscreenIndiana’s Sophie Cunningham (center) reacts to DiJonai Carrington’s hard foul during Saturday’s game.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesIn the third quarter, Fever starCaitlin Clarkwas assessed a technical foul after she made contact with a referee when she was forced out of bounds. The technical was Clark’s eighth of the season, triggering a one-game suspension for Indiana’s next game.After the game, Clark said the contact was inadvertent and that no words were exchanged. She was hopeful theWNBAwould rescind the foul.“She said I ran into her,” Clark said of the referee. “I have already watched it on the tape. So, we’ll let the league decide. But, it wasn’t anything intentional or anything. So, I hope it gets rescinded. And, nothing was said.”Fever coach Fever coach Stephanie White said it was “a bad call”.Cunningham has frequently come to Clark’s defense after physical play by opponents and has become one of the higher-profile players in the league this season. In an ESPN article published last month, she voiced support for barring transgender girls and women from girls’ and women’s sports, which led to small protests and rallies outside Fever games in Seattle and Portland.In a memo to teams on Friday, WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert said the leaguewould have ongoing discussionsabout the issue of transgender participation in women’s basketball.Explore more on these topicsWNBAIndiana FeverChicago SkyCaitlin ClarkShareReuse this content

title: Fifa launches new attack on media over alleged ‘concerted effort’ to undermine Gianni Infantino  | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: Fifa has issued a new statement alleging there is a ‘concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president’ as pressure increases on Gianni Infantino
Author: David Hills
Headline: Fifa has issued a new statement alleging there is a ‘concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president’ as pressure increases on Gianni Infantino
Content: Fifa has issued a new statement defending its under-fire president, Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Jaime Saldarriaga/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFifa has issued a new statement defending its under-fire president, Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Jaime Saldarriaga/AFP/Getty ImagesGianni InfantinoFifa launches new attack on media over alleged ‘concerted effort’ to undermine Gianni InfantinoFifa issues statement defending under-fire president‘Insinuation should not be presented as fact’David HillsSat 8 Aug 2026 18.17 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 18.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa has issued a new statement alleging there is a “concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president” as pressure increases onGianni Infantino.Fifa president Gianni Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged ‘lover’Read moreThe governing body issued the statement in response toUefa confirming on Saturdaythat a “departure payment” was made to a female employee who is alleged to have been in a relationship with Infantino while he was the organisation’s general secretary – allegations Fifa dismissed as “categorically untrue”.The Daily Telegraph reported on Friday night that the woman received a six-figure sum following the alleged relationship with Infantino. In a statement, Uefa confirmed a payment was made along with covering the fees for an MBA course, which it said was “in line” with regulations at the time.Fifa told the Telegraph that “any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory”, and late on Saturday issued a new, broader statement attacking Infantino’s critics.A Fifa spokesperson said: “The Fifa president was democratically elected by Fifa’s member associations and continues to serve with their mandate. It is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president.“Those who do not have the support of Fifa’s member associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through Fifa’s established democratic processes. Recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning Fifa and its president. Speculation and insinuation should not be presented as fact, and repetition does not make an allegation true.”Two weeks that rocked Fifa: how Gianni Infantino unravelled, day by dayRead moreDefending Infantino as a leader who has “dedicated more than 30 years of his professional life to European and world football”, the statement added: “Fifa welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to distort facts, amplify unsubstantiated allegations or manufacture distractions designed to undermine progress.“Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading, Fifa will challenge it directly and vigorously. Fifa’s responsibility is to its 211 member associations and to football around the world. We will not be distracted or diverted from strengthening the organisation, delivering for our member associations and continuing the work of making football truly global.”Pressure has continued to mount on Infantino after theexposure and collapse of his planto seek private investment in a company which would run Fifa’s competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cups. Fifa has said it will not accept any challenge to Infantino’s position before the election next March.Uefa’s threat that its 55 member countries could boycott Fifa competitions remains in place, with the European confederation saying on Thursday that the withdrawal of the scheme “changes nothing”.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: WNBA commissioner says league will continue discussing issue of transgender eligibility | WNBA | The Guardian
description: Cathy Engelbert says league will consult teams and players’ union as debate over transgender participation draws growing political attention
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cathy Engelbert says league will consult teams and players’ union as debate over transgender participation draws growing political attention
Content: WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert smiles as she talks to media at a news conference before last month’s All-Star game in Chicago.Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APView image in fullscreenWNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert smiles as she talks to media at a news conference before last month’s All-Star game in Chicago.Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APWNBAWNBA commissioner says league will continue discussing issue of transgender eligibilityCommissioner sends memo to teams on eligibility rulesPlayers’ union refuses to be used as a political pawnCunningham remarks have prompted rallies and protestsAssociated PressSat 8 Aug 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert has sent a memo to teams that addresses ongoing discussions around transgender athletes in women’s basketball.“I know many of you have received questions in recent weeks regarding transgender athlete participation in women’s basketball, and I expect this topic will continue to receive significant attention,” Engelbert wrote in the memo, which was sent Friday afternoon and obtained by the Associated Press. “I wanted to reach out to share how we are approaching these conversations at the league office and to thank those of you who have responded to questions from the media with thoughtfulness and professionalism.”WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert has a hard job. Here's how to make it easier | Jordan RobinsonRead moreThe memo said the topic will be discussed further by a task force of team presidents and general managers at a previously scheduled meeting next week.In an ESPN article published last month, Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham voiced support for barring transgender girls and women from girls’ and women’s sports. Cunningham’s comments sparked small rallies and protests in Seattle and Portland when the Fever were on the road last week.There was a lone protester at the Fever’s home game against Las Vegas on Thursday night. Indiana visits Chicago on Saturday. Members of two conservative groups are planning a rally in support of Cunningham ahead of that game.The league hasn’t made any public comments on the issue.Engelbert wrote that the league will “always approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league. Second, our player eligibility rules, unlike the eligibility rules of some other leagues and governing bodies, are collectively bargained. Lastly, preserving the integrity of our game and ensuring fair competition will always remain among the league’s highest priorities.”The league’s collective bargaining agreement states that “only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA”, but it does not include any more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth. On Friday, two former NBA players, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, declared themselves eligible for the WNBA draft, saying they identify as women.“We recognize that this is a complex and nuanced topic, and we will continue to have important conversations with all of you and the Players Association in the weeks and months ahead,” Engelbert said in the memo. “We also plan to convene additional discussions and offer listening sessions for any team leaders who would like to participate. Your perspectives and feedback are invaluable, and I appreciate those who have already reached out to share their thoughts.”The WNBA players’ association released a statement on social media Friday that emphasized diversity and inclusion while saying the group “will not be used as political pawns”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We embrace justice equity, diversity, and inclusion,” the statement read. “Those are the values that unite this Union and allow it to protect women’s sports while creating transformational change. Hate, abuse, and demonization of any person or group of people, including transgender people, only fuel fear, division, and harm. We will continue to have hard conversations. But we will not be used as political pawns.”Some WNBA players and coaches have come out in support of transgender athletes, including Seattle Storm center Stefanie Dolson and Minnesota Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve .“We need to protect trans kids,” Reeve said on 1 August. “To me, it’s a human rights issue. Every kid has a right to sports.”Explore more on these topicsWNBABasketballShareReuse this content

title: Skye Blakely and Claire Pease share lead at US gymnastics championships | Gymnastics | The Guardian
description: Skye Blakely and 17-year-old Claire Pease are tied after Friday’s opening session, with Charleigh Bullock just 0.2 points behind
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Skye Blakely and 17-year-old Claire Pease are tied after Friday’s opening session, with Charleigh Bullock just 0.2 points behind
Content: Skye Blakely competes on the balance beam during the US gymnastics championships ⁠on Friday in ⁠Phoenix.Photograph: Chris Coduto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSkye Blakely competes on the balance beam during the US gymnastics championships ⁠on Friday in ⁠Phoenix.Photograph: Chris Coduto/Getty ImagesGymnasticsSkye Blakely and Claire Pease share lead at US gymnastics championshipsBlakely and Pease score 55.6 points in PhoenixBullock third as defending champion Rivera sits fourthWomen’s all-around competition concludes SundayReutersSat 8 Aug 2026 08.10 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 08.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe University of Florida’s Skye Blakely and 17-year-old Honolulu native Claire Pease are tied for ⁠the all-around lead after the first day of women’s competition at the US gymnastics championships ⁠on Friday in ⁠Phoenix.Each ​earned 55.6 points.‘It just means more’: Black college gymnasts competing in a divided southRead moreSixteen-year-old Charleigh Bullock from Virginia holds third place at 55.4, with defending all-around champion ⁠Hezly Rivera (55.0), Jade Carey (54.4) and Reese Esponda (54.1) also in contention.Blakely, 21, was part of the United States’ winning ⁠teams at the 2022 and 2023 world championships, but she missed ​the 2024 Paris Olympics ‌due to an ‌achilles injury she sustained at the US trials. She returned to ‌competition last year and shared the uneven bars crown with Rivera at the US championships.She said of her performance on Friday, according to Olympics.com, “That felt really good. I’m really proud of myself. It’s not easy, but I feel like I handled ‌each moment the best of my ability.“Pease called being the co-leader “definitely a dream”, per Olympics.com. Looking ahead, she ​added, “I just like to stay focused on what I’m doing in the gym.“Rivera, 18, was a member of the gold-medal-winning US team at the 2024 Olympics. Her Friday score was hurt by ⁠a fall on the uneven bars, but she ended the ​day with the ​best score on the ​balance beam (14.3) and the second- best mark on the ​floor exercise (14.0), ‌behind only Esponda’s ​14.45.Bullock produced ​the best uneven bars score (14.25), just ahead of Pease and Blakely, who were both at 14.2.Pease (13.9) and Blakely (13.75) were second and third, respectively, behind Rivera on the balance beam.The women’s event concludes on Sunday.Explore more on these topicsGymnasticsUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: High divers take the plunge in Paris for a new test of reclaimed Seine’s water | Diving | The Guardian
description: Paris is staging its first high-diving competition in the Seine, with athletes launching themselves from a 20-metre platform in front of the Eiffel Tower
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Paris is staging its first high-diving competition in the Seine, with athletes launching themselves from a 20-metre platform in front of the Eiffel Tower
Content: Germany’s Maike Elena Halbisch competes in the women’s 20m high diving event during the European Aquatics Championships, alongside the Seine, with the Eiffel Tower in the background.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGermany’s Maike Elena Halbisch competes in the women’s 20m high diving event during the European Aquatics Championships, alongside the Seine, with the Eiffel Tower in the background.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty ImagesDivingHigh divers take the plunge in Paris for a new test of reclaimed Seine’s waterEuropean Aquatics Championships taking place in cityThreat to water quality tested two years after GamesAssociated PressSat 8 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParis is staging its first high-diving competition in the Seine, with athletes launching themselves from a 20-metre platform in front of the Eiffel Tower – a spectacular new test of the city’s effort to reclaim its river for sport. The event on the Pont de Bir-Hakeim has also exposed the fragility of that ambition.Organisers suspended training on Thursday when traces of hydrocarbons were detected upstream. By Friday, the FrenchSwimmingFederation said the affected area had been treated, allowing athletes to return to the water and the event to proceed as planned. High diving concludes on Saturday with the final two rounds and medal events, while the broader European Aquatics Championships run through to 16 August.View image in fullscreenFrance’s Gary Hunt in the men’s 20m high diving event.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty Images“There are things that are within our control and there are uncertainties that are inevitably linked to any outdoor activity,” said Maxime Sauvage, the Paris deputy mayor in charge of sports, sports facilities and equal access to sport. Among the things within the city’s control, he said, are the massive investments made before the 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Gamesto make the river safe for swimming, such as work to prevent sewage from flowing directly into the Seine to improvements in stormwater management.“There is always a small risk, but that is also part of what makes outdoor events special,” he said. “When they work, it is magical.”Hundreds of people gathered along the banks on Friday to watch the divers. Some stopped during their lunch break, while others stumbled across the competition by chance. Among them was Rebecca Kapogiannis, a 45-year-old visitor from London, Ontario, who was visiting Paris with her daughter to celebrate her graduation. Her daughter had even packed a bathing suit in case she got the chance to swim in the Seine.View image in fullscreenA diver during practice with the Eiffel Tower in the background.Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/AP“We just headed down to the [Eiffel] Tower today and thought we would walk along the Seine and stumbled upon this and thought it was a really cool activity to watch,” she said. “I was not expecting a competition to take place in the Seine, but it’s such a cool use of this water that runs right through the city.”For Cynthia Matz, who was visiting with her husband, Sean, the setting was part of the draw. She said they probably would not have sought out the competition had it been held inside. “Anybody can go. I don’t have to know anything about diving. I can just say: ‘This is really cool to see’. Having it out in public, people will just stop and go, ‘huh, what’s going on?’ and stop and spend some time and enjoy it.”View image in fullscreenSpectators watch the action from the riverbank.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty ImagesThat ability to stumble across elite sport in the middle of the city reflects a broader transformation Paris officials have been pushing for years: turning the Seine from a river associated largely with commerce, transport and tourism into a place where people can also swim, play and compete.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe 38th European Aquatics Championships mark the centenary of the inaugural championships, held in Budapest. For Paris, they are a return of another kind: the capital last hosted the event in 1931. More than 1,000 athletes are competing in five disciplines: swimming, diving, artistic swimming, open-water swimming and high diving.The Seine is hosting the open-water swimming and high diving, placing the river back at the centre of a major international sporting event two years after the Paris Oympics. Swimming in the Seine was banned in 1923 because of pollution and the dangers of river traffic. Public swimming returned in 2025, after Paris and its partners mobilised €1.4bn to make the river swimmable, an effort accelerated by the Olympics.View image in fullscreenSwimmers compete in the men’s 10km open-water event.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty ImagesFor many French people, making the Seine clean enough for swimming again seemed a distant dream. But images of athletes competing – and now residents swimming – in the river have become almost familiar. “Paris is not just a postcard image, it is also a magnificent sporting venue,” said Sauvage.Explore more on these topicsDivingSwimmingParisFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: A tale of two Murrays: when Ewan met Ewen to talk Tiger Woods, stiff gins and 15 years of mistaken identity | Golf | The Guardian
description: Guardian journalist Ewan Murray and Sky Sports Golf commentator Ewen Murray on being mixed up by irate fans and ‘canteen commandos’
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Guardian journalist Ewan Murray and Sky Sports Golf commentator Ewen Murray on being mixed up by irate fans and ‘canteen commandos’
Content: The Guardian’s Ewan Murray (left) with Sky Sports Golf commentator Ewen Murray at Royal Birkdale.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Guardian’s Ewan Murray (left) with Sky Sports Golf commentator Ewen Murray at Royal Birkdale.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianGolfInterviewA tale of two Murrays: when Ewan met Ewen to talk Tiger Woods, stiff gins and 15 years of mistaken identityEwan MurrayGuardian journalist Ewan Murray and Sky Sports Golf commentator Ewen Murray on being mixed up by irate fans and ‘canteen commandos’Sat 8 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt started with an email in early 2011. “I don’t know what it is like in your country, sir,” wrote angry of Arizona. “But here in America we SPIT!!!”The penny eventually dropped. Ewen Murray’s commentary on Sky Sports about Tiger Woods emptying his mouth on a putting surface in Dubai triggered a reaction fired directly towards Ewan Murray of the Guardian. Murray of Sky fame can still recall it.“Tiger spat on the green with three groups playing behind him,” Ewen says. “I remember my words. ‘For a person who is an inspiration, not just to golfers but to everyone, there are times when he is arrogant and disrespectful.’ I switched the mic off straight away. I knew there would be trouble. But if I don’t say anything, people close to me are going to ask why I didn’t comment.Maguire survives missed cuts and controversy to headline Solheim Cup wildcard picksRead more“There was no bigger supporter of Tiger than me but the email you got, I got an awful lot more of ‘Who the hell are you to tell …’ I wasn’t telling, I was only saying it wasn’t acceptable.”Months later, at the Scottish Open, I explained the email episode to Ewen. He was concerned at the impact of this tirade on me. My response related to my ongoing coverage of Scottish football, a domain where even mild opinion fuels abuse. Water, duck’s back.Fast forward to 2026 and we are together again, this time in the Open Championship’s media centre. “If only we knew,” says Ewen. Indeed. If only we knew.It is coincidental enough for two individuals whose names are one letter apart to work in media coverage of the same sport. Freakish in this instance is that we both joined Twitter in October 2010. Before long, confusion reigned. We may be almost three decades apart in age and of totally different stock – Ewen a former professional golfer who competed in the Open, me an erratic amateur – but social media criticism (plus the odd element of praise) intended for Sky’s esteemed commentator flew this way. Lots and lots of it.My response was to fight fire with fire in an alter ego; to take on the canteen commandos in a manner that is considerably more pretentious than Ewen in reality. The man himself soon roared with approval.“I think if you don’t have humour in life; and let’s face it, there isn’t much nowadays … ” he says. “Laughter is the best medicine. I have found it all very funny and everyone I have spoken to about it is the same. What I should have been doing is answering some more of the messages meant for you but the trouble was the language was so bad. People just Google the name. ‘That’s him, there he is, Ewan Murray!’View image in fullscreen‘Laughter is the best medicine’: Ewen Murray (left) chats to Ewan Murray at Royal Birkdale.Photograph: Gary Calton/The Guardian“Some of your answers are very, very funny. Darren Clarke had tears coming out of his eyes when I showed him a few of them. He used to collapse with laughter. ‘Look what he has written now.’ Something about buggers upstairs not paying you properly, sinking stiff gins and dancing on the table. People started looking forward to the next one. I certainly do.”Just for clarity: “I don’t drink stiff gin any more. And I found dancing on tables was bad for the hamstrings.”Quick GuideIn characterShowWhen the Guardian's Ewan masquerades as Sky's Ewen"Ewan - do you like everyone in your @SkySportsGolf team? Does that impact your ability to be a good broadcaster?"Ryder Cup, 2021The buggers upstairs get on my wick sometimes – lack of a pay rise, lack of appropriate air time – but the majority of the riff raff are fine. I am, however, a GREAT broadcaster because of ME. Yours in golf."Contrary to your comments - I think you will find that Dubai have now moved weekends to Saturday/Sunday from previously Friday/Saturday as mentioned. Good move too I think."Jan 2022Gary, if I want to know the days of the week, I’ll consult a calendar. Not a backseat driver on Twitter. If you want lifestyle chatter, take out a Hello subscription. Yours in golf"Are you not commentating at the Phoenix Open this week? Missing your lovely Scottish voice."Feb 2023Alas, Syl … I’m at the bottom of a Tanqueray 10 bottle in deepest Sussex. Pringle sweater on, Dire Straits playing. Lamb madras demolished. Take it up with The Buggers Upstairs … Yours in golf"The lads need to sort out the delay that’s going on between the broadcast and the commentary. Rich Beem] asking a ball to stop when it’s already gone into the water."Players Championship, 2023When you have a problem with your ears, do you phone your podiatrist? Production types – common lackeys – are nothing to do with me. Take it up with them. Yours in golf"Matthew Jordan's home town is West Kirby not Liverpool ....for the avoidance of doubt the city of Liverpool is some 11 miles away from Hoylake on the other side of the River Mersey!"The Open, 2023Tell you what, George: why don't you pitch up at my booth with a map of Liverpool in your hand? You'll discover I can ram it into a place that doesn't have a postcode. Yours in golf"Why oh why were we subjected to 4 hours of Faldo droning on? Presumably yourself and Coltart were face down in the members bar?!"The Masters, 2024What goes on tour, stays on tour, my friend. I can however safely assure you that a gentleman's measure at Augusta would knock out a horse"Good to hear you on commentary, hopefully we will see @ShaneLowryGolf in green tonight."The Masters, 2026Niall, you are a fine man. Perhaps 24 hours early but I was atop the piano in Surrey Tavern at 1am, belting out "When Irish eyes are smiling."  Enjoy the finaleWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.There have been high-profile victims. Mick Fitzgerald, the famed jockey, praisedmytelevision commentary on a recent major. Rory McIlroy sought me out mid-round at the 2018 Open having been so tickled that a multiple world champion in another sport (who shall remain nameless) asserted, “you’re not Ewen Murray” when we first met.Other moments have flirted with danger. One punter threatened to seek me out in a public house close to Hoylake after some Ewan/Ewen antics during the Open of 2023. “He was going to findme,”Ewen says. “If people don’t find it funny, if people take offence to that, I think they have a major problem. It’s actually quite lucky to have this because so many people are involved; the players, the fans, the press, the TV. Because it is funny.“If I say something wrong on air, I know what is coming to you. You get the brunt of it but you also get the joy of answering them. ‘Do you know how many Opens I have played in? I have played with Arnold Palmer, you know.’” He is spurting with laughter once more.View image in fullscreen‘You get the brunt of it but you also get the joy of answering them,’ says the Sky Sports Golf commentator Ewen Murray.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianThis frivolity is a mere footnote on Ewen’s rich career. He combines commentary skill with an unrivalled, intense knowledge of golf and its courses. Now 71, he is still going strong in the booth and intends to do so for some time.Ewen’s time in broadcasting began almost by accident in 1990, after an executive at Emirates airlines called a professional’s shop in Sussex looking to offer Brian Barnes the gig at the second edition of the Desert Classic. “I said, ‘I’ll do it,’” Ewen says. “That was the start, a two-minute phone call. They sent me an air ticket and £500. I was lucky in that I had just finished playing so I knew all the players. I knew their strengths, their weaknesses and their characters. I still have the tapes.”He had lost his European Tour card a year earlier. Ewen’s confidence, primarily on the greens, had left him. “Too much negativity,” he says of his mindset. “When I was a kid, it was the other way round. I would dream then about hitting shots and they were all good shots. As I got older, that changed. I could see the end coming; then there was a big problem. What do you do now?”He left home in Edinburgh at 18 for an assistant professional’s job at Walton Heath. “I sat on the bed and thought ‘What the hell have I done?’ I had no car. My wage was £5 a week, my digs was £5 for the week.” Teaching, playing, commentating. A life in golf was colourful enough before online mischief-making. Not that all condemnation is swatted aside.“I ignore it unless I think they might be right,” Ewen says. “Constructive criticism is vital in life. I haven’t had it too bad, though. Nowhere near as bad as you.” Long may it continue.Explore more on these topicsGolfinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France Femmes: Vollering’s late escape for yellow leaves Niewiadoma fuming | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Demi Vollering will take an eight-second lead into the final stage of the Tour de France Femmes after winning the penultimate stage in Nice
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Demi Vollering will take an eight-second lead into the final stage of the Tour de France Femmes after winning the penultimate stage in Nice
Content: Demi Vollering sports the yellow jersey after a blistering attack in the hills near Nice.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemi Vollering sports the yellow jersey after a blistering attack in the hills near Nice.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesTour de France FemmesTour de France Femmes: Vollering’s late escape for yellow leaves Niewiadoma fumingVictory on penultimate stage secures eight-second leadPrevious leader claims she was blocked by rival’s teamJeremy Whittlein NiceSat 8 Aug 2026 13.09 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 16.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDemi Vollering took the overall lead from Kasia Niewiadoma in theTour de France Femmeswith a vicious attack in the hills behind Nice to lead the race by eight seconds from the 2024 winner, with just one stage remaining.“It’s very special to be back in yellow,” Vollering, leader of French team FDJ United-Suez said. “Tomorrow I start in yellow and I will do everything in my power to keep it. So much can happen – it’s still a big fight.”It was Vollering’s fifth stage victory in the Tour Femmes and also her fifth yellow jersey and came after she had regretted failing to mount a meaningful pursuit of Niewiadoma on Friday’s summit finish to Mont Ventoux.Tour de France Femmes 2026: stage eight heads to Nice on penultimate day – liveRead moreVollering took the initiative on the final climb of the Cote de la Ginestière and after a breakneck descent, extended her lead on the long straight road to the finish on the Promenade des Anglais in Nice.But Niewiadoma was critical of the tactics of Vollering’s team. “I was annoyed at the beginning of the climb because Gery, on purpose, just blocked me to the barriers where I had to stop pedalling,” she said of Célia Gery, Vollering’s teammate.“They should compete fair play and not look to block me on the barriers because it is so childish. I lost all the respect for them for that.” Vollering responded by saying she had not seen the incident, which was studied at length by race commissaires after the stage. “I didn’t see anything, I just saw what was in front of me,” she said. “It happened behind me. I don’t have eyes in the back of my head. Celia probably didn’t see Kasia and I’m sure she didn’t do it on purpose. I’m sure Kasia knows deep in her heart that those kinds of things just happen sometimes in racing.
