It’s the shit part of racing.”While the critical attacks came in the suburbs of Nice, the stage was animated by a two-rider breakaway, featuring Breton rider Maëva Squiban and Loes Adegeest, of the Netherlands.The duo might have hoped to remain clear to the finish, but Squiban, winner of two stages in last year’s race, crashed on a left-hand bend on the descent of the Côte de Colomars and howling in pain, was swallowed up the peloton.That left her former companion riding alone at the front of the Tour, but her escape ended nine kilometres from the finish as Vollering’s team attacked the bends leading to the Cote de la Ginestière.It was there that Vollering attacked, and while Niewiadoma stuck to the task, she lost ground in the final cruel metres of the short steep climb.View image in fullscreenKasia Niewiadoma (second left) relinquished the yellow jersey in Nice.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesNow only eight seconds separate the pair. Every second will count in Sunday’s final stage of the Tour, based around Nice, which takes in four climbs of the Col d’Eze, overlooking the corniche roads of Villefranche-sur-Mer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe rivalry between Vollering and Niewiadoma goes back to the 2024 Tour, when the Dutch rider lost to the Pole by just four seconds, the narrowest margin of defeat in the history of any Tour de France, after an epic duel to Alpe d’Huez.Meanwhile, French favourite Pauline Ferrand-Prévot’s title defence came to a predictable end. From her listless performance in the stage four time trial, to her major losses of time on Mont Brouilly and Mont Ventoux, her performance has been a stark contrast to that of a year ago.The Olympic gold medallist’s exit from the race was sudden and dramatic. Her bike was prepared and readied outside the Visma Lease-a-bike team bus at the start of stage eight in Sisteron, when she was reported by French TV crews to have told team staff “I can’t do it, I can’t do it.”An announcement confirming her withdrawal was made on social media afterwards stating that Ferrand-Prevot “was not feeling well this morning” and adding “in consultation with medical staff, it has been decided that she will not start”.Ferrand-Prévot’s vulnerability was evident as early as stage three, something her trainer, Rutger Tijssen, acknowledged.“When she couldn’t hold on in the fifth stage, the signals were clearer,” he said. “We knew then that it wasn’t realistic to talk about winning the Tour.”Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League managers have never been less English, title-winning or secure in their jobs | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Huge turnover between seasons means 11 clubs start the 2026-27 campaign led by people with under a year in their dugout
Author: Andrew Beasley
Headline: Huge turnover between seasons means 11 clubs start the 2026-27 campaign led by people with under a year in their dugout
Content: (From left) Frank Lampard, Michael Carrick and Gary O'Neil are the only three English managers currently in charge of Premier League sides.Composite: Getty Images, ReutersView image in fullscreen(From left) Frank Lampard, Michael Carrick and Gary O'Neil are the only three English managers currently in charge of Premier League sides.Composite: Getty Images, ReutersPremier LeaguePremier League managers have never been less English, title-winning or secure in their jobsHuge turnover between seasons means 11 clubs start 2026-27 led by people with under a year in their dugoutAndrew BeasleySat 8 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNine of the 20Premier Leagueclubs will begin the 2026-27 season with a different man in the dugout than the one who ended the last campaign. Opta recently revealed that the only other seasons which started with so many men making their managerial debut for top flight clubs were 1888-89 and 1946-47; the inaugural season of league football and the first following the second world war. Neither occurred under normal circumstances yet the level of turnover this summer does not feel unusual. Job security has never meant less in the Premier League.Adding in the recently appointed pair of Roberto De Zerbi and Michael Carrick – confirmed in March and May respectively – means this season will start with 11 teams led by coaches with less than a year in their hotseat. The median tenure of Premier League managers at the start of each season has never been so low.Chart showing median time in charge for Premier League managers at the start of each seasonThe most recent similar season was 2016-17. Heading into that campaign, 10 clubs had managers with under one year in the role. But with respect to the current Premier League crop, the relatively new head coaches that summer included Antonio Conte, Pep Guardiola, Jürgen Klopp and José Mourinho. All had either already won the Premier League or would go on to do so.With Arsène Wenger still at Arsenal, four of those consideredthe five big beasts of Premier League managementwere competing, with the other (Alex Ferguson) having retired three years earlier. By contrast, Mikel Arteta is the only man who has won the English league who will be starting 2026-27 with the chance to do so again. There was also only one such manager two years ago, albeit it was Guardiola with his bulging trophy cabinet.As Arteta has a single championship win, this season begins with the fewest English league titles on the division’s collective CV in the Premier League era. The previous lowest at the beginning of a campaign was three in 1995-96 (thanks to Ferguson having two and Howard Wilkinson one) and 2019-20 (Guardiola two, Manuel Pellegrini one).This is a natural byproduct of managers being younger and less experienced. The median age of Premier League managers is 46.9 years old. It was the same heading into 2024-25 but was last younger 20 years ago. The drop in age has not led to further opportunities for Englishmen.Chart showing breakdown of Premier League managers by geographical region across seasonsEddie Howe’s departure from Newcastle means there will be three English managers when 2026-27 gets under way. The total was the same at the start of the last two campaigns, though interestingly it will be a different trio this year (Carrick, Frank Lampard and Gary O’Neil) than 12 months ago (Howe, Scott Parker and Graham Potter). The standing of the six clubs led by these men is worth considering. Two of the current coaches are at teams that have just been promoted, while two from last season’s group were with sides that went on to be relegated. Opportunities with even relatively secure Premier League clubs are now rare for English managers, never mind at those with realistic title ambitions.The top end of the division is likely to have a Spanish feel. TheBasque region of Gipuzkoais providing more head coaches to England’s top division than England, with Arsenal, Aston Villa, Chelsea and Liverpool led by men from that relatively small area of Spain. It’s plausible none of them will win the league given the presence of Manchester City (who themselves are under new management after a decade of Guardiola) but Arteta, Xabi Alonso and Andoni Iraola are in charge of three of the leading four clubs in the title betting market, with Unai Emery’s Villa seventh.Managers from overseas lessening opportunities for English coaches in the Premier League is simply following the trend on the pitch. Just 8.6% of available minutes went to players from outside Britain or Ireland in 1992-93 yet a new high of 69.6% was reached last season. It is a truly global competition at every level, including ownership and sporting directors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChart showing percentage of Premier League involvement by players and managers not from UK or Ireland by seasonThe influence of the latter on recruitment decisions has blurred the line between being a head coach and a manager. Liam Rosenior said he was “extremely humbled and honoured to be appointed head coach of Chelsea Football Club” when he was appointed by the Blues in January. “It fills me with immense pride to become manager of this great club,” was Xabi Alonso’s line when he secured essentially the same gig less than six months later. Based on the announcements clubs made to herald news of their appointments, the Premier League currently employs 14 head coaches and six managers.Regardless of what the sign says on Alonso’s office door, he should reflect upon his new club giving him a four-year contract when they haven’t kept a manager for as long as two years since Conte left in 2018, or three years since Mourinho’s first spell in charge over a decade earlier.Rosenior learned this the hard way. He signed a six-and-a-half year deal yet Chelsea previously employed both Rafael Benítez and Guus Hiddink on interim bases for longer than the young Englishman lasted at the club. Head coach or manager, call it what you will. The profession has never offered shorter-term employment, or felt less English, in the Premier League.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mason Mount injury overshadows Manchester United’s draw with PSG | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Manchester United managed a creditable 1-1 draw with Paris Saint-Germain but the result was overshadowed by a foot injury for Mason Mount
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Manchester United managed a creditable 1-1 draw with Paris Saint-Germain but the result was overshadowed by a foot injury for Mason Mount
Content: Bryan Mbeumo scored Manchester United’s equaliser in a 1-1 friendly draw with Paris Saint-Germain.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBryan Mbeumo scored Manchester United’s equaliser in a 1-1 friendly draw with Paris Saint-Germain.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesManchester UnitedMason Mount injury overshadows Manchester United’s draw with PSGBryan Mbeumo scores United’s goal in 1-1 drawMount taken off with foot injury in GothenburgAFPSat 8 Aug 2026 15.10 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 16.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United managed a creditable 1-1 draw with the European champions, Paris Saint-Germain, in a Gothenburg friendly on Saturday but the result was overshadowed by an injury to Mason Mount.The England midfielder, whojoined United from Chelsea in 2023, has been hampered by injury problems since arriving at Old Trafford and he lasted fewer than 20 minutes after starting against PSG.Premier League managers have never been less English, title-winning or secure in their jobsRead moreMount, 27, appeared to suffer a foot injury in Sweden and, after discussions with coaches on the touchline, left the field to be replaced by Tyler Fletcher. Mount has been restricted to 54 league appearances – many of them as a substitute – during his first three seasons with United.His side were 1-0 down to PSG at the time of his injury, having gone behind in the second minute through an Ibrahim Mbaye goal even though the French giants were missing many of their star players.But Bryan Mbeumo equalised in the 32nd minute when Amad Diallo played him in after winning the ball back.There were more injury concerns for United early in the second half when their 40-year-old goalkeeper Tom Heaton suffered a right hamstring problem while rushing out to make a clearance.Mbeumo might have doubled his tally but for the fine form of PSG’s Matvey Safonov but the goalkeeper left the pitch to jeers after escaping punishment for clattering into Joshua Zirkzee way outside his area – an incident that may well have led to him being punished in a competitive match.There were late chances for Fletcher, Shea Lacey and the captain, Bruno Fernandes, who linked up well withnew arrival Youri Tielemansin an encouraging sign for the United manager, Michael Carrick.View image in fullscreenMason Mount (back right) started the friendly in Gothenburg but had to be removed with an apparent injury.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty Images“I enjoyed it,” Carrick told MUTV, United’s in-house television station. “Good challenge. Slightly different with the way they play. We should’ve scored more goals.“It’s good for the boys sometimes to have to problem-solve and find their own way and I thought we did that. That prepares them for the season as well. In that respect there were a lot of things that maybe people don’t always see that we were quite happy with. There were some good signs there.”United have two more friendly fixtures, against bitter rivals Leeds in Dublin on Wednesday and AC Milan in Wroclaw three days later, before launching their Premier League campaign away to newly promoted Hull on 22 August.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: West Ham sink Pompey in Carabao Cup as Sullivan ignores advice to stay away | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: West Ham began the season with a 3-1 win over Portsmouth in the Carabao Cup as their former co-chair David Sullivan watched from the stand
Author: John Brewin
Headline: West Ham began the season with a 3-1 win over Portsmouth in the Carabao Cup as their former co-chair David Sullivan watched from the stand
Content: Taty Castellanos heads home West Ham’s third goal early in the second half.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAView image in fullscreenTaty Castellanos heads home West Ham’s third goal early in the second half.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PACarabao CupWest Ham sink Pompey in Carabao Cup as Sullivan ignores advice to stay awayJohn Brewinat the London StadiumSat 8 Aug 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 16.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn an unseasonable black bomber jacket, with heavy duty company beside him, David Sullivan took his seat. Against the advice of the stadium’s operators, unbowed by serious allegations placed against his name and the weight of public opinion, West Ham’s major shareholder, the former co-chair, sat with arms crossed, always conspicuous by his presence.By beating Portsmouth in relative comfort, West Ham, the club where Sullivan’s name is no longer above the door, had secured a hearteningCarabao Cuppassage to the second round. There, they will be reunited with their former Premier League peers. The serious Championship business begins next Sunday at Burnley. Whether Sullivan travels north for that remains to be seen. It cannot be ruled out.Carabao Cup: Preston prevail in Goodison home game, Millwall keeper saves four penaltiesRead more“Neither me nor the players,” said Nuno Espírito Santo when asked about the effect of the uninvited guest’s presence. “We’ll focus on the pitch. The noise that comes from outside cannot distract at all; we’re going to find a lot of noise. We focus on the game, they do their job, they did it well.”Before kick-off, the London Stadium big screen showed a “countdown to walkout”, referring to the players’ arrival rather than to fans deserting the scene in protest. This being West Ham in 2026, any confusion would be understandable. Taking previous mutinies into account, and despite a summer of intrigue and anger, there were surprisingly few audible or visible signs of insurrection as season 2026-27 began, and an extended 90 minutes was played out.Even with Sullivan’s arrival expected, the gate to the directors’ car park did not stage a welcoming committee, the lanes around the London Stadium quiet. Protests there have been a regular sight, targeting Sullivan and his departed associate Karren Brady.Even once Sullivan’s presence was confirmed there was nothing resembling the barracking of last season. Instead, the loudest boos of the first half came at a hydration break at its midway point, with an odd choice of 90s rave musical accompaniment. The legacy of a North American World Cup continues to darken.View image in fullscreenDavid Sullivan takes his seat at the London Stadium just after kick-off.Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty ImagesPerhaps still-searing temperatures and a dose of early optimism had doused the fires raging when theHammers’ drop was confirmed in May. Time-served Irons know plenty about relegation; their club has dropped down each decade since the 1970s; West Ham heritage indeed.The kick-off chorus of I’m Forever Blowing Bubbles drowned out the Pompey Chimes ringing out from 9,000 away fans. As is usual at the London Stadium, the visiting contingent decried their surroundings and the Faustian pact struck for West Ham’s tenancy.Football has rarely been in focus during West Ham’s summer of tumult, boardroom battles after Sullivan’s defenestration. So what of football? Carabao Cup Saturday served as a decent dry run for their attempt at a promotion campaign. The new West Ham closely resembled the former West Ham, though shorn of the £151m worth of player sales that took inMateus Fernandes, Crysencio Summerville and Freddie Potts. Joël Veltman, the sole summer signing so far, came on with three minutes left.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBoardroom struggle deepens gloom as West Ham prepare for life on the outsideRead moreIn midfield, Edson Álvarez, who spent last season on loan to Fenerbahce, lined up alongside Lewis Orford, a 20-year-old it is hoped can follow the path of Frank Lampard, Michael Carrick and Mark Noble, the latter a mentor, into becoming a first-team regular. His was a successful introduction into the first team.“The energy of the young players is really really important for us,” said Nuno. “It’s up to us to develop the young academy players. That’s the vision for the future.”The torpor of a first 30 minutes of little footballing consequence was broken by aPortsmouthgoal, scored by Adrian Segecic, via a deflection off Maximilian Kilman, an expensive purchase far too regularly on the crime scene.It took 10 minutes for West Ham to awaken before Mohamadou Kanté’s pirouetting feint laid up Taty Castellanos to equalise. Mere moments later, Jarrod Bowen, the club captainstaying on to lead his club back up, a rare adult in the room last season, lashed in their second. “Jarrod shows us every day his commitment,” said Nuno.The goals evidenced a quality that ought to guide the club back to the Premier League with some comfort, though nothing should be taken for granted. “If you give them a slight opening they’re going to take it,” said the Portsmouth manager, John Mousinho.Sullivan kept any celebrations to himself and returned for a second half that began with Castellanos nodding in Bowen’s cross. An afternoon that might have descended into a familiar seething pit of rage and resentment now offered grounds for optimism. Though just beyond the hour, a chorus of “Stand up if you hate the board”.If Sullivan is no longer a board member he was its undoubted target. He has turned many a deaf ear down the years and continues to do so.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupWest Ham UnitedPortsmouthmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Versatile Bruno Guimarães gives Mikel Arteta options to shuffle midfield pack  | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: While able to play deeper, the onus will also be on Arsenal’s £75m signing to provide creativity in an attack that has struggled to break down the low block
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: While able to play deeper, the onus will also be on Arsenal’s £75m signing to provide creativity in an attack that has struggled to break down the low block
Content: While emotional over his Newcastle departure, Bruno Guimarães knew that at 28, the chance to join Arsenal might never come again.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWhile emotional over his Newcastle departure, Bruno Guimarães knew that at 28, the chance to join Arsenal might never come again.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesArsenalAnalysisVersatile Bruno Guimarães gives Mikel Arteta options to shuffle midfield packEd AaronsWhile able to play deeper, the onus will also be on Arsenal’s £75m signing to provide creativity in an attack that has struggled to break down the low blockData shows deal could be another set-piece masterstrokeSat 8 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTShareIf there was one of his many assets Newcastle supporters grew to love above all about Bruno Guimarães then it was best summed up by the man himself after being unveiled asArsenal’s new £75m signing. “That’s a tough one,” said the Brazil midfielder when asked what fans in north London can expect from him. “I would say I can pass the ball, run a lot and play like a warrior. I’ll never give up.”After more than four years on Tyneside and having seen Alexander Isak, Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali precede Eddie Howe’s departure, Guimarães – who was devastated after missing a penalty for theSeleçãoin their defeat against Norway in the last 16 of the World Cup – was determined to seize his opportunity.Data shows Bruno Guimarães deal could be another Arsenal set-piece masterstrokeRead moreWhile his emotional statement released by Newcastle as his move toArsenalwas confirmed on Saturday said they “did everything they could to keep me”, at the age of 28 he clearly felt it may never come again.Andrea Berta’s pursuit of Vinícius Júnior came up short this week after the Brazil forward signed an improved six-year deal with Real Madrid. But at least Arsenal’s sporting director was finally able to bring in a player who was first courted by the club in the early days of Mikel Arteta’s reign, and who will add to the outstanding crop of central midfielders at his disposal.Edu Gaspar, Berta’s predecessor, is understood to have first enquired about Guimarães when he was still at Athletico Paranaense in Brazil before he joined Lyon in the January 2020 transfer window – a few weeks after Arteta’s arrival at the Emirates.They were also interested when Newcastle won the race to sign him in January 2022 for €40m, which came back to haunt Arsenal when he scored in a 2-0 win that went a long way to them missing out on Champions League qualification that season.That first of nine appearances is the only time he scored against Arsenal, but Guimarães always impressed in a variety of roles whenever he came up against them, including in the Carabao Cup semi-final Newcastle won 4-0 on aggregate in 2025. He has covered more distance, won more duels and committed more fouls against Arsenal than any other side since making his Premier League debut.It was no surprise that Declan Rice – the only player in the division to have covered more distance than Guimarães in that period and who enjoyed their fair share of battles – was one of the first to welcome him to Arsenal with a message that said “come here and please no more fights, now we’re friends”.It is hard to argue with Guimarães that Arsenal have “one of the best midfields” in Europe because last season proved it. Yet having gone all the way to the Champions League final before spending the summer with England, after suffering with neural pain in his hamstring and lower back since December, Rice must be treated with the utmost care in the coming months. Guimarães can provide cover for him in a box-to-box role and gives Arteta options to rotate his other midfielders more frequently.View image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães will provide box-to-box cover for Declan Rice, rather than engage him in midfield combat.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesHe did not seem to trust Christian Nørgaard, who has joined Everton, to deputise for Martín Zubimendi in the Premier League last year, and that led to the Spain midfielder running out of steam in the spring.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt was telling that the teenager Myles Lewis-Skelly started in his preferred position at the base of midfield during the title run-in, and against Paris Saint-Germain in Budapest for the Champions League final, having begun the campaign as a left-back. Guimarães showed at Newcastle he is capable of playing in a deeper role as well and Arteta must decide how to balance his plethora of options in a crucial part of the pitch.While he could not match Mikel Merino’s goalscoring exploits for Spain,Martin Ødegaard showed signs that he is back to his best during the World Cup after another disappointing season for Arsenal that was again interrupted by injury.Having missed out on Morgan Rogers, the onus will be on the Norway captain, Guimarães and last summer’s big signing, Eberechi Eze, to provide some creativity to an attack that struggled to break down the low block at times last season.Arsenal are still in the market for a defender to cover the absence of William Saliba for an extended period, while they would like to bring in another forward to add to the signing of Christos Tzolis. Atlético Madrid’s Julián Alvarez or Bradley Barcola of Paris Saint-Germain would fit the bill, although it remains to be seen if they will bring in a marquee player without offloading Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus – who has interest from Napoli. Even if they do depart, the presence of another familiar face in the Brazil centre-back Gabriel should also help Guimarães settle into his new home.“Big Gabi was very excited,” he told Arsenal’s website. “Every time he sent me the message: ‘We’ll wait for you, when will you come?’ I’m so excited to join them, not only the Brazilians, we have an amazing squad here. I’m so excited to meet the other players, to start training. I just want to give my best.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Carabao Cup: Millwall keeper saves four penalties, Preston prevail in Goodison home game | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Millwall’s manager, Alex Neil, said Lukas Jensen deserved his moment of glory after the fit-again goalkeeper saved all four QPR penalties to take Millwall through to the second round of the Carabao Cup
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Millwall’s manager, Alex Neil, said Lukas Jensen deserved his moment of glory after the fit-again goalkeeper saved all four QPR penalties to take Millwall through to the second round of the Carabao Cup
Content: Lukas Jensen of Millwall is mobbed by teammates at Loftus Road.Photograph: Andrew Fosker/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLukas Jensen of Millwall is mobbed by teammates at Loftus Road.Photograph: Andrew Fosker/ShutterstockCarabao CupCarabao Cup: Millwall keeper saves four penalties, Preston prevail in Goodison home gameLukas Jensen the shootout hero for Millwall at QPRKyle Walker hits winner in Burnley shootout victoryPA MediaSat 8 Aug 2026 14.37 EDTFirst published on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlex Neil felt Lukas Jensen deserved his moment of glory after the fit-again goalkeeper saved all fourQPRpenalties to takeMillwallthrough to the second round of theCarabao Cup.After a 1-1 draw, with a late Mark Sykes own goal bringing Rangers level after Luke Cundle’s opener,Millwallwon 2-0 in a shootout which included six missed spot-kicks. Jensen, back after a long injury lay-off, kept out penalties from Ilias Chair, Harvey Vale, Koki Saito and Kwame Poku.The Millwall manager said: “To save four penalties is really, really rare. And to put in the context behind that, Lukas has been missing for 15 months – he had a bad injury and then came back and had a setback. I think he would have been dreaming about that moment for 15 months – making four penalty saves and being the reason we’re through to the next round. And I’m absolutely delighted for him because he’s a great professional and a good lad, so fair play to him.”View image in fullscreenLukas Jensen saves from Harvey Vale during Millwall’s shootout victory.Photograph: Andrew Fosker/ShutterstockBurnleyprevailed 4-3 in a shootout to book their place in the second round after the Championship club had been held to a 1-1 draw by League OneNotts Countyat Turf Moor. Veteran defender Kyle Walker held his nerve with the winning kick after Clarets goalkeeper Max Weiss had saved from Emile Acquah and Jacob Bedeau.West Ham sink Pompey in Carabao Cup as Sullivan ignores advice to stay awayRead moreRussell Martin celebrated his first competitive game in charge ofLeicesterwith a 1-0 victory overNorthamptonthanks to Caleb Okoli’s first-half goal. The former Southampton and Rangers manager has been tasked with leading Leicester’s recovery following relegation to League One and overcame a spirited showing from League Two opponents at the King Power Stadium.Andre Brooks scored on his debut asNorwichcruised to a 4-1 victory over visitorsMK Dons. The Canaries made a blistering start at Carrow Road, pouncing on some sloppy defending to grab an early two-goal advantage. Mohamed Touré was put clean through by Kenny McLean after the Dons had made a hash of their first attempt to play out from the back and blasted home with just 40 seconds on the clock.The hosts then made it 2-0 after seven minutes as Touré picked out Anis Ben Slimane who calmly found the corner. Norwich effectively settled the issue on 43 minutes when Brooks’ shot found the net via a deflection off Ben Chrisene, who was credited with the goal. The Dons pulled one back on 56 minutes through Ryan Wintle, but Brooks made it four just before the hour.Tony Mowbray wants to see more cutting edge from hisBlackburnside after his return to the club began with a comeback 2-1 win at League OneBurton. Substitutes Andri Gudjohnsen and Jayden Fevrier netted late goals to secure victory after Zac Scutt’s opener. “We got there in the end.” Mowbray said. “We said at half-time that we should have scored four or five goals. Not could have. Should have.”View image in fullscreenJayden Fevrier celebrates scoring Blackburn’s second at Burton.Photograph: Andrew Kearns/CameraSport/Getty ImagesDelano Burgzorg scored the winning penalty in the shootout after Jusef Erabi equalised in stoppage time for 10-manPrestonto knock outHuddersfield. The game took place at Goodison Park, the former Everton men’s ground, due to Preston’s Deepdale pitch not being ready. Daniel Iversen saved two penalties, after a thrilling end to normal time that ended 1-1 when Erabi cancelled out Radinio Balker’s strike. Preston played 69 minutes without Lewis Gibson who was shown a red card.Sheffield Wednesday’s manager, Henrik Pedersen, praised his team’s performance after they beat Championship sideBolton1-0. Substitute Jamal Lowe scored in the 70th minute. Bolton had Xavier Simons sent off in the 56th minute when he received a red card after clashing with Harry Gray.Pedersen said: “I saw a lot of steps in the right direction for our aggressive pressing, for our quick transition, more players higher up when we won the ball, more forward mindset. We keep on going, and they keep on working as a group. It means everything in this situation where we are.”View image in fullscreenPlayers confront each other before Bolton’s Xavier Simons is shown a red card.Photograph: Lee Parker/CameraSport/Getty ImagesArkell Jude-Boyd scored the decisive spot-kick asShrewsburybeatSalford4-3 on penalties after a 1-1 draw. Both goalkeepers starred in a remarkable shootout in which nine penalties were missed before Jude-Boyd fired into the top corner.An unlucky own goal from Ollie Norburn and a late strike from Robert Bozenik gaveStokea 2-0 win overOldham, whileBirminghambooked their place in round two with a narrow 1-0 win at Championship rivalsSwansea. August Priske’s goal a minute before the break proved decisive at the Swansea.com Stadium, the big Danish striker steering the ball into the far corner after Carlos Vincente had sent a cross back across goal following a long free-kick into the box.Fleetwood’s manager, Matt Lawlor, described the only goal in his side’s victory overChesterfieldas “Ched Evans in a nutshell”. New captain Evans struck 14 minutes in to seal the Cod Army’s place in the second round. Lawlor said: “He was brilliant. He sets standards at 37, while also challenging the young lads. We can use him as a reference point. That’s how you prepare for a game of football, whatever he does, replicate it.”Readingbeat League One new boysBromleyon penalties as they sunk five flawless spot-kicks to go through to the second round after a 1-1 draw. Goalkeeper Joel Pereira proved the match winner, saving Ethon Archer’s spot-kick to claim a 5-4 victory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDerbycrashed out after a 2-1 home defeat by Championship new boysLincoln, who deserved their victory in the sunshine at Pride Park and could have won by a bigger margin. It took the Championship newcomers less than three minutes to go ahead when Ben House steered in a corner via a deflection off Matt Clarke. Lincoln extended their lead when a superb pass from Freddie Draper released Dom Jefferies to fire into the bottom right corner in the 23rd minute. Derby offered little until first-half stoppage time when Sam Szmodics struck from 25 yards.View image in fullscreenLincoln’s Ben House, centre, celebrates scoring their opener against Derby.Photograph: Chris Vaughan/Getty ImagesThe newWatfordhead coach, Alessio Dionisi, admitted he was relieved after his first game in charge needed a dramatic 99th-minute winner to sink League TwoCrawley1-0 at Vicarage Road. Dionisi, the Hornets’ 15th full-time appointment in seven years, watched his side squander a string of chances until Marc Bola’s 25-yard rocket.The Italian said: “In the first half we played good, in the second only so-so. It is true we had a lot of shots and I agree it is better to win 1-0, but after 90 minutes it was 0-0 and to win football matches you have to score.”Cambridge Unitedmounted a speedy comeback to beatBarnet2-1. The visitors went ahead soon after half-time, but the Us hit back through Ben Knight and Isaac Heath to lead only eight minutes later.Leyton Orientstruck late to seal a 2-0 win overOxfordat Brisbane Road, with both goals coming from crosses by Charlie Wellens, the son of manager Richie, who only came on after 84 minutes.AFC Wimbledonscored a late equaliser before beating League TwoNewport County5-4 on penalties.Luca Moore’s late header earnedCrewea 2-1 victory overAccrington. The tie appeared destined to end in spot-kicks, but there was late drama five minutes from the end of normal time when Moore pounced just as John Doolan’s side seemed to be gathering momentum.Doncasteradvanced into the second round with a 5-4 penalty shootout win overStockportafter the game had finished 1-1 over 90 minutes. Rovers’ keeper Tommy Simkin proved the hero, keeping out efforts from Ben Osborn and Eoghan O’Connell.Charltonprogressed with a 3-1 win at League TwoCheltenham. Nathan Jones’ side opened up a three-goal lead before half-time, with Matty Godden, Sonny Carey and Tyreece Campbell on target.Substitutes Cyle Larin and Romeo Akachukwu scored inside the last 18 minutes to giveSouthamptona 2-0 victory atColchester, whileWestBromcoasted into the second round with a 4-1 win overRotherham. The damage was done early on with goals coming from debutant Jimmy Jay-Morgan and Harry Whitwell to make it 2-0 at the break. Albion then doubled their lead in a dominant second half.BarnsleybeatWiganon penalties after the tie had finished 1-1 in normal time. The first 10 spot-kicks were scored before Jon Mellish’s effort was saved by the knee of Rogan Ravenhill and Josh Earl scored to make it 6-5. Jack Moylan scored the winner on hisCardiffdebut as the Championship new boys squeezed into the second round with a 3-2 win over League TwoSwindon. Moylan – who joined Cardiff in midweek from Lincoln – curled in the winner in the 77th minute.View image in fullscreenCardiff’s Jack Moylan celebrates with Joel Colwill after scoring their third against Swindon.Photograph: Gareth Everett/Huw Evans/ShutterstockLeague OneLutoncruised to a comfortable 3-0 victory over League TwoGillingham. Goals from Nahki Wells, Benny Benagr and Gideon Kodua made sure Jack Wilshere’s side impressed at the Priestfield Stadium.Blackpoolsecured progression with a 3-1 victory overGrimsbyat Blundell Park, while League OneBradfordeased their way into the second round with a 2-0 win overRochdale.Harry Leonard ensuredBristol Rovers’ poor run in the Carabao Cup continued, his penalty securingPeterborougha 1-0 win at the Memorial Stadium. Leonard’s first-half spot-kick for the League One side meant Rovers have exited the competition at the first hurdle for seven consecutive seasons.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupMillwallQPRBurnleyNotts CountyLeicester CityNorthamptonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jorge Messi, father and agent of Argentina great, dies aged 68  | Lionel Messi | The Guardian
description: Lionel Messi’s father and agent Jorge has died at the age of 68 at a medical clinic in the ⁠Argentinian city of ⁠Rosario after ​a long illness, the family have announced
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Lionel Messi’s father and agent Jorge has died at the age of 68 at a medical clinic in the ⁠Argentinian city of ⁠Rosario after ​a long illness, the family have announced
Content: Jorge Messi, father and agent of Lionel Messi, holding his son's Golden Ball World Cup trophy in 2022.Photograph: Jean Catuffe/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJorge Messi, father and agent of Lionel Messi, holding his son's Golden Ball World Cup trophy in 2022.Photograph: Jean Catuffe/Getty ImagesLionel MessiJorge Messi, father and agent of Argentina great, dies aged 68Messi family report death at medical clinic in RosarioInter Miami are due to play Monterrey on Saturday nightGuardian sportSat 8 Aug 2026 10.49 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLionel Messi’s father and agent, Jorge, has died aged 68 at a medical clinic in the ⁠Argentinian city of ⁠Rosario after ​a long illness, the family have announced. Jorge Messi spent his final months ⁠alternating between a medical centre in Rosario and his home, accompanied by his wife, Celia, and his ⁠children Rodrigo, Matías and María Sol.Lionel Messi ​spent time with his ‌father after the World ‌Cup before rejoining his club,Inter Miami, for whom he ‌returned to action a week ago. Inter Miami are due to play Monterrey on Saturday at home in the 2026 Leagues Cup, but the MLS club have yet to announce whether he will feature.Newell’s Old Boys announced the death in a social media post that said he had undergone treatment in recent months for an unspecified illness. The post described him as “the pillar and the person who, with vision, rigour and affection, supported the career of the best player of all time, alongside his wife, Celia Cuccittini”. The Argentinian FA also expressed its ⁠condolences in a statement, saying: “From here, we stand in solidarity ​with the entire family ​during this difficult time and send ​the most heartfelt, warm, and affectionate embrace. Strength to you all.”View image in fullscreenLionel Messi poses with his brother Rodrigo, sister María Sol, father Jorge, mother Celia, nephew Tomás and brother Matías in Rosario, Argentina, in 2003.Photograph: El Grafico/Getty ImagesAt the World Cup, Lionel Messi said afterArgentina’s 3-0 victory over Algeria– when he broke down in ​tears while celebrating ​his first goal in the team’s opening match – that he was going through a difficult personal situation. Later, he explained his tears ​were due ‌to “something unrelated to ​football” after ​going through “a few difficult, complicated days”.There was speculation that the player’s emotional reaction toArgentina’s last-16 victory over Egyptwas due in part to his father’s deteriorating condition. A few days later, the family issued a statement regarding Jorge Messi’s “health situation”, informing the public that he was undergoing medical treatment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJorge Messi closely accompanied his son throughout his career, beginning with his early years at Barcelona. He acted as a crucial pillar of support and, for several years, served as his representative. “I always ‌needed my dad’s approval, ever since I was a kid. After every match, I’d ask him ​what he thought of how I played,” said Lionel Messi.Explore more on these topicsLionel MessiInter MiamiArgentinaUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

Content: Ronald Araújo has made more than 200 appearances for Barcelona but was not a regular last season, playing 11 games.Photograph: Ryan Pierse/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRonald Araújo has made more than 200 appearances for Barcelona but was not a regular last season, playing 11 games.Photograph: Ryan Pierse/Getty ImagesLiverpoolLiverpool agree to sign Barcelona’s Ronald Araújo on loan as Jacquet coverAndoni Iraola moves to improve defensive optionsUruguay defender expected to complete his medicalEd AaronsSat 8 Aug 2026 06.44 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiverpool have agreed to sign Ronald Araújo on a season-long loan from Barcelona after Andoni Iraola wasfaced with lack of defensive optionsfor the start of the new season.Concerns over Jérémy Jacquet – the France Under -21 defender who arrived last seasonfor more than £50m– and injuries to Joe Gomez and Giovanni Leoni have left Liverpool short of options at the back after the departure of Ibrahima Konaté on a free transfer to Real Madrid.Araújo, who was part of the Barça side that won La Liga last season, will add much-needed cover in the short-term. title: Why Super Furry Animals joined music’s dash to cross over football’s vinyl frontier | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The sponsorship deal between Cwmbran Celtic and the Welsh indie-rockers is part of a trend to monetise ‘adjacent audiences’ as much as it is a nostalgia trip
Author: Emma John
Headline: The sponsorship deal between Cwmbran Celtic and the Welsh indie-rockers is part of a trend to monetise ‘adjacent audiences’ as much as it is a nostalgia trip
Content: ‘In the last couple of years, the relationship between bands and football teams has turned serious.’Illustration: David Lyttleton/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘In the last couple of years, the relationship between bands and football teams has turned serious.’Illustration: David Lyttleton/The GuardianSoccerWhy Super Furry Animals joined music’s dash to cross over football’s vinyl frontierEmma JohnThe sponsorship deal between Cwmbran Celtic and the Welsh indie-rockers is part of a trend to monetise ‘adjacent audiences’ as much as it is a nostalgia tripSat 8 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 16.53 EDTShareAs someone born on the cusp of the gen X-millennial divide, I am the perfect target for today’s 90s nostalgia. I played my modest, teenage part in the Battle of Britpop (verbal skirmisher, Blur division); I fervently sang – and, God help me, believed – thatThings Can Only Get Better. Super Furry Animals were a band I knew only distantly, via the transgressive thrill ofthat song they had with all the swearing in. And yet the news they’ll be shirt sponsor for a Welsh football club this season has managed to whisk me straight back to a time when things seemed simpler, kinder and more hopeful.Nearly three decades have passed sinceSuper Furry Animalslast had their logo on a football kit. Back in 1999, their frontman Gruff Rhys and bassist Guto Pryce, both Cardiff City fans, persuaded their Bangor-born bandmates to lay down their north Wales allegiances for the duration of the Bluebirds’ Welsh Cup run – which was, incidentally, all they could afford. The cup shirts cost them £2,000 and were, according to Rhys, knock-offs made for ice hockey. This year’s beneficiaries are a more modest outfit: Cwmbran Celtic, just relegated from Wales’s second tier. Cwmbran is the town where the band send their stage props for repair, and given the props in question are giant inflatable bears, you wonder whether they could get one installed in goal.Sing when you’re winning: the 20 greatest songs about football – ranked!Read moreSuper Furry Animals aren’t the only 90s band involved: Scottish post-rockersMogwaihave sponsored the men’s away strip, with 10% of the profits from all shirt sales going to a grassroots music charity.There has traditionally been an element of patronage when famous musicians do football, from Elton John’s time as chair of Watford, to Robbie Williams’s 2024 elevation to Port Vale club president. The pattern is a repeating one: local lads (they’re usually lads) make good, and want to give back to the team they’ve followed since they were little. Wet Wet Wet were the first to go down the shirt-sponsorship route with Clydebank in 1993. The team’s shirts turned out to be a more timeless design than the loud, oversized suits that Marti Pellow’s crew wore the day they unveiled them.Slapping your logo on your home side’s shirt was a charitable endeavour, rather than an investment. Nothing underscored this point better than Fatboy Slim’s relationship with Brighton & Hove Albion. The DJ’s record label first sponsored their shirts in the late 90s, back when the team’s financial straits had left them flirting with extinction, and Tony Bloom’s billions were still waiting to be won. It was particularly appropriate back then that Micky Adams’s men should run out on to the field with their chests declaring them SKINT.View image in fullscreenBobby Zamora in Brighton’s home kit sponsored by Fatboy Slim.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesMusical match-ups have tended, therefore, towards the endearing, not the cool. Jake Bugg sponsored Notts County not to market his own music, but to evangelise the Midlands team on his global tours. And it’s even cuter when bands have sponsored kids’ teams. The late Lemmy of Motörhead was tickled by the thought of a Lincolnshire under-10s team sporting his Snaggletooth skull mascot on their fronts; unfortunately the resultant all-black kit too closely resembled referees’ uniforms and the children were banned from wearing it in league matches. Still, the idea had an enduring appeal: the Prodigy, Biffy Clyro, Sleaford Mods and Franz Ferdinand have all paid for youth kits.In the last couple of years, though, the relationship between bands and football teams has turned serious. The move to monetise the “adjacent audiences” of pop and sporting fandom means shirt sponsorship is no longer a way of artists showing their support, but a marketing and merchandising opportunity in its own right.Spotify’s deal with Barcelona got the ball rolling, with Coldplay, Karol G, Rosalía and Travis Scott each briefly appearing on the shirtfront, and limited-edition replicas costing more than £340 a pop. The footie-kit-as-streetwear trend means bands aren’t “sponsors” any more, they’re “collaborators”. Hence Manchester United’s pre-match shirts don’t bear the name of the Stone Roses, just their album artwork. And while that may have baffled a few younger fans – the club’s website ran a post explaining who the Madchester group were for the gen Z-ers – it still reflects a genuine connection. Ian Brown is a lifelong Red, and the team has walked out to This Is the One since Gary Neville first requested it two decades ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenColdplay show off their Barcelona shirts.Photograph: Fc Barcelona Handout/EPAWhereas a year ago, if you’d been asked at a pub quiz what Paris Saint-Germain had in common with a K-pop band, or what Pink Floyd had to do with a Serie A team, you’d have been within your rights to say “nothing”. The answer, now, is clothing ranges – PSG teamed up with the girl group Blackpink to optimise fan engagement in Asia, while Inter marked the 50th anniversary of the album release of Wish You Were Here.All this can be confusing for the simple-minded sports lover like me. What is a culture-forward lifestyle capsule, anyway? It sounds like something Musk and Bezos want to blast to Mars in. Creating a sporting look now involves an advanced understanding of fashion arithmetic: at last year’s Euros it was Admiral x Spice Girls, now it’s the Rolling Stones x England Cricket x Castore. These are powerful equations, as when a 2025 Bohemian FC x Fontaines DC shirt (raised tothe power of Greta Thunbergwhen she wore it on her flotilla to Gaza) = £££££ for charity. Maybe Ed Sheeran’s Mathematics tour top for Ipswich was an omen. Or perhaps this is a fad, and the music industry will soon move on to something new. GQ, which has declared “blokecore” over, says we’ll be wearing classic rugby tops by autumn/winter. Sounds delightfully 90s to me.Explore more on these topicsFootballMogwaiSuper Furry AnimalscommentShareReuse this content

Author: Jonathan Howcroft
Headline: Minute by minute: The Wallabies began a new era under coach Les Kiss with a Test win against old boss Eddie Jones’ side
Content: 12h ago09.50 EDTMatch reportAngus FontaineThere was good, bad and plenty of ugly but the Les Kiss era is off to a winning start. Despite searing heat and a brave home side, the Wallabies shrugged off an early red card and a litany of reckless errors to welcome their new coach to international rugby with a brave but dramatic victory over Japan in Osaka.New coach Kiss off to a winning start as Wallabies rumble past bold JapanRead moreShare

title: New coach Kiss off to a winning start as Wallabies rumble past bold Japan | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: The Wallabies shrugged off an early red card and a litany of reckless errors to welcome their new coach Les Kiss to international rugby with a 35-32 victory over Japan in Osaka
Author: Angus Fontaine
Headline: The Wallabies shrugged off an early red card and a litany of reckless errors to welcome their new coach Les Kiss to international rugby with a 35-32 victory over Japan in Osaka
Content: Harry Potter surges forward to score Australia's first try against Japan.Photograph: Paul Miller/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHarry Potter surges forward to score Australia's first try against Japan.Photograph: Paul Miller/Getty ImagesRugby unionNew coach Kiss off to a winning start as Wallabies rumble past bold JapanJapan 32-35 AustraliaWallabies withstand early red card and heatAngus FontaineSat 8 Aug 2026 09.42 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 22.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was good, bad and plenty of ugly but the Les Kiss era is off to a winning start. Despite searing heat and a brave home side, the Wallabies shrugged off an early red card and a litany of reckless errors to welcome their new coach to international rugby with a brave and dramatic victory over Japan in Osaka.Against an unpredictable Brave Blossoms side coached by the former Wallabies mentor Eddie Jones, the former rugby league player, who iscoaching Australia’s union sidedespite never having played the game, escaped the ambush Jones laid for him and comes home with a heartening triumph.Japan 32-35 Australia: rugby union international – as it happenedRead moreBut it was not easy. Japan’s frantic play had Australia under siege early, with rapid breakdown work and precision passes feeding their express pace on the edges. With Naoto Saito’s clever kicks keeping Australia pinned in their half, the heatwave hit the visitors allowing Ryunosuke Ito to zip behind the lines and score.The Wallabies hit back quickly, Hunter Paisami bursting through out wide to scatter the defence and allow Harry Potter to slice through and equalise. But with just 35% possession, Australia were on the back foot for most of the first quarter, clumsy errors and disjointed link play kiboshing each attacking raid.Kiss had reshuffled Joe Schmidt’s pack, making nine changes to the side thatbeatItaly 57-10 last month. The initial disconnection soon settled and despite Japan’s dominance, Australia took the lead in the 27th minute as a lineout sparked a lovely looping charge that climaxed with Tom Wright crossing in the corner.Miles Amatosero had won a first Test start, but the big lock’s impetuosity cost his side a third try as a reckless high shot within sight of the try line earned him a yellow card. Japan successfully salted the wound, barrelling downfield through Shuhei Takeuchi and sending Faulua Makisi under the posts.It left the Test locked at 14-all at half-time and when Amatosero’s yellow card was upgraded to a red, leaving Australia a man short for 20 minutes, the advantage tipped to the home side.View image in fullscreenLes Kiss oversaw a victory in his first game as Australia coach.Photograph: Philip Fong/AFP/Getty ImagesAustralia had allowed nine line breaks in the half and their three-Test playmaker, Declan Meredith, was struggling, spraying his kicks and passes.Jones had tuned his tactics to the heat Osaka had endured all week, aiming to exhaust and frustrate Australia, but Kiss had a counter plan. Knowing the Wallabies had led all three Tests in 2026 at half-time yet converted only one into victory, he had created his own Bomb Squad of finishers to arrest the second-half struggles.One of those bombers, the prop Angus Bell, got Australia rolling in the second half, splitting Japan up the middle. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii bent the line further, deftly flick-passing to Max Jorgensen on the fly. He popped a pass over the top to Ryan Lonergan then looped back to crash over as Australia snatched back the lead.That ascendancy lasted a minute as Japan’s speedboats outflanked the slow-moving tankers in gold, Kazuma Ueda waltzing into space and bolting away. But Australia did not sulk. Bell won a turnover, Meredith drilled a kick and Fraser McReight iced the pick-and-drive with a low punch run over the line.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs Lonergan’s fourth conversion extended the Wallabies’ lead to nine, Kiss went for broke, sending out Taniela Tupou and Jeremy Williams to muscle his men home. Japan refused to yield, emptying their own bench. Australia’s discipline again cost them dearly as Japan calmly cut the margin to three with two penalty goals.Springboks and All Blacks flex financial muscles with ‘Greatest Rivalry’ tourRead moreHarryWilson had two chances for penalties of his own, but instead the captain backed his scrum from close range. The gamble backfired when Meredith tapped and ran without consent, giving the ball back when his side were close to scoring again. Australia made it worse by fumbling more kicks and throwing needless wild passes.The Wallabies had been averaging 38 points a Test in 2026, the most since 1985. But only one of those had ended in victory asIreland ran them down in SydneyandFrance ran them ragged in Brisbane. Now Japan, the world No 10, were looming larger than theGreat Waveoff Kanagawa.Australia shrugged off their woes by grinding grimly and slowly. Jorgensen made some slicing runs and Charlie Cale, off the bench for his first Test since 2024, lifted the tempo further. Finally, the Wallabies staggered into the red zone for Tupou to rumbleover.Although Japan scored a late try, Australia had done enough to win. They now come home to Kiss’s home state of Queensland for a rematch in Townsville. The mercury is not likely to drop there, but when you are a Wallabies coach with a home World Cup looming, the heat will always be on.Explore more on these topicsRugby unionAustralia rugby union teamJapan rugby union teamAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bruno Guimarães completes £75m Arsenal move: ‘I needed a new challenge’ | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Bruno Guimarães has said he ‘needed a new challenge in my life’ after joining Arsenal from Newcastle for £75m and has targeted winning trophies with the champions
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Bruno Guimarães has said he ‘needed a new challenge in my life’ after joining Arsenal from Newcastle for £75m and has targeted winning trophies with the champions
Content: Bruno Guimarães said he wanted to join Arsenal after his first meeting with Mikel Arerta.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães said he wanted to join Arsenal after his first meeting with Mikel Arerta.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesArsenalBruno Guimarães completes £75m Arsenal move: ‘I needed a new challenge’Four-year deal signed after Newcastle’s reluctant sale‘I want to win trophies and I’m in the right place to do it’Ed AaronsSat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBruno Guimarães says he “needed a new challenge in my life” after joining Arsenal from Newcastle for £75m and has targeted winning trophies. Guimarães is understood to have signed a four-year contract that contains a further one-year optionafter Newcastle reluctantly agreed to sell their captain.The 28-year-old, who captained Newcastle to their first trophy since 1955 when theywon the Carabao Cup last year, had made it clear that he wanted to join the Premier League champions after meeting the club’s new manager, Matthias Jaissle, this week.Why the data shows Guimarães deal could be another Arsenal set-piece masterstrokeRead moreArsenal have previously shown an interest in signing Guimarães on two occasions – in 2020 when he was playing for Athletico Paranaense in Brazil and then 18 months later when he was at Lyon and went on to move to the north-east. But the Brazil midfielder said he wanted to joinArsenalafter his first meeting with Mikel Arerta and the sporting director, Andrea Berta.“I was excited. I just felt inside of me that I need a new challenge in my life and to be an Arsenal player is going to be an exciting challenge in my life,” he told Arsenal’s website. “After playing two World Cups, I’m at the point of my life, I need a challenge like this. I want to win trophies, I want to make history and I think I’m in the right place to do it.“I’m so excited to start. We have tough games to play this season, so the squad is going to be very, very important and I’m hopeful we can achieve our dreams.”The arrival of Guimarães significantly boosts the midfield options available to Arteta, who now has a formidable squad that contains Declan Rice, Martin Ødegaard, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Myles Lewis-Skelly.“We are further strengthening the heart of our team,” said Berta. “As we have all seen, Bruno can play as a defensive midfielder and as a box-to-box player. He combines quality with quantity and has provided goals and assists for his team every year. Bruno will allow Mikel to further develop our playing style and will also increase our internal competitiveness, which is essential for maintaining the standards required when we are aiming to win major trophies.”Guimarães revealed he has already received a message from Rice welcoming him to Arsenal that said “come here and please no more fights, now we’re friends”. “I was happy he messaged me, but the midfield we have here, is one of the best in Europe,” said Guimarães. “Everyone is an amazing player. I’m so excited to start chatting and play, and know the players very, very well,”View image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães said leaving Tyneside was ‘one of the toughest decisions of my life’.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesGuimarães also released a statement to Newcastle. He said: “I fell in love with this place. I really mean that. From my first day, the supporters, my teammates, Eddie [Howe] and the staff, and everyone connected with the club made me and my family feel at home.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“This is one of the toughest decisions of my life. When I arrived, the club was in a challenging position and I am incredibly proud of what we achieved together. I thank PIF, our chair, Yasir Al-Rumayyan, and Jamie Reuben for everything they have done for me and for this football club. I also want to say thank you to David [Hopkinson, the Newcastle CEO] and Ross [Wilson, Newcastle’s sporting director] for the huge respect to me throughout this process. They did everything they could to keep me at Newcastle, and I am very grateful for our time together.”On Friday, Wilson said they had no option but to allow Guimarães to leave. “What we had to weigh up was, very respectfully from Bruno with his behaviour towards us, very emotionally as well, he effectively told us he wanted to leave,” he said.“That doesn’t mean he can go, but it certainly plays a part in what our thinking is when we hit a certain range of number. There’s no part in saying it was part of our strategy and was in our thinking this summer – it wasn’t. But we have got to be flexible and react to things that happen.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalNewcastle UnitedTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Rising number of UK children report seeing explicit deepfakes of themselves | Deepfake | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: anonymous flagging service says cases have surged, as watchdog says AI is making sexualised or ‘nudified’ content easier to produce
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Exclusive: anonymous flagging service says cases have surged, as watchdog says AI is making sexualised or ‘nudified’ content easier to produce
Content: The Report Remove service said it had received 420 reports from children so far this year.Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Report Remove service said it had received 420 reports from children so far this year.Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty ImagesDeepfakeRising number of UK children report seeing explicit deepfakes of themselvesExclusive: anonymous flagging service says cases have surged, as watchdog says AI is making sexualised or ‘nudified’ content easier to produceDan MilmoGlobal technology editorSat 8 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChildren in the UK have reported a surge in explicitdeepfakeimages featuring their likenesses, as a safety watchdog warned AI is making such content easier to produce.The Report Remove service, which blocks intimate images from appearing online, said there had been a rapid increase in imagery that had been digitally manipulated or “faked” in some way, including with AI andnudification tools.In the first six months of this year it received 420 reports from children of images of themselves that they believed had been faked or manipulated to appear explicit. The number has already exceeded its 2025 total of 397.Dan Sexton, chief technology officer at the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF),which operates Report Removealongside the NSPCC children’s charity, said the figures underscored the difficulty of preventing online images from being manipulated in an age of widely available and capable AI tools.“If someone can take a benign image of a child from the internet and create child sexual abuse material with it, there is nothing that child can do to stop it from happening apart from preventing anyone from taking pictures of them – or not putting pictures of themselves online,” he said.Report Removehas received so many reports of manipulated images from under-18s in recent years that it has added a check box to its online submission form allowing them to flag the material as deepfaked.Sexton said the figures confirmed a fear that AI would improve in capability and be used to manipulate images of real people.“This is one of the harms we were worried about when we first saw AI image generators being used, that they would be used to create child sexual abuse material featuring real children,” he said.“Everyone in the world is at risk,” Sexton added.View image in fullscreenDan Sexton, the chief technology officer at the Internet Watch Foundation, said it was becoming easier to manipulate benign images of children.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianThe IWF, which monitors the distribution of child sexual abuse material [CSAM] online, said the majority of the reports of manipulated images made to Report Remove in 2025 and 2026 were so severe that they passed the CSAM threshold. AI-generated CSAM is illegal in the UK and the government has made it illegal to adapt an AI model to create abuse material or to distribute such models to others.Rani Govender, an online safety expert at the NSPCC, said tech companies must put stronger safety protections in their AI products to prevent the creation of explicit material.Misleading AI-generated doctors pose ‘huge danger to public safety’Read more“This rise in children reaching out because fake or AI‑generated sexual images have been created of them is alarming but also sadly predictable,” she said. “Tech companies cannot keep pushing out AI products without embedding strong protections that prevent this material from being created in the first place.”Sexton said some victims who had contacted Report Remove about manipulated images had been targeted for sextortion, where a blackmailer threatens to publish the material unless they receive financial payment or demands more explicit images from the victim.Report Remove is a service that allows children to anonymously flag intimate images or videos of themselves that have been sent to former partners, sextortion fraudsters or could appear online. The service turns those images into a “hash”, or digital fingerprint, which is shared with major tech platforms, which can take the image down or prevent it from being uploaded.The rise of AI-enabled deepfakes has prompted a series of warnings about posting identifiable pictures of children online.Last month the National Crime Agency and IWFencouraged parents and guardiansto keep pictures of their children away from public display online. They suggested making social media accounts private or sharing pictures of children through a “close friends” group only.The guidance also followed cases in which cybercriminals had attempted to blackmail schools by scraping pictures of children, using AI to convert them into child sexual abuse material, then threatening to publish the imagery. Schools have been urged to remove identifiable pictures of pupils’ faces from their websites and social media accounts.Explore more on these topicsDeepfakeInternet safetyChildrenChild protectionAI (artificial intelligence)Social mediaInternetnewsShareReuse this content

title: Google DeepMind enters a new era as co-founder Demis Hassabis shifts AI role | DeepMind | The Guardian
description: Observers express concern that the division has lost its independence and commercial reality has taken over
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Observers express concern that the division has lost its independence and commercial reality has taken over
Content: Demis Hassabis at Google's offices in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDemis Hassabis at Google's offices in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianDeepMindGoogle DeepMind enters a new era as co-founder Demis Hassabis shifts AI roleObservers express concern that the division has lost its independence and commercial reality has taken overDan MilmoandAisha DownSat 8 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenSir Demis Hassabissaid AI had brought the world to a “pivotal moment in human history” last month, he knew another big change was imminent.This shift was closer to home. TheNobel prize-winninghead of Google DeepMind, Google’s AI unit, announced this week he wasrelinquishing his day-to-day duties as chief executiveand becoming chair. He is also taking on the role of chief scientist at DeepMind’s parent, Alphabet.Hassabis andDeepMindhave been key players in AI’s breakthrough era. The 50-year-old co-founded DeepMind and sold it to Google in 2014, which gave him the resources to oversee a number of advances.These included building the AlphaGo system that mastered theChinese board game Goand developing AlphaFold, a programme that predicts the 3D structure of proteins. The latter resulted in Hassabis being jointly awarded the 2024 Nobel prize in chemistry.A formerGoogleexecutive said the leadership overhaul showed London-based DeepMind being brought firmly into the orbit of its parent in Mountain View, California. DeepMind will now be run by Hassabis’s longstanding colleague, the US-based Koray Kavukcuoglu, who will take the non-CEO role of senior vice-president of DeepMind.“The era of DeepMind as an independent actor is over and the obvious sign of that is you have gone from a charismatic founder-leader to appointing Koray in a non-CEO leadership role. Koray is a technical character, not an inspirational figure like Demis,” said the former executive.The ex-Google employee added that it would be “galling” for Google and Hassabis that the latest iterations of Google’s flagship AI model series, Gemini, have lost ground to rival models developed by its US rivals Anthropic and OpenAI.Hassabis has said he was looking forward to focusing more on the “big picture” for AI and believed he was handing over operational management of a unit that was well placed for the competitive battles ahead.View image in fullscreenThe London DeepMind office will be brought into the orbit of its parent in Mountain View, California, a former Google executive said.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesInternally, DeepMind is a workplace where there have been political tensions. Employees who spoke to the Guardian said there was internal disquiet over the company’s work with the Pentagon. Earlier this year, a former Google DeepMind employee launched a legal challenge against Google, claiming they wereunfairly dismissedfor their views on Gaza.That employee was involved in unionisation efforts at Google DeepMind, which have taken place against a backdrop of concern that Google’s AI could assist militaries, including the Israel Defense Forces. Another Google DeepMind employeeresignedfrom the company in mid-July, citing Google’s work with the Pentagon and the US Department of Homeland Security.One said to the Guardian that Hassabis’s departure was the “end of an era”.“Now the person we were supposed to trust to get the right outcomes for humanity has stepped away,” they said. Google DeepMind “has become just another subdivision of Google”, they added.Rosa Curling, the executive director of Foxglove, a campaign group that supported the Google DeepMind employee in their legal challenge, said: “The departure of the co-founder of a company that once prided itself on its ethical credentials is likely to cause further concern among its frontier AI staff about how their work will end up being used in the real world.”Google has said it is committed to the “private and public sector consensus” that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without “appropriate human oversight”. While Google has declined a voluntary union recognition agreement in London, it has said it valued “the constructive and direct dialogue that we have with our employees about building a positive and successful workplace”.View image in fullscreenSome Google staff have been uncomfortable about its work with the Pentagon.Photograph: Joshua Roberts/ReutersOn the commercial side, a new cutting-edge model, Gemini 3.5 Pro, has yet to be released amid reports it has been delayed owing to attempts to improve its code-writing abilities – a core part of the appeal of Anthropic and OpenAI’s best products.Google’s two AI labs, London-based DeepMind and California-based Google Brain, were merged into Google DeepMind under Hassabis’s leadership three years ago. Control now appears to be moving back to the US, where Google’s co-founder Sergey Brin is reportedly playing a bigger role in AI development.Citing the departure of the leading AI researcher Yann LeCun from Meta and Geoffrey Hinton from Google as another example of “the end of an era in the AI ecosystem”, the former executive added: “This is very clearly a sign that the science-driven agenda of leadership in these labs has given way to cold, hard commercial reality that all of these companies want to make a return on the hundreds of billions of dollars they have invested in AI.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe source added, however, that Google still had the benefit of being able to combine its Gemini models with an impressive suite of products, from its all-conquering search product to its cloud platform and YouTube. Thanks to its search business it also has the money to continue investing heavily in AI, having generated net income – a US measure of profit – of $132bn (£98bn) last year.View image in fullscreenHassabis has called for a US safety body to assess cutting-edge AI models.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersHassabis has also taken on a more statesman-like role in recent years. The reference to a “pivotal moment” came in a blogpost in which he called for a US safety body to assess cutting-edge models, with the hope it would lead to the establishment of global standards.The need for such a body, Hassabis argued, was pressing because the tech industry was approaching the “pivotal” point of achieving AGI, the term for a theoretical state of AI where a system can perform any human cognitive task – which also means being capable of performing white collar jobs in sectors such as law, finance and health.A Google spokesperson said: “This is a move Demis has been thinking about for a while. He is very excited, and this will give him more time to focus on AI-driven scientific breakthroughs.” They disputed that the changes had anything to do with the performance of Gemini.Hassabis’s move was announced alongside the departure of Jeff Dean, a veteran Google engineer and DeepMind’s chief scientist, who is leaving along with three other top researchers to form an AI startup called Discovery Loop.According to one former Google employee, Dean’s departure could augur further personnel losses. Dean’s move also follows OpenAI’s poaching in June of Google’s Noam Shazeer, a leading figure in the field as co-author of the2017 research paperAttention is All You Need, a crucial step in developing chatbots.“It’s hugely problematic for Google,” said Jeremy Nixon, a former AI researcher at Google and founder of Infinity Artificial Intelligence Institute, a startup. “It’s problematic because of who Jeff will hire and because the primary reason people want to work at Google is because of him and Noam Shazeer and all these other phenomenal researchers. It’s no longer true to say that if you want to work with the greatest researchers on the planet, you go to Google DeepMind.”Nixon added that Dean was an “angelic diplomat” who could “deal with these complex political organisations”.Google denies it faces a post-Dean talent crisis, pointing to attrition rates for AI talent for the first half of this year being lower than they were at this time last year.If AI is indeed facing a pivotal moment, Google has just had one.Explore more on these topicsDeepMindGoogleAI (artificial intelligence)AlphabetComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI to pause some work on AI model Astra due to security concerns | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Agent found to be able to find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, and to carry out cyber-attacks
Author: Eric Berger
Headline: Agent found to be able to find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, and to carry out cyber-attacks
Content: ‘The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them.’Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them.’Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAI to pause some work on AI model Astra due to security concernsAgent found to be able to find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, and to carry out cyber-attacksEric BergerSat 8 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTFirst published on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI will pausesomework on an artificial intelligence model because of security concerns, the company stated on Friday, following a series of incidents in which AI agents have escaped containment.The company had evaluated the agent, Astra, and found “significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity”, which had moved to a “critical” threshold where it can find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, or devise and execute cyber-attacks when given only a “high level desired goal”.OpenAI stated that the model was not involved in an incident in which one of its AI agentswent rogueduring a test, accessed the open web and hacked a startup, Hugging Face. The company discovered other instances in which autonomous agents had escaped containment,Reuters reportedin July.Google DeepMind enters a new era as co-founder Demis Hassabis shifts AI roleRead moreThe reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them. Still, critics of the AI industryhave warnedthat such disclosures from OpenAI and its competitors Anthropic and Meta could be designed to generate hype about the technology’s power and thus spur additional interest from investors.To prevent potential rogue behavior from AI agents,OpenAIis “implementing stricter security controls for higher-capability models and associated activities, including isolated testing environments, restricted network and tool access”, the company’s blogpost stated. It will also install “enhanced model weight protections and encryption, additional monitoring and detection capabilities”.The company will pause internal activities involving Astra that do not meet these new requirements.“We’re committed to working alongside governments, safety institutes, and civil society to ensure that the frontier capabilities of models like Astra, and those that follow, are deployed responsibly and broadly for the benefit of all humanity,” the company stated.Metaalso disclosedthis week that one of its models hacked another company during cybersecurity testing.
