And the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) announced on 4 August that agents powered by OpenAI and Anthropic had senttargeted emailsto software developers in an attempt to pass a cyber challenge.“These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world,” theinstitute statedin a blogpost.The organisation cautioned that the models’ sending of harmful software was not a case of a “model escaping its secure test environment” but rather that the group had intentionally permitted internet access to “best assess the maximum capability of models”.Still, the “behaviour was possible, sustained and new; that alone warrants attention”, the AISI said.The reports emerged while the Trump administrationwas finalizinga framework on how to test AI models for safety and cybersecurity risks. OpenAI and Anthropic, which have increased competition from China and other tech firms, have argued that open-source models, meaning those that allow anyone to see and modify the underlying program code, pose asecurity riskand pushed for additional federal regulations on them.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAInewsShareReuse this content

title: The ornithological artist drawing 1,000 birds by hand – all for an app that wants you off your phone | San Francisco | The Guardian
description: The mission of the Flock app is quietly subversive: to encourage users to ditch their screens and explore the wonderful world of birding
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The mission of the Flock app is quietly subversive: to encourage users to ditch their screens and explore the wonderful world of birding
Content: Keith Hansen puts the finishing touches to his illustration of a painted bunting bird.Photograph: Nick CzapView image in fullscreenKeith Hansen puts the finishing touches to his illustration of a painted bunting bird.Photograph: Nick CzapSan FranciscoThe ornithological artist drawing 1,000 birds by hand – all for an app that wants you off your phoneThe mission of the Flock app is quietly subversive: to encourage users to ditch their screens and explore the wonderful world of birdingNick Czap in San FranciscoSat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a brilliantly bright afternoon in his gallery and studio in Bolinas, a small town on the northernCaliforniacoast, Keith Hansen was putting the finishing touches on a watercolor of an almost improbably flamboyant painted bunting.With an ultra-fine sable brush, he made a few intricate additions to the cobalt blue plumage on the bunting’s head, and, satisfied with his work, slipped the watercolor into a stout binder that every few days welcomes a new addition.“That was number 420,” he said. Or to put it another way, just 584 to go.Hansen, a renowned ornithological illustrator and author, has a monumental task – a hand-painted compendium of every one of the roughly 1,000 bird species ever recorded from the US and Canada, including those found in waters up to 200 miles from shore, Hawaiian birds not included. When finished, it will complete the visual backbone of an app called Flock, whose mission, compared with that of most apps, is quietly subversive.For rather than seeking to monopolize and monetize its users’ attention, it deftly employs elements of computer gaming and social networking to draw people outward, into the world of birding, with the broader aim of cultivating a community of conservationists.View image in fullscreenHansen’s illustration of the painted bunting appears in Flock, an app conceived and created by Hansen’s friends Adam Donkin and Bob Stevenson.Photograph: Nick CzapFlock was conceived and created by two of Hansen’s friends, Adam Donkin and Bob Stevenson. Both have impressive tech industry CVs. Donkin, 52, who lives not far from Hansen in Marin county’s San Geronimo valley, worked for many years as a product and user experience designer. As a lead product designer at Amazon, he led the charge on design for several models of the Kindle e-reader.Stevenson, a 58-year-old Scotsman, lives in St Helena in the Napa valley. He founded his first company in Edinburgh at 18, and at 24, moved to California to work as an art director for Richard Branson’s Virgin Games, embarking on a decades-long career as an art or design director, or as a producer, for more than 50 video games.Despite their disparate disciplines, the three friends are united by a shared passion for birds and birding.Hansen fell in love with the avian world in sixth grade, when, on a walk in the Maryland woods, his brother, Rob, drew his attention to a cedar waxwing. “It’s just an exquisite bird,” Hansen recalled. He began illustrating birds during his senior year of high school, and in 1986 – after a decade and a half observing and studying birds on numerous expeditions – he settled in Bolinas, opening his gallery there in 1991.Donkin grew up on theSan Franciscopeninsula and began birding at the age of four under the wing of his father’s friend Rich Stallcup, an esteemed ornithologist and birder, and a founder of the Point Reyes Bird Observatory. “He was like a nature wizard,” said Donkin. “Birds and animals would appear when you were in the field with him. He knew every bird by call and by sight.”View image in fullscreenFrom left to right: Stevenson, Donkin and Hansen, all avid birders, in Marin county, California.Photograph: Nick CzapDonkin moved to Marin in 2012. “When I moved to Marin,” he said, “Rich introduced me to the thriving birding community here, including Keith.”That same year, Stevenson was looking for a designer for his new company. “One of our investors recommended that we chat with this designer, Adam,” said Stevenson. “It was meant to be a quick call, but we ended up talking for over an hour. We became friends on the first call.”In 2016, Donkin visited Stevenson at his home in the southern Marin town of Tiburon, overlooking Richardson Bay, a major habitat for migrating waterbirds. “One day Adam came round to the house,” Stevenson recalled. “I didn’t know that he was an avid birder. He turned up and said, ‘Hey, dude, you’ve got to bird! Do you have binoculars?’”Stevenson, who had recently stepped away from his company to focus on his family, fell hard and fast for birding. He bought binoculars, scopes and cameras, began birding from his deck, and, as an outlet for his avian photography, opened his own gallery in Tiburon.He was also struck by the ways in which birding resembled multi-player gaming, in that it involved learning new skills, a mastery curve, collecting (by way of so-called yard lists and life lists – tabulations of the bird species sighted in one’s yard, or over a lifetime), an awareness of how one is progressing relative to others, and a community which, while competitive, helps its members learn more quickly. He also recognized, at the age of 48, what he had given up by trading the beauty of the natural world for computer screens. “It was such a revelation, because going back to nature at that age, you realize what you’ve been missing.”Shortly after, he and Donkin began discussing the idea of building an app around birding. For Donkin, his friend’s newfound passion was a catalyst. “I had the experience with Bob of turning someone on to it, and seeing what a huge impact it had on him.”For Stevenson, the spark was a conversation with Robert Snow, the president of the Fresno Audubon Society, who said the organization was concerned about its ability to bring future generations into birding, as this was critical to perpetuating its mission of protecting birds and their habitats.View image in fullscreenAn American robin in Kirkland, Washington.Photograph: Wolfgang Kaehler/LightRocket/Getty ImagesTo Donkin, the path from birding to conservation is a natural progression. “Birding creates an infinite well of curiosity,” he said. “You start to notice things and think, ‘Well, how can I help?’ You might start with providing water, providing food, providing shelter. By restoring habitat in your area, you can have an impact. It could be your yard, a park in your neighborhood, sometimes ranch land, sometimes public land.”Initially Stevenson and Donkin thought they might develop an app in partnership with Audubon, or with the Cornell Lab of Ornithology in Ithaca, New York, where they had given a presentation on the parallels between birding and gaming, with an eye towards how aspects of game design could be employed to increase engagement with the Cornell Lab’s Merlin app, which identifies birds based on their songs and calls, or images.double quotation markWe’re trying to get your attention away from your phone so that you can then turn your attention outwardAdam DonkinThey ultimately decided to strike out on their own and, in 2017, set to work on Flock. Having worked on projects backed by publishers and by investors in Silicon Valley, Stevenson said they decided to fund it themselves “so we would not be bound by anyone’s rules”. They also set out to break the addictive conventions of app design. “The games industry is so comfortable making experiences that are so engaging that you can’t look away,” said Donkin, “and we were very aware of the negative aspects of social media.”“We didn’t want to make something that got you addicted to the dopamine hit of getting a like, or followers,” Donkin continued. “We wanted to make something that was a companion to the experience of birding. In an attention-based economy, we’re going to use that same system, but we’re going to flip it. We’re not trying to get your attention on the app, we’re trying to get your attention away from your phone so that you can then turn your attention outward.”View image in fullscreenBolinas, California, a small coastal town where Keith Hansen has his studio.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesThe result is an app whoseinterface is refreshingly spare and minimalistic, with a tab where users can search for birds or for other users; another for recording sightings, made, perhaps with the aid of the Merlin app or an old-fashioned field guide; a leaderboard which ranks users according to the number of unique species they saw in the current month; and a community tab where users can upload photos, message one another, and congratulate other users on their sightings.As with every detail of the app, even the way in which users cheer one another on was carefully considered. Instead of a “like” button, there is a “high-five” button. “We put ‘high five’ rather than ‘like’,” Stevenson explained, “because kids were using it, and we wanted it to be, ‘Nice job on seeing that bird!’ rather than, ‘I like you.’ We didn’t want kids to collect likes.”They enlisted their longtime friend Hansen, whose artistic sensitivity brought a unique beauty to the app. While Stevenson coded, Donkin scanned and processed new batches of illustrations as Hansen completed them, following an algorithm that sorted the bird species in order from the most- to the least-commonly seen. Given that it can take Hansen up to four days to complete an illustration, this prioritized the birds Flock users are more likely to encounter: an American robin or a northern cardinal, for instance, rather than a Steller’s sea eagle, a huge Siberian raptor, one of which, acting on some unknown impulse in 2020, flew from northern Asia to Alaska and then Texas, before settling on the coast of Maine.View image in fullscreenHansen, in his gallery and studio in Bolinas.Photograph: Nick CzapIn early 2025, they released Flock on Apple’s app store. By April of that year, Flock had about 100 users. Today, although Donkin and Stevenson have not yet done anything in the way of marketing, it has on the order of 1,000. Among the recent enhancements they enjoy are uncannily realistic animations that bring Hansen’s illustrations to life. The short animations – which Stevenson created with AI, with Hansen’s guidance – give a sense of the way each particular bird moves. The formerly static white-crowned sparrow now darts its head this way and that in a most sparrow-like fashion, peering inquisitively at its viewer; the great blue heron, meanwhile, tiptoes along a sandy bank, and pausing, stealthily lowers its bill to the water’s surface, preparing to strike.Among Flock’s growing flock is Amy Tan, the bestselling writer whose most recent work, The Backyard Bird Chronicles, grew from a series of pencil sketches, color portraits and journal notes she collected on her avian neighbors during the pandemic. A friend of Hansen’s for 10 years, and more recently of Stevenson’s, Tan logged her first sightings in the app late last summer. In an email, Tan wrote that Flock was “hands down the most beautiful bird app and the easiest one to track and share sightings of my backyard birds. With each bird I add to my daily list, I feel rewarded when its illustration suddenly comes to life. All my friends are blown away and become instant fans.”This reporter, meanwhile, who entered his first sighting – a western gull – in Flock last spring, has found himself growing ever more attuned to the sights, sounds and habits of his feathered compatriots in San Francisco, and has recently begun shopping for a hummingbird feeder.Explore more on these topicsSan FranciscoBirdsCaliforniaAppsAnimalsWildlifeWest CoastfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rest assured, the new CDC director thinks ‘abortion surveillance’ is essential | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: An exchange between Dr Erica Schwartz and Senator Josh Hawley during her confirmation hearing is alarming
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: An exchange between Dr Erica Schwartz and Senator Josh Hawley during her confirmation hearing is alarming
Content: ‘Overturning Roe v Wade was just the beginning of the new war on reproductive rights in the US.’Photograph: Mariam Zuhaib/APView image in fullscreen‘Overturning Roe v Wade was just the beginning of the new war on reproductive rights in the US.’Photograph: Mariam Zuhaib/APThe Week in PatriarchyTrump administrationRest assured, the new CDC director thinks ‘abortion surveillance’ is essentialArwa MahdawiAn exchange between Dr Erica Schwartz and Senator Josh Hawley during her confirmation hearing is alarmingSat 8 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 18.03 EDTShareRobert F Kennedy Jr’snew cooking showisn’t the only big news out of the public health world this week. On Wednesday, Dr Erica Schwartzwas confirmedby the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), making her the first Black woman to hold the position. This is the first time in almost a year that the agency has had a permanent leader; the previous director, Susan Monarez, onlylasted 29 daysbefore she was ousted for butting heads with RFK about US vaccine policies. Translation: she was a little too keen on following accepted science for the Trump administration.So is Schwartz an RFK-approved vaccine skeptic who thinks you can cure cancer by praying to trees? Surprisingly: no. Schwartz, who served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first term, actually has government experience and a public health background. During her confirmation hearing in July, she walked acareful tightropewhen asked about her stance towards vaccines. Schwartz said she “will never betray the science” but also dodged questions about how she would handle pressure from Kennedy.But don’t breathe a sigh of relief quite yet. During that same confirmation hearing, Schwartz made some chilling remarks aboutabortion surveillancewhen quizzed on the issue by Missouri senator Josh Hawley, an anti-abortion lawmakerwho wants tobanthe abortion pill mifepristone nationwide.“The CDC collects data on abortions that are committed in the United States of America through a system called the Abortion Reporting System,”Hawley saidwhen asking Schwartz whether she would commit to collecting detailed data on abortions. “This system is voluntary, and so a number of states, not coincidentally large blue states, do not turn over any data, so that it’s difficult to get a picture of just how many abortions and under what circumstances are committed in this country. We do know the numbers are going way up.”“Senator, you have my commitment,” Schwartz replied. “Abortion surveillance is absolutely a critical component of what the CDC is currently doing.”“I also want to make sure that certain states are not conflating emergency services and hiding abortions in that emergency services case definition,” she added. “We need to make sure we’re pulling out true abortions and making sure that we’re really having clear case definitions regarding abortions so the data is actually accurate.”“Tremendous,” Hawley replied. He seemed very happy with her response.If you are concerned about the growingcriminalization of abortionand surveillance of pregnant women in the US, then absolutely nothing about this is tremendous. I’ve quoted the majority of the exchange between Hawley and Schwartz instead of paraphrasing it, because the choice of language is so alarming. First, look at the way in which Hawley frames the issue. He talks about abortions beingcommitted:a loaded word which makes you think of murder. (Imagine it in another medical context:I’m having a mammogram committed tomorrow!)Then he insinuates that blue states are hiding abortion data for nefarious reasons. As it is, 44 states plus Washington DC have some form of mandated abortion reporting, according tothe Guttmacher Institute, and there is no evidence that these states are hiding anything. New York is anoutlierin that it only requires abortion reporting when a patient makes a request related to the disposition of the fetus’s remains. Which seems like a sensible policy that protects the privacy of people who have had abortions.Now look at Schwartz’s reply. Why would abortion surveillance be “a critical component” of what the CDC is doing? Data collection around abortions can serve legitimate purposes, sure, but isn’t it rather more important for the CDC to be, I dunno, controlling and preventing diseases? Her reference to “true abortions” (as opposed to fake ones?) and to states “hiding abortions” is also worrying. Pregnant people are already dyingpreventable deathsbecause providers in states with abortion bans are terrified of treating them. This sort of language from the CDC director is going to make the situation even worse.Donald Trump has called Schwartz “a STAR”. If her exchange with Hawley is anything to go by, however, she seems to be yet another stooge: happy to facilitate the Trump administration’s anti-abortion agenda and politicization of public health.“Erica Schwartz’s testimony … should alarm everyone who believes private medical decisions belong to patients, not politicians,” Mini Timmaraju, the president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, said in a statement. She added that, under theTrump administration, “abortion surveillance could be expanded or weaponized to collect more intrusive information, spread disinformation about reproductive health care, and support efforts to investigate or criminalize patients and providers”.As activists and experts have repeatedly said, overturning Roe v Wade was just the beginning of the new war onreproductive rightsin the US – a war facilitated by an unprecedented network of surveillance technology. Theconvicted felonin the White House seems intent on treating every pregnant woman as a potential criminal.Todd Blanche pledged to roll back abortion access nationwideDuring a private call with religious groups, the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche, said effortsto reversethe Biden administration’s efforts to protect abortion were “taking longer than we want”. He seemed to suggest that the administration was working to restrict access toabortion pills and said: “We don’t have complete victory yet, but we will have victory, and victory will be soon, and it will be permanent.” Blanche has faced a rocky road to confirmation as attorney general. The bad news is that the government’s anti-abortion agenda will continue whether he gets the role or not.Arizona clergy who learn of child abuse in confessions aren’t required to report itThat’s according to a new ruling by thestate’s supreme court. No doubt they’ll soon be forced to report abortions, though!skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnya Taylor-Joy has a theory about why method acting is associated with men“If you’ll notice, women don’t method act because we have things to take care of,” Taylor-Joy said in aninterview promotingher new Apple TV show Lucky (which is extremely good, by the way). Back in 2024, Natalie Portmansimilarly describedmethod acting as a “luxury women can’t afford”. She added: “I don’t think that children or partners would be very understanding of, you know, me making everyone call me ‘Jackie Kennedy’ all the time.”Sydney Towle, who shared cancer journey on TikTok, dies aged 26More than a million people watched Towle navigate her cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer of the bile ducts. Sheraised awarenessof the disease and built community. However, because the internet is often toxic, she was alsoaccused by trollsof exaggerating or even faking her cancer. It even got to a point where Towle’s doctor had to confirm to the New York Times that she had stage 4 cancer.Miscarriages are surging in Gaza and births are decliningThis is not someunfortunate byproductof war; it is by design. Last year, a UN report found that Israel’s systemic attacks on women’s healthcare in Gaza amount to “genocidal acts”. The report noted that Israel’s destruction of maternity wards, an IVF clinic and control on essential supplies into Gaza “destroyed in part the reproductive capacity of Palestinians in Gaza as a group”.The week in pawtriarchyA cat called Toast Malonesurvived a firethat destroyed an apartment complex in Utah by hiding in a closet for three days. Toast did not get burned, and has now beenreunitedwith their family. Now they’re the toast of the town.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationThe Week in PatriarchyAbortionHealthWomenVaccines and immunisationUS SenateReproductive rightscommentShareReuse this content

title: Parenting is hard. Should we let AI do it for us? | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: Tech companies offer eye-movement trackers, personalized podcasts and ‘optimized nap predictions’. Who actually needs this?
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: Tech companies offer eye-movement trackers, personalized podcasts and ‘optimized nap predictions’. Who actually needs this?
Content: ‘What about the eight to 10 hours a day when your child has the gift of blissful solitude?’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘What about the eight to 10 hours a day when your child has the gift of blissful solitude?’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionParents and parentingParenting is hard. Should we let AI do it for us?Dave SchillingTech companies offer eye-movement trackers, personalized podcasts and ‘optimized nap predictions’. Who actually needs this?Sat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 08.56 EDTShareWhat job in our world is less lucrative than being a parent? A Hollywood internship? Volunteering at a soup kitchen? Professional writer? Parenting is the only job you have to pay money to do.Lots of money. Lodging, clothes, food, school, Pokémon cards – it really adds up. And it’s getting worse. According to the tech industry, I have to strap my drooling offspring to a computer in order to ensure the baby’s survival.Parents are being offered life-altering advancements in artificial intelligence that purport to make this taxing endeavor a tiny bit easier. OpenAI is suggesting its latest products can make child-rearing more efficient: its boss, Sam Altman, suggestsgenerating a podcast about your kid’s lifethat you can listen to in the morning on the way to school. How entertaining would a podcast “that talks about one kid’s soccer game that afternoon, one kid’s upcoming birthday, some news, etc” actually be? “Jimmy needs to work on his dribbling.” Great. I think he knows already. He’s not going to be the next Messi, so how about we switch back to music?Momfluencers are co-parenting with AI. Is it better than a man? | Arwa MahdawiRead morePresumably, this idea renders the need for conversation moot. The computer already knows everything about our lives and has now regurgitated it into digital mush delivered by a generically cheery voice. But why I would find it helpful to have a machine reiterate information I have at my disposal already is a grand mystery even Philip Marlowe couldn’t solve. I’m a functioning, alive adult human being. This is like giving me an extra tooth with the promise that I can chew my food faster.But what about the eight to 10 hours a day when your child has the gift of blissful solitude? Surely, they can’t be left alone at bedtime, lest they swallow a Hot Wheels car or open your favorite jar of loose razor blades. That’s whereNanitcomes in – a startup that promises the kind of 24-hour surveillance that would make the Department of Homeland Security salivate. Nanit sells a camera and monitor set that observes your kid during sleep, tracking eye movements, “sleep efficiency”, and breathing patterns. Nanit’s rival, a company called Owlet, attaches a pulse oximetry tracker to your child’s foot through a sock. That’s not quite hooking your kid up to a terminal from the novel Neuromancer, but it feels like a decent first step in that direction. An app called Huckleberry offers “optimized nap predictions” and a chatbot assistant.Of course, all of this costs money. A Nanit kit is $474, plus $100 a year in subscription fees. Owlet’s robo-sock is $300. Huckleberry’s app is free, but its nap predictions, like expert sports betting advice, will cost you. For $120, you can be told when your kid might go to sleep. I doubt there’s a money-back guarantee if they get it wrong, and the kid ends up spilling Legos all over the floor instead of going to bed.These services promise to save lives by identifying health issues early in a child’s development. Nanit claims it offers more sleep and peace of mind, so parents can move their babies into their own rooms, thereby giving mom and dad a chance to go back to having regular intercourse. Yes, Nanit has looked intoparents’ sex habits, too. If you went back to when I was married, you’d find there wasn’t much to look into.None of this is anything people actually need to be parents. Babies need food, toys, diapers and a regular bath. Those all cost money. If I have to choose between saving for my son’s college and a spreadsheet with a bunch of biometric data, I’m skipping the spreadsheet. I realize, of course, these products are not for me. I don’t have an unlimited supply of disposable income. I have to prioritize and be practical. These devices are for people who optimize every single shred of their daily lives, thinking it will protect them from the reality of failure, illness and death. I’m sorry to report that a $400 camera isn’t going to fix any of that.Is the promise of AI living up to the hype? | Fiona KatauskasRead moreSociety has been trying to offer solutions to solve the conundrum of parenting for decades: self-help books, classes, the legendary (and expensive)Snoo cribthat shakes your child like it’s a gin martini until it stops crying. In every case, these aids cost money, turning parenting into a lucrative sector of the economy. If you can’t afford these modern “miracles”, where can you turn?Parenting is hard, and we all need help. But there was a time when grandparentslived with their kids and grandkids, or at least lived close enough to help. I grant that the idea of living with my mother is akin to pitching a tent next to a cave filled with grizzly bears, but I’d do that before I got an AI-powered camera system to take a video of my kid sleeping. The best part of extended family childcare is that people can do something an AI can never do. It can teach children about someone besides themselves.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsParents and parentingOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)FamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: President Xi never wastes a good crisis. As Iran, Ukraine and Palestine distract the world, he tightens his grip  | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: Ever the strategist, the Chinese leader is taking the offensive, both abroad and at home. That’s bad news for global order, and minorities in his country, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: Ever the strategist, the Chinese leader is taking the offensive, both abroad and at home. That’s bad news for global order, and minorities in his country, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: China's Xi Jinping with Donald Trump during a visit to Zhongnanhai Garden in Beijing on 15 May 2026.Photograph: Evan Vucci/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChina's Xi Jinping with Donald Trump during a visit to Zhongnanhai Garden in Beijing on 15 May 2026.Photograph: Evan Vucci/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionXi JinpingPresident Xi never wastes a good crisis. As Iran, Ukraine and Palestine distract the world, he tightens his gripSimon TisdallEver the strategist, the Chinese leader is taking the offensive, both abroad and at home. That’s bad news for global order, and minorities in his countrySat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.05 EDTShareImagine what would happen if a British prime minister in London told the Scots they could not have their own parliament, national football team or fly the saltire. Or if the Welsh were told their language and poetry were banned and must no longer be taught in schools. The ensuing uproar would probably destroy the United Kingdom. Yet that’s exactly what Xi Jinping, China’s communist emperor, is telling the roughly 125 million members of the 55ethnic and religious minoritieswho together comprise about 9% of the country’s (majority Han Chinese) population.Xi claims his sinicisation policy, embodied in a new “ethnic unity” law, will boost national identity and integration and, by expanding compulsory use of the Mandarin language, improve life and work prospects. Minorities should “hug tightly like pomegranate seeds” to build a strong, united China, he says. But Tibetans, Mongolians,Uyghursand others who value their separate language and customs fiercely object to what they see asforced assimilationinto a conformist, intolerant monoculture dominated by the Communist party’s tunnel vision. For them, it’s ethnic cleansing by another name.The new law has been condemned, though not too loudly, by western governments and more vociferously by rights organisations such asAmnesty International. The death of Lobga Rangzen, a Free Tibet activist whoset himself on firein protest outside the UN in New York last month, briefly drew international attention. But such tragedies are not new. Wholesale repression in Tibet and brutal “re-education” camps in Xinjiang are but two longstanding aspects of Xi’s intensifying nationwide war on dissent, difference and diversity. The law and its harsh penalties, which extend toChinese citizens based abroad, adds legal weight to existing efforts to enforce his and the party’s will (much the same thing these days) by creating a politically compliant, cowed population that dare not answer back.A debilitating fatalism has taken hold in the west about China’s behaviour, whether it involves persecution of minorities, evisceration of democracy in Hong Kong, vindictive prosecutions of pro-democracy activists such as the former Apple Daily publisherJimmy Lai, or vicious suppression of independentChristian churchesand “unapproved” religious groups. It’s as though Xi’s China is now seen as simply too big, too economically powerful and too militarily threatening to influence, let alone contain or control. When China’s internal affairs are the issue, it’s easier to steer clear. Awkwardly balancingtrade against security, and culpably silent on human rights, Britain is far from alone among western democracies in failing to articulate a coherent China policy.But Xi’s increasingly aggressive, uncompromising policies are not confined to domestic matters. In power for nearly 15 years, Xi, 73, is growing ever more confident and abrasive in pursuit of his international legacy bucket list: establishing China asthe dominant global power, relegating the US to second place and making his country the essential hub of a new multipolar security, economic and diplomatic order. His legacy list includes a takeover of Taiwan before he stands down, and unchallenged supremacy across the Asia-Pacific region. It all points one way: to Xi’s coronation as the greatest Chinese leader since Mao Zedong.With the 21st party congress approaching, 2027 could be a big year for Xi – and he is already getting his ducks in a row. His dictatorship looks unassailable. Top regime cadres,meeting this week in secretive conclaveat the Beidaihe seaside resort in Hebei province, are expected to endorse his redoubled drive to enforce loyalty and discipline in the ranks – the official phrase is “sustained advancement of full and rigorous party self-governance”. The Beidaihe gathering, andanother meeting due in October, come amid almost Stalinistpurgesofsenior politicaland military figures.Signs of a more assertive international posture are everywhere. In recent months, China has stoked nationalisttensions with Japanand deliberatelyprovoked the Philippinesin disputed areas of the South China Sea. Its intimidation of Taiwan is unceasing. This week, Japan’s latest defence white paper singled out China as presenting “an unprecedented strategic challenge” and warned the threat was moving closer to home. Admiral Samuel Paparo, head of US Pacific Command,fired a broadsideat China’s “coercive actions” in pursuit, he said, of regional dominance.Xi is now actively challenging the US and the west on several other fronts. China is reportedly planning toprovide Iranwith up to 400 shoulder-fired missiles and new air defence systems. It is already materially assisting Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. And an emboldened Beijing is deploying the sort oftrade weaponsbeloved of Donald Trump. Last year it restricted exports of vital rare earth minerals, to Washington’s great alarm. Only this week, China hit back at Trump’s new tariffs byblocking sales of drone technology.Xi’s ever more bullish stance owes much to Trump’s trashing of the post-1945 global order, disdain for international law and national sovereignty (as seen in Venezuela and Greenland), andstrained relationswith traditional allies such as Japan, South Korea and European Nato countries. Many now view the US as an unreliable partner. For China, Trump’s shifting focus away from Asia and towards the western hemisphere is a golden opportunity to be exploited while it lasts. That may be one reason why Xi has taken the unusual step of agreeing to visit Trump in Washington next month, so soon after their May meeting in Beijing.The main focus of the summit is expected to be artificial intelligence, amid US worries that it is in danger oflosing the AI race. According to Chinese commentators, at least, Trump asked for the meeting after China agreed AI partnerships with 28 countries, mostly from the global south. AI is “probably the biggest thing anybody’s ever seen”, Trump said last month. “Whoever wins that race is probably going to win, period.” By which he presumably means, win the 21st century’s superpower crown.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe summit is likely to confirm the impression left bythe last one: that Xi, outmanoeuvring Trump on Asia-Pacific security and Taiwan, accumulating geopolitical clout, and winning trade and tech wars, is well on the way to fulfilling his ambition of gaining the upper hand over the US. Yet in the end, Xi is still an unelected autocrat, a thug in a suit who relies on force to stay in power. He’s failing to deliver economically and, as in India and elsewhere, young urban Chinese may not tolerate his old-school brand of suffocating authoritarianism indefinitely. Who knows? Perhaps his ethnic unity law may ultimately prove a step too far – as it certainly would in Britain.All should be on their guard. Xi, no friend of the west, may be morphing into an outright enemy while all eyes are onIran, Gaza and Ukraine. Symbolically if not yet physically, a dangerously unconstrained Xi is shutting the door on peaceful coexistence at home and abroad.Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsXi JinpingOpinionChinaHuman rightsTariffsAI (artificial intelligence)Asia PacificDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Australian families are losing loved ones to gambling. The industry’s ‘I know nothing’ defence beggars belief | Zoe Daniel | The Guardian
description: Australians are the biggest gambling losers in the world. Labor’s feeble ‘reforms’ aren’t close to good enough
Author: Zoe Daniel
Headline: Australians are the biggest gambling losers in the world. Labor’s feeble ‘reforms’ aren’t close to good enough
Content: Luke Bateman, former NRL player and reformed problem gambler, centre, told the Senate inquiry he attended a private Gold Coast event hosted by a gambling company at which senior figures took illicit drugs with clients.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenLuke Bateman, former NRL player and reformed problem gambler, centre, told the Senate inquiry he attended a private Gold Coast event hosted by a gambling company at which senior figures took illicit drugs with clients.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPOpinionGamblingAustralian families are losing loved ones to gambling. The industry’s ‘I know nothing’ defence beggars beliefZoe DanielAustralians are the biggest gambling losers in the world. Labor’s feeble ‘reforms’ aren’t close to good enoughFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesSat 8 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 19.51 EDTShareReaders of a certain age will recall the Hogan’s Heroes TV series with affection and the implausibility of the Sergeant Schultz defence: “I know nothing.”But that’s pretty much what the multibillion-dollar gambling industry giants would have us believe.It wasn’t us.That’s the response from the industry that has turned Australians into the biggest gambling losers in the world after the deplorable allegations made to a Senate inquiry this week.It’s not our fault.It’s not part of our “customer offering”, a euphemism for inducements, to supply drugs and escorts to problem gamblers.Not to mention bonus bets and the incentives presented to those who are hooked by their VIP “handlers” whose entire job it is to encourage people to pour their money into the profit-making machines of these largely multinational companies.Labor faces fierce backlash from gambling giants as Coalition and Greens push for new controls on inducementsRead moreAs federal parliament prepares to debate the government’s gambling “reforms”, the nexus between high-earning sportsmen and the gambling companies that are sponsoring their sports and then preying on their wages should also be homed in on.Luke Bateman, former NRL player and reformed problem gambler, told the inquiry he attended a private Gold Coast event hosted by a gambling company at which senior figures took illicit drugs with clients.He rightly pointed out that, at age 23, he was a vulnerable young man. He was also part of the 18-24 cohort that is the fastest growing problem gambling group in the country.“There were times I would be flown interstate and taken to race days, put in marquees with alcohol and food provided, but before getting there your VIP manager would [ask] … ‘Hey mate, what drugs do you want? Do you want a couple of bags for the weekend?’”What was alleged is utterly disgraceful. The gambling industry denies it.Jules Norton Selzer, the director of corporate affairs for Sportsbet, told the inquiry the company had “zero evidence of the allegations”.Tabcorp’s head of government affairs, Julian Whealing, said the provision of illicit drugs, sex workers and alcohol was not “part of Tabcorp’s customer offering”.“Any evidence of this illegal activity should be referred to the relevant authorities.”It certainly should.Mark Kempster, who uses his own experience of problem gambling to advocate for the Alliance forGamblingReform and also fronted the inquiry, can list a bunch of others who have contacted him relating similar experiences.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“I know dozens of examples of what Luke said as well, with the people I’ve worked with. That is a regular occurrence. Those types of things happen across nearly all the major VIP programs that I’ve seen,” he told the inquiry.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd beyond the drugs and prostitutes allegedly offered to high rollers such as Bateman,who says he lost $1m and considered taking his own life as a result, there’s the constant badgering with offers of bonus bets and more.Anyone who has spent time with a problem gambler will know that the government’sleaky BetStop self-exclusion programis not solving this.Now, the government plans to cap TV ads at three per hour until 8.30pm (apparently the industry found that amount tolerable), ban radio ads during school drop-off and pick up, ban ads in sports venues and logos on uniforms, ban the use of stars in ads and restrict online ads to adults only.All of this amounts to the kind of tinkering that has previously increased the number of ads that Australians are being exposed to.It avoids the substantive recommendations made by the committee led by Labor’s own Peta Murphy more than 1,100 days and$104bn dollars in losses ago; that all betting inducements should be banned, along with gambling ads and a national regulator with teeth stood up to hold the companies to account.Prioritising the profitability of sport, broadcasting and gambling corporations is a befuddling approach from the federal government, which is being at best pig-headed and at worst negligent as families face collapse caused by the toxic normalisation of betting on sport. The flow-on effects can include family breakdown, domestic violence, mental health issues, financial collapse and, sometimes, death.Labor’s gambling reform friendless as Coalition withholds support amid drug and sex worker allegationsRead more“The inducements really destroyed my life because that’s what kept you coming back … when you wanted to get out,” Bateman said. “But it also destroyed the lives of the people who loved me.”Too many Australian families know this. Some have lost sons and daughters to suicide due to gambling debt. This was a theme that threaded the Senate inquiry evidence.“There is no gap in knowledge, no gap in evidence and no gap in understanding. The only gaps are in regulation, in oversight and in the willingness to uphold the moral and ethical responsibility that a government owes its people,” said Anna Bardsley, co-founder of Gambling Harm Lived Experience Experts (GHLEE).“It’s beyond frustrating to know that we have a blueprint in the form of the Murphy report that could end the exploitation and manipulation of people and that this bill is all we get. Frankly, it’s piss-weak.”We can’t say we didn’t know.Zoe Daniel is a three-time ABC foreign correspondent and the former independent member for GoldsteinExplore more on these topicsGamblingOpinionAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: This burning summer is the proof: the voices of climate denial aren’t just delusional, they’re deadly | Sadiq Khan | The Guardian
description: Look at our blazing forests and parched cities. Green policies aren’t a ‘luxury’, and we can’t burn more oil and gas. People need the truth, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Author: Sadiq Khan
Headline: Look at our blazing forests and parched cities. Green policies aren’t a ‘luxury’, and we can’t burn more oil and gas. People need the truth, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Content: Parched grass near the Houses of Parliament in London, 3 August 2026.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenParched grass near the Houses of Parliament in London, 3 August 2026.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionClimate crisisThis burning summer is the proof: the voices of climate denial aren’t just delusional, they’re deadlySadiq KhanLook at our blazing forests and parched cities. Green policies aren’t a ‘luxury’, and we can’t burn more oil and gas. People need the truthReport: Sadiq Khan calls on Andy Burnham to commit to climate action as pressure grows over North Sea oilSat 8 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 13.47 EDTShareEurope is burning. This summer, an unprecedented series of heatwaves hasswept throughthe continent and across many parts of the globe. The consequences have been nothing short of catastrophic. In recent weeks deadly blazes have torn through France, Greece and Spain, killing firefighters, forcing people from their homes and robbing them of their livelihoods.With Tuesday marking Britain’s 34th day of temperatures exceeding 30C (86F) this year, the UK has also found itself reckoning with ferocious heat. Wildfires have forced evacuationsin Suffolkandthe Cairngorms. In London – where parks have become burnt, brittle and brown – hundreds of grass fires have put our firefighters under pressure like never before. In July, the weather station at Kew Gardens recorded its first ever month without rain since it started operating in 1871. As rivers run dry and reservoirs run low, farmers are warning of food shortages amid the deepening drought. Withthousands of deathsalready estimated to be linked to the extreme heat we saw in May and June alone, it’s likely this figure will climb higher still.The terrifying scenes we’ve seen so far this summer are the latest part of a pernicious long-term pattern. This is the third drought London has experienced in the past five years. Across the world, the past 11 years have been the 11 hottest ever recorded – and with a super strengthEl Niño forming in the Pacificwhich could pour yet more fuel on the fire, that trend is all but certain to continue. The climate emergency is here – and no one can say they didn’t see it coming.When I was first elected mayor back in 2016, I warned that our rapidly warming world would be the defining challenge of our time. I was the first mayor of a global city todeclare a climate emergency. Since then, a coalition of climate deniers and delayers has been relentless in condemning the green policies I’ve introduced. When I announced my intention to expand the Ulez – creating thelargest clean air zonein the world – they unsuccessfully attempted to drag down the debate and whip up a crude culture war. On social media, people were blinded by a dark blizzard of disinformation designed to discredit climate action. Radicalised by what he’d seen online, one man even detonated ahomemade bomb, destroying a Ulez camera in a shocking act of domestic terrorism.Looking back now, it feels like the fierce fight over Ulez marked the beginning of something else: a new age of extreme climate scepticism. In the years since, the horrifying reality of the climate crisis has come into sharp relief – and yet somehow the clamouring voices of denial and delay have grown louder than ever. Having dismissed climate change as a “con job”, Donald Trump has sought to sabotage global climate action, withdrawing the United Statesfrom the Paris agreementfor the second time, cutting support for clean energy, and boosting oil and gas production. In the UK, where cross-party consensus on the climate crisis has collapsed, his ideas have been echoed by opposition politicians and rightwing populists who veer wildly between denialism and fatalism. As some claim the climate crisis is a hoax, others insist it’stoo late to act.Both arguments are bogus. The climate crisis is getting worse, but inLondonwe’ve shown that – with courage and creativity – we can prepare ourselves for its impacts. We’ve planted more than 640,000 trees across the capital, shading our streets from the summer sun. We’ve embraced rewilding while creating and improving more than 2,000 football pitches’ worth of green space, providing natural drainage to prevent flooding. And just last month, we set out a plan to clean up our rivers and create safe swimming sites where Londoners can cool down in the heat. We have more zero-emission buses than any city in Europe and about a third of our country’s electric charging points.At the same time, since I’ve been mayor our city’s carbon emissions have fallen by about a quarter, while our economy has continued to grow. And last year the Ulez helped us to get levels of nitrogen oxide – one of the most toxic pollutants in our air–within legal limitsalmost two centuries before experts predicted we would. Between 2019 and 2024, estimated deaths associated with air pollution in Londonfell by an estimated 40%.Through C40 Cities, a network of almost 100 global cities I co-chair, London is working side by side with cities around the world to take on the climate emergency – from rolling out new green buses to boosting the supply of renewable energy – but we cannot do this alone. National governments across the globe must step up and meet the gravity of this moment with renewed focus, funding and resolve. This includes our own government, which should reassure the public by reaffirming its commitment to net zero and making clear that it will continue to reduce our reliance on oil and gas and to invest in green projects.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExtreme heat breaks temperature records in central and eastern EuropeRead moreThe most common refrain I hear from climate deniers is that green policies are some kind of luxury divorced from the worries of working people who are just trying to get by. But the idea that you can separate the climate crisis from the cost of living is patently absurd. What happens when droughts cause food prices to rise and when oil-price shocks squeeze household budgets? When hospitals are overwhelmed by vulnerable people struggling in the heat? When railways and roads buckle, workplaces close and schools are shuttered? The notion that climate action represents “woke nonsense” relies on the ridiculous premise that the climate crisis isn’t real – or that if it is, we won’t feel its impact on our lives. This year has proven just how wrong that is.We are living in an era of extremes, and my fear is that – without urgent action – the worst is still to come. In this context, climate denial and delay isn’t just delusional – it’s deadly. Because it won’t be President Trump and the fossil fuel companies paying the price for failure – it will be the rest of us. If we are to protect our planet and the people who call it home, we must turn the tide on climate denial by preparing for a hotter future and embracing net zero like never before.Sadiq Khan is mayor of LondonExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionClimate science scepticism and denialExtreme heatSadiq KhanLondonAir pollutionLow emission zonescommentShareReuse this content

title: Lime bikes hurtling around the city: is this the revenge of a priced-out generation? | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: From running red lights to dumping bikes, some Lime users get a bad rap. But many who grumble about them don’t appreciate their own privilege, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: From running red lights to dumping bikes, some Lime users get a bad rap. But many who grumble about them don’t appreciate their own privilege, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: A 2023 report commissioned by Lime found that ‘20% of Lime riders in London had never cycled before’.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/AlamyView image in fullscreenA 2023 report commissioned by Lime found that ‘20% of Lime riders in London had never cycled before’.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/AlamyOpinionEbikesLime bikes hurtling around the city: is this the revenge of a priced-out generation?Andy BeckettFrom running red lights to dumping bikes, some Lime users get a bad rap. But many who grumble about them don’t appreciate their own privilegeSat 8 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 10.48 EDTShareThe night belongs to Lime bikes in the capital this summer. Buses and tube carriages are boiling, cars crawl between low traffic neighbourhoods and Thames Water roadworks, and pedestrians plod through the sticky heat. But Lime riders exist in a different, breezier realm: whirring along, chatting in pairs or blissfully alone, weaving through the city’s tree-lined maze, choosing impulsively between destinations, rarely stopping for anything or anyone.“My favourite part of a night out is Lime biking home,” writesAnnie Lord, a dating columnist and author, in Freewheeling: Essays on Cycling. “As I ride up a hill, the bike’s electrics click … And, for a little while, I’m free.”According to the confidently expansive Californian company that owns Lime, Neutron Holdings Inc, theaverage ageof its London riders is 34. With the capital’s weather becoming warmer and drier, and social media and other online sources making more information about things riders could do instantly available, rented e-bikes seem a perfect tool to unlock the city’s possibilities. Across the globe, they are changing urban life: speeding it up, connecting previously out-of-the-way places, and making many women feel safer at night. Where I live in Hackney, once one of the capital’s more isolated boroughs and now one ofthe busiest Lime markets, many pubs are enjoying a bike-driven boom on summer nights, with the bright green bikes glowing outside like lurid cocktails before their riders wobble home.Yet since Limes became available in London and other British cities in 2018, the narrative has focused on their negative impacts. The way their riders often run red lights and cycle on pavements. How bikes are oftendumped in pedestrian spacesafter use, blocking entrances and vulnerable people’s safe routes. The fact that riders sometimes don’t share space considerately with traditional cyclists, and take over footpaths in parks. The strong sense that some Lime users can barely cycle at all. A2023 reportcommissioned by Lime found that “20% of Lime riders in London had never cycled before”. That is not as straightforwardly positive a statistic as the company likes to think.Other data about Lime usage is hard to come by, as the company considers it commercially sensitive. But information from Transport for London suggests Limes are disproportionately responsible for injuries to pedestrians. It estimates that in 2024 about 12% of the city’s cycling journeys were made on rented e-bikes, of which Lime is by far the biggest provider, yet rented bikes were reportedly responsible foralmost a thirdof cyclist collisions with pedestrians that required police intervention. As anyone who walks much in London knows, Limes have changed the experience of crossing a road.In truth, the Lime phenomenon is both an imposition and a liberation; an improvement to city life, and a sign of its sometimes alienating intensification; an expression of a certain kind of urban privilege (a half-hourLondonride can cost over £10), and evidence of its diminution. It shows how the relationship has changed between mobility and property, especially among the young.In 1975, Peter Ambrose and Bob Colenutt, two far-sighted British analysts of urban places, wrote in their book The Property Machine: “The city is a zone of conflict between competing claims for land.” In today’s London, as in other cities where space is sought-after and expensive, many Lime riders are young professionals, who in the past would have owned or rented homes close to the best public transport. Nowadays, that’s unaffordable for most of them, as is property ownership of any kind – as shown by the fact that the age of the average London first-time buyer has recently overtaken that of the average Lime rider,at 35.E-bike rental, whether for commuting or pleasure, is a solution to the scattering of these people to less-connected suburbs. Young Lime riders in a hurry, you could say, represent the revenge of a generation priced out of living near tube stations. Meanwhile, some of those who complain about Lime users are older Londoners who were able to buy properties in more convenient locations. They say Lime bikes are starting to dominate the city, but late-20th-century homebuyers have a much deeper hold on the capital.Tensions between the two groups can be reduced. This year, Hackney councilsays it has“worked with Lime … to install a high density of dedicated parking bays for the bikes, and compliance [by riders] is generally good”. To discourage riders from running red lights – a practice Lime’s critics claim is encouraged by its policy of charging by the minute – the council has also agreed with Limea flat fee for local residents: £1.75 for trips of up to 25 minutes that start in the borough, the same price as a bus fare, and the lowest Lime rate in London. Amid all the acrimony about rental bikes, it’s often forgotten – deliberately so by the much more powerful motoring lobby – that in polluted cities with unequal public health, more cycling is good.Yet a collaborative, responsible bike rental culture involving Lime, its customers and the overworked local authorities tasked with regulating both is some way off. Partly, this is because of commercial pressures: despite having big investors such as Uber, Lime isheavily in debtand not yet profitable. Meanwhile, as with many tech-enabled enterprises, key aspects of its business model have social costs. “People love the flexibility of being able to start and end their journey anywhere”said oneof Lime’s senior executives, Andrew Savage, last year. What he would not – could not – acknowledge was that absolute convenience for his customers can mean inconvenience for everyone else. As usual last night, despite Hackney’s ban on leaving Lime bikes anywhere but official parking bays, someone left one blocking some of my road.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnless divided, expensive cities such as London build more affordable homes, provide more widely available public transport, and make bicycle ownership less vulnerable to criminals – in other words, make mobility and housing less competitive and hierarchical – the sometimes petty, sometimes dangerous rental bike wars are likely to carry on. But at least we won’t all be stuck in cars.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsEbikesOpinionCycle hire schemesLondonCyclingEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve always felt too old and too young at the same time’: The Last of Us star Bella Ramsey on swapping child stardom for cult television – and Celebrity Traitors | Bella Ramsey | The Guardian
description: At 22, Ramsey has already been on our screens for a decade, and nominated for every award going. So why do they find it strange to be called an actor?
Author: Rebecca Nicholson
Headline: At 22, Ramsey has already been on our screens for a decade, and nominated for every award going. So why do they find it strange to be called an actor?
Content: Bella Ramsey: ‘I’m going to be more famous for a bit.’ All portraits: Linda Brownlee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBella Ramsey: ‘I’m going to be more famous for a bit.’ All portraits: Linda Brownlee/The GuardianBella RamseyInterview‘I’ve always felt too old and too young at the same time’: The Last of Us star Bella Ramsey on swapping child stardom for cult television – and Celebrity TraitorsRebecca NicholsonAt 22, Ramsey has already been on our screens for a decade, and nominated for every award going. So why do they find it strange to be called an actor?Sat 8 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBella Ramsey often feels more comfortable around older people. The actor, 22, who is non-binary and uses they/them pronouns, has been working professionally since they were 11, when they got their first TV job as the child noblewoman Lyanna Mormont inGame of Thrones. For half of their life, they have been in adult environments, talking to adults, working with adults. Even so, the London cafe in which Ramsey has chosen to meet makes any retirement home look like a creche. It is full of old men with their dogs, popping in for a cup of tea and a morning chat.“It feels like it belongs in the Midlands. It feels a bit, like, shit and familiar,” says Ramsey, who grew up in the East Midlands and can say that with affection. Their curly hair is short, pushed back off their face, and they have a single gold hoop in one ear. The plan had been to go for a walk this morning, but it is raining so we have a cup of tea and wait for the drizzle to pass. Ramsey seems both younger and older than 22, depending on the moment. Sometimes, within a single sentence, they sound ancient and wise, and also like a bookish teenager, discovering with amazement how they think they might feel about the world.Perhaps this, too, is a result of being on film and television sets for so long. Legend has it that Ramsey’s character in Game of Thrones was only supposed to be in a single scene, but their performance was one of pure grit, and they remained in the show for three seasons, almost until its bitter end. That grit took another shape in Lena Dunham’s charming medieval comedy filmCatherine Called Birdy, in which they played a young English noblewoman scheming to reject the suitors who wanted to trap her, and it appears again in the British prison drama Time, in which Ramsey was a pregnant heroin addict. But it was HBO’s massive, dystopian drama The Last of Us, an adaptation of the popular video game, that made them a name internationally.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenRamsey with Pedro Pascal in The Last of Us (2024), top, and in Catherine Called Birdy (2022), bottom. Photographs: AP; Capital Pictures/AlamyRamsey was cast as its young lead, Ellie, an orphan who, in the midst of a zombie-like apocalypse, joins forces with Joel (Pedro Pascal), who becomes a father figure to her. When it first aired in 2023, Ramsey and Pascal found themselves at the centre of one of the year’s most successful and hyped new shows. The duo became the object of parasocial ardour, with fans rooting for their cross-generational friendship, and both were nominated for every acting award going – Ramsey for two Emmys, two Golden Globes, two Critics Choice awards, an Actor award and a Bafta.Ellie is a complex character, brittle and petulant, yet Ramsey’s performance gives her vulnerability and heart. As with Time and Game of Thrones, the actor has a knack for conveying rough-edged softness, for young women who mask their inner turmoil by fronting up to the world.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenIn Time (2021), top, and in Game of Thrones (2011). Photographs: Album/Alamy; HBOIn person, Ramsey seems so earnest and gentle that it is easy to forget just how much they have done over the past 10 years. One benefit of working so hard, for so long, is that they have been able to buy their first flat, close to where we’re sitting today, on the edge of a lovely park in a suburban area of London. They have been unpacking boxes this morning. “I feel like this cafe might become my regular eating spot,” says Ramsey. “They also do jacket potatoes, which is my favourite thing. No one does jacket potatoes any more, properly.”Ramsey feels guilty about the fact that they have bought a flat at 22. “It feels very wrong! You’re not supposed to do that until you’re older.” The flat is small, cosy, one-bedroom, and they are living alone, happily. Their thoughts about it unspool at length, as they talk out the good and the bad, each argument undulating softly, taking its turn. Ramsey often seems as if they are in discussion with themselves, carefully weighing up both sides of a point before they decide to make it.“I’ve done it a bit early. I started working when I was 11 and I’m now 22, so it’s been 10 years, and I guess people maybe start working when they’re 21 and then buy a house when they’re 31, so I don’t know. Buying a house is impossible now, and it’s only because I ended up in this industry, that pays people too much money, that I’ve been able to do it.” They take a breath. “It just feels like a glitch in the system. I feel so embarrassed by it.”Living alone suits Ramsey; they need it. “Else I sort of become almost less of a person. I become whoever I’m around, in a way. I just meld to the people around me.” Is that a people-pleasing thing? “I think so, but it’s also aneverythingthing.” For example, they say, right now they are looking at me, so they can’t see themselves. “In my head, it’s like you’re the only one who’s here. So, yeah, I don’t know. It’s an interesting thing that I’m just beginning to understand.” I am not quite sure I do understand, but it sounds like an excess of empathy. It also sounds as if Ramsey relishes being alone, and being alone is not common when they are working. “It’s really nice to be able to come home and just be me and I’m not having to worry about how anyone else is feeling.”View image in fullscreendouble quotation markAged 11, I was away from home for 16 weeks, over the summer. Home at weekends, but in a hotel room by myselfRamsey prefers to keep their family’s lives private, and does not want to specify where they come from in the East Midlands, but it sounds rural and remote. “It was quite specific and wonderful.” School was a drive away, and it wasn’t the kind of place where you could walk to a friend’s house, or vice versa, so they kept themselves busy with after-school clubs. When they were 10, they auditioned for theTelevisionWorkshop in Nottingham, the young actors’ group that has been called the working‑class Rada, and which counts Samantha Morton, Jack O’Connell, Vicky McClure and Felicity Jones among its attenders. Ramsey failed to get in the first time, but was invited back to re-audition at age 11. “And then I got in. It was such a good lesson. For your very first introduction to be a rejection, I think, is perfect.”Did they audition because they wanted a career in acting? “No! I definitely didn’t go there with that in mind.” The Workshop is firm about that not being the point of the group, and Ramsey insists that they only took part for their own enjoyment. “And then I started to get auditions for things. And even then, I never thought about it as being a career. It was just fun, and then when it did become my career, and everyone started calling it that, I found it very strange, and still do.” Can they call it a career now? “Nooo,” Ramsey says, cringing a little. “Feels wrong.” Maybe in time? “I mean, it has definitely been an experience that is now feeling like work, which it hadn’t when I was younger.”Ramsey seems to have escaped the notorious curse of the child star. They seem nice and normal, in so much as it can be normal that32 million people watched them in the season one finale ofThe Last of Us. As a child, they were protected from some of the industry’s cruelties, yet, ever the pragmatist, they suggest that such protections were both good and bad for them. Take The Worst Witch, an adaptation of the beloved children’s books by Jill Murphy. Ramsey was 11 when they were cast as Mildred Hubble, the main character. They were not allowed to have a parent chaperone them on set – “I think to avoid pushy stage parents,” they say today. “But it was terrible for me. I’d never been away from home, even for a sleepover. I didn’t like school trips. I wanted to be around my parents. And then I was away from home for 16 weeks, over the summer. Home at weekends, but in a hotel room by myself [while working], at age 11.”View image in fullscreenThe young cast were looked after by professional chaperones, but, as the lead, Ramsey felt the weight of responsibility. “I was put in an interconnecting room with one who was 10 and told that I was to help look after her,” they recall. At the time, that felt fine. “I felt like I could just do it. I didn’t feel that young.” And now? “Now I look at 11-year-olds, and I’m like, God, you’retiny.” People like to ask Ramsey if they feel as if they missed out on having a traditional childhood. “I think some of the freedom and innocence of it, sure. But I was having so much fun. I didn’t want to be anywhere else other than on set.” They loved acting, loved being part of something. “It was one of the worst times and the best times of my young little life. I guess it sealed the thing that was already there, of being older than I was.”Recently, for the first time since The Worst Witch, Ramsey found themselves acting with a group of their peers. In the film Sunny Dancer, they play a teenage cancer survivor called Ivy, who heads off to summer camp with other teenagers who have had, or who have, cancer. Ivy is angry at the world, and feels isolated by what she has been through. It is a sweet, wonky coming-of-age film, with a very British eye on the teenage experience. There is banter, there is sex in a tent, and there is a lot of vodka being swilled from the bottle.“I was so nervous that I’d be on the edge of things, and that they’d all get along really well, and that I’d be the odd one out, or not as included,” Ramsey admits. They have spoken before about being miserable at school and not fitting in with people their own age. “I’ve always felt slightly on the outside, too old and too young at the same time,” they say today, which makes sense. They were more comfortable around adults, yet their silliness and sense of fun seemed childish to their schoolmates. “It’s probably a neurodiverse thing as well,” they say. Ramsey had long suspected that they were neurodivergent, and received a formal diagnosis when filming the first season of The Last of Us. “I just felt like I couldn’t access anyone, or that people couldn’t access me. I just felt a bit strange.”Sunny Dancer sounds as if it was liberating for Ramsey. “As I’ve got older, I’ve found people my age easier. I think everyone levelled out.” The film’s cast was effectively living out a version of the summer camp that they were depicting on screen. “Everyone got on with each other in slightly different ways, and started to annoy each other a little bit, in a familial, sibling way. It wassofun.” There is a lot of drinking in the film. Ramsey once said that they had never been drunk. Is that still the case? “I’d say I’ve got a little bit closer to that,” they reply, coyly. “Maybe a little bit happy? But I’ve still never had a hangover.” Suddenly, Ramsey sounds exactly like a 22-year-old.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenAged 11, in The Worst Witch (2017), top, in Sunny Dancer (centre) and with Daisy Haggard in Maya (bottom), both 2026. Photographs: BBC; Sunny Dancer Distribution Ltd; Channel 4The film was supposed to be the last time that Ramsey would play a teenager. “It was going to be my final big bang,” they say. But they’re playing another one, in Maya, a new thriller for Channel 4, in which Ramsey stars as a teenage girl forced into a witness protection programme with her mother, played by Daisy Haggard, who also writes and co-directs the series. “I really thought that I wanted to move away from that, but then, also, I’m only going to be able to play teenagers for a very limited amount of time in my life. I may as well, if they’re interestingly written.” It has been produced by the company behind The Tourist and Fleabag, so may well be worth that brief return to adolescence.It sounds as if Ramsey is as busy as ever, then, but right now they’re not filming anything at all. They are writing a TV series, which they can’t yet talk about, and working on music with friends. “I really don’t want to just be an actor who makes music. I really want them to be separate,” they say. They are taking it seriously. “I don’t want people to listen just because it’s me.” Later in the summer, they will go back to Vancouver for the third and final season of The Last of Us. Filming has already begun, but Ramsey’s services are not yet needed. Ellie is absent from the story for a period of time, as the focus has shifted to her nemesis, Abby, played by Kaitlyn Dever.Ramsey has enjoyed this time off. “I was getting to a place where I’d done a bit too much and was starting to not enjoy it, a bit, and not feel inspired, and feel a bit resentful of it.” They never wanted to feel that way about acting. “I couldn’t do that, for my 11-year-old self. It was their favourite thing in the world. So I took a step away, and now I am really excited to go back and I miss it.”They can’t talk about what is coming up in The Last of Us, not because of any restrictions, but because they have yet to see the scripts. During season one, their friendship with Pascal became a fan favourite. Ramsey called Pascal “Pedge”. Pascal called Ramsey “Bellie”. For plot purposes, he was barely in season two. Are they still in touch? “Yeah. But, like, yes, loosely in touch, yeah. But it feels like an entirely separate thing.” Their friendship has been endlessly clipped and memed – him calling Ramsey his “blessing”; Ramsey talking of their “deep-rooted connection” – and when the topic comes up, Ramsey has the look of someone who has been asked about it several thousand times before. “People get invested in the characters,” they say, but now seems weary of the fuss and won’t go any deeper. “I’m not sure. It’s sort of weird to talk about it … Let’s move on to a different topic.”It is still wet outside, but it feels like we need a change of scene. “I’m like a dog: I need to be walked,” says Ramsey. “If I don’t walk in a day, I feel it. I have to move my body somehow.” They have sturdy boots and an outdoorsy jacket, so we decide to go for a stroll through the rain. Ramsey turned 18 while making the first season of The Last of Us. It sounds as if that time was a transformative one. It was when they realised that they were neurodivergent. It was when they talked about their gender identity. In 2023, they told the New York Times that their gender “has always been very fluid” and that they would tick a box marked “non‑binary”, if asked.double quotation markThere’s a misconception that if you get someone’s pronouns wrong, they’ll be offended. It’s no big deal, as long as you’re respectfulView image in fullscreenStyling: Lucy Tempest Walker. Hair and makeup: Wendy Turner using Dr Levy for skin, Lisa Eldridge for makeup and Sam McKnight for hair.  T-shirt: Sandro. Sweater: With Nothing Underneath. Denim jacket: Levi’s at RokitRamsey has always talked about this with sensitivity and nuance, but they say now that they feel they weren’t given enough warning about how much of a talking point it might become. Just before press for The Last of Us began, they were asked which pronouns they would be using. “I’d expressed being in the middle.” For Ramsey, it was just a “helpful descriptor. And then suddenly it became a huge thing, where it’s, like, this is your identity and it’s who you are. I wasn’t aware of the impact of that, both positively and negatively. But I think the positive impact outweighs the negative, in terms of being visible or giving a name to an experience.”They remain relaxed about pronouns. “Like, people will see me and they’re going to go ‘she’ because, of course, I would. I accidentally misgender people. It’s a thing that even I have to learn. There’s a misconception that if you get someone’s pronouns wrong, they’re going to be offended and it’s a big thing. It’s just not a big deal as long as you’re respectful, and I think if somebody does correct you, then you respect that and you try your best. And so I’m pretty chill about it.”What is different now is that their family also uses they/them pronouns for them. “I just think it feels the most accurate, is all that it is. They’ve been lovely about it. They always got a free pass, but it started to be weird because everyone in my life was calling me ‘they’ except them, and they know me the best. They were, like, maybe we can just try. And so it’s very sweet, hearing them try.” Again, they say, they are very laid‑back about it. “I understand why it has become such a thing that people want to talk about and talk to me about, but it really is just a descriptive word for part of my experience of being in the world.”In the same interview, Ramsey also said that they were not 100% straight. “I said something about being a bit wavy,” they laugh. “I mean, I think most people are, slightly. Like, who knows who you’re falling in love with, you know? You just meet a person and you fall in love with them, and that’s kind of all there is to it.” What has your experience of that been, so far? “I’ve experienced it and I just think it’s a beautiful part of life.” I ask if they’re in love now. “I’m not talking about that!” they say, squirming a little, like the teenager that they have only recently been.Ramsey may have enjoyed some time off recently, but managed to fit in filming the second series of The Celebrity Traitors, alongside a pleasantly eccentric cast, including Miranda Hart, Richard E Grant, Maya Jama and Ross Kemp. They said yes to doing it because they love the party game Mafia, on which the show is loosely based. “I started playing it in the Television Workshop, so I’ve been playing it since I was 11. I love it so much. I’ve done Mafia nights at my flat. So fun. In my head, it was just, like, I’m going to go to this castle and play this game for two weeks.” Had they seen the first series? “Yeah. So I’m, like, you just go and you do that. But I’m too naive. I should know, after doing this for so many years, that what you see on screen isn’t actually what it is,” they say, with a smile.Sunny Dancer review – ‘chemo camp’ gives teen drama a fresh spinRead moreAre they nervous about it coming out? “No, not really.” A pause. “Well, actually, I might try to be out of the country,” they say, laughing.
