They are aware that it will bring them attention, and for the most part, right now, they can wander around the park, with the old men and the dogs, without many second glances coming their way. “So the idea that I’m going to be more famous for a bit … ” they say, and taper off.Ramsey has learned, over the past decade, that fame is fleeting and it comes and goes. “Suddenly everyone recognises you and you’re famous for two weeks, and then there’s somebody else. So it will be a bit of a thing for a few weeks and then people will move on, you know?” They say this with the wisdom of an old hand, someone who has been at this for a long time already. “So I’m not too worried,” they say, sweetly, and set off home, to unpack more boxes.Sunny Dancer will be in cinemas across the UK from 14 AugustExplore more on these topicsBella RamseyThe Last of UsGame of ThronesTelevisionPedro PascalinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘She’s the voice of a really particular moment’: how Phoebe Bridgers became her generation’s defining songwriter | Phoebe Bridgers | The Guardian
description: The US songwriter’s third album has drawn rave reviews, she counts Taylor Swift as a fan and pop bears the imprint of her wit and pathos. Her peers explain how she did it
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: The US songwriter’s third album has drawn rave reviews, she counts Taylor Swift as a fan and pop bears the imprint of her wit and pathos. Her peers explain how she did it
Content: ‘Her music is so precise and weird and beautiful’ … Phoebe Bridgers performing on The Tonight Show With Jimmy Fallon, 15 July 2026.Photograph: NBC/Todd Owyoung/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Her music is so precise and weird and beautiful’ … Phoebe Bridgers performing on The Tonight Show With Jimmy Fallon, 15 July 2026.Photograph: NBC/Todd Owyoung/Getty ImagesPhoebe Bridgers‘She’s the voice of a really particular moment’: how Phoebe Bridgers became her generation’s defining songwriterThe US songwriter’s third album has drawn rave reviews, she counts Taylor Swift as a fan and pop bears the imprint of her wit and pathos. Her peers explain how she did itKatie HawthorneSat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis week, indie star Phoebe Bridgers releases her long-awaited third album, six years since her pandemic-era breakthrough. Alongside a slew of glittering reviews for Lost Weekend, includingfive stars from the Guardian, with it comes her first solo charting single in the UK – although the Californian musician’s influence runs far deeper than reviews or record sales could measure. Just how did a RuneScape-referencing, Halloween-costumed Berklee drop-out become the most influential songwriter of the 2020s?Bridgers’ idiosyncratic writing has shaped the sound of the decade. Her second album Punisher, released in June 2020 (and recorded many months before), spookily anticipated that strange, lonely year: in her eerie double-tracked vocals (a nod to Bridgers’ musical hero, Elliott Smith), Bridgers sang of empty shopping malls and conspiracy theories over lush, unsettling music made from watery electric guitar, Mellotron, strings, screams and birdsong. Today, Bridgers’ distinctive mix of dry wit and pathos is traceable in the lyrics of pop’s new chart toppers, such as Olivia Rodrigo andGracie Abrams, while heavyweights across generations and genres, including Paul McCartney, Taylor Swift and SZA, have clamoured for collaborations. “Sheisthe reference now,” Swifttold the Guardian in 2022.“She’s the voice of a really particular moment,” says author Carmen Maria Machado, who first met Bridgers when she attended an event for Machado’s prize-winning memoirIn the Dream House. There is a kinship between Machado’s prose and Bridgers’ lyrics – both are candid, haunted, unafraid to get gruesome – and it resulted in Machado publishing a short story to accompany Punisher. “Phoebe’s never looking directly on, rather looking askance,” says Machado. “Her music is so precise and weird and beautiful; it’s a prayer or an ode to this place that we’re living in, while also watching it fall apart.”Phoebe Bridgers: Lost Boys – videoReviews for Lost Weekend have highlighted the album’s deeply personal subject matter – it discusses the death of Bridgers’ father, and the end of her engagement to actor Paul Mescal – but also Bridgers’ enduringly surreal sense of humour. When performing single Lost Boys on the Tonight Show, she played it first with a band of children, who were fizzing with excitement, and then again in an acoustic arrangement with veteran folk legend Dan Reeder. The effect was trippy, sweet and faintly morbid: distinctly Phoebe.For Naomi McPherson, a member of synth-pop three-piece Muna, it’s this mixture of matter-of-fact and magical that makes Bridgers so distinct. “It’s infuriating and inspiring how good she is,” McPherson says, pointing to a forthcoming Lost Weekend song with a line about turning down the stereo volume to better parallel park: “To be able to put that in a song in a way that isn’t stupid, but is actually brilliant and somehow deeply touching, is an enormous feat.”Muna signed to Bridgers’ record label Saddest Factory in 2021, joining a cohort of imaginative, predominantly queer musicians united under Bridgers’ mentality of “getting cool stuff out to people as fast as possible”. Singer-songwriter Claud (whose song A Good Thing soundtracked the finale to queer romance series Heartstopper) was the label’s first signee. They emphasise the value of Bridgers’ support at a vital time for both artists: “I knew I could trust her opinions and instincts for my project, because I love everything she does with hers.”The label was rolled into parent company Dead Oceans earlier this year after a trademark dispute, but its lasting influence reflects Bridgers’ determination to change the music industry for the better – as didher supergroup, Boygenius, formed with songwriter friends Lucy Dacus and Julien Baker. Together the trio played their biggest stages to date and clinched three Grammy awards, while Bridgers took the award ceremony as an opportunity to condemn former Recording Academy boss Neil Portnow, who had beenaccused of sexual assault, for his disparaging“step up”comment towards women in music: “Rot in piss!”View image in fullscreenFrom left: Bridgers, Lucy Dacus and Julien Baker of Boygenius accepting the award for best rock performance at the 2024 Grammy awards.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APBridgers’ plain-talking has won her a passionate fanbase, many of whom are easily spotted by their matching ghost tattoos – a reference to the cover of her 2017 debut Stranger in the Alps – and her concerts are intense: Claud, who has toured with Bridgers, describes “crowds of tens of thousands where you can actually hear a pin drop”. It tracks, then, that Bridgers decided to promote Lost Weekend not with sit-down interviews but a series of secretive pop-up shows across the US, taking the new songs straight to fans.‘We have to nurture each other’: how Olivia Rodrigo and Gen Z reinvented the power balladRead moreFan Baleigh Epperly, an environmental advocate, DJ and co-founder of queer, female-led local DJ collective Their House, “freaked out” when Bridgers rolled in to play at the Loud, a 500-capacity venue in her home town of Huntington, West Virginia. “We never get shit,” she laughs, saying it meant “everything” that Bridgers was visiting “the overlooked places, the places where she knows her fans are”.The tiny shows were first come, first served, capped at $50 a ticket, and mobile-phone free. Epperly says they all sat cross-legged, watching Bridgers play as if it were a house show. “It was the talk of the town, literally,” she marvels, predicting that the performance will have a lasting impact on young musicians who may have internalised damaging stereotypes about Appalachia: “If Phoebe is good enough for West Virginia, then you’re good enough to play here, to live here, to be from here.”Muna’s Katie Gavin describes Bridgers’ influence in similar terms. “She’s an aspirational songwriter for me. Seeing her make art makes me want to do it, which is what the best music does.”Explore more on these topicsPhoebe BridgersIndienewsShareReuse this content

title: [seagull] review – silence proves golden in innovative if puzzling shot at Chekhov | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Magnificently expressive performances make this ambitious sign-language production feel viscerally new. But what’s with the square brackets?
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Magnificently expressive performances make this ambitious sign-language production feel viscerally new. But what’s with the square brackets?
Content: Startling … [seagull].Photograph: Kurt van der Elst/Kvde.beView image in fullscreenStartling … [seagull].Photograph: Kurt van der Elst/Kvde.beEdinburgh festival 2026Review[seagull] review – silence proves golden in innovative if puzzling shot at ChekhovStudio theatre, EdinburghMagnificently expressive performances make this ambitious sign-language production feel viscerally new. But what’s with the square brackets?Arifa AkbarSat 8 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 10.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe silence in this adaptation “after” Anton Chekhov’s The Seagull is startling. Performed straight through at two and a half hours, the intakes of breath, tears, screams of anguish and, of course, the gunshots when they come arrest the senses. So do the intermittent spoken words, which sound almost like an intrusion, and occasional lines of music.Directed by Stijn Van Opstal, this is a sharp, ambitious, modern-dress chamber piece at the Edinburgh international festival by Belgian theatre companies Toneelhuis and Olympique Dramatique, with numerous translators and adapters. For the first 30 minutes, there is just signing on stage (Flemish Sign Language translated into British Sign Language), with screens translating dialogue.The story is the same but appears new and visceral. Konstantin (Yana Wuytjens) is an aspiring writer intent on discovering innovative forms of storytelling, but is overshadowed by his grand actor-mother, Arkadina (Sofie Decleir), who comes back to the family’s country estate with her lover, Trigorin (Serge Vlerick), in tow. He is a distinguished novelist and his presence gives rise to a love triangle involving Konstantin’s companion, Nina (Yousra Boukantar), who is an aspiring actor.Performers are a mix of D/deaf and hearing, magnificently expressive across the board – though Lobke Leirens, as ancillary character Masja, has a particularly formidable presence. Arkadina is a good blend of thespy self-importance, charm and maternal concern. Konstantin is performed by a woman, which makes his relationship with Nina somehow more tender and intimate, while Wuytjens brings a good blend of anger, tantrum and earnestness to the part.View image in fullscreenFormidable … [seagull].Photograph: Kurt van der Elst/Kvde.beCharacters swill in boredom and sometimes seem ridiculous. Humour sits close to anguish. Sound clangs. Damiaan De Schrijver and Van Opstal’s set design on a traverse stage exposes the construction of its effects. A host of techniques amplify the sense of overt theatricality.A Trial: After An Enemy of the People review – Wagner Moura upends Ibsen and keeps us guessingRead moreActors bring on the props, sometimes create sound effects and take up the wooden boards towards the end, which brings a plaintive, packed-up, autumnal quality to both the summer home and the drama. But the production is hampered by too many of these techniques; they come to seem like tricks, there for the sake of clever contrivance. Why, for instance, is there a seemingly random freezing of some scenes? Why do the surtitles become non-grammatical and seemingly a literal translation before returning back to standardised English? What, for that matter, is the point of the square brackets of the title? These questions are frustratingly unanswered.Then again, at its best, this play dazzles and contains a fresh, dangerous quality, as physical as a gut-punch in its climatic moments. Silence has never sounded louder or more loaded.AtStudio theatre, Edinburgh, until 11 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalAnton ChekhovDeafness and hearing lossBelgiumreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Is it OK to talk about Ariana Grande’s body? There is no right answer | Ariana Grande | The Guardian
description: I wish I could say that expressing concern for the pop star’s health is helpful – but I know from experience it’s not that simple
Author: Emma Madden
Headline: I wish I could say that expressing concern for the pop star’s health is helpful – but I know from experience it’s not that simple
Content: Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignAriana GrandeIs it OK to talk about Ariana Grande’s body? There is no right answerI wish I could say that expressing concern for the pop star’s health is helpful – but I know from experience it’s not that simpleEmma MaddenSat 8 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTShareThe last time I opened X, a photo ofAriana Grandeleaning over in a low-cut black dress, clavicle showing, was at the top of the feed. The post read: “hey @grok make Ariana Grande healthy and fat”.Images of celebrities at their most skeletal regularly rise to the top of social feeds because they generate enormous, dissenting engagement. Social media platforms have made half-hearted efforts tosuppressexplicit pro-eating disorder content; Instagram and TikTok redirect searches for “thinspo” toward support resources. Yet over the past couple weeks, Grande has sent users into a frenzy that outstrips the platforms’ attempts.The screenshot the user posted was taken from Grande’s music video for Petal, the title track from her latest album. Grande and her team have not said that she lives with any kind of eating disorder. Nevertheless, promotion for Petal has been thoroughly overshadowed by discussion of the singer’s ultra-thin body.double quotation markSomeone who is suffering can mistake isolation for self-preservationOther replies to the screenshot ranged from vicious attacks on Grande and other users’ bodies, to earnest, almost desperate pleas for empathy. Having lived with an eating disorder as a teenager, I recognize in these reactions a familiar pattern. People often respond to the visibly suffering body with a visceral pity intertwined with a kind of disgust. Whether that response actually protects anyone, or instead solidifies the very dynamics it seeks to resist, is a question worth returning to.Those of us who have lived through eating disorders and are witnessing this news cycle feel compelled to offer our own interpretations – to explain what this moment means, and to argue for the “right” way to speak about it. But precisely because disordered eating is so idiosyncratic and so forceful, there may be no single correct language for confronting it. The only honest response may be to acknowledge its contradictions.In the case of Grande, all of the prayers, best wishes and outcries so far haven’t provoked the public response so many have hoped for. Instead, it appears to have pushed her in the opposite direction. Over the weekend, just days after the release of Petal, arepresentative toldPeople magazine that Grande would be “taking a step back from visibility” after her current tour, cancelling future promotional plans and withdrawing from an upcoming West End revival of Sunday in the Park With George. At a recent concert, Grandeexplained to fansthat stepping back from the spotlight was something she had planned “a long time ago” and that it came from a “thoughtful and empowered place”.‘I had fantasies about how it would eventually serve me’: my struggle with disordered eatingRead moreIf this were a case of disordered eating, a retreat from public life might seem like a positive step towards recovery. But I know from experience that someone who is suffering can mistake isolation for self-preservation. The cruelty of an eating disorder is how easily it convinces you that it is the only thing standing between you and a world trying to take control away from you.Concerns over Grande’s body have hovered since the beginning of her teenage acting career. In 2013, the year she released her debut album, Yours Truly, she took to her old Tumblr account – which has itself been accused of “pro-ana” content, or content promoting disordered eating – to address “the rumors going around.” In ablogpostshe wrote that reports of “this whole ‘eating disorder thing’” had been “a bit blown out of proportion”.“Yes, I lost a bit of weight last year,” she continued. “It’s because I stopped eating junk food and started making healthy choices. I was happy with the way I was before and I’m still happy now! Just healthier!”More than a decade later, she made much the same point in a TikTok after people posted side-by-side photos of her during the Wicked press tour and the years when she acted on the Nickelodeon show Victorious. “The body you’ve been comparing my current body to was the unhealthiest version of my body,” she said in April 2023. “I was on a lot of antidepressants and drinking on them.”Her response reminded me of something the singer Fiona Apple said in 2013, after years of speculation about her weight. While performing on stage, Apple exploded at a heckler who shouted: “get healthy”. “I’m healthy and I shouldn’t even have to say any of that,” AppletoldPitchfork the next day. “What makes me unhealthy and puts me in danger is that kind of scrutiny itself.”double quotation markThe confused discourse surrounding Grande’s weight mirrors the paradox [of disordered eating]Avoiding scrutiny can become part of an eating disorder itself. I know this because I suffered for many years with bulimia, and I now realize my years spent hiding in the bathroom after every meal was an attempt to withdraw from any kind of outside opinion. When friends hugged me and recoiled at the touch of my bones, that only influenced me to raise the wall between myself and the rest of the world. It was an untenable and, frankly, devastating attempt to cope with the terror of puberty, trying all I could to stay both in control and independent of my body and its radical changes.On several levels, disordered eating is built on irreconcilable tensions. It requires relentless self-control while submitting to an all-consuming fixation. In seeking to disappear, the thin body only becomes a spectacle of morbid curiosity. What usually begins as an effort to master the self soon becomes an act of self-destruction. The confused discourse surrounding Grande’s weight mirrors the paradox. Every word feels stuck in place, because we don’t yet have a cultural script capable of holding all these ambiguities.It is obvious and true that the bodies of female celebrities are uniquely surveilled. It’s why Billie Eilishresisted that surveillanceby wearing oversized clothing and criticizing the public’s sense of entitlement to judge her body – a tacticGrande employed, too, in 2018, a year after the devastatingManchester Arena bombing.For much of the 2010s, the body positivity movement supplied a simple injunction against prying eyes: don’t comment on women’s bodies. It corrected for the smarmy and misogynistic tabloid treatment of celebrities in the aughts, discouraging public discussion of other people’s bodies as intrusive, harmful and unnecessary.But it might have been an overcorrection. Grande’s appearance presents a case where that consensus no longer feels entirely adequate, or ethically tenable. But it’s complicated. Two feminist arguments are at odds. The first is that women should not have to submit their bodies to public interpretation or explanation. The second is that eating disorders thrive in secrecy and denial. We do not want a culture that treats visible suffering – and conversations around them – as too taboo to acknowledge.After all, Grande has long featured in thinspo Pinterest boards. On private pro-ana message boards, users have found recognition in her public statements. “The whole ‘don’t worry about me’ and ‘the old me was sad and unhealthy’ sounds like people responding to an intervention lol,” one user wrote. On the pro-ana internet, Grande’s body is both hailed as aspirational and a huge trigger. In eating-disorder recovery Reddit communities, users describe her as the reason for their “relapse”, putting them back into the mindset of their illness. Beneath the now widely circulated photograph of Grande bending over, users in the underground X communityknown as EDTwthave openly compared themselves to her body and wondered how they might achieve a similar appearance.Ozempic is hailed as a miracle drug. But how does it affect people with eating disorders?Read moreMore broadly, her body has also become a proxy on to which wider cultural anxieties are projected. In a moment of GLP-1 drugs reinstating the aspiration of thinness, body positivity in retreat, bonesmashing still on the up, and Maga tradwives once again moralizing fatness, fears about the return of aughts-era anorexia have settled on to Grande herself. Whether or not those fears belong to her alone is almost beside the point. Her body has become the site through which the culture argues with itself.She is hardly the first celebrity on to whom those anxieties have been projected. From Karen Carpenter’s collapse from starvation at her parent’s home in 1983 to the many stars who have since publicly disclosed eating disorders – including Demi Lovato, Taylor Swift and Kesha – it is almost assumed that a significant portion of the female entertainment industry has, or has had, some form of eating disorder. The illness is simultaneously embedded within ordinary culture and yet treated as an aberration whenever it becomes visible.The desire to resolve those contradictions might even keep us at the distance the illness relies on, allowing us to imagine that a single correct response will absolve us of having to deal with it in the first place. Instead we could try broadening our concern towards the millions living with eating disorders by petitioning to improve a medical system that has so oftenfailedthem; insurers that routinelydeny careif the patient’s BMI is anything other than extremely emaciated; and clinicians who stillstigmatizethe illness.Grande’s visibility isn’t moving down the feed. People are continuing to debate it, defend it, plead for us to find another way to talk about it. But ultimately, another person’s physical and mental reality is out of our control; no one person’s recovery can be crowdsourced. If only it were all as simple as Grok editing Grande into health.In the US, help is available atnationaleatingdisorders.orgor by callingANAD’seating disorders hotline at 800-375-7767. In the UK,Beatcan be contacted on 0808-801-0677. In Australia, theButterfly Foundationis at 1800 33 4673. Other international helplines can be found atEating Disorder Hope

title: ‘Can’t stop smiling!’ The wait is over for epic Game of Thrones prequel The Mad King  | Theatre | The Guardian
description: New play, which has been a decade in the works, opens at the Royal Shakespeare theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon after five previews were cancelled
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: New play, which has been a decade in the works, opens at the Royal Shakespeare theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon after five previews were cancelled
Content: Tanisha Spring, Elizabeth Ayodele, Mariah Gale, Callum Woodhouse, Michael Shaeffer, Harmony Rose-Bremner, Luke Brady, Noah Ritter and Michael Abubakar, the cast of Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Seamus Ryan © RSCView image in fullscreenTanisha Spring, Elizabeth Ayodele, Mariah Gale, Callum Woodhouse, Michael Shaeffer, Harmony Rose-Bremner, Luke Brady, Noah Ritter and Michael Abubakar, the cast of Game of Thrones: The Mad King.Photograph: Seamus Ryan © RSCTheatre‘Can’t stop smiling!’ The wait is over for epic Game of Thrones prequel The Mad KingNew play, which has been a decade in the works, opens at the Royal Shakespeare theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon after five previews were cancelledChris WiegandStage editorSat 8 Aug 2026 06.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 06.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA winter of discontent is anticipated by the embattled characters in Game of Thrones, but the Royal Shakespeare Company is banking on a glorious summer with itsworld premiereof a prequel to the hit TV series based on George RR Martin’s fantasy novels.The new play,The Mad King, arrives 30 years to the month after the original publication of A Game of Thrones, the first novel in Martin’s series A Song of Ice and Fire. It has a gala performance in Stratford-upon-Avon on Saturday evening in a reconfigured Royal Shakespeare theatre with a capacity of 870. Tickets for the entire run, priced from £10 to £95, have already sold out.The RSC’s co-artistic directors,Daniel Evans and Tamara Harvey, have said that the epic play – which lasts 225 minutes including an interval – “thrillingly imagines events teased in the books” and they trumpet it as the “first-ever stage production arising from the canon of George RR Martin”. The Mad King bookmarks, handy for all those doorstop novels, are on sale in the RSC gift shop – although scripts for the play are not currently purchasable, leading to heated discussions on message boards about its plot, which involves familiar characters from the houses of Targaryen, Stark, Lannister, Baratheon and Martell. To “protect the magic” of the play, theatregoers with cameraphones are asked to cover them with stickers labelled “sworn shield”, a reference to a dutiful oath in Game of Thrones.View image in fullscreenNoah Ritter as Prince Rhaegar Targaryen and Harmony Rose-Bremner as Lyanna Stark in The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonThe play is adapted by Duncan Macmillan, who has worked on it for almost a decade. In the programme, Macmillan writes that its focus is a jousting tournament at Harrenhal – “a major event in Game of Thrones lore that has never been depicted on the page or on screen”. Macmillan added that he and director Dominic Cooke wanted to make a play “for fans and novices alike, a piece of theatre that sits inside the wider history but is also complete in its own right”. Macmillan and Cooke werefirst announcedin 2021 as collaborating on a Game of Thrones project for an unspecified venue.The Mad King – which unfolds on a cross-shaped stage with the audience all around and has a cast of three dozen – weathered a challenging period of previews. Five early performances were cancelled, with an announcement that “the actors, creative and technical teams [were taking] the additional time necessary to progress and refine the work in real time, owing to the ambitious and epic nature of the production and, as a knock-on effect of unforeseen delays to the fit-up process”. (A spokesperson for the RSC said that affected audiences were contacted to arrange refunds or to rebook their tickets.)The demand for tickets, alongside a sold out run ofThe Cherry Orchard(starringHelen Huntand Kenneth Branagh) in its Swan theatre, will help fill the company’s coffers after what Evans described last year as a“perilous situation”. A recent restructure has enabled the company to reduce its cost base by £2.8m a year. The RSC said the process was “not solely based on reducing our financial overheads” but also to help it “work as effectively and efficiently as possible and to position us to generate additional income to invest in the creation of theatre and learning through theatre, which is our founding purpose”.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Daniel Evans, Duncan Macmillan, George RR Martin, Tamara Harvey and Dominic Cooke.Photograph: Seamus Ryan © RSCBy transforming its stage into the world of Westeros for The Mad King, the RSC hopes to welcome audiences who are new to either its Stratford venue or to theatre more generally. In recent years, it has drawn upon existing IP with considerable success, including an adaptation of the Studio Ghibli filmMy Neighbour Totoro, also powered by imaginative puppetry like The Mad King. My Neighbour Totoro opened at the Barbican in London in 2022 andtransferred to the West End, where it will end its run in January.Among the audience at the Royal Shakespeare theatre on Friday night wasGame of Thronesfan Edward, 29, from Dudley, who said he had visited Birmingham Hippodrome and Wolverhampton Grand but it was his first time at the RSC. “I just can’t stop smiling – it’s so fun,” he said of the production, despite initially being “shocked when I saw the run time”. Another newcomer to the building was Aisha, 28, who had travelled from London. A fan of the franchise, Aisha said the play “compares very well to the books and films – they’ve done an amazing job”.View image in fullscreenMichael Shaeffer as King Aerys II Targaryen in The Mad King.Photograph: Johan PerssonRachel, 51, comes to the RSC a couple of times a year, most recently foran adaptation of Roald Dahl’s The BFG, and said that mixing Shakespeare with such adaptations provides “a good variety”. Diane, 66, was there to see The Cherry Orchard and expressed frustration that the company’s two main stages had no Shakespeare this summer (a trimmed version ofA Midsummer Night’s Dream, made with the Unicorn children’s theatre, ison at its third venue, The Other Place.) “For me personally it’s disappointing. I know that sounds snobby, I don’t mean it to, but the name’s the RoyalShakespeareCompany … The balance is off. It’s a little bit of a betrayal of their name and raison d’etre but I’m well aware they have financial difficulties.” Diane acknowledged: “I’m probably the only one on earth who hasn’t watched [the TV series] … I know there’s a following that’s very loyal.”On the fan forumTheatreboard, people who had seen The Mad King variously praised its “full Shakespearean tragic resonance” and “Shakespearean-ish cadence”, with one saying that it was “on a par in theatrical terms with the London 2012 opening ceremony”.Steven and Bethany, both 30, recently moved to Stratford and saw theRSC’s Henry Vearlier this year. Bethany arrived “hoping for a dragon tonight!” and Steven said that they hadn’t expected the RSC to stage such a production. “It brings in more people who wouldn’t usually come to the theatre,” said Bethany. “They might enjoy the experience and see what else is on offer as well. With it being in Stratford, rather than London, you’re bringing in different crowds.”“You’d expect to see it on the West End rather than Stratford,” agreed Steven. TheRSC’s Hamlet Hail to the Thief, another bid to draw new audiences by accompanying the tragedy with a Radiohead album, opens in London this winter. The Mad King is widely tipped to follow hot on its heels.Explore more on these topicsTheatreGame of ThronesRoyal Shakespeare CompanyGeorge RR MartinFantasy booksFantasy TVTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: A kids’ film taught me the power of delusion – and helped me chase my standup dreams | Comedy | The Guardian
description: The protagonist of A Little Princess wills reality to bend to her desires. Comedians need that same idiot confidence when we’re starting out, or else we’d all give up
Author: Olivia Ladanyi
Headline: The protagonist of A Little Princess wills reality to bend to her desires. Comedians need that same idiot confidence when we’re starting out, or else we’d all give up
Content: Illustration: Martin O’NeillView image in fullscreenIllustration: Martin O’NeillMy cultural awakeningComedyA kids’ film taught me the power of delusion – and helped me chase my standup dreamsThe protagonist of A Little Princess wills reality to bend to her desires. Comedians need that same idiot confidence when we’re starting out, or else we’d all give upExplore the rest of our coverage of the Edinburgh festival 2026Sarah Roberts; as told toOlivia LadanyiSat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwas 28 the first time I did standup. It was an open-mic competition where the audience decided the winner. As I held the tiny gold trophy, I decided to quit my job the next day. Some people might call that crazy, and it probably was. But I’d been honing that delusional self-belief since I was eight when I first watched the film adaptation of Frances Hodgson Burnett’s story A Little Princess.I already almost had the same name as its protagonist, Sara, a young girl who is sent off to boarding school while her father fights in the war. I wanted to be exactly like her. She was so sure of herself, and believed so completely in the worlds she created, that all the other girls at school wanted to be her friend. My favourite scene is the one where the girls sit on Sara’s bed, forming a circle round her as she tells fantastical stories. I would watch it and think: I want to tell stories that make people gather round me.But unlike Sara, I was shy and making friends didn’t come easily. I did, however, understand how to use my inner world to escape my reality. My imagination became my most powerful asset. It’s why I told everyone the reason I didn’t get into S Club Juniors was because I would overshadow the other members, when the reality was that I couldn’t sing or dance and hadn’t even got through the first round of auditions.double quotation markYou have to believe in what you’re doing, even after bombing to a room full of stag dos“Don’t you ever do that? Believe in something just to make it seem real?” Sara says in the film. At the boarding school, Sara’s belief that she’s a princess – “All girls are! Even if they live in tiny old attics, even if they dress in rags, even if they aren’t pretty, or smart or young” – helps her to stand up against the cruel headteacher, Miss Minchin.As a teenager, I wrote poems and short stories about boys I fancied, imagining they fancied me back. As an adult, I would fantasise about being anywhere else to escape my meaningless nine-to-five that largely involved sending emails. Those fantasies were a refusal to believe that this was my fate. It was as if by having them, I was preparing myself for a bigger, more exciting life.As a standup comedian, delusion is your greatest asset: you have to believe in what you’re doing more than anyone else. When it’s 2am and you’re at a service station on the M6 after bombing to a room full of stag dos, knowing you have to do it all again tomorrow, you tell yourself that it’s just one show, and you’re building towards something bigger.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEuphoria gave me the courage to come out to my friend – now we’re togetherRead moreSara never loses her resolve. Even after everyone believes her father has died and left her penniless, and she’s forced to live in the attic as a servant girl, she still insists she’s a princess. One day, when Miss Minchin locks her in with no breakfast, lunch or dinner, Sara imagines a feast with candles and trays of good things to eat, and there, laid out in the morning, are platters of sausages, muffins and fresh fruit. Her imagination helps her to survive her reality until her fantasy becomes her reality. That’s the thing about delusion: you have to believe it’s real until it becomes real. Fantasy isn’t just escapism, it’s strategy.I have been doing standup consistently for five years now. The longer you do it, the more you embrace failing: you don’t get better if you don’t bomb. You need delusion, resilience and persistence, the same qualities I admired in Sara all those years ago. You have to believe in your version of reality even when everything around you seems to prove the opposite.Every time I do standup now, I want to feel exactly like Sara, enchanting her classmates at her boarding school. I didn’t realise until I rewatched A Little Princess as an adult that she’s not just a fantasist – she’s a standup comedian.Sarah Roberts: Scary Movie 7is at theMonkey Barrel 2,Edinburgh, to 30 August.Did a cultural moment prompt you to make a major life change? Email us at cultural.awakening@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsComedyMy cultural awakeningEdinburgh festivalEdinburgh festival 2026featuresShareReuse this content

You’re probably either in or out by this point but, in case it makes a difference, the film stars Ari Millen of Orphan Black fame as the titular dispenser of summer treats.A Child of My OwnOut nowA true-crime docudrama based on the real-life case of a Mexican woman who abducted a baby from the hospital where she worked as a nurse. Chilean director Maite Alberdi’s factual account is interwoven with a telling of the story from the perpetrator’s point of view.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenUrine for a treat … Joji.Photograph: Evers PundJojiDublin,11 August; London,13 August; touring to 16 AugustThe Japanese-Australian YouTube prankster turned serious musical artist arrives in arenas in support of February’s fourth album of ornate electronic ballads, Piss in the Wind. The night’s singalong moment is likely to be Glimpse of Us, which is now on 1.8bn Spotify streams and counting.Michael CraggJohn Grant with Richard HawleyKelvingrove Bandstand, Glasgow,10 AugustOriginally brought together in 2023 as part of the Manchester international festival, Grant and Hawley reunite for this unique collaboration celebrating the work of late country star Patsy Cline. With Cline’s songs steeped in romance and heartbreak, expect them to come to life anew on a Glasgow bandstand.MCThe Galloping CureFestivaltheatre, Edinburgh,9 to 12 AugustAdvertised as “an opera for the opioid age”, this is the latest collaboration between Missy Mazzoli, one of the most successful composers working in opera today, and librettist Royce Vavrek, dubbed “the indie Hoffmannsthal”. Its world premiere production by Scottish Opera is a musical must-see at this year’s Edinburgh international festival.Flora WillsonDenys Baptiste, Gary Crosby, Cassie KinoshiBristol Beacon: Lantern Hall, 8 AugustJoining the BBC’s wider Proms season, this live-broadcast Radio 3 Bristol concert showcases successive generations of African-Caribbean jazz artists who have transformed the UK scene over the past half-century. Soulful Coltrane-inspired saxophonist Denys Baptiste, Jazz Warriors co-founder Gary Crosby and saxophonist/composer Cassie Kinoshi highlight this diversely creative gig.John FordhamGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenFigures of fun … Kira Freije’s Unspeak the Chorus.Photograph: Rob HarrisKira FreijeModernArtOxford, to 16 AugustIt’s your last chance to catch a clutch of exhibitions this week before they close, including strange, lifesize figures frozen in moments of emotional anguish created by Freije, who is nominated for this year’s Turner prize.New Contemporaries 26Mima, Middlesbrough, to 16 AugustThere’s no better place to spot the art stars of the future than the annual New Contemporaries exhibition, which brings together work by recent graduates and early-career artists.Rachel Maclean: They’ve Got Your EyesFact, Liverpool, to 16 AugustThis Scottish artist combines film and sculpture, fairytale and horror for a terrifying immersive exploration of AI and how it’s tearing apart the idea of art and authorship.Flare-UpGoldsmith’s Centre for Contemporary Art, London, to 16 AugustHealth and illness are the focus of this show about the body and disability, featuring a stellar lineup of artists including Derek Jarman, Félix González-Torres and Racheal Crowther.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenBetween the sheets … Alan Cumming and Shirley Henderson in rehearsals for A History of Paper.Photograph: Chris KeatchA History of PaperPitlochry Festivaltheatre,9 Augustto 19 SeptemberOliver Emanuel and Gareth Williams’s thoughtful and romantic new musical charts a burgeoning relationship between a man and woman through the scraps of paper they leave behind – tickets, letters, menus and shopping lists. Alan Cumming and Shirley Henderson star.Miriam GillinsonLove’s Labour’s Lost and Much Ado About NothingThomas’s College, Richmond, to 22 AugustThis enticing Shakespearean double bill transforms his two comedies into a sweeping single love saga set around the second world war.MGKevin Bridges8 Augustto 20 February; tour starts YorkThe Glaswegian comic’s gritty, relatable and masterfully constructed observational fare made him a standup institution in his homeland long ago. Now, more than two decades on from his debut, the (still only) 39-year-old heads back out on the road with new show Here If You Need Me.Rachel AroestiTchaikovsky: Child of GlassOpera Holland Park, London,13to 15 AugustA music-dance-drama about the life and forbidden loves of composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. This is a real meshing of forms, the play written by Tama Matheson (artistic director of the Brisbane Shakespeare festival), with pianist Jayson Gillham playing live, and Royal Ballet soloist Téo Dubreuil performing choreography by Stephen Wicks.Lyndsey Winshipskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenTunnel vision … Warren’s Vortex.Photograph: Rebecca McMillan Photography/ FremantleWarren’s VortexNow & Sky Comedy,10 August, 9pmThis sister show to the New Zealand comedy Wellington Paranormal (itself a What We Do in the Shadows spin-off) sees a teenage girl fall into the transdimensional wormhole her dad has been hiding in his shed, leading the pair into a host of absurd alternate timelines.Hit PointU&Dave,13 August, 9pmMisfits creator Howard Overman’s twisty romcom-thriller ramps up the standard-issue police procedural suspense with a hefty dose of sexual tension. Saffron Hocking and Nick Blood are two detectives trying not to get distracted by their mutual attraction while investigating a gangland robbery that doesn’t quite add up.A House Through TimeiPlayer & BBC Two,13 August, 9pmDavid Olusoga’s particular brand of braininess may not have made him much of a Traitor hunter, but the softly spoken historian is the perfect fit for this gently fascinating series which chronicles British life through the prism of a single dwelling. This sixth instalment focuses on an Edinburgh home that dates back to 1765.MourinhoNetflix,11 AugustThe Special One (a nickname he loudly disavows in the trailer while standing in front of a huge self-portrait) and his 20-year winning streak is the subject of this new series from Joe Pearlman, director of arch documentaries on Robbie Williams and Bros. Ferguson, Terry, Lampard, Ibrahimović and Drogba are among the talking heads.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenPlaying the Bond markets … Agent 64: Spies Never Die.Photograph: Replicant D6Agent 64PC, out11 AugustAimed squarely at those who played and loved GoldenEye 007 on the Nintendo 64 nearly 30 years ago, this homage keeps the lo-fi graphics and much-loved split-screen multiplayer mode but has its own story campaign and the ability to play online. Relive your youth – now with updated modern design.Servant of the LakePC, out13 AugustEye-catching for its charming mix of bold line-drawn characters and muted sketched backgrounds, this point-and-click adventure hs charming characters and hides a darker mystery.Jordan Erica WebberStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenClubbing together … Flo.Photograph: Alexander PiperFlo – Therapy at the ClubOut nowThe British R&B trio return with the follow-up to their Grammy-nominated debut, Access All Areas. Led by the salacious banger Leak It and the retro-soul stomper Remedied, the album also features throwback soul jams on the title track and Don’t Break Her Heart.Overmono – Pure DevotionOut nowWelsh brothers Tom and Ed Russell continue to push the boundaries of electronic music on this follow-up to 2023’s debut, Good Lies. As well as incorporating vintage synthesisers and destabilising vocal techniques, the pair also literally baked a crash cymbal in the oven. Why not?Ravyn Lenae – Blue IslandOut nowAfter releasing a couple of if-you-know-you-know alt-pop albums, Chicago singer-songwriter Lenae scored an unexpected smash last year with Love Me Not. As a result, this third album should garner more attention, and thankfully songs such as the Solange-esque Saturday Night and the loping Handle live up to the hype.The Anchoress – As We Once WereOut nowWhen she’s not hosting her own podcast, or writing books about epic poetry, Welsh polymath Catherine Anne Davies also makes music. On her first album of new material in five years, her decadent art-rock is augmented by guests including Gwenno and James Dean Bradfield.MCStaying in:Brain foodView image in fullscreenWriter’s RoutinePodcastDan Simpson’s long-running series finds nuggets of wisdom in writers’ mercurial schedules. A treasure trove of advice for anyone looking to be creative, Simpson’s bestselling guests explore how to build confidence and set your own pace.Bayeuxmuseum.comOnlineAs the Bayeux tapestry prepares to open to the public at London’s British Museum, this high-resolution interactive panorama from Normandy’s Bayeux Museum allows those who can’t get their hands on tickets to experience the next best thing.Women Not Included: Drugs and Clinical TrialsBBC World Service,10 August, 8.30pmDr Ella Hubber’s investigation into the ways that women have been overlooked across decades of research is a deeply troubling yet necessary listen. Alongside expert commentary, she explores how biological differences affect the ways drugs work.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Water Colour review – an elegant, expertly handled study of depression | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Milly Sweeney’s award-winning two-hander about an art student and a kitchen porter draws power from its clever structure and light touch
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Milly Sweeney’s award-winning two-hander about an art student and a kitchen porter draws power from its clever structure and light touch
Content: Doesn’t overstate its case … Molly Geddes and Ryan J Mackay in Water Colour.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenDoesn’t overstate its case … Molly Geddes and Ryan J Mackay in Water Colour.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewWater Colour review – an elegant, expertly handled study of depressionTraverse theatre, EdinburghMilly Sweeney’s award-winning two-hander about an art student and a kitchen porter draws power from its clever structure and light touchMark FisherSat 8 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is rare to come out of a show raving about the structure, but the unusual plotting distinguishes Milly Sweeney’s two-hander. The young playwright’s theme is the way everyday social pressures – the stress of completing an art degree show, the anxiety of starting a job – can take a toll on mental health. With sensitivity, she traces the step-by-step process that might take someone from depression, compounded by circumstance, to thoughts of suicide.Her characters are Esme (Molly Geddes) – friendless at Prestwick Academy, isolated at Glasgow School of Art – and Harris (Ryan J Mackay), seemingly on the up after landing a job as a kitchen porter in a Michelin-star restaurant.The novelty in Water Colour, namedbest new play in the 2026 Cats awards, is that the two young people are unknown to each other. Their stories play out independently, except for the significant moment when they cross, one inadvertently helping the other at the point of greatest need. It is built with the elegance of a figure of eight.A Trial: After An Enemy of the People review – Wagner Moura upends Ibsen and keeps us guessingRead moreA joint venture by the Byre theatre, Pitlochry Festival theatre and the Traverse, it is punchily performed by Geddes and Mackay, who help narrate each other’s stories to create the illusion of their happening at the same time. She plays his tyrannical head chef, while he plays her opinionated tutor, the two revelling in their malevolent caricatures in Sally Reid’s buoyant production.This lightness of touch leavens the play’s serious intent. When Esme is suffering from debilitating inertia, still in bed at 3pm, Harris is the partying carouser with money to burn. The roles are reversed as the play loops round on itself, illustrating the fragility of our emotional health without overstating the case. It is a clever piece of writing, brisk and confident, portraying isolation even as it celebrates the power of mutual support.AtTraverse theatre, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreMental healthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Trial: After An Enemy of the People review – Wagner Moura upends Ibsen and keeps us guessing | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: At the Edinburgh international festival, the Narcos star and director Christiane Jatahy transform the 1882 classic into a resonant, fourth wall-breaking event
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: At the Edinburgh international festival, the Narcos star and director Christiane Jatahy transform the 1882 classic into a resonant, fourth wall-breaking event
Content: Original … Wagner Moura in A Trial: After An Enemy of the People.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOriginal … Wagner Moura in A Trial: After An Enemy of the People.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewA Trial: After An Enemy of the People review – Wagner Moura upends Ibsen and keeps us guessingLyceum theatre, EdinburghAt the Edinburgh international festival, the Narcos star and director Christiane Jatahy transform the 1882 classic into a resonant, fourth wall-breaking eventArifa AkbarSat 8 Aug 2026 08.25 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis dramatised trial takes Henrik Ibsen’s 1882 play about a man’s campaign to expose the secret scandal of contaminated water in his town and turns it into a modern day interrogation: of speaking out versus remaining silent, of a family at war and of fiction and reality itself.In fact, is this a drama at all? It starts off as such but minutes later, the celebrated Brazilian screen actorWagner Moura, playing Ibsen’s Thomas Stockmann, seemingly breaks character to talk to us directly. Stockmann still sits invisibly on stage and we as an audience are here to judge him, he says, before returning to inhabit him.View image in fullscreenFamily drama … A Trial: After An Enemy of the People.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianSo Stockmann’s trial begins. Here he is: a family man living in contemporary Brazil, in a spa town whose tourism is dependent on the water that he insists is poisoning people. Is he a heroic truth-teller, belligerent anti-hero or self-serving villain? A 12-strong jury made up of audience members (have actors infiltrated this lineup? We don’t know, it is all uncertain ground) are called to sit on stage for most of the play before leaving to deliberate their verdict.Christiane Jatahy, who has conceived the show and written it with Moura and Lucas Paraizo, knows how to reinvent a classic. Often using post-dramatic techniques and incorporating screens on stage, she has repurposed the works of Anton Chekhov and August Strindberg, and three years ago broughtDusk, her documentary-style adaptation of Lars von Trier’s film Dogville, to the Edinburgh international festival.A blend of documentary and drama forms, it dismantles the fourth wall, at times, in a similar vein toThomas Ostermeier’s version of the play, staged in London two years ago. But this is more radical in its ambitions. Its central scandal certainly chimes in our world, too – as shown in the recent docudramaDirty Business– but also resonates with the“forever chemicals” investigationsin the US. Jatahy has taken an old story and turned it into a tale of our time.Despite this resonance, there is just not enough force in the moral debate at the heart of this production. The question of whether Thomas was right to reveal the truth is a foregone conclusion, with not enough to mitigate it. That his truth-telling affects the town’s tourism seems like an inadequate argument in the face of mass water poisoning.You wish for greater complexity or more skin in the game.View image in fullscreenUncertain ground … the jury of A Trial: After An Enemy of the People.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianIn the Black review – rewarding drama about the Faustian pact of big businessRead moreStill, it is gripping and original. Moura is an immensely charismatic force on stage, at ease with his fissured role – as Thomas and an observing commentator of Thomas. Everyone around him gives powerful performances, too. There are two young sons off stage and a wife who has died – partly, it is implied, from the stress of Thomas’s campaigning. We see these characters on screen, in videos that bring grief and betrayal to the storyline. His daughter Petra (Julia Bernat) sits on stage with him, presenting evidence and conducting cross-examinations opposite his brother, Peter (Danilo Grangheia), who is Thomas’s most vocal adversary. They bring raised passions, fights and tears. Ultimately, it is this traditional element, of turbulent family drama, that grips the most.At theLyceum theatre, Edinburgh, until 10 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreHenrik IbsenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Supposing: review – only ancient Greek rage will suffice in our exasperating times | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A modern, secular woman is transformed into a Hellenic heroine as she sees visions of the future in Zinnie Harris’s minimalist drama
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: A modern, secular woman is transformed into a Hellenic heroine as she sees visions of the future in Zinnie Harris’s minimalist drama
Content: She is getting intense … Nicole Cooper in Supposing:.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicView image in fullscreenShe is getting intense … Nicole Cooper in Supposing:.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewSupposing: review – only ancient Greek rage will suffice in our exasperating timesTraverse theatre, EdinburghA modern, secular woman is transformed into a Hellenic heroine as she sees visions of the future in Zinnie Harris’s minimalist dramaMark FisherSat 8 Aug 2026 12.09 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you found Christopher Nolan’sThe Odysseytoo bombastic, you might prefer your Greek drama filtered like this. Written and directed by Zinnie Harris, Supposing: could scarcely be staged more simply. Designer Alisa Kalyanova outlines a white-edged circle on the floor of an otherwise empty space. It could be the hole on the high street that Sally trips into for want of a protective bollard. Or it could be the kitchen where she tells her husband, Richard, about her strange concern. “I think I’ve been cursed,” she says, imagining him react in a hundred different ways – incredulous, mocking, shocked – none of them good.Either way, the circle defines the relationship between actors Nicole Cooper and Richard Conlon – both excellent as they revolve around each other, desiring to get close but so often repelled, twisting apart because of the import of Sally’s revelation. Is this modern day secular woman, who does not believe in gods but in concrete facts, suffering some kind of mental collapse, or does her curse mean she can she really see the future? And if she can, what to do with the prophecies?With a 17-strong Greek chorus in her head, nagging her like a guilty conscience, she reads up about satyrs and tragedies, portents and sacrifices, in case they have something to do with her. She even tries a bit of libation, with water, salt and wine, to make it all stop. Like Greek antecedents such as Medea, Clytemnestra and Penelope, she is getting intense.View image in fullscreenTroubled times … Nicole Cooper and Richard Conlon in Supposing:.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicShe admits as much and, delivered in a tone of helpless irony by Cooper, it is one of this elliptical play’s funnier observations. The ancient heroines are a comically imperfect fit for Sally, an ordinary wife and mother, yet something in our own troubled times calls for the kind of full-blooded response that only the Greeks can provide.In the Black review – rewarding drama about the Faustian pact of big businessRead moreSally’s frequent references to pregnancies and miscarriages suggest there is a future, but an uncertain one. In a society beset by political extremism, she sees visions of a racist neighbour and an unknown refugee housed in accommodation targeted by rightwing protesters. In such exasperating times, perhaps only ancient rage will suffice. Or perhaps, as the play’s closing moments hint at, there is still a possibility of healing the fractures.AtTraverse theatre, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Human Centipede director Tom Six reveals multiple sclerosis diagnosis in ‘final film’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Dutch creator of the controversial trilogy set to detail struggles with neurological disease in homemade documentary, after spending six years ‘as a recluse’
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: The Dutch creator of the controversial trilogy set to detail struggles with neurological disease in homemade documentary, after spending six years ‘as a recluse’
Content: ‘I’m a morbid lump of untouchable howling flesh’ … a scene from The End of Tom Six.Photograph: Courtesy of Tom SixView image in fullscreen‘I’m a morbid lump of untouchable howling flesh’ … a scene from The End of Tom Six.Photograph: Courtesy of Tom SixMoviesHuman Centipede director Tom Six reveals multiple sclerosis diagnosis in ‘final film’The Dutch creator of the controversial trilogy set to detail struggles with neurological disease in homemade documentary, after spending six years ‘as a recluse’Philip OltermannEuropean culture editorSat 8 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom Six, the film-maker behind schlock horror phenomenon The Human Centipede, has revealed that he has been living as “a full-blown recluse” in a darkened Amsterdam apartment for six years after being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis.In The End of Tom Six, a homemade documentary that the Dutch director said would be his final film, he says that the stress over his failure to find a distributor for the follow-up to the Centipede trilogy significantly exacerbated his condition.Released in 2009, independently produced The Human Centipede tells the story of a crazed scientist, played by German actor Dieter Laser, who kidnaps three tourists and surgically conjoins them in a chain, mouth to anus.The film performed modestly at the box office but the horrific medical experiment of its title became global pop culture lore, cited in South Park and The Simpsons.In 2011 and 2015, Six made two sequels that each referenced the previous film, to create a “movie centipede”. In 2018 the film-maker released a trailer for The Onania Club, about a group of wealthy women who get turned on by extreme human suffering, but the film failed to pick up a distributor.View image in fullscreen‘A strong appetite for self-destruction’ … The End of Tom Six.Photograph: Courtesy of Tom SixIn The End of Tom Six, which is being released on a pay-what-you-want model on YouTube on 15 August, Six reveals he has spent the last six years “as a recluse” after being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS) in 2020.MS is a neurological disease that affects the brain and spinal cord. Symptoms and the severity of the condition vary from patient to patient, but can include extreme fatigue, vision and memory problems, muscle cramps, spasms and stiffness, and difficulties with or loss of mobility.“I can’t walk any more, reducing me to worming through my house like [a] fucking gargoyle,” the 52-year-old says in the film, in which he plays both himself and the director conducting the interview. “I’m a morbid lump of untouchable howling flesh.”While Six notes that many MS sufferers make an effort to eat healthily and exercise after their diagnosis, he says he has a “strong appetite for self-destruction”, with “a black belt in ego demolition”.He describes a daily routine that consists of lying on a Chinese opium bed in silk pyjamas, bingeing opioids and film noir movies, smoking Havana cigars and eating chicken curry, chocolate mousse and peanut butter. He doesn’t leave his home apart from night-time trips to a nearby cafe, for decaffeinated coffee.Six says he did not reveal his medical condition at the time of his diagnosis because “I hate being a victim and get pity”.The second half of his final film is mostly a complaint against “woke cowardice” and “safe-space crybabies” in the film industry, which he blames for the failure to get The Onania Club released. He said that the project was densely interwoven with references to global elite conspiracies and which would have become “even more of a success than The Human Centipede”.Throughout the film, a “censor nazi” in an SS uniform interrupts the interview to point out which scenes will need to be cut or fitted with trigger warnings.“The prolonged, extremely stressful battle accelerated his disease and totally ravaged his body up to the point that he is now nearing the end of his life,” Six’s producer Maartje Willems said in a statement accompanying the film’s release.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMultiple sclerosisnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a joyous night of live music with Paul Heaton  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: A hugely fun performance of all the Beautiful South and Housemartins hits. Plus: how deep were Elvis Presley’s connections to organised crime? Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: A hugely fun performance of all the Beautiful South and Housemartins hits. Plus: how deep were Elvis Presley’s connections to organised crime? Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: It’s happy hour again! … Paul Heaton: Live at Bramall Lane on BBC Two.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyView image in fullscreenIt’s happy hour again! … Paul Heaton: Live at Bramall Lane on BBC Two.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a joyous night of live music with Paul HeatonA hugely fun performance of all the Beautiful South and Housemartins hits. Plus: how deep were Elvis Presley’s connections to organised crime? Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Graeme Virtue,Jack SealeandSimon WardellSat 8 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePaul Heaton: Live at Bramall Lane10.10pm, BBC TwoThe Sheffield United fan and maker of some of pop’s most fun melodies performed at Bramall Lane last year – and it was 90 minutes packed with joy. In this recording, he is joined by Rianne Downey as they perform all the Housemartins, Beautiful South and solo hits to a lively crowd. The opening half-hour alone boasts Bell Bottomed Tear, Old Red Eyes Is Back, Song for Whoever and I’ll Sail This Ship Alone.Hollie RichardsonSandi Toksvig’s Hidden Wonders7pm, Channel 4Before launching her TV career, Sandi Toksvig earned a degree in archaeology. This fascinating series sees her returning to her academic roots, joining a dig in Dorset. There’s an iron age cemetery to be unearthed and, somewhat troublingly, some secrets about human sacrifice to be revealed.PHBettany Hughes’ Lost Worlds: Dawn of Civilisations8pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenAdventure time … Bettany Hughes’ Lost Worlds : Dawn of Civilisations.Photograph: Channel 4For her latest historical adventure Hughes heads to Turkey to explore the legacy of ancient Anatolia, a region that “left its mark on every era of human history”. Highlights include the otherworldly Cappadocia and the spectacular architecture of a 13th-century mosque.Graeme VirtueElvis, the Colonel and the Mob10pm, Channel 4Blame it on Colonel Tom Parker but Elvis Presley’s links to organised crime were, according to this two-part documentary, surprisingly strong. Parker was a denizen of Las Vegas and, along with taking care of Elvis’s business, he forged a few shady connections. Eventually, as this film shows, this court became a mixed blessing for the King.Phil HarrisnThe Staircase10.20pm, ITV1Colin Firth continues to excel in the drama about murder suspect Michael Peterson, despite the production being less essential than the original documentary. In 2003, the Petersons’ son Clayton makes an important discovery; in 2017, Michael’s new partner Sophie considers how meeting him changed her life.Jack SealeGhosts Australia10.50pm, BBC ThreeThe genius of the Ghosts premise is its adaptability to any cultural context. This Australian version is a case in point, this week touching on issues around colonisation but with the lightest and wittiest of touches. In the present, Kate and Sean handle an invasion of their own as the odious neighbours turn up.PHFilm choiceParallel Mothers, 11.10pm, BBC FourView image in fullscreenBumps in the road … Parallel Mothers on BBC Four.Photograph: Sony/AllstarJust before his latest twisty film, Bitter Christmas, hits cinemas, here’s another chance to see Pedro Almodóvar’s equally knotty 2021 drama, which explores family secrets in the domestic and national spheres. It features a standout performance from Penélope Cruz as photographer Janis, who gets pregnant by a forensic anthropologist investigating the forgotten civil war victims of Franco – including her ancestors. When her newborn gets swapped with that of the young Ana (Milena Smit), fate intertwines their lives. A forceful experience.Simon WardellLive sportWomen’s Hundred Cricket: MI London v Trent Rockets, 11am, Sky Sports Main EventFrom Kia Oval in London.Cycling: Tour de France Femmes, 2.30pm, TNT Sports 1Stage eight from Sisteron to Nice.EFL Cup Football: Colchester v Southampton, 5pm, Sky Sports Main EventOn Sunday, Mansfield v Sheffield Utd is at 3.45pm.
